paragraphs: On a scorching hot evening in early July, a young man left the tiny attic room where he lived in S. Place and walked slowly, almost hesitantly, toward K. bridge.

He had managed to avoid running into his landlady on the stairs. His attic room was at the top of a tall, five-story building and felt more like a closet than a real apartment. The landlady, who gave him the attic, meals, and did chores for him, lived on the floor beneath. Every time he went out, he had to walk past her kitchen, which was always open. Each time he did, he felt sick and nervous, his face twisting in shame. He owed her a lot of money and was terrified of bumping into her.

It wasn’t that he was a coward; actually, he was the opposite. But lately, he had been so stressed and irritable, almost depressed. He had gotten so wrapped up in his own thoughts and cut off from everyone else that he was scared of meeting not just his landlady, but anyone at all. Poverty weighed him down, but lately he didn’t even care about his money problems. He had stopped bothering with practical things and lost any motivation to try. Nothing his landlady could do really scared him. But to be stopped on the stairs, forced to listen to her pointless gossip, her nagging about rent, threats and complaints, and then to have to make up excuses or even lie—no, he’d rather sneak down the stairs quietly, like a cat, and slip out unseen.
But this evening, when he stepped out into the street, he felt his fear more strongly than ever.

“I’m planning something huge, and yet I’m scared of little things like this,” he thought, giving a weird smile. “Hmm… yeah, everything’s in a person’s hands, but they let it slip because they’re afraid. That’s just how it is. I wonder what people are most afraid of? Taking a new step, saying something new—that’s what scares them most… But I’m talking too much. Maybe I talk so much because I never do anything. Or maybe it’s the other way around—I talk because I don’t act. I’ve spent a whole month lying around thinking… about Jack the Giant-Killer. Why am I going there now? Am I actually capable of it? Is this serious? No, it’s not serious at all. It’s just a fantasy to entertain myself, a toy! Yeah, maybe it’s just a game.”

The heat outside was unbearable. The air felt heavy and dirty, full of noise, construction, bricks, and dust everywhere, plus that awful Petersburg smell that everyone who can’t escape the city in summer knows all too well. It all made his already frayed nerves even worse. The horrible stink from the bars—there were lots of them in this part of town—and the sight of drunk men everywhere, even though it was a workday, made everything feel even more disgusting. For a moment, his handsome, refined face showed just how grossed out he felt. He was actually a good-looking guy: tall, slim, well-built, with striking dark eyes and brown hair. Soon, though, he sank into deep thought—or really, into a kind of blankness—walking along without noticing or caring about anything around him. Sometimes he would mumble to himself, a habit he had just admitted. At those times, he would realize his thoughts were all tangled up and that he felt very weak; he had barely eaten in two days.

He was dressed so poorly that even someone used to shabby clothes would be embarrassed to be seen in public like that. But in this part of town, near the Hay Market, with all its sketchy places and so many working-class people packed into the streets, no one really noticed what anyone else was wearing. There were so many different types of people here that nothing looked out of place. Still, the young man felt so bitter and angry inside that, despite being young and usually picky about appearances, he barely cared about his rags in public. It was only when he ran into someone he knew, like an old classmate or acquaintance, that he really minded. And yet, when a drunk guy being hauled somewhere in a big wagon suddenly yelled at him, “Hey, German hatter!” and pointed at him, the young man stopped and grabbed for his hat. It was a tall, round hat from Zimmerman’s, but it was so old and worn-out, rusty, torn, and bent that it looked ridiculous. But what he felt wasn’t shame—it was something more like fear.

“I knew it,” he mumbled, embarrassed. “I thought this would happen! That’s the worst part! Something stupid and tiny like this could ruin everything. Yeah, my hat stands out… It looks ridiculous and people notice it… With these rags, I should be wearing any old flat cap, not this weird thing. No one else wears a hat like this—it stands out from a mile away, people would remember it. And that would give them a clue. For what I’m planning, I need to be as unnoticeable as possible… The little things, it’s always the little things that mess everything up.”

He didn’t have far to go; he knew exactly how many steps it was from his apartment’s gate: seven hundred and thirty. He had counted once while daydreaming. Back then, he hadn’t taken his dreams seriously and was just teasing himself with how wild they were. Now, a month later, he thought about them differently. Even though he made fun of his own weakness, he had started to see this “awful” idea as something he might actually do, even if he didn’t fully realize it. He was basically going now for a “practice run” of his plan, and with each step, he felt more and more nervous.

Heart pounding and hands shaking, he walked up to a huge building that looked out on the canal on one side and the street on the other. The place was divided into tiny apartments for all kinds of working people—tailors, locksmiths, cooks, Germans, women scraping by, office clerks, and more. People were always coming and going through the two main doors and courtyards. Three or four doormen worked the building. The young man was relieved not to run into any of them and slipped in through the right-side door without being noticed, quickly making his way up the back stairs. The stairway was dark and narrow, but he already knew his way and actually liked the shadows—no one could really see him there.

“If I’m this scared now, what would I be like if I were actually going to do it?” he wondered as he reached the fourth floor. Some porters were moving furniture out of an apartment. He knew the place had belonged to a German clerk from the government and his family. Now that they were moving out, the only one left on this floor would be the old woman. “That’s good, at least,” he thought as he rang her doorbell. The bell made a weak, tinny sound, not a proper ring. Apartments in buildings like this always had bells like that. He’d forgotten what her bell sounded like, and now its odd jingle brought memories back, making him jumpy. His nerves were totally shot. After a moment, the door opened just a crack. The old woman peeked out suspiciously, only her beady eyes visible in the dark. But when she saw there were people out on the landing, she got braver and opened the door all the way. The young man stepped into a dark hallway that was separated from the tiny kitchen. The old woman stood facing him, silent, with a questioning look. She was small, dried-up, about sixty years old, with sharp, mean eyes and a pointy nose. Her thin, grayish hair was greasy and she didn’t wear a scarf. Around her long, skinny neck—like a chicken’s—was a flannel rag, and even though it was hot, she wore a gross, old fur cape over her shoulders. She coughed and groaned constantly. The young man must have looked at her in a strange way, because she seemed even more suspicious.
“Raskolnikov, a student. I came here a month ago,” the young man hurried to say, giving a half-bow, remembering to be polite.
“I remember, young man, I remember quite well when you came,” the old woman replied clearly, still eyeing him up and down.
“And… I’m here for the same reason,” Raskolnikov went on, a bit thrown off by her suspicion. “Maybe she’s always like this, and I just didn’t notice last time,” he thought, feeling uneasy.
The old woman paused, like she was unsure. Then she stepped aside and pointed to the door of the room, letting him go in ahead of her:
“Go on in, young man.”
The small room Raskolnikov entered had yellow wallpaper, potted geraniums, and thin curtains in the windows. The setting sun was shining brightly through the glass right then.

“So the sun will shine like this then, too!” flashed through Raskolnikov’s mind. He quickly looked around, trying to notice and remember everything in the room. But there was nothing special: all the old yellow furniture—a sofa with a huge curved back, an oval table in front of it, a dressing table with a mirror between the windows, chairs lined up along the walls, and a couple of cheap prints of German girls holding birds. In the corner, a small lamp burned in front of an ikon. Everything was super clean; the floor and furniture shined from being polished.
“Lizaveta’s work,” thought Raskolnikov. There wasn’t a speck of dust anywhere.

“Only mean old widows keep places this clean,” he thought again, sneaking a look at the cotton curtain over the door leading to another tiny room, where the old woman’s bed and dresser were. He’d never seen in there before. These two rooms made up her whole apartment.
“What do you want?” the old woman asked sharply, coming into the room and standing in front of him so she could look him right in the face.
“I brought something to pawn,” he said, pulling an old, flat silver watch from his pocket, with a globe engraved on the back and a steel chain.
“But your last pawn is overdue. The month was up the day before yesterday.”
“I’ll bring you the interest for another month; please wait a little.”
“That’s up to me, young man, whether I wait or sell your pawn right away.”
“How much for the watch, Alyona Ivanovna?”
“You bring such little things, young man. It’s hardly worth anything. I gave you two roubles for your ring last time, and you could buy a new one at the jeweler’s for a rouble and a half.”
“Give me four roubles for this. I’ll get it back, it was my father’s. I’ll have money soon.”
“A rouble and a half, and you pay the interest in advance, if you want.”
“A rouble and a half?” the young man burst out.
“Take it or leave it,” the old woman said, handing the watch back. He almost turned to leave, angry, but stopped himself—he had nowhere else to go, and he actually had another reason for coming.
“Fine, take it,” he said gruffly.
The old woman dug in her pocket for her keys and went behind the curtain into the other room. Left alone, the young man listened closely, thinking. He could hear her unlocking a drawer.

“Must be the top drawer,” he thought. “So she keeps her keys in her right pocket, all together on a steel ring… And there’s one key, three times bigger than the others, with deep notches; that can’t be for the dresser… so there must be another chest or strongbox. That’s good to know. Strongboxes always have big keys like that… but this is so pathetic.”
The old woman came back.

“Here you go, young man: as we say, ten kopecks for every rouble a month, so I’ll take fifteen kopecks from a rouble and a half, for the month in advance. And from the two roubles I lent you before, you owe me twenty kopecks up front. That adds up to thirty-five kopecks. So I’ll give you a rouble and fifteen kopecks for the watch. Here.”
“What! Only a rouble and fifteen kopecks?”
“That’s right.”
The young man didn’t argue and took the money. He looked at the old woman and didn’t leave right away, as if he still had something to say or do, but he wasn’t even sure what.
“I might bring you something else in a day or two, Alyona Ivanovna—a valuable thing—silver—a cigarette box, as soon as I get it back from a friend…” he said, trailing off, embarrassed.
“Well, we’ll talk about it then, young man.”
“Goodbye—are you always here alone, is your sister ever with you?” He tried to sound casual as he moved toward the hallway.
“What’s it to you, young man?”
“Oh, nothing really, just curious. You’re awfully quick to snap… Goodbye, Alyona Ivanovna.”

Raskolnikov left, feeling completely unsettled. His confusion just got worse and worse. Going down the stairs, he even stopped a few times, struck by sudden thoughts. Out in the street, he blurted, “Oh God, how disgusting this all is! Can I really… could I possibly…? No, that’s crazy, it’s nonsense!” he told himself firmly. “How could such a horrible thing even cross my mind? My heart is capable of such ugly, filthy thoughts. Yes, filthy, disgusting, awful! And for a whole month I’ve been…” But no words could really express how upset he felt. The sense of disgust that had started while he was on his way to the old woman now became so strong, so real, that he didn’t know what to do with himself. He wandered along the pavement like he was drunk, bumping into people without even noticing, until he finally snapped out of it in the next street. Looking around, he realized he was right next to a tavern, with steps going down from the sidewalk. Just then, two drunk men came out, cursing and holding each other up as they climbed the steps. Without thinking, Raskolnikov went down into the tavern. He had never been in one before, but now he felt dizzy and so thirsty. He longed for a cold beer and blamed his weakness on not eating. He sat at a sticky little table in a dark, dirty corner, ordered a beer, and drank the first glass quickly. Right away, he felt a bit better, his thoughts clearer.

“It’s all nonsense,” he thought hopefully. “There’s nothing to worry about! It’s just my body acting up. A glass of beer, a piece of dry bread—and suddenly your brain is stronger, your thinking is clearer, and your will is steady! Phew, how small all my problems seem.”

But even though he told himself this, he actually felt cheerful now, almost like a weight had been lifted off him. He looked around at the people in the tavern with a friendly gaze. Even then, though, he had a strange feeling that this good mood wasn’t normal either.

There weren’t many people in the tavern at that hour. Besides the two drunks he’d seen on the steps, a group of about five men and a girl with a concertina had just left, so the room felt quiet and almost empty. The only ones left were a man who looked like a craftsman—drunk, but not totally out of it—sitting with a mug of beer, and his friend, a huge, fat man with a gray beard and a short, full coat. This man was very drunk and had fallen asleep on the bench; every now and then, even while half-asleep, he’d snap his fingers, throw out his arms, bounce his upper body around, and hum some random song, trying to remember lines like:
“His wife a year he fondly loved
His wife a—a year he—fondly loved.”
Or suddenly waking up again:
“Walking along the crowded row
He met the one he used to know.”

But no one else was enjoying his singing; his silent friend looked at him with obvious annoyance and suspicion. There was another man in the room who looked a bit like a retired government clerk. He sat off to the side, sipping his beer and glancing nervously at the others. He seemed agitated too.

Raskolnikov wasn’t used to being around crowds, and, as we’ve said before, he avoided people whenever he could—especially recently. But suddenly, he felt like being with others. Something inside him was changing, and he craved company, almost like he was thirsty for it. After a month of feeling miserable and wound up, he just wanted a break, even if it was in a place as dirty as this tavern. For once, he was actually glad to be there.

The owner of the tavern was in another room, but he kept coming down a few steps into the main room, his flashy, black boots with red tops usually appearing before the rest of him. He wore a long coat and a disgustingly greasy black satin vest with no tie, and his face looked as shiny as if he’d smeared it with oil. Behind the counter stood a boy about fourteen, and another, even younger, helped hand things out. There were sliced cucumbers, dried black bread, and bits of chopped fish on the counter, all of it smelling terrible. The air was suffocating and thick with the smell of alcohol; spending only five minutes there could make a person tipsy.

Sometimes, you meet a stranger and feel immediately interested before anyone even speaks. That’s how Raskolnikov felt about the older man sitting a little ways from him, who looked like a retired office worker. Raskolnikov would remember this feeling later and call it a kind of premonition. He kept glancing at the man, partly because the man was watching him too, clearly wanting to strike up a conversation. The man looked at everyone else in the tavern with a kind of annoyed superiority, like he was used to them and bored, considering them beneath him and not worth his time. He was over fifty, bald with gray hair, stocky, and his face was puffy and yellowish-green from drinking, with swollen eyelids and sharp red eyes that gleamed strangely. There was something odd about him—a kind of burning feeling in his eyes, maybe intelligence or maybe a hint of craziness. He was wearing an old, hopelessly ragged black coat with only one button left, which he’d carefully fastened, clinging to the last bit of respectability. His shirt front was crumpled and stained, sticking out from his canvas vest. He had no beard or mustache, but his chin was so unshaven it looked like a gray scrub brush. He acted official and respectable, but he was restless, messing up his hair and sometimes dropping his head sadly into his hands on the sticky table. At last he looked Raskolnikov straight in the eye and spoke loudly and confidently:

“May I ask, sir, if I can talk with you for a moment? Because, even though your clothes are nothing special, my experience tells me you’re educated and not a regular drinker. I always respect education when it comes with good feelings, and besides, I’m a titular counsellor—that’s my rank. My name is Marmeladov—titular counsellor. May I ask, have you been in government service?”

“No, I’m a student,” the young man replied, surprised by Marmeladov’s fancy way of speaking and by the directness. Even though Raskolnikov had just wanted company, the moment someone actually talked to him, he instantly felt his usual annoyance and discomfort around strangers.

“A student, then, or used to be,” the clerk said, excited. “I knew it! I have a lot of experience, sir,” he said, tapping his forehead proudly. “You’ve studied, or been to some college! But wait a moment…” He stood up, swayed, grabbed his jug and glass, and moved to sit beside Raskolnikov, turning a bit toward him. He was drunk, but spoke clearly and confidently, only sometimes losing his train of thought or dragging his words. He latched onto Raskolnikov as eagerly as if he hadn’t talked to anyone in ages.

“Sir,” he began, almost seriously, “poverty isn’t a crime, that’s true. But I also know being drunk isn’t a virtue, and that’s even more true. But begging—begging is a crime. When you’re just poor, you can keep your pride, but if you’re a beggar—never. Nobody can. Beggars aren’t just pushed out of society—they’re swept out with a broom, to make it even more humiliating. And that’s fair, because as a beggar, I’m the first to embarrass myself. That’s why I’m here in this tavern! Sir, a month ago, Mr. Lebeziatnikov beat my wife, and she’s nothing like me! Do you understand? Let me ask you something out of curiosity: have you ever spent the night on a hay barge on the Neva River?”
“No, I haven’t,” said Raskolnikov. “What are you talking about?”

“Well, I just came from one, and it’s the fifth night I’ve slept like that...” He filled his glass, drank it, and stopped. Bits of hay stuck to his clothes and hair, making it clear he hadn’t changed or washed in five days. His hands were especially dirty: red, fat, with black fingernails.

Their conversation drew some lazy interest. The boys at the counter started snickering. The innkeeper came down, apparently just to listen to this “funny guy,” and sat nearby, yawning with a certain pride. Clearly, Marmeladov was a regular here, and probably picked up his habit of flowery speeches from talking to random people in the tavern. Drunks who are watched closely at home often develop this craving to defend themselves and get some respect among strangers.
“Funny guy!” said the innkeeper. “So why don’t you work? Why aren’t you at your job if you’re in the service?”

“Why am I not at my job, sir?” Marmeladov continued, talking only to Raskolnikov, as if he’d asked the question. “Why am I not at my job? Doesn’t it hurt me to think I’m useless? A month ago, when Mr. Lebeziatnikov beat my wife and I was lying drunk, didn’t I suffer? Tell me, young man, have you ever… hmm… begged hopelessly for a loan?”
“Yes, I have. But what do you mean by hopelessly?”

“Hopelessly means knowing for sure you’ll get nothing. For example, you know a certain respectable person will never lend you money—why should he? He knows I won’t pay it back. Out of kindness? But Mr. Lebeziatnikov, who’s up-to-date with modern ideas, said the other day that science doesn’t allow compassion anymore, at least in England, where there’s political economy. So why should he help me? But still, even knowing I’ll get nothing, I go to him and…”
“Why do you go?” Raskolnikov asked.

“Because I have no one else, nowhere else I can turn! Everyone needs somewhere to go. Sometimes you just need it! When my own daughter first got her yellow passport, I had to go… (my daughter has a yellow card),” he added, glancing uneasily at Raskolnikov. “No matter, sir, no matter!” he rushed on when the boys at the counter burst out laughing and even the innkeeper smiled. “I’m not ashamed of their snickering; everyone knows everything already, everything secret is out in the open. And I accept it, not with anger but with humility. Let it be! ‘Behold the man!’ Tell me, young man, can you… no, better yet, do you dare, looking at me, say I am not a pig?”
Raskolnikov said nothing.

“Well,” Marmeladov continued, sitting up straighter, waiting for the laughter to die down, “so be it, I am a pig, but she—she’s a lady! I may look like a beast, but Katerina Ivanovna, my wife, is educated and an officer’s daughter. Yes, I’m a scoundrel, but she’s a noble woman, raised right. And yet… oh, if only she cared for me! Sir, every man needs at least one place where someone cares! But Katerina Ivanovna, even though she’s generous, she’s unfair… And even though I know she only pulls my hair out of pity—yes, I’m not ashamed to admit it, she pulls my hair,” he said, hearing the snickers again, “but, God, if only one time… but no, it’s pointless! No use talking! Sometimes, I’ve gotten my wish and she’s felt for me… but that’s my fate, I’m just a beast by nature!”
“You got that right,” yawned the innkeeper. Marmeladov hit the table with his fist.

“That’s my fate! Do you know, sir, I’ve sold her very stockings for booze? Not her shoes—that’d be normal—but her stockings! I sold her mohair shawl too, a gift from long ago, her own, not mine. We live in a freezing room, and she got sick this winter and started coughing and coughing up blood. We have three little kids, and Katerina Ivanovna works from morning to night—cleaning, scrubbing, washing the children, because she’s used to cleanliness. But her lungs are weak, she’s getting tuberculosis, and I feel it! Don’t you think I feel it? The more I drink, the more I feel it. That’s why I drink. I look for sympathy in drink… I drink so I can suffer even more!” And, as if in despair, he lowered his head onto the table.

“Young man,” he went on, lifting his head again, “I can see some kind of trouble in your face. I noticed it when you came in, that’s why I spoke to you. I’m not telling my story to amuse these people—they already know it all. I’m hoping to talk to someone who can understand. My wife was educated at a fancy girls’ school, and when she graduated, she even danced for the governor, and got a gold medal and a certificate. The medal… well, it was sold long ago, but the certificate is still in her trunk. Not long ago, she showed it to our landlady, even though they’re always fighting—she just wanted someone to know her past glories. I don’t blame her; remembering the past is all she has left. Yes, she’s proud and strong. She scrubs floors and only eats black bread but won’t let anyone disrespect her. That’s why she wouldn’t let Lebeziatnikov’s rudeness go, and when he beat her, she took to her bed more from hurt feelings than pain. She was a widow when I met her, with three kids, each smaller than the last. She married her first husband, an infantry officer, for love and ran away from her father’s house. She really loved him, but he gambled, got in trouble, and died. He used to beat her at the end, and even though she fought back (I’ve got proof), she still talks about him with tears and compares me to him; and I’m glad she still dreams of being happy once. She was left in such poverty, out in the middle of nowhere, that even I can’t describe it. Her family abandoned her, and she was so proud… Then, sir, I was a widower too, with a fourteen-year-old daughter from my first wife, and I offered to marry her because I couldn’t stand to see her suffer. You can see how desperate she was, that a woman of education and good family would agree to marry me. But she did, sobbing and wringing her hands, because she had nowhere else to go. Do you understand what it’s like to have absolutely nowhere to turn? No, you don’t. For a whole year, I was a good husband and didn’t touch this—” (he tapped the jug) “—because I have feelings. But even then, I couldn’t please her, and then I lost my job—not my fault, just changes at work—and then, I started drinking again. It’s been about a year and a half since we ended up here in this great city, with its monuments. I found a new job… and lost it again. That time it was my fault—my weakness showed. Now we only have part of a room at Amalia Fyodorovna Lippevechsel’s place; I don’t even know what we live on or how we pay rent. The place is crowded, dirty, and chaotic... yes. My daughter from my first marriage, Sonya, has grown up—and I won’t even say what she’s endured from her stepmother. Katerina Ivanovna, though generous, is quick-tempered... But never mind that! Sonya never got much education. Four years ago, I tried to teach her geography and history, but I wasn’t good at it and we didn’t have the books. We stopped at Cyrus of Persia. Later, she read some romantic novels, and more recently, a science book she got from Mr. Lebeziatnikov—Lewes’ Physiology—ever heard of it? She even told us about it. That’s all her education. Now let me ask you something personal, sir—do you think a respectable poor girl can earn much by honest work? Not even fifteen kopecks a day, if she has no special skills! And Ivan Ivanitch Klopstock—the civil counselor, you know him?—still hasn’t paid her for the shirts she made, and kicked her out, saying she botched the collars. Meanwhile, the little ones are hungry. Katerina Ivanovna paces, wringing her hands, her cheeks red from her illness: ‘You live with us, eat and drink, and do nothing to help.’ And what does she eat, when there’s no bread for the kids? I was lying there… well, whatever, I was drunk, and I heard Sonya say—she’s so gentle, with fair hair and a pale, thin face—‘Katerina Ivanovna, do I really have to do that?’ Darya Frantsovna, a well-known troublemaker, had tried to get to her through the landlady. ‘Why not?’ says Katerina Ivanovna sarcastically, ‘you’re nothing special.’ But don’t blame her, sir, don’t blame her! She was out of her mind with illness and the kids crying from hunger. When children cry, she even beats them. Around six, I saw Sonya quietly put on her headscarf and cape and leave, and around nine she came back. She silently laid thirty roubles on the table in front of Katerina Ivanovna. She didn’t say a word or even look at her, just took our big green shawl, covered her head and face, and lay down on the bed facing the wall; her shoulders kept shaking... And I just lay there. Then I saw Katerina Ivanovna, just as silently, go to Sonya’s bed, kneel, and kiss her feet all evening and wouldn’t get up, then they both fell asleep in each other’s arms... together… and I... lay there, drunk.”
Marmeladov stopped, like he’d lost his voice. Then he quickly poured himself another glass, drank, and cleared his throat.

“Since then, sir,” he went on after a short pause, “because of some bad incident and because of gossip from nasty people—Darya Frantsovna was the main one, pretending she’d been disrespected—since then, my daughter Sofya Semyonovna had to get a yellow passport, and now she can’t live with us anymore. Our landlady, Amalia Fyodorovna, wouldn’t allow it, even though she’d supported Darya Frantsovna before, and Mr. Lebeziatnikov too... All the trouble between him and Katerina Ivanovna was about Sonya. First he tried to get close to Sonya, then suddenly acted all high and mighty: ‘How can an educated man like me live with a girl like that?’ Katerina Ivanovna wouldn’t stand for it—she defended Sonya, and that’s how it all happened. Now Sonya comes to see us only at night, brings what she can, comforts Katerina Ivanovna... She has a room at the Kapernaumovs’—they’re tailors. Kapernaumov is lame and has a cleft palate, and so does his whole family, even his wife. They all live in one room, but Sonya has a sectioned-off corner... yes, very poor, and all with cleft palates. In the morning, I put on my rags, lifted my hands to heaven and went to see his excellency Ivan Afanasyvitch. You know him? No? Well, then, you’ve missed a saint of a man. He’s like wax before God; he melts with kindness… His eyes filled with tears when he heard my story. ‘Marmeladov, you’ve let me down before, but I’ll give you another chance—just remember, now it’s on my responsibility.’ That’s what he said. I wanted to kiss the ground at his feet—in my thoughts, because in reality he’d never let me, being a modern, enlightened man. I went home and announced I had my job back and a salary coming—oh, what a celebration there was!”

Marmeladov paused again, now extremely worked up. Just then, a group of drunk partygoers came in from the street, and you could hear a hired concertina and a little kid singing “The Hamlet” in the entryway. The room filled with noise. The tavern-keeper and the boys were busy with the newcomers, but Marmeladov ignored them and kept talking. He seemed weaker now, but the drunker he got, the more he talked. Just remembering his recent success at getting the job again seemed to cheer him up, and it even showed in his face. Raskolnikov listened closely.

“That was five weeks ago. Yes… As soon as Katerina Ivanovna and Sonya heard, it was like I’d brought them to heaven. Before, I’d get nothing but insults; suddenly, they were walking on tiptoe, hushing the kids: ‘Semyon Zaharovitch is tired from work, let him rest, shh!’ They made me coffee before work, even boiled cream for me! They actually got real cream—imagine that! And how they scraped together money for a proper outfit—eleven roubles and fifty kopecks—I’ll never know. Boots, shirts, a uniform, all for that price. The first day I came home from the office, Katerina Ivanovna made two dinner courses—soup and salted meat with horseradish—luxuries we’d never dreamed of. She didn’t have any nice clothes, but she made herself look like she was visiting someone important—did her hair, put on a clean collar, cuffs, and looked younger and prettier. Sonya, my darling, only helped with the money ‘for now,’ she said, ‘I shouldn’t visit too often. Maybe after dark, so no one sees.’ Do you hear that? I lay down for a nap after dinner, and guess what: even though Katerina Ivanovna had just had a huge fight with our landlady a week before, she couldn’t resist inviting her in for coffee. They sat together for two hours, whispering. ‘Semyon Zaharovitch is working again, getting a salary,’ she says, ‘and his boss even brought him into his office ahead of everyone else.’ Do you hear? And all that, I swear, she made up for herself—not just for show, but because she really believes it and makes herself happy with her own stories. I don’t blame her, not at all! Six days ago, when I brought her my first pay—twenty-three roubles and forty kopecks—she called me her ‘poppet.’ When we were alone—imagine, nobody would call me handsome or a catch—she pinched my cheek and called me her little poppet.”

Marmeladov broke off, tried to smile, but his chin started to tremble. He controlled himself. The dirty tavern, Marmeladov’s pitiful appearance, five nights on a hay barge, the pot of booze, and yet his deep love for his family all confused Raskolnikov. He listened closely, but with a sick feeling, and regretted coming.

“Sir, sir,” Marmeladov cried, pulling himself together—“Maybe you think all this is just silly, just like the others do, and maybe I’m boring you with all these details of my life, but it’s not funny to me. I feel it all! That whole glorious day and evening, I dreamed about fixing everything, dressing the kids, giving my wife some rest, saving my daughter from shame, and much more… All normal dreams, sir. Well then,” (Marmeladov suddenly jerked upright and stared at Raskolnikov), “the very next day after all those dreams—exactly five days ago, in the evening—I snuck the key to Katerina Ivanovna’s chest, stole what was left of my wages, however much it was, I can’t remember, and look at me now! I’ve been gone five days, they’re looking for me, my job is lost, my uniform is in a pawn shop by the Egyptian Bridge—I traded it for these rags. It’s all over!”

Marmeladov hit his forehead with his fist, clenched his teeth, closed his eyes, and leaned heavily on the table. But a minute later, his face changed, and with a sly, almost proud look, he glanced at Raskolnikov, laughed, and said:
“This morning I went to see Sonya, to ask her for a ‘pick-me-up!’ Ha-ha-ha!”
“You mean she gave it to you?” yelled one of the newcomers, bursting out laughing.

“This very quart came from her money,” Marmeladov said, talking only to Raskolnikov. “She gave me thirty kopecks with her own hands—her last, all she had, I saw it. She didn’t say a word, just looked at me. Up in heaven, they grieve for people, they weep, but they don’t blame them, they don’t! But that hurts even more—when they don’t blame you! Thirty kopecks! And maybe she needs it now, eh? What do you think, sir? She has to keep up appearances—costs money to look decent, you know! There’s hair oil, petticoats, shoes, nice ones to show off when she steps over a puddle. Do you get it, sir, what all that ‘smartness’ means? And here I am, her father, I took thirty kopecks of that for booze! And I’m drinking it! And it’s already gone! Who could feel sorry for someone like me, huh? Tell me, sir, do you pity me or not? Ha-ha-ha!”
He tried to pour another glass, but the pot was empty.
“Why should anyone pity you?” shouted the tavern-keeper, who was back again.
Shouts of laughter and a few curses followed. The noise came from people listening and from others who hadn’t heard a thing but just saw the shabby clerk.
“Pity? Why pity me?” Marmeladov suddenly boomed, standing up and stretching out his arm, as if waiting for that question.

“Why pity me, you ask? Yes! There’s nothing to pity me for! I should be crucified, not pitied! Crucify me, judge me—but then feel sorry for me! I’d go to the cross myself, because I don’t want a party—I want tears, suffering! Do you think your pint was sweet to me? I was looking for sorrow, for suffering, and I found it, I tasted it; but He will pity us—He who pitied everyone, who understood all people, He alone is the judge. He’ll come one day and ask: ‘Where’s the daughter who gave herself up for her dying stepmother and hungry children? Where’s the daughter who forgave her drunken, disgusting father?’ And He’ll say, ‘Come to me! I’ve already forgiven you once... Your many sins are forgiven because you loved so much…’ And He’ll forgive my Sonya, I know it… I felt it today with her! And He’ll judge and forgive everyone, good and bad, smart and gentle. And after He’s done with them, He’ll call us: ‘You too come, you drunkards, you weak ones, you outcasts!’ And we’ll all come, without shame, and He’ll say, ‘You’re pigs, made in the image of the Beast, but come anyway!’ And the smart people will ask, ‘Lord, why do you let them in?’ And He’ll say, ‘This is why: not one of them thought he deserved it.’ And He’ll open His arms, and we’ll fall down and cry and understand everything! Then we’ll all understand—even Katerina Ivanovna will understand… Lord, let Your kingdom come!” And he collapsed, exhausted, staring at nothing, lost in thought. His words made an impression; for a moment, everyone was quiet. But soon, laughter and cursing started up again.
“That’s his idea!”
“Talked himself silly!”
“What a government clerk!”
And so on, and so on.
“Let’s go, sir,” Marmeladov said suddenly, raising his head and speaking to Raskolnikov. “Come with me… Kozel’s house, looking into the yard. I’m going to Katerina Ivanovna—it’s time.”

Raskolnikov had already been wanting to leave and planned to help Marmeladov. Marmeladov was much less steady on his feet than in his speech and leaned heavily on Raskolnikov as they walked. They had to go a few hundred steps. The drunk seemed more and more confused and scared as they got closer to his home.

“It’s not Katerina Ivanovna I’m scared of now,” he mumbled nervously, “not that she’ll start pulling my hair. Who cares about my hair! Let her pull it—it’s better that way. I’m not afraid of that… it’s her eyes I’m scared of… yes, her eyes… and the red in her cheeks, that’s scary… and her breathing too. Have you noticed how sick people breathe when they’re upset? I’m scared the kids will cry… If Sonya hasn’t fed them… I don’t know what’s happened! But I’m not afraid of being hit. For me, that isn’t pain—it’s almost a pleasure. I need it. It’s better that way. Let her hit me, it makes her feel better… there’s the house. Kozel’s house, the carpenter—he’s German, well-off. Lead the way!”

They entered from the yard and climbed to the fourth floor. The staircase got darker and darker as they went up. It was almost eleven at night, and although in summer St. Petersburg never gets truly dark, it was pitch black at the top.

A dirty little door at the top of the stairs was open. A shabby room about thirty feet long was lit by a stub of candle; you could see it all from the doorway. The place was a mess, full of rags, mostly kids’ clothes. Across the far corner, a ragged sheet hung, probably covering a bed. There were only two chairs and a ripped-up sofa covered in fake leather, with an old, unpainted kitchen table in front. On the edge of the table was a burning candle in an iron holder. It looked like the family had a whole room, not just part of one, but it was basically a hallway. The door to the other rooms—really just closets—was half open, and there was shouting, laughing, and card playing inside. Rude words kept coming out.

Raskolnikov recognized Katerina Ivanovna right away. She was a tall, thin, graceful woman, but terribly skinny, with beautiful dark brown hair and red cheeks from fever. She was pacing back and forth, pressing her hands to her chest; her lips were dry, and her breathing was fast and broken. Her eyes glowed like she had a fever, staring fixedly. That sick, excited face, lit by the dying candle, was shocking. She looked about thirty and seemed a strange wife for Marmeladov. She hadn’t heard them come in and didn’t notice them, lost in thought. The air was stuffy, but she hadn’t opened a window; there was a stink from the stairs, but the door was open. From the other rooms came clouds of cigarette smoke; she kept coughing, but didn’t close the door. The youngest child, a six-year-old girl, was asleep curled up on the floor by the sofa. A boy a year older stood crying and shaking in a corner, probably after a beating. Next to him was a thin nine-year-old girl, wearing a ragged old shirt and an outgrown cashmere coat over her bare shoulders. Her skinny arm was around her brother’s neck, trying to comfort him and keep him from crying again, but her big dark eyes, huge on her thin face, kept watching her mother. Marmeladov didn’t enter, but fell to his knees in the doorway, pushing Raskolnikov ahead of him. The woman, seeing a stranger, stopped and looked at him, surprised and wondering why he was there. But she guessed he was just passing through to the next room. Ignoring him, she went to close the outside door and screamed suddenly when she saw her husband kneeling in the doorway.
“Ah!” she shrieked, “he’s come back! Criminal! Monster! Where’s the money? What’s in your pocket? And your clothes are different! Where are your clothes? Where’s the money! Speak!”
She started searching him. Marmeladov obediently held up his arms to make it easier. Not a single coin was found.

“Where’s the money?” she yelled. “Oh, God, did he drink it all? There were twelve silver roubles left in the chest!” In a rage, she grabbed his hair and dragged him into the room. Marmeladov helped by crawling along on his knees.

“And this is a comfort to me! It doesn’t hurt me, it’s a real con-so-la-tion, ho-nou-red sir,” he called out, getting shaken by his hair and even hitting his head on the floor. The sleeping child woke up and started crying. The boy in the corner began screaming in terror and rushed to his sister; the oldest girl shook like a leaf.

“He drank it! He drank it all!” the poor woman screamed. “And his clothes are gone! And they’re hungry, hungry!” She pointed to the kids, wringing her hands. “Oh, what a life! And you, aren’t you ashamed?” she suddenly yelled at Raskolnikov. “From the tavern! You’ve been drinking with him? You too? Get out!”

Raskolnikov hurried out, silent. The inner door flew open and curious faces peered in—rough, laughing men with pipes, cigarettes, and caps stuck their heads through the doorway. Further back, you could see people in dressing gowns, half-dressed, some holding cards. They were especially entertained when Marmeladov, being dragged by his hair, shouted that it was a comfort. Some even started coming into the room; finally, a shrill scream was heard: Amalia Lippevechsel herself forced her way in, trying to restore order by yelling at Katerina Ivanovna, threatening for the hundredth time to kick her out the next day. As he left, Raskolnikov quickly put the change he’d gotten at the tavern on the windowsill, unnoticed. Out on the stairs, he thought about going back.

“What a stupid thing I’ve done,” he thought. “They have Sonya, and I need the money myself.” But then he realized it was impossible to take it back now and, honestly, he wouldn’t have anyway, so he just waved it off and headed home. “Sonya needs hair oil too,” he thought as he walked, and he laughed bitterly. “That kind of ‘smartness’ costs money… Hm! And maybe Sonya will be out of luck tonight—there’s always a risk, chasing big money… hunting for gold… then they’d all be starving tomorrow, except for my money. Hurrah for Sonya! What a gold mine she is! And they’re cashing in! Yes, they’re making the most of it! They’ve cried about it and gotten used to it. People get used to anything—what scoundrels!”
He fell into deep thought.

“But what if I’m wrong,” he suddenly cried to himself after a moment, “what if people aren’t really scoundrels—humans in general, I mean, the whole human race—then everything else is just prejudice, made-up fears, and there are no real barriers, and everything’s just as it should be.”

Raskolnikov woke up late the next day after a night of restless sleep. But he didn’t feel any better—he was grouchy, irritated, and angry, especially at his tiny, cramped room. The place was barely big enough to walk across, with faded yellow wallpaper peeling off the walls and a ceiling so low that anyone even a little tall would be afraid of hitting their head. The furniture was just as shabby: three old wobbly chairs, a small painted table in the corner covered with a thick layer of dust and untouched books and papers. A large, awkward sofa took up most of the wall and almost half the room; it used to be covered in chintz but now the fabric was torn and ragged. This was where Raskolnikov slept, usually without even changing out of his clothes, just wrapping himself up in his old student’s coat, using a single small pillow and piling all his linen—clean and dirty—under it for extra support. A little table stood in front of the sofa.

It would have been hard for the room to get messier, but oddly enough, Raskolnikov kind of liked it this way right now. He’d shut himself away from everyone, like a turtle hiding in its shell. Even seeing the servant girl who sometimes peeked into his room made his nerves twitch. He was completely obsessed with his own thoughts, barely noticing anything else. For two weeks, his landlady had stopped sending him meals, but he hadn’t even bothered to complain, just skipped dinner instead. Nastasya, the cook and only servant, actually liked that Raskolnikov was so withdrawn, so she stopped cleaning his room except maybe once a week. She was the one who woke him up that morning.
“Get up, why are you still sleeping?” Nastasya called. “It’s past nine. I brought you some tea; want a cup? You must be starving.”
Raskolnikov opened his eyes, startled, and saw that it was Nastasya.
“Is that from the landlady?” he asked slowly, his face pale and sick as he sat up on the sofa.
“From the landlady? Hardly!”
She put down her own cracked teapot, full of weak, old tea, and placed two yellowish lumps of sugar next to it.

“Here, Nastasya, take this,” he said, digging around in his pocket—since he’d slept in his clothes—and pulling out some small coins. “Go buy me a loaf of bread. And get a little sausage, the cheapest kind, from the pork shop.”

“I’ll get you the bread right away, but wouldn’t you rather have some cabbage soup instead of sausage? It’s really good, leftover from yesterday. I saved it for you, but you came home late. It’s tasty.”
When Nastasya brought the soup and he started eating, she sat down next to him on the sofa and began to chat. She was a country woman and loved to talk.
“Praskovya Pavlovna is planning to report you to the police,” she said.
He frowned.
“The police? What for?”
“You don’t pay your rent, and you won’t leave the room. That’s what she wants, obviously.”
“Damn, that’s just what I needed,” he muttered through his teeth. “No, that won’t do for me... not right now. She’s an idiot,” he added out loud. “I’ll go talk to her today.”
“Idiot she is, just like me. But if you’re so smart, why are you lying here like a sack doing nothing? You used to go out and tutor kids. Why don’t you do anything now?”
“I am doing something...” Raskolnikov started, sounding grumpy and annoyed.
“What are you doing?”
“Work...”
“What kind of work?”
“I’m thinking,” he answered seriously, after a pause.
Nastasya burst out laughing. She had a habit of laughing so hard and silently that her whole body shook until it made her feel sick.
“And have you made much money just from thinking?” she finally managed to ask.
“Can’t go out to give lessons without boots. And I’m sick of it anyway.”
“Don’t complain about your bread and butter.”
“They pay so little for lessons. What’s the point of a few coins?” he answered, mostly talking to himself.
“So you want to get rich all at once?”
He gave her a strange look.
“Yes, I want to be rich,” he answered firmly, after a short pause.
“Don’t be in such a rush, you’re scaring me! So, should I get the bread or not?”
“Do whatever you want.”
“Oh, I almost forgot! A letter came for you yesterday while you were out.”
“A letter? For me? From who?”
“No idea. I paid three kopecks of my own money to the postman for it. Will you pay me back?”
“Then bring it here, please, bring it!” Raskolnikov cried, suddenly excited. “Oh God!”

A minute later, she brought him the letter. That was it—his mother’s handwriting, from the province of R——. He turned pale as he took it. He hadn’t gotten a letter in a long time, but something else suddenly stabbed at his heart, too.
“Nastasya, leave me alone, please; here’s your three kopecks, but please hurry up and go!”

The letter shook in his hand; he didn’t want to open it while she was there—he needed to be alone with it. When Nastasya left, he quickly pressed the letter to his lips and kissed it. Then he stared at the address, at the small, slanted handwriting he knew so well from his mother, who had taught him to read and write. He hesitated, almost afraid. Finally, he opened it; it was thick and heavy, more than two ounces, two big sheets of paper covered in tiny handwriting.

“My dear Rodya,” wrote his mother, “It’s been two months since I last wrote to you, which has really upset me and kept me awake at night. But I hope you won’t be angry with me for not writing. You know how much I love you; Dounia and I have always counted on you, you’re our everything, our one hope. It broke my heart when I heard you had to leave university because you couldn’t afford it, and lost your tutoring jobs! How could I help on my tiny pension of a hundred and twenty roubles a year? The fifteen roubles I sent you four months ago I had to borrow, using my pension as security, from Mr. Vahrushin, a kind local merchant and a friend of your father’s. But since I had to let him collect my pension until the debt was paid, I couldn’t send you anything else until now. Thank God, things are better now, and I have some good news for you. First, would you have guessed, dear Rodya, that your sister Dounia has been living with me for six weeks now? We won’t be separated again. Thank God her troubles are over, but I’ll explain everything in order. When you wrote me two months ago that you’d heard Dounia was having a hard time at the Svidrigailovs’ house, and asked me to tell you what happened—how could I answer? If I told you the whole truth, I know you’d have dropped everything and come to us, even if you had to walk, because you’d never let your sister be insulted. I was desperate too, but I didn’t know the full story then. The hardest part was that when Dounia started as a governess with them, she got a hundred roubles in advance, with part taken out of her pay every month—so she couldn’t just quit without paying it back. (Now I can finally explain, my dear Rodya.) She took most of that money to send you sixty roubles when you needed it so badly last year. We told you it was from Dounia’s savings, but that wasn’t true, and I want you to know now, because—thank God—things have turned out better, and you should know how much Dounia loves you. At first, Mr. Svidrigailov was rude and made nasty remarks at dinner... but I won’t go into every detail and upset you now that it’s all over. In short, even though Marfa Petrovna, Svidrigailov’s wife, was kind, Dounia had a really hard time, especially when Mr. Svidrigailov was drunk. Later, we found out that he’d secretly fallen in love with Dounia, but hid it by being rude and mean, maybe because he was embarrassed or ashamed, especially since he was older and married. Eventually, he lost control and made Dounia a disgraceful offer, promising her all kinds of things and even suggesting they run away together. You can imagine how she felt! She couldn’t quit right away—not just because of the money, but also to avoid hurting Marfa Petrovna’s feelings, which would have caused a scandal. Dounia had no way out for six more weeks. You know Dounia—she’s clever and strong-willed, and can put up with a lot. She didn’t even tell me everything, afraid to worry me, though we stayed in touch. In the end, something unexpected happened: Marfa Petrovna overheard her husband begging Dounia in the garden, misunderstood what was happening, and blamed Dounia. There was a terrible scene; Marfa Petrovna even struck Dounia, wouldn’t listen to her, and after shouting for an hour ordered Dounia to be sent to me at once, piling all her things into a peasant’s cart without packing—and it poured rain, so Dounia had to ride seventeen versts to town, soaking wet and humiliated. You can see why I couldn’t answer your letter honestly—I was desperate, but what could you have done? Only made yourself miserable, and Dounia wouldn’t have allowed that. For a whole month, the town gossiped about us; we didn’t even dare go to church because of the stares and whispers. All our friends ignored us, no one even said hello on the street. I heard that some clerks were planning to shame us by smearing pitch on our door, and even our landlord wanted us to leave. Most of this was started by Marfa Petrovna, who slandered Dounia everywhere, telling her story to the whole town and countryside. It made me sick, but Dounia handled it better than I did—she’s an angel! But by God’s mercy, it ended: Mr. Svidrigailov repented and gave Marfa Petrovna proof of Dounia’s innocence—a letter Dounia had written, refusing his secret offers, scolding him for his behavior and reminding him that he was a husband and father. The letter was so noble and heartfelt that I cried when I read it. The servants also testified for Dounia; they’d seen more than Svidrigailov realized. Marfa Petrovna was shocked and realized she’d been wrong. The next day, she went to the Cathedral to pray, then came to us, told us everything, begged Dounia for forgiveness, and spent days going house to house to tell everyone Dounia was innocent, even reading the letter to them and letting them copy it. In my opinion, she went a bit overboard, but that’s her way. In the end, Dounia’s reputation was completely restored, and everyone blamed her husband. Dounia was offered new teaching jobs, but she refused. Suddenly, everyone treated her with respect, which led to a big change for our family. Rodya, Dounia now has a suitor, and she’s agreed to marry him. I wanted to tell you as soon as possible, and although we didn’t wait for your permission, I hope you won’t be upset, as you couldn’t possibly know all the details from afar. The man is Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin, already a counsellor, distantly related to Marfa Petrovna, who helped arrange the match. He visited, drank coffee with us, and the next day sent a polite letter proposing marriage, asking for a quick and clear answer. He’s in a hurry to get to Petersburg for work, so time matters to him. At first, we were surprised—it all happened so quickly. He’s well-off, reliable, has two government jobs, and has already made his fortune. He’s forty-five, but looks good and is very respectable, though a little gloomy and proud, though maybe that’s just the first impression. Be careful, Rodya, not to judge him too quickly when you meet him—he’s probably a good man. At his first visit, he said he was practical but shared many ideas of ‘the younger generation’ and didn’t believe in old prejudices. He may be a bit full of himself, but that’s not a crime. Dounia says he’s clever and seems kind-hearted, even if not highly educated. You know Dounia—she’s sensible, patient, generous, but also passionate. There’s no great love on either side, but Dounia is determined to be a good wife, and he wants to make her happy. It’s all happened fast, but he’s cautious and will surely realize he’ll be happier if Dounia is happy. As for his flaws or differences of opinion, Dounia says she can handle them as long as their marriage is honorable and straightforward. He did say, for example, that he wanted to marry a respectable girl who had no dowry and had experienced poverty, because, as he explained, a husband shouldn’t be in debt to his wife, and it’s better for the wife to see her husband as a benefactor. He put it more politely than I do, and it just slipped out in conversation, but it did sound a bit rude. Dounia was annoyed when I mentioned it, saying ‘words aren’t deeds,’ and she’s right. She stayed up all night thinking before she decided and prayed for a long time before telling me her answer.”

“I already mentioned that Pyotr Petrovitch is about to leave for Petersburg, where he has lots of work and wants to start a law office. He’s been handling cases for years, and just won an important one. He has to be in Petersburg for a big case in the Senate. So, dear Rodya, he could really help you in lots of ways, and Dounia and I think this means your future is safe and planned out. Oh, if only it works out! It would be such a blessing for us. Dounia is obsessed with the idea. We’ve even hinted to Pyotr Petrovitch that you could work for him as a secretary. He answered carefully, saying that it’d be better to hire a relative than a stranger if they’re qualified—but he wondered if your university work would leave you time for his office. That was the end of that conversation, but Dounia can’t stop thinking about it and has already made plans for you to become his partner one day, since you study law. I totally agree, and I think it’s possible. Even though Pyotr Petrovitch seems a bit distant now (since he doesn’t know you yet), Dounia believes she can convince him once they’re married. Of course, we don’t talk to him about these bigger plans—it might sound too much like daydreaming for his taste. Also, we haven’t mentioned our hope that he’ll help pay for your studies; we figure he’ll offer that himself later, especially if you help in his office and earn a salary, not charity. Dounia wants it to work that way and I agree. Another reason we haven’t said anything is that I want you to feel equal when you first meet him. When Dounia praised you, he said he’d rather meet you in person before forming an opinion. Rodya, I have a feeling—nothing to do with Pyotr Petrovitch, just an old woman’s instinct—that after the wedding, I should live separately instead of with them. I’m sure he’ll invite me to stay with them, but I’d rather not get in anyone’s way, and I’d like my own independence as long as I have enough to live on and have you and Dounia. If possible, I’ll settle somewhere near you, which brings me to the happiest news: soon we might all be together again, after almost three years apart! Dounia and I plan to leave for Petersburg very soon, maybe in a week, depending on when Pyotr Petrovitch is ready. He wants the wedding as soon as possible, maybe even before the Feast of Our Lady, or right after. Oh, how happy I’ll be to hug you! Dounia is so excited to see you that she joked she’d marry Pyotr Petrovitch just for that. She’s an angel! She isn’t writing herself, but told me to send all her love and kisses, and says she has so much to tell you that it’s better to wait. Even though we’ll see you soon, I’ll try to send you money in a few days. Now that people know about Dounia’s engagement, my credit is better and I think I can borrow up to seventy-five roubles, so I hope to send you twenty-five or thirty roubles. I wish it could be more, but I worry about our travel costs. Pyotr Petrovitch is paying for our bags and trunk, but we’ll need some money for our first days in Petersburg. We’ve planned every detail and should be able to travel third class comfortably. So, I may be able to send you thirty roubles. I’ve already filled two sheets with everything that’s happened! So, my dear Rodya, I hug you and send you a mother’s blessing until we meet. Love Dounia the way she loves you—she loves you even more than herself! You’re everything to us. If you’re happy, we’ll be happy. Do you still say your prayers, Rodya, and believe in God’s mercy? I worry that you might have lost your faith, like so many young people these days. If you have, I pray for you. Remember, when you were little and your father was alive, how you used to say your prayers with me and how happy we were. Goodbye until we meet—I hug you tightly, with many kisses.”
“Yours forever,
Pulcheria Raskolnikov.”

Almost as soon as he started reading, Raskolnikov’s face was streaked with tears; but when he finished, he was pale and twisted with emotion, and a bitter, angry smile appeared on his lips. He buried his head in his dirty, worn-out pillow and thought and thought for a long time. His heart pounded and his mind was spinning. Finally, he felt trapped and suffocated in his little yellow box of a room. He craved space. He grabbed his hat and left, not even caring who might see him. He walked toward Vassilyevsky Island, heading down Vassilyevsky Prospect, moving quickly as if on an urgent errand—but really, he didn’t notice where he was going, mumbling and even talking out loud to himself. Passers-by looked at him with surprise—some thought he was drunk.

His mother’s letter had been absolute torture for him, but when it came to the main point in it, he didn’t hesitate for even a second—not even while reading it. The most important thing was decided, and in his mind, it was final: “That marriage will never happen as long as I’m alive, and Mr. Luzhin can go to hell!” “It’s completely clear,” he muttered to himself, with a bitter grin, already picturing how he’d win in the end. “No, Mother, no, Dounia—you can’t fool me! And then you apologize for not asking my advice, saying you made the decision without me! Sure, right. You both think it’s all arranged now and can’t be undone. But we’ll see about that! What a great excuse: ‘Pyotr Petrovitch is such a busy man, even his wedding has to be rushed.’ No, Dounia, I see through all of this. I know what you want to say to me; I know what was going through your head when you walked up and down all night, and how you were praying before the icon of the Virgin Mary in Mother’s bedroom. The road to Golgotha is bitter.... Hm... so it’s finally settled; you’ve decided to marry a practical businessman, Avdotya Romanovna (Dounia), someone wealthy, someone with two government jobs, someone who, as Mother says, shares the latest ideas, and who, according to Dounia herself, seems kind. That ‘seems’ is everything! And for that ‘seems,’ Dounia is marrying him! Wonderful! Just great!”

“... But why did Mother write ‘our most rising generation’? Was it just to describe him, or was she trying to make me like Mr. Luzhin? Oh, how sneaky they are! I’d like to know one more thing: how honest have they been with each other about all this, that day and night and since then? Did they talk openly, or did they both just know what the other was thinking, so they didn’t have to say it out loud? Probably some of both—Mother’s letter shows it. She thought he was a bit rude, and in her innocence, she told Dounia about it. Dounia probably got annoyed and ‘answered her angrily.’ Of course! Who wouldn’t, when it’s all so obvious and not worth discussing? And why does she write, ‘love Dounia, Rodya, and she loves you more than herself’? Does she feel guilty about sacrificing her daughter for her son? ‘You are our only comfort, you are everything to us.’ Oh, Mother!”
He felt more and more bitter, and if he had met Mr. Luzhin right then, he might have killed him.

“Hm... yes, that’s true,” he went on, chasing the wild thoughts spinning in his head, “it’s true that ‘it takes time and care to get to know someone,’ but there’s no mistake about Mr. Luzhin. The main thing is, he’s ‘a businessman and seems kind’—and that’s enough to send them the bags and big box! Such kindness! But his fiancée and her mother have to ride in a peasant’s cart covered with old sacks (I know what that’s like). No big deal! It’s only ninety versts, and then they can ‘travel very comfortably, third-class,’ for a thousand versts! Right, you have to live within your means. But what about you, Mr. Luzhin? That’s your bride... and you know her mother has to pawn things from her pension just to afford the trip. Of course, it’s a business deal—a partnership where everything’s split—food and drink included, but you pay for your own tobacco. The businessman wins again! Their luggage will cost less than their tickets, and probably get shipped for free. How do they not see all this? Or do they just not want to see? And they’re happy, so happy! And this is just the beginning—the real problems will come later. What really matters isn’t the cheapness or stinginess, it’s the whole attitude. That’s what marriage to him will be like, just a preview now. And Mother, why is she being so generous? When she gets to Petersburg, she’ll have maybe three silver roubles or two ‘paper’ ones, like she says... poor old woman... hm. What does she expect to live on in Petersburg? She already guesses she can’t live with Dounia after the marriage, even for a few months. Luzhin probably hinted at that, though Mother would deny it: ‘I’ll refuse,’ she says. Who does she think will support her then? Is she counting on what’s left of her pension after she pays back Afanasy Ivanovitch’s loan? She knits shawls and embroiders cuffs, ruining her old eyes for barely twenty roubles a year extra. So she’s putting all her hopes on Luzhin’s generosity—‘he’ll offer money himself, he’ll insist on it.’ She’ll be waiting forever! That’s how these noble, romantic types are; every goose is a swan to them until reality smacks them in the face. Does Luzhin have any medals, I wonder? I bet he wears his Anna medal at dinners with merchants. He’ll definitely wear it at his wedding! Enough about him, curse him!”

“Well... I’m not surprised at Mother, that’s just how she is, God bless her. But how could Dounia? Dounia, my dear, as if I don’t know you! You were almost twenty when I saw you last—I understood you even then. Mother writes, ‘Dounia can put up with a lot.’ I know that. I’ve been thinking about that for the past two and a half years—if she could put up with Mr. Svidrigaïlov and all that happened, she can put up with anything. And now Mother and Dounia think she can put up with Mr. Luzhin, who actually says out loud that wives who are rescued from poverty owe everything to their husbands—he says that, almost at the first meeting. Maybe he just let it slip, but maybe he meant to be clear from the start. But Dounia? She knows what kind of man he is, but she’ll have to live with him. She’d rather live on black bread and water than sell her soul or trade her freedom for comfort; she wouldn’t do it for all the gold in the world, much less for Luzhin’s money. No, Dounia wasn’t like that when I knew her, and I’m sure she’s the same now. Yes, the Svidrigaïlovs were awful to deal with! It’s rough being a governess in the provinces for two hundred roubles, but I know she’d rather be a slave on a plantation than lower herself by tying herself forever to a man she doesn’t respect, just for her own gain. If Luzhin were made of pure gold, she still wouldn’t agree to be his legal mistress. So why is she agreeing now? What’s the point? The answer’s obvious: for herself, for her own comfort, she wouldn’t do it—but for someone she loves, she will. For her brother, for her mother, she’ll sacrifice everything. In these cases, people convince themselves it’s their duty, and start making excuses for themselves. That’s just how we are. It’s clear that Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov (me) is at the center of all this. Yes, with her help, he’ll be happy, stay at university, get a good job, maybe even become rich and famous someday! But what about Mother? It’s all for Rodya, precious Rodya, her firstborn! For a son like that, who wouldn’t sacrifice a daughter! Oh, loving, too-loving hearts! For his sake, they’d even go through what Sonia does. Sonia Marmeladov, the eternal victim. Do you realize what you’re sacrificing, both of you? Is it right? Can you stand it? Does it make sense? And let me tell you, Dounia, Sonia’s life isn’t any worse than life with Luzhin. ‘There can be no question of love,’ Mother writes. But what if there can’t even be respect—if it’s all disgust and contempt, then what? You’ll have to ‘keep up appearances,’ is that it? Do you get what that means? Do you see that Luzhin’s version of being respectable is the same as Sonia’s life, maybe even worse, because for you it’s a trade for comfort, but for Sonia it’s just to avoid starving. There’s a price to pay, Dounia. What if it’s more than you can handle? What if you regret it? The bitterness, misery, the secret tears—because you’re no Marfa Petrovna who can handle anything. And how will Mother feel then? Even now she’s worried, but later, when she really sees it? And me? What do you take me for? I won’t let you sacrifice yourself, Dounia. I won’t let you, Mother. Not while I’m alive. No way! I won’t allow it!”
He suddenly stopped, caught in his thoughts, and stood still.

“Won’t allow it? But what am I going to do about it? Forbid it? What right do I have? What can I offer them to give me that right? I promise them my whole life, my whole future, once I finish my studies and get a job? They’ve heard that before—it’s just talk. But now? Something has to be done now, do you get that? And what am I doing? Living off them. They borrow money from their hundred-rouble pension. They borrow from the Svidrigaïlovs. How am I supposed to save them from people like Svidrigaïlov, or Afanasy Ivanovitch Vahrushin, or any other ‘savior’ who wants to fix their lives? In ten years? In ten years, Mother will be blind from knitting shawls, maybe from crying too. She’ll be just a shadow from fasting. And Dounia? Imagine what could happen to your sister in ten years! What might she go through?”

So he tortured himself with these questions, almost enjoying the pain. But these weren’t new problems; they were old, familiar wounds. His current agony had started long ago, slowly growing until it became a wild, terrifying question that ate at his heart and mind, always demanding an answer. Now, his mother’s letter had hit him like thunder. He realized he couldn’t just sit and suffer anymore—he had to do something, and fast. He had to decide, or else...

“Or just give up on life altogether!” he suddenly cried out in a frenzy. “Just accept things as they are, kill all hope inside myself, and give up on ever doing anything, having a life, or even love!”
“Do you understand, sir, do you understand what it means when you have absolutely nowhere to turn?” Marmeladov’s question suddenly popped into his mind. “Every man has to have somewhere to turn....”

He jerked in surprise; another thought from yesterday came back to him. But he wasn’t surprised that it returned—he knew, he’d felt it would come back. It wasn’t just yesterday’s thought. The difference was, a month ago, or even yesterday, it was just a dream. But now... now it didn’t feel like a dream at all—it felt real and dangerous, and he suddenly realized that. His head started pounding, and his vision went dark.

He looked around quickly, searching for something. He wanted to sit down and was looking for a bench. He was walking along K—— Boulevard. There was a bench about a hundred steps ahead. He hurried toward it, but on the way, something happened that caught all his attention. While looking for the bench, he’d noticed a woman walking about twenty steps in front of him, but at first, he didn’t pay more attention to her than to anyone else on the street. He often walked home without noticing his route, and he was used to just wandering lost in thought. But there was something strange about this woman that slowly drew his attention—first reluctantly, almost annoyed, and then more and more focused. He suddenly wanted to figure out what was so odd about her. First, she looked very young. She was walking in the blazing heat with no hat, no umbrella, no gloves, waving her arms in a weird way. She wore a light silky dress, but it was on wrong, not buttoned properly, torn at the waist with a big ripped piece hanging down. She had a little scarf around her bare neck, but it was crooked. She was walking unsteadily, stumbling and swaying from side to side. Finally, she had all of Raskolnikov’s attention. He caught up to her at the bench, but as he reached it, she dropped onto it in the corner, let her head fall back, and closed her eyes, completely exhausted. Looking closely, he saw right away that she was completely drunk. It was a shocking sight. He could hardly believe it was real. She looked so young—sixteen, maybe not even fifteen—with a pretty face, but it was flushed, puffy, and heavy-looking. She seemed barely aware of what she was doing; she crossed her legs carelessly, not even noticing she was on the street.

Raskolnikov didn’t sit down, but he didn’t want to just leave her, so he stood there, confused. The boulevard was never very busy, and now, at two o’clock in the sweltering heat, it was almost empty. But on the other side of the boulevard, about fifteen paces away, a man was standing on the sidewalk’s edge. He also wanted to approach the girl for some reason. He’d probably seen her from a distance and followed her, but now Raskolnikov was in his way. The man looked at Raskolnikov angrily, trying to ignore him, and waited impatiently for the “ragged stranger” to leave. His intentions were obvious. The man was short and chubby, about thirty, dressed fashionably, with a red face, red lips, and a mustache. Raskolnikov felt a sudden urge to insult this fat dandy. He left the girl for a moment and walked toward the man.
“Hey! You Svidrigaïlov! What are you doing here?” he shouted, clenching his fists and laughing angrily.
“What do you mean?” the man asked, frowning and glaring at him with pride.
“Get lost, that’s what I mean.”
“How dare you, you lowlife!”

The man raised his cane. Raskolnikov rushed at him with his fists, not thinking that the man was much stronger. But just then, someone grabbed him from behind—a police officer had stepped between them.
“That’s enough, gentlemen. No fighting in public. What’s going on? Who are you?” he asked Raskolnikov sternly, noticing his shabby clothes.
Raskolnikov looked at him closely. The officer had an honest, sensible face, with gray mustache and whiskers.
“You’re just the man I need,” Raskolnikov said, grabbing his arm. “I’m a student, Raskolnikov.... Just so you know,” he added, glaring at the other man. “Come on, I have something to show you.”
Taking the officer by the hand, he pulled him toward the bench.

“Look here,” he said, “she’s hopelessly drunk, and she just came down the boulevard. There’s no telling who she is, but she doesn’t look like a prostitute. More likely, someone gave her drinks and tricked her... for the first time, maybe... you get it? Then they shoved her out onto the street like this. Look at her torn dress, and how it’s put on. Someone else dressed her—clumsy hands, probably a man’s. And now, look over there: I don’t know that dandy I almost fought, I’ve never seen him before, but he saw her too, drunk and lost, and now he’s desperate to get her alone while she’s like this... I’m sure of it. I saw him watching her and following her, but I stopped him, and now he’s just waiting for me to leave. He’s pretending to make a cigarette, but he’s not leaving. So, how do we keep her away from him, and how do we get her home?”
The officer understood right away. The fat man’s intentions were obvious, so he turned his attention to the girl. He bent down to look more closely, and his face showed real sympathy.

“Ah, what a shame!” he said, shaking his head. “She’s just a child! She’s been tricked, you can see that right away. Listen, young lady,” he said to her, “where do you live?” The girl opened her tired, sleepy eyes, looked blankly at him, and waved her hand.
“Here,” Raskolnikov said, digging out twenty copecks from his pocket, “take this, get a cab, and send her home. The only problem is finding out her address!”
“Miss, miss!” the officer said, taking the money. “I’ll get you a cab and take you home myself. Where to? Where do you live?”
“Go away! They won’t leave me alone,” the girl mumbled, waving her hand again.
“Oh, oh, how terrible! It’s shameful, miss, shameful!” the officer said, shaking his head, shocked and angry but also feeling sorry for her.
“It’s not easy,” the officer told Raskolnikov, glancing him up and down quickly. Raskolnikov, in his ragged clothes, must have looked odd, especially offering money!
“Did you meet her far from here?” he asked.
“No, she was walking in front of me, staggering, right here on the boulevard. She just made it to the bench and collapsed.”

“Ah, the shameful things people do these days, God help us! An innocent girl like that, already drunk! She’s definitely been tricked. Look how her dress is torn... So much evil these days! She probably comes from a good family, maybe a poor one.... There are so many like that. She even looks like a lady,” he said, leaning over her again.
Maybe he had daughters at home growing up like that too—looking proper, trying to seem like ladies...
“The main thing,” Raskolnikov insisted, “is to keep her away from that creep! Why should he get to do anything to her! It’s obvious what he wants—what a monster, he still hasn’t left!”
Raskolnikov said this out loud, pointing at the man. The dandy heard him, looked furious for a moment, but then just gave him a scornful look, walked another ten steps away, and stopped again.
“We can keep her away from him,” the officer said thoughtfully, “if only she’d tell us where to take her. But like this... Miss! Hey, miss!” He bent over her again.

Suddenly, the girl opened her eyes wide, stared at him like she was realizing something, stood up, and walked back the way she’d come. “Oh, awful people, they won’t leave me alone!” she said, waving her hand again. She walked quickly, but still staggered. The dandy followed her, but on a different path, still watching her.
“Don’t worry, I won’t let him get her,” said the officer firmly, and he set off after them.
“There’s so much evil in the world today!” he said out loud, sighing.
At that moment, Raskolnikov suddenly felt something sting him, and his feelings flipped completely.
“Hey, you there!” he shouted after the officer.
The officer turned around.
“Let them be! Why do you care? Let her go! Let him have his fun.” He pointed at the dandy. “Why do you care?”
The officer looked confused, staring at him wide-eyed. Raskolnikov laughed.
“Fine!” the officer said, waving his hand in disgust, and walked after the dandy and the girl, probably thinking Raskolnikov was crazy or worse.

“He stole my twenty copecks,” Raskolnikov muttered angrily when he was alone. “Well, maybe he’ll get the same amount from the other guy for letting him have the girl. And that’s how it ends. Why did I even get involved? Is it my job to help? Do I have the right? Let them eat each other alive—why should I care? How dare I even give him twenty copecks? Was it even my money?”

Even with those harsh words, he felt miserable. He sat down on the empty bench. His thoughts wandered aimlessly... He couldn’t focus on anything. He just wished he could forget everything, and wake up as someone new....

“Poor girl!” he said, looking at the empty spot where she had sat. “She’ll wake up and cry, and then her mother will find out.... She’ll get a terrible beating, and maybe her mom will kick her out.... Or even if she doesn’t, people like Darya Frantsovna will hear about it, and soon the girl will start sneaking out. Then it’ll be the hospital (that always happens to girls from good families who get into trouble), and then... more hospital... more drinking... bars... and again the hospital, and in a couple years, she’ll be ruined, her life over by eighteen or nineteen.... Haven’t I seen it before? And how does it happen? It always starts like this. Disgusting! But what does it matter? That’s just how things are, they say. Every year, a certain percentage has to end up like this... so everyone else can stay pure. A percentage! What a nice word—so scientific, so comforting....
