Once you call it a ‘percentage,’ you don’t have to worry. If we didn’t have that word, maybe we’d feel more uncomfortable.... But what if Dounia was one of the ‘percentage’? Or someone else I care about?”

“But where am I going?” he suddenly thought. “Weird, I left for a reason. As soon as I read the letter, I went out.... I was going to Vassilyevsky Island, to see Razumihin. That’s it... now I remember. But why? And what made me think of going to Razumihin just now? Strange.”

He was surprised at himself. Razumihin was an old friend from university. It was strange, because Raskolnikov barely had any friends there; he kept his distance from everyone, never visited anyone, and didn’t like visitors. People eventually left him alone. He never joined in student events or parties or talks. He studied intensely and was respected for it, but no one really liked him. He was very poor, and always seemed proud and reserved, as if he was hiding something. Some classmates thought he looked down on everyone else, as if he was better than them in every way.

But with Razumihin, he got along—or at least, he was more open and talkative with him. It was impossible not to like Razumihin. He was cheerful and honest, so kind it was almost simple, but there was real depth and dignity underneath. The better students saw this and all liked him. He was very smart, but sometimes a bit of a goof. He was tall, skinny, black-haired, and always a bit scruffy. He could be loud, and was known for his strength. One time, he knocked down a giant policeman in one punch. He could drink a lot, but could also quit any time; sometimes he went too far with jokes, but he could also be totally serious. He never let failure get him down, and nothing seemed to crush him. He could live anywhere and survive any hardship. He was poor, and lived off whatever work he could find. He knew a thousand ways to make money. One winter, he didn’t light his stove at all, saying he liked sleeping in the cold. For now, he’d had to drop out of university, but just for a while, and was working hard to save up to go back. Raskolnikov hadn’t visited him in four months, and Razumihin didn’t even know his address. Two months before, they’d passed each other in the street, but Raskolnikov turned away and even crossed to the other side to avoid being seen. Razumihin noticed, but didn’t push—he didn’t want to bother him.

“I’ve been thinking about going to see Razumihin to ask for some work, maybe tutoring or something,” Raskolnikov thought. “But what good would that do right now? Even if he gets me some students and shares his last coins with me, so I could buy boots and look decent enough to teach... hmm. Then what? What would I do with the little money I earn? That’s not what I really need. It’s kind of pointless for me to go to Razumihin...”
The question of why he was even heading to Razumihin’s place bothered him more than he realized. He kept searching for some dark or hidden reason behind what should have been a normal thing to do.
“Did I really expect that Razumihin alone could fix everything and help me find a way out?” he wondered, feeling confused.
He thought hard and rubbed his forehead. Then, strangely, after a long time lost in thought, a wild idea suddenly popped into his head.

“Hmm... to Razumihin’s,” he said out loud, sounding calm, like he’d made up his mind. “I’ll go to Razumihin’s, sure, but... not now. I’ll go to him... the day after It happens, when It’s all over, and everything starts again....”
And all at once, he realized what he had just been thinking.

“After It,” he shouted, jumping up from the bench. “But is It really going to happen? Is it really possible?” He left the bench and almost started running. He meant to turn back towards home, but the idea of going home made him feel sick. In that tiny, awful room of his, all these thoughts had been growing for a month; he just wandered off without thinking about where he was going.

The shaky feeling in his nerves turned into a feverish chill, even though the weather was hot. Without really meaning to, he started staring at everything around him, as if searching for something to distract himself, but it didn’t help. He kept sinking back into brooding. Every time he snapped out of it and looked around, he forgot what he’d just been thinking, or where he was heading. Like this, he crossed all the way over Vassilyevsky Ostrov, reached the Lesser Neva, crossed the bridge, and walked toward the islands. The green trees and fresh air were a relief to his tired eyes after the city’s dust and crowded buildings. Here, there were no noisy bars, no suffocating heat, no bad smells. But soon, even these good feelings turned into irritation. Sometimes he stopped and stared through the fence at a brightly painted summer house surrounded by trees. He saw fancy women on the balconies and kids playing in the garden. The flowers especially caught his eye; he looked at them longer than anything else. He also saw fancy carriages and people on horseback, but he lost interest in them as soon as they passed. Once, he stopped and counted his money: thirty copecks. “Twenty for the policeman, three to Nastasya for the letter—so I must have given forty-seven or fifty to the Marmeladovs yesterday,” he thought, for no clear reason. He soon forgot why he’d even pulled out his money. He remembered when he passed a tavern and felt hungry. He went inside, drank a glass of vodka, and ate some kind of pie. He finished it as he walked away. It had been a long time since he’d had any vodka, and it hit him right away, even though it was just a small glass. His legs felt heavy, and he got very sleepy. He started home, but when he got to Petrovsky Ostrov, he was too tired to go on. He left the road, collapsed into the bushes, and instantly fell asleep on the grass.

When someone’s mind is sick, their dreams can feel frighteningly real and vivid. Sometimes dreams are filled with strange, twisted images, but the details and setting are so lifelike that even a great artist couldn’t come up with them while awake. These nightmares stick in the memory and make a big impression on someone whose nerves are already frayed.

Raskolnikov had a terrifying dream. He dreamed he was a little kid again, back in his hometown. He was about seven, walking with his father into the countryside on the night of a holiday. The day was gray and heavy, and everything looked just like he remembered—actually, even clearer than in his real memories. The town was flat and empty, not even a willow tree nearby; far away, there was a patch of trees, just a dark smudge on the horizon. Past the last gardens, there was a big tavern that always creeped him out when he walked by with his dad. There was always a crowd there—shouting, laughing, loud singing, sometimes fights. Drunk, scary-looking people hung around outside. He used to cling to his father’s hand, shaking with fear whenever they passed. Near the tavern, the road turned into a dusty black path, winding around, and about a hundred steps later, it turned toward the graveyard. In the graveyard stood a stone church with a green dome. He went there two or three times a year with his parents for services in memory of his grandmother, who had died long ago, before he was born. They would bring a special rice pudding with raisins in the shape of a cross. He loved that church—the old icons, the ancient priest with a shaky head. Near his grandmother’s grave was a small grave for his baby brother who had died at six months. He never knew him, but he always made the sign of the cross and kissed the grave. Now, in his dream, he was walking with his father past the tavern toward the graveyard, holding his father’s hand, scared of the tavern. Something caught his attention: there was some kind of party going on, with crowds of townspeople, peasants, women, their husbands, and all kinds of rough people—everyone singing and drunk. Near the tavern’s door was a cart, but it was strange. It was a huge cart, the kind usually pulled by big, strong horses carrying heavy loads. He always liked watching those horses with their long manes and thick legs, pulling huge loads like it was nothing. But now, weirdly, in the cart’s harness was a skinny, tired little brown mare—the kind of horse he’d seen struggling to pull heavy wood or hay, especially when stuck in mud. He’d seen peasants beat those horses so cruelly, even hitting their faces and eyes, and it always made him want to cry. His mother would pull him away from the window when that happened. Suddenly, there was a burst of noise—shouting, singing, and balalaika music—and a bunch of big, very drunk men in red and blue shirts came out of the tavern.
“Get in, get in!” yelled one of them—a young peasant with a thick neck and a face as red as a carrot. “I’ll take you all, get in!”
But right away, the crowd burst out laughing and yelling.
“Take all of us with a horse like that?”
“Mikolka, are you nuts? That little thing can’t pull a cart like that!”
“That mare must be at least twenty years old!”

“Get in, I’ll take you all!” Mikolka yelled again, jumping into the cart, grabbing the reins, and standing up at the front. “The good horse is gone with Matvey,” he shouted from the cart, “and this useless thing is just eating up all my food. I feel like killing her. She’s no help. Get in, I tell you! I’ll make her run! She’ll gallop!” He picked up his whip, obviously eager to beat the poor little mare.
“Get in! Come on!” The crowd laughed. “Did you hear that? She’s going to gallop!”
“Gallop? She hasn’t galloped in ten years!”
“She’ll barely stagger along!”
“Don’t worry, guys. Grab a whip each. Get ready!”
“All right! Hit her!”

They all climbed into Mikolka’s cart, joking and laughing. Six men piled in, and there was still room for more. They pulled in a fat, rosy-cheeked woman in a red dress, with a pointed beaded hat and thick shoes; she was cracking nuts and laughing. The crowd was laughing too—how could they not? That poor little horse was supposed to pull all those people at a run! Two young men in the cart already had their whips ready to help Mikolka. When Mikolka yelled “now,” the mare pulled as hard as she could, but she could barely move. She gasped for air and shrank away from the three whips raining down on her like hail. Everyone in the cart and the crowd laughed even harder, but Mikolka got angry and whipped the mare even harder, as if he really thought she could gallop.
“Let me get in too, guys!” yelled a young man in the crowd who wanted a turn.
“Get in, all of you!” Mikolka yelled. “She’ll pull you all! I’ll beat her to death!” He whipped the mare over and over, wild with anger.
“Father, father!” Raskolnikov cried. “Father, what are they doing? They’re beating the poor horse!”

“Come on, let’s go,” his father said. “They’re drunk and stupid, just fooling around. Don’t look!” He tried to pull Raskolnikov away, but the boy tore himself free, terrified, and ran to the horse. The poor animal was in terrible shape. She was gasping, standing still, then trying to pull again and almost falling.
“Beat her to death!” shouted Mikolka. “That’s it! I’ll finish her!”
“What are you doing, you devil? Are you even a Christian?” yelled an old man in the crowd.
“Have you ever seen anything like this? A miserable old mare trying to pull all that weight,” said another.
“You’re going to kill her!” shouted a third.
“Don’t interfere! She’s mine, I can do what I want. Get in, more of you! Get in, everyone! I’ll make her gallop...”
Suddenly, everyone started laughing loudly. The mare, whipped so hard, started kicking weakly. Even the old man had to smile. Imagine a poor little horse like that trying to kick!
Two boys from the crowd grabbed whips and ran over to hit the mare on her sides—one on each side.
“Hit her in the face, in the eyes, in the eyes!” Mikolka yelled.
“Sing us a song, guys!” shouted someone in the cart, and everyone started singing loudly, shaking a tambourine and whistling. The woman kept cracking nuts and laughing.

... Raskolnikov ran beside the mare, then in front of her, watching as she was whipped right in the eyes. He was crying, choking up, tears streaming down his face. One of the men even hit him with a whip across the face, but he didn’t feel it. Wringing his hands and screaming, he ran up to a gray-haired old man who was shaking his head sadly. A woman tried to pull him away, but he tore himself free and ran back to the mare. She was almost dying, but managed to kick one more time.
“I’ll show you how to kick!” Mikolka shouted angrily. He threw down his whip, bent down, and picked up a long, heavy pole from the bottom of the cart. With both hands, he lifted it over the mare.
“He’s going to crush her!” people shouted. “He’ll kill her!”
“She’s mine!” Mikolka shouted, and brought the pole down hard. There was a heavy thud.
“Hit her! Don’t stop!” voices shouted from the crowd.

Mikolka raised the pole and slammed it down again on the poor mare’s back. She fell back on her rear legs, but still tried to pull the cart—first one way, then the other. But six whips were hitting her from all sides, and the pole kept coming down: a third blow, a fourth—each heavy and slow. Mikolka was furious that she wouldn’t die in one hit.
“She’s tough!” someone shouted.
“She’ll be down in a minute, guys. This won’t last long,” said someone in the crowd, almost admiring.
“Get an axe! Finish her off!” yelled a third.

“I’ll show you! Stand back!” Mikolka screamed, throwing down the pole. He bent down in the cart and grabbed an iron crowbar. “Watch out!” he shouted, and smashed the poor mare with all his strength. The bar hit, and the mare staggered, tried to pull, but then Mikolka hit her again, swinging the bar onto her back. She collapsed on the ground like a log.

“Finish her!” Mikolka yelled, jumping out of the cart in a frenzy. Several drunk young men grabbed whatever they could—whips, sticks, poles—and rushed at the dying mare. Mikolka stood aside, wildly swinging the crowbar. The mare stretched out her head, took a long breath, and died.
“You butchered her!” someone yelled from the crowd.
“Why wouldn’t she gallop, then?”
“She’s mine!” Mikolka shouted, his eyes bloodshot, still holding the bar. He looked like he wished there was something else to hit.
“No way you’re a real Christian,” many people in the crowd shouted.

But the poor boy, out of his mind, forced his way through the crowd to the dead mare, put his arms around her bleeding head, and kissed her eyes and lips. Then he jumped up, furious, and rushed at Mikolka with his tiny fists. Right then, his father—who had been chasing after him—grabbed him and carried him out of the crowd.
“Come on, let’s go home,” his father said.
“Father! Why did they... kill... the poor horse?” he sobbed, his voice cracking and coming out in shrieks from his chest.
“They’re drunk... they’re cruel... it’s not our business,” his father said. Raskolnikov clung to his father, but he felt like he was choking, couldn't breathe, wanted to scream—and woke up.
He woke up gasping for air, his hair soaked with sweat, and stood up in terror.
“Thank God, it was just a dream,” he said, sitting down under a tree and taking deep breaths. “But what’s wrong with me? Is this some kind of fever coming on? What a horrible dream!”
He felt completely broken—his mind was full of darkness and confusion. He put his elbows on his knees and held his head in his hands.

“Oh God!” he cried. “Is it possible—could I really take an axe, hit her on the head, smash her skull... step into the hot blood, break the lock, steal, and hide—covered in blood... with the axe... Oh God, could I really do that?”
He was shaking all over as he said this.

“But why am I acting like this?” he went on, sitting up in shock. “I knew I could never actually do it, so why have I been driving myself crazy? Yesterday—yesterday, when I went to try that... experiment, I realized for sure I could never go through with it... Why am I still thinking about it? Why am I hesitating? Even as I came down the stairs yesterday, I felt it was disgusting, sickening, horrible... just the thought of it makes me sick and fills me with fear.”
“No, I couldn’t do it, I just couldn’t! Even if all my reasoning over the past month is perfectly logical... My God! I just couldn’t bring myself to do it! I couldn’t! So why, why am I still...?”

He stood up, looked around in confusion—almost surprised to find himself in this place—and headed toward the bridge. He was pale, his eyes burning, his whole body exhausted, but suddenly he felt like he could breathe more easily. It was like he had thrown off a terrible weight that had been crushing him for so long, and suddenly he felt a rush of relief and peace inside. “God,” he prayed, “show me my path—I give up that cursed... idea of mine.”

As he crossed the bridge, he looked calmly at the Neva River and the red sun setting in the sky. Even though he was weak, he didn’t feel tired. It was like a wound in his heart that had been festering for a month had finally burst. Freedom, freedom! He was free from that strange spell, that obsession!

Later, when he looked back on those days, remembering every detail, Raskolnikov was always struck by one thing. It wasn’t even a very unusual thing, but he always felt it was the exact turning point in his life. He could never figure out why, when he was so tired and it would have been easier to go home by the shortest route, he ended up walking through the Hay Market, where he had no reason to go. It was a little out of his way, but not much. He’d sometimes gone home before without noticing which streets he took. But why did such a huge, life-changing meeting happen in the Hay Market (where he had no business going) at the exact time and place when it could have the biggest effect on his fate? It was like it was waiting for him there on purpose!

It was around nine o’clock when he walked through the Hay Market. The market people were closing up their stalls and shops, packing up their goods, and heading home. Rag pickers and street vendors crowded around the taverns in the dirty, stinky yards. Raskolnikov actually liked this area and the nearby alleys when he wandered around. Here, no one cared if he was dressed in rags; you could walk around however you wanted and no one would judge you. At the corner of an alley, a huckster and his wife had two tables with things like ribbons, thread, and handkerchiefs. They were packing up to go home, but were still talking with a friend who had just come by. This friend was Lizaveta Ivanovna—everyone called her Lizaveta—the younger sister of the old pawnbroker, Alyona Ivanovna, whom Raskolnikov had visited the day before to pawn his watch and try his “experiment.” He already knew about Lizaveta, and she knew him a bit, too. She was about thirty-five, tall, awkward, shy, and almost simple-minded. She was totally under her sister’s control, scared of her, and Alyona made her work all day and even hit her. Lizaveta was standing there with a bundle, listening to the huckster and his wife, who were talking with a lot of excitement. As soon as Raskolnikov noticed her, he felt a strange shock, almost like he was incredibly surprised, even though there was nothing surprising about seeing her.
“You can decide for yourself, Lizaveta Ivanovna,” the huckster was saying loudly. “Come over tomorrow around seven. They’ll be here too.”
“Tomorrow?” Lizaveta said slowly, as if she couldn’t make up her mind.

“Honestly, you’re so scared of Alyona Ivanovna,” said the huckster’s wife, a lively little woman. “You look like a little kid. And she’s not even your real sister—just your stepsister, but she treats you like a servant!”
“But this time don’t say anything to Alyona Ivanovna,” her husband interrupted. “Just come, without telling her. You’ll be glad you did. Maybe later your sister will want to do the same.”
“Should I come?”
“Around seven tomorrow. And they’ll be here. You can decide then.”
“And we’ll have some tea,” his wife added.
“All right, I’ll come,” Lizaveta said, still thinking it over, and slowly started to walk away.

Raskolnikov had just passed by and heard no more. He moved quietly, making sure not to miss anything. First he was shocked, then a chill of horror ran down his spine. He had suddenly, and totally by accident, learned that the next day at seven o’clock, Lizaveta—the old woman’s sister and only companion—would be out of the house, and the old woman would be home alone.

He was only a few steps from his place. He went in like a man heading to his own execution. He couldn’t think about anything, didn’t even try; he just felt, all at once, that he had no more control over his thoughts or his will, and that everything was suddenly and finally decided.

Honestly, even if he’d waited years for the perfect chance, he couldn’t have hoped for a better opportunity than the one that had just appeared. There was almost no way to find out, with this much certainty and without any risk, that the old woman—who he was planning to attack—would be home alone at a specific time the next day.

Later, Raskolnikov would figure out why the dealer and his wife had invited Lizaveta over. It was nothing unusual; just a simple matter. A family new to the city had fallen on hard times and wanted to sell their household things—mostly women’s clothes and belongings. Since those items wouldn’t sell for much at the market, they needed a dealer. That was Lizaveta’s job. She often helped people like this, because she was honest and always set a fair price. She was usually quiet, and, as had already been said, very meek and shy.

But lately, Raskolnikov had become superstitious. This superstition stuck with him for a long time afterward, almost impossible to get rid of. He started to see everything as strange and mysterious, as if fate or coincidences were guiding him toward something. Last winter, a student he knew, Pokorev, had randomly given him the address of Alyona Ivanovna, the old pawnbroker, in case he ever needed to pawn something. He didn’t go there right away; he still had some tutoring work and got by. But six weeks ago, he remembered her address because he had two things he could pawn: his father’s old silver watch and a small gold ring with three red stones, a gift from his sister when she left. He decided on the ring. When he met the old woman, he instantly felt a strong dislike for her, even though he didn’t know her. She gave him two roubles for the ring, and on his way home, he stopped in a shabby tavern for some tea, sinking into deep thought. A strange idea kept pecking at his mind, almost like a chick trying to break out of an egg, and he couldn’t stop thinking about it.

Almost right next to him, at the next table, sat another student he didn’t know, along with a young officer. They had played billiards and were now drinking tea. Suddenly, Raskolnikov heard the student mention Alyona Ivanovna, the pawnbroker, and give her address to the officer. That seemed weird to Raskolnikov—he had just left her place, and now someone was talking about her. It could have been a coincidence, but it made a deep impression on him, as if someone was saying these things just for him to hear. The student started telling the officer all sorts of details about Alyona Ivanovna.

“She’s great,” the student said. “She always gives you money. She’s as rich as a Jew, she can lend you five thousand roubles at once and still take tiny pledges for just one rouble. Lots of students go to her. But she’s an awful old witch…”

Then he described how mean and unpredictable she was—if you were even a day late with your interest, she’d keep your stuff. She only gave a quarter of what your things were worth, and charged five or even seven percent a month in interest. He kept talking, adding that Alyona Ivanovna had a sister, Lizaveta, whom she was always beating and bossing around like a little kid, even though Lizaveta was at least six feet tall.
“Now that’s a sight for you,” the student joked loudly, laughing.

They started talking about Lizaveta. The student seemed to enjoy talking about her, laughing often, and the officer listened with interest, even asking if Lizaveta could come do some sewing for him. Raskolnikov listened to every word, learning all about her. Lizaveta was younger than Alyona Ivanovna, her half-sister from a different mother, and thirty-five years old. She worked constantly for her sister, doing the cooking, washing, sewing, cleaning—she handed over all her earnings. She couldn’t accept any job without Alyona’s permission. Alyona had already made her will, which Lizaveta knew about. Lizaveta would get nothing but the furniture; all the money was left to a monastery in another province so prayers would be said for Alyona forever. Lizaveta was poorer than her sister, unmarried, awkward-looking, extremely tall, with big feet that turned outward. She always wore old goatskin shoes, but she was clean. What the student found most surprising and funny was that Lizaveta always seemed to be pregnant.
“But you said she’s ugly?” the officer asked.

“Yeah, she’s dark and looks almost like a soldier in a dress, but really, she’s not ugly at all. She has a kind face and kind eyes. Honestly, a lot of people like her. She’s gentle, always willing to help anyone, never complains. And she has a really sweet smile.”
“So, you think she’s cute?” the officer laughed.

“It’s just because she’s so odd. But seriously, I’ll tell you this: I could kill that awful old woman and take her money, and I wouldn’t feel the slightest bit guilty,” the student said, getting excited. The officer laughed again, while Raskolnikov shivered. How strange!

“Listen, I want to ask you a serious question,” the student said, suddenly intense. “I was joking, but think about this: on one side, there’s this useless, mean, sick old lady who does more harm than good, who doesn’t even know why she’s alive, and who’ll probably die soon anyway. Do you get what I mean?”
“Yeah, I get it,” the officer said, watching his friend closely.

“Okay, now think about this. On the other side, there are thousands of young lives ruined just because they don’t get help! With the money the old woman’s leaving to the monastery, you could do a hundred thousand good deeds. Maybe save hundreds, even thousands, of people—families who’d otherwise fall into poverty, ruin, or crime. If you killed her and used that money to help people, wouldn’t that one little crime be made up for by all the good you could do? One life traded for a hundred others—it’s just math! Besides, what’s the life of such a mean, useless old woman worth? Less than a bug, really, since she actually hurts people. Just recently, she bit Lizaveta’s finger so badly it almost had to be cut off.”
“Of course she doesn’t deserve to live,” the officer said, “but that’s just how things are.”

“Well, brother, that’s why we need to fix and guide nature. If we didn’t, we’d all drown in old-fashioned ideas. If nobody ever challenged things, there’d never be any great people. They talk about duty and conscience—I don’t mean to insult those ideas, but what do those words really mean? Wait, I have another question for you. Listen!”
“No, wait, let me ask you something. Listen!”
“Well?”
“You’re making all these speeches, but tell me, would you actually kill the old woman yourself?”
“Of course not! I was just arguing the point… It’s not my business…”
“Well, I think if you wouldn’t do it yourself, then it’s not really just, is it? Come on, let’s play another game.”

Raskolnikov was really shaken. Of course, this was just the kind of talk young people have all the time—he’d heard similar things before. But why did he overhear it now, right when he was starting to have the exact same thoughts? And why, right after leaving the old woman’s place, did he walk straight into a conversation about her? That coincidence always seemed weird to him. This random chat in a tavern had a huge effect on what he did later, as if it was fate or some kind of sign….

When he got back from the Hay Market, he collapsed onto his sofa and sat there for an hour without moving. It got dark, but he didn’t light a candle—he didn’t even think about it. He couldn’t remember what he was thinking about, if anything. Finally, he noticed he still felt feverish and shivery, but at least he could lie down. He soon fell into a heavy, dreamless sleep that felt like it was crushing him.

He slept for an extremely long time, without any dreams. Nastasya came in at ten the next morning and had a hard time waking him up. She brought him tea and bread, but the tea was once again the second brew and in her own teapot.
“Wow, he sleeps like a rock!” she said irritably. “He’s always asleep.”
He forced himself up. His head hurt, he walked around his tiny attic room, then collapsed back onto the sofa.
“Going back to sleep again?” Nastasya called. “Are you sick or what?”
He didn’t answer.
“Want some tea?”
“Later,” he mumbled, turning to the wall and closing his eyes.
Nastasya stood and stared at him.

“Maybe he really is sick,” she said. She left, but came back at two with some soup. He was still lying there, the tea untouched. Nastasya felt honestly annoyed and started trying to wake him up, this time angrily.
“Why are you lying there like a log?” she shouted, looking at him with disgust.
He sat up and then sat down again, saying nothing and staring at the floor.
“Are you sick or not?” Nastasya asked, but got no answer. “You should go out and get some fresh air,” she said after a moment. “Are you going to eat or not?”
“Later,” he said weakly. “You can go.”
He waved her away.
She stayed a bit longer, looked at him with pity, and then left.
A few minutes later, he looked up and stared at the tea and soup for a while. Then he took the bread, picked up a spoon, and began to eat.

He ate a little, three or four spoonfuls, without really wanting it—almost automatically. His headache was a bit better. After eating, he lay back down on the sofa, but now he couldn’t sleep. He just lay there, not moving, face buried in the pillow. Strange daydreams haunted him, especially one that kept coming back: he imagined he was in Africa, in Egypt, at an oasis. The caravan was resting, camels lying down, palm trees all around; everyone was eating dinner. He was drinking cool water from a spring nearby, so cold and blue, running over colorful stones and bright sand that sparkled like gold. Suddenly, he heard a clock chime. He jumped, shook himself awake, looked out the window, and realized how late it was. Instantly, he jumped up as if someone had yanked him off the sofa. On tiptoe, he crept to the door, listened on the stairs. His heart pounded wildly. But everything was quiet outside, as if everyone was asleep. It seemed unreal that he had slept so long and done nothing, prepared nothing yet—while time was slipping by. Now his tiredness turned into a panicky, feverish rush. But there wasn’t much left to do. He focused all his energy on remembering every detail and forgetting nothing, his heart pounding so hard he could barely breathe. First, he had to make a noose and sew it into his coat—something that would just take a minute. He dug under his pillow, found an old, dirty shirt, and tore off a long strip of fabric. Folding it in two, he took off his only coat, a sturdy cotton summer overcoat, and sewed the ends of the rag onto the inside under his left arm. His hands shook, but he managed it so nothing showed on the outside. The needle and thread were already ready on his table. This noose was for the axe—he couldn’t just walk down the street holding it, and even if he hid it under his coat, he’d have to hold it, which would look suspicious. With this trick, he could slip the head of the axe in the noose under his arm, holding the end of the handle in his pocket so it wouldn’t swing, and with his baggy coat, no one would notice. He’d come up with this idea two weeks before.

After this, he reached into a small gap between his sofa and the floor, felt around in the left corner, and pulled out the “pledge” he’d prepared and hidden ahead of time. But it was really just a smooth piece of wood, about the size of a cigarette case. He’d found the wood during a walk in a workshop yard, and later added a thin piece of iron he found in the street. He tied the iron to the wood with thread and wrapped it neatly in clean white paper, tying it up so it would take a while to undo. This was meant to distract the old woman while she tried to open it, giving him a moment. The iron was just to add weight, so she wouldn’t realize right away it was just wood. He had hidden all this under the sofa earlier. He’d just gotten the pledge out when he heard someone moving in the yard.
“It’s already past six.”
“Past six! Oh God!”

He rushed to the door, listened, grabbed his hat, and started down the thirteen stairs, moving quietly and carefully, like a cat. He still had the most important thing to do—steal the axe from the kitchen. He had decided a long time ago that he’d have to use an axe. He did have a small pocket knife, but he didn’t trust it or his own strength, so he finally settled on the axe. It was strange, but the more he finally made up his mind about something, the more awful and ridiculous it seemed to him. No matter how much he argued with himself, he could never fully believe he was actually going to go through with his plan.

Really, if there ever came a time when every detail was planned out and settled, and nothing was uncertain, he probably would have dropped the whole thing as something stupid and impossible. But there were still so many things he hadn’t figured out. As for getting the axe, he didn’t worry much. Nastasya was almost always out in the evenings—visiting neighbors or running errands—and always left the door open, which the landlady always scolded her for. So when the time came, he just had to slip into the kitchen, grab the axe, and later (when everything was done) put it back. But there were problems. What if he came back to return the axe and Nastasya was there? He’d have to wait until she left again. Or what if she noticed the axe was missing and started shouting? That could mean trouble, or at least suspicion.

But these were little things he hadn’t really thought through, and he didn’t have time to worry about them now. He was focused on the main point and left the small details for later, for when he actually believed he could do it. But that belief felt impossible. It was hard for him to even imagine that he’d stop thinking, get up, and just go do it… Even his recent “practice run” (when he went to check the place) was really just a test, not the real thing, and he’d freaked out and run away, furious with himself. When it came to the moral questions, he’d thought it all through; his reasoning was sharp, and he couldn’t find any arguments against it. But deep down, he just didn’t believe in himself and kept searching for reasons to go through with it, as if something was pushing him toward it.

For a long time, he’d wondered why almost all crimes are so easy to discover, and why criminals always leave so many clues. He came to lots of different conclusions, but he thought the main reason wasn’t that it was impossible to hide a crime, but that the criminal himself messed up. Almost every criminal makes stupid mistakes right when it’s most important to be careful. Raskolnikov believed that this “loss of reason” was like a sickness—it grew slowly, peaked just before the crime, stayed strong during and after it, and then eventually went away. He wasn’t sure if the sickness caused the crime, or if crime always came with a bit of madness, but he didn’t have an answer yet.

After coming to these ideas, he decided that in his case, he wouldn’t have this kind of breakdown; his mind and will would stay strong, because what he was planning “wasn’t even a crime.” The story of how he reached this conclusion is long, so we’ll skip it for now. Just know that the practical problems didn’t bother him much. “If you just keep your willpower strong and focus, you can handle them when the time comes, as long as you know every tiny detail…” But he never really started that kind of preparation. He trusted his final decisions the least, and when it finally happened, it all happened differently, almost by accident.

One small thing ruined his plan before he even left the staircase. When he reached the kitchen (the door was open as usual), he peeked in to see if the landlady was there, or if at least her door was shut so she wouldn’t see him take the axe. To his shock, Nastasya was not only home, but in the kitchen, taking laundry out of a basket and hanging it up. She stopped and stared right at him the whole time he walked by. He quickly looked away and acted like he didn’t notice her. But that was it—he couldn’t get the axe! He felt crushed.
“Why did I think,” he wondered as he walked under the gate, “why did I just assume she wouldn’t be home right now? Why was I so sure?”
He was defeated and even embarrassed. He almost wanted to laugh at himself, he was so angry. A heavy, animal-like rage boiled inside him.

He stood hesitating under the gateway. The idea of walking around outside just to look normal disgusted him; going back to his room was even worse. “And I’ve lost my chance forever!” he muttered, standing there with nothing to do, just opposite the porter’s little dark room, which was also open. Suddenly, something shiny under the bench in the porter’s room caught his eye. He looked around—no one was there. He tiptoed into the room, went down two steps, and called softly for the porter. “He’s not here! But he must be nearby, since the door’s open.” Quickly, he grabbed the axe (it was an axe!) from under the bench, where it was lying between two logs. Before leaving, he slipped it into the noose under his coat, put both hands in his pockets, and walked back out—no one saw him! “When logic fails, the devil helps!” he thought with a strange grin. This bit of luck cheered him up a lot.

He walked calmly and slowly, not hurrying, so he wouldn’t attract attention. He barely looked at anyone passing by, trying not to look at their faces, and wanted to be as invisible as possible. Suddenly, he thought about his hat. “Oh no! I had money two days ago and didn’t buy a cap to wear instead!” He cursed himself deep down.
Peeking into a shop window, he saw a clock on the wall—it was ten past seven. He had to hurry, but also needed to take a roundabout route so he’d approach the house from a different direction.

When he imagined this moment earlier, he thought he’d be terrified. But now, he wasn’t scared at all. His mind kept wandering to random things, but nothing stuck. As he passed the Yusupov garden, he started thinking about building huge fountains and how much fresher the city would feel with them. Then he imagined expanding the summer garden all the way to the Field of Mars and maybe connecting it to the Mihailovsky Palace gardens—what a great thing that would be for the city! Then he wondered why people in big cities always seem to end up living in the dirtiest, smelliest parts instead of near gardens or fountains. Suddenly, he remembered his own walks through the Hay Market and snapped back to reality. “What nonsense!” he scolded himself. “Better not to think at all.”

“Maybe people being led to their executions grab on to every little thing they see on the way,” flashed through his mind, but only for a second—he quickly pushed the thought away. And now he was there: the house, the gate. Somewhere, a clock struck once. “What? Can it be half-past seven already? No way—it must be fast!”

Luckily, everything worked out at the gates. Right then, a huge hay wagon drove in, blocking the gateway and hiding him as he slipped in. The wagon had barely passed through into the yard before he darted to the right. On the other side, he heard shouting and arguing, but no one saw him or stopped him. Many windows overlooking the big square yard were open, but he didn’t look up—he didn’t have the strength. The stairs to the old woman’s room were right by the gateway, just to the right. He was already climbing the stairs.

He paused, trying to catch his breath, pressing his hand to his pounding heart, and checked that the axe was still in place. Then he started up the stairs, moving softly and carefully, listening constantly. But the stairs were empty; all the doors were shut, and he saw no one. One apartment on the first floor was wide open, with painters working inside, but they didn’t even glance at him. He stopped, thought for a second, then kept going. “It would be better if they weren’t here, but… it’s two floors above them.”

Now he was on the fourth floor. There was the door, and the empty apartment across from it. The flat below the old woman’s was empty too; the name card had been ripped off—they must have moved away! He was out of breath. For a second, he wondered, “Should I just go back?” But he didn’t answer himself, just started listening at Alyona Ivanovna’s door. Silence. He listened again on the stairs, for a long time, very carefully. Then he looked around one last time, straightened up, made sure the axe was hidden. “Am I pale?” he wondered. “Do I look nervous? She’s so suspicious… Maybe I should wait until my heart stops pounding?”
But his heart wouldn’t calm down. In fact, it was beating even harder. He couldn’t wait anymore, so he slowly reached out and rang the bell. Half a minute later, he rang again, a bit louder.

No answer. There was no point in ringing again. The old woman was probably home, but she was suspicious and always alone. He knew her habits a little. He put his ear to the door again. Maybe his senses were extra sharp, or maybe the sounds were really clear, but suddenly he heard what sounded like a careful hand on the lock and the swish of a skirt right at the door. Someone was standing on the other side, listening just like he was. He moved a little on purpose and muttered something out loud, so it wouldn’t look like he was hiding. Then he rang a third time, more quietly and calmly. Later, he would remember this moment clearly for the rest of his life—he couldn’t believe how clever he’d been, since his mind felt cloudy and he was almost out of it. A second later, he heard the latch being undone.
The door opened just a tiny bit, just like before, and two sharp, suspicious eyes stared at Raskolnikov from the darkness. Suddenly, Raskolnikov panicked and almost made a huge mistake.

Worried that Alyona Ivanovna would be scared to be alone with him, and knowing she probably wouldn’t trust him just because she saw his face, Raskolnikov grabbed the door and pulled it toward himself so she couldn't close it again. She didn’t fight back much, but she wouldn’t let go of the handle, so he nearly dragged her out onto the stairs. Since she was blocking the doorway, he moved straight toward her. She backed away, scared, and tried to say something, but couldn't find the words and just stared at him with wide, frightened eyes.
“Good evening, Alyona Ivanovna,” he said, trying to act casual, but his voice cracked and shook. “I’ve come… I brought something… but maybe we should go inside… where there’s more light…”
Leaving her behind, he walked right into the room without waiting to be invited. The old woman hurried after him, finally able to talk.
“Good heavens! What is it? Who are you? What do you want?”
“Why, Alyona Ivanovna, you know me… Raskolnikov… I brought you the pledge I promised the other day…” He held out the package.

The old woman glanced at the pledge, but then stared right into his eyes. She looked at him carefully, with a nasty, distrustful look. A whole minute passed; he thought he even saw her sneer, like she already knew everything. He felt himself losing control, getting more and more scared—so scared that if she kept looking at him like that without saying a word, he thought he might just run away.
“Why are you looking at me like you don’t know me?” he burst out suddenly, sounding angry. “Take it if you want. If not, I’ll go somewhere else. I’m in a hurry.”
He hadn't planned to say that, but the words just came out. The old woman seemed to snap out of it, and his confident tone seemed to make her less suspicious.
“But why, my good sir, all of a sudden… What is it?” she said, looking at the pledge.
“It’s that silver cigarette case; I told you about it last time, remember?”
She reached out her hand.
“But you look so pale… and your hands are shaking? Have you been swimming or something?”
“I’ve got a fever,” he replied quickly. “You can’t help looking pale… if you’ve got nothing to eat,” he added, struggling to get the words out.
He felt his strength fading again. But his answer sounded believable; the old woman took the pledge.
“What is it?” she asked again, staring at Raskolnikov and weighing the package in her hand.
“It’s just… a cigarette case… silver… take a look.”
“It doesn’t really look like silver… And why did you wrap it up like this?”

She started untying the string and turned to the window for better light (even though all the windows were closed, even though it was so hot inside). For a few seconds, she had her back to him. Raskolnikov unbuttoned his coat and slipped the axe out of its loop, but kept it hidden under his coat, just holding it in his right hand. His hands felt horribly weak, getting more numb and stiff every second. He was scared he might drop the axe. Suddenly, he felt dizzy.
“Why did he tie it up like this?” the old woman complained, moving closer to him.

He couldn’t waste another minute. He pulled out the axe, swung it with both hands, hardly aware of what he was doing, and brought the blunt side down on her head. It didn’t even feel like he was using his own strength. But as soon as the axe struck, he felt all his strength come rushing back.

The old woman, as usual, wasn’t wearing anything on her head. Her thin, gray-streaked hair, oily and messy, was braided into a rat’s tail and held by a broken horn comb sticking out at the back of her neck. Since she was so short, the blow landed right on top of her skull. She let out a weak cry and collapsed on the floor, hands going to her head. She still held the “pledge” in one hand. Then he hit her again, and again, in the same spot, with the blunt side of the axe. Blood spurted out like it was poured from a glass. Her body fell back. He stepped away and let her drop, then leaned over her face; she was dead. Her eyes bulged out, her forehead and face twisted and tight from the blow.

He set the axe down next to her body and quickly searched her pocket—the same right pocket where she’d taken out the keys last time. His mind was clear now, no confusion or dizziness, but his hands still shook. He remembered later how careful and alert he’d been, always trying not to touch the blood. He pulled out the keys right away—they were all together on a steel ring, just as before. He ran into the bedroom with them. It was a tiny room, filled with religious icons. Against one wall was a big, spotless bed covered with a silk quilt. On another wall there was a chest of drawers. As soon as he started trying the keys in the chest and heard them jingling, he shuddered all over. For a second, he thought about just giving up and running away. But it was too late to turn back. He even smiled a little at himself—then a terrifying idea popped into his head. What if the old woman wasn’t dead? What if she woke up? Leaving the keys in the chest, he hurried back to the body, grabbed the axe, and raised it over her again—but didn’t bring it down. She was definitely dead. Leaning closer, he saw that her skull was smashed in on one side. He started to reach out to touch it, but pulled back—he didn’t need to. There was a huge pool of blood. Suddenly he noticed a string around her neck; he tugged at it, but it wouldn’t break, and it was soaked with blood. He tried to pull it out from the front of her dress, but something held it in place. Frustrated, he almost used the axe to cut it off, but didn’t dare and, after two minutes of struggling, got it off by hand, getting blood on himself and the axe. He was right—it was a purse. On the string were two crosses, one made of Cyprus wood, one of copper, and a small silver icon. With them was a greasy little chamois leather purse with a steel rim. The purse was stuffed full; he shoved it in his pocket without looking, threw the crosses onto the old woman’s body, and rushed back into the bedroom, this time bringing the axe with him.

He was panicking, snatched the keys, and tried them again. But they wouldn’t fit. It wasn’t just his shaking hands—he kept making mistakes, trying keys that obviously didn’t fit. Suddenly, he remembered that the big key with deep notches, hanging with the other keys, couldn’t be for the chest of drawers (he’d thought of that last time), but probably for some sort of strongbox. That must be where she hid everything. He left the chest and felt under the bed, guessing that old ladies usually keep boxes there. He was right: there was a good-sized box, about a yard long, with a curved lid covered in red leather and studded with steel nails. The big key fit perfectly. At the top, under a white sheet, was a fancy red brocade coat lined with rabbit fur. Under that was a silk dress, then a shawl, and it looked like everything else was just clothes. First, he wiped his bloody hands on the red brocade. “It’s red, so the blood won’t show,” he thought—then suddenly snapped out of it. “God, am I losing my mind?” he thought, terrified.

But as soon as he touched the clothes, a gold watch slipped out from under the fur coat. He quickly turned everything over. There were all sorts of gold things among the clothes—probably all unclaimed pledges: bracelets, chains, earrings, pins, and more. Some were in cases, others wrapped in newspaper and tied with tape. Without wasting time, he stuffed his pockets with as much as he could carry, not bothering to unwrap them—but he didn’t have time to take much.

Suddenly, he heard footsteps in the room where the old woman lay. He froze, perfectly still. But everything was quiet, so maybe he imagined it. Then he heard a faint moan, like someone quietly crying out. Then silence for a minute or two. He crouched by the box, holding his breath. Suddenly, he jumped up, grabbed the axe, and ran out of the bedroom.

Lizaveta was standing in the middle of the room, holding a big bundle. She stared in shock at her murdered sister, pale as a ghost, too stunned to even scream. When she saw him run out of the bedroom, she started shaking all over, like a leaf. She opened her mouth, lifted her hand, but couldn’t get a sound out, as if she couldn’t breathe. She slowly backed into the corner, eyes locked on him, but still said nothing. He rushed at her with the axe; her mouth twisted pitifully, like a scared baby about to cry. Poor Lizaveta was so innocent and frightened that she didn’t even try to protect her face, even though the axe was raised over her. She just held her empty left hand out in front of her, as if to push him away. The axe came down, splitting her skull with one blow. She fell heavily. Raskolnikov completely lost his head, grabbed her bundle, dropped it, and ran into the entryway.

Fear took over him, especially after this second, unexpected murder. He wanted to get out of there as fast as possible. And if he’d been able to think clearly, if he understood how hopeless and horrible the situation was, and just how many more problems—or even crimes—he’d have to face just to get home, he might have given up completely and turned himself in—not out of fear, but out of disgust for what he’d done. He felt sick to his stomach, and the feeling just kept getting worse. Now, nothing could make him go back to the box or even into the room.

But his mind was going blank, almost like he was dreaming. Sometimes he forgot what was important and focused on little things. Glancing into the kitchen, he saw a bucket half full of water on a bench and thought about washing his hands and the axe, which were sticky with blood. He dropped the axe in the bucket, grabbed a piece of soap from a broken saucer on the window, and washed his hands. Then he cleaned the blade of the axe, and spent a long time, maybe three minutes, scrubbing the wood where there were blood spots. He dried it all with some linen hanging to dry in the kitchen, then carefully checked the axe at the window—no blood left, though the wood was still damp. He hid the axe back under his coat. In the dim light, he checked his overcoat, trousers, and boots. At first, he only saw stains on his boots, so he wiped them off with the wet rag. But he knew he wasn’t checking carefully—there could be something obvious he was missing. He stood in the middle of the room, lost in thought, dark, panicked ideas swirling in his head—maybe he was going mad, maybe he couldn’t think straight or protect himself, maybe he should be doing something totally different. “Oh God!” he muttered. “I have to get out, get out,” and he rushed into the entryway. But then something happened that terrified him even more than anything so far.

He stared in shock: the front door, the one from the stairs where he’d waited earlier and rung the bell, was wide open—at least six inches! No lock, no bolt, all that time! The old woman must not have closed it after him, maybe as a precaution. But wait—he’d seen Lizaveta come in after that! How could he not have realized that she must have used the door? She couldn’t have come through the wall!
He rushed to the door and latched it shut.
“No, wrong move again! I have to leave, have to get out…”
He unlatched the door, opened it, and listened on the stairs.

He stood there listening for a long time. Somewhere far off, maybe in the main entrance, two people were yelling and arguing loudly. “What are they fighting about?” he wondered. He waited. Finally, everything went quiet—they’d gone. He was about to go out, but then, on the floor below, a door banged open and someone started going downstairs, humming a tune. “Why is everyone so noisy?” he thought. He closed the door and waited again. At last, everything was silent—no one around. He was just about to go to the stairs when he heard new footsteps.

The steps were far away, down at the bottom of the stairs, but from the first sound, Raskolnikov got a strange feeling—like this person was coming up to the fourth floor, to the old woman’s place. Why? Maybe the footsteps sounded different, more purposeful? The steps were heavy, even, and slow. Now the person was past the first floor, then climbing higher; the steps got louder. He could hear heavy breathing. Now they were on the third floor—coming here! Raskolnikov suddenly felt frozen, like in a nightmare where you’re being chased and can’t move or even lift your arms.

Finally, as the stranger was climbing to the fourth floor, Raskolnikov snapped out of it and quickly slipped back inside the apartment, closing the door behind him. He quietly hooked the door shut. Instinct took over. Done, he crouched by the door, holding his breath. The visitor was now at the door. They stood face to face, separated only by the wood, just like Raskolnikov had just been with the old woman.
The visitor panted a few times. “He must be a big, heavy man,” Raskolnikov thought, gripping the axe. It really did feel like a dream. The visitor grabbed the bell and rang it loudly.

As soon as the little bell rang, Raskolnikov thought he heard something move inside the room. He listened seriously for a few seconds. The stranger rang again, waited, then yanked hard, impatiently, at the door handle. Raskolnikov stared in horror at the hook shaking, expecting any second that it would pull loose. It really seemed possible, the way the man was shaking it. Raskolnikov was tempted to hold the hook in place, but then the man might notice. He felt dizzy again. “I’m going to faint!” he thought, but then the stranger began to speak and Raskolnikov snapped back to himself.

“What’s going on? Are they asleep or murdered in there? Damn them!” the man yelled in a thick voice. “Hey, Alyona Ivanovna, old witch! Lizaveta Ivanovna, hey, my beauty! Open up! Ugh, are they asleep or what?”
The stranger, now angry, yanked the bell a dozen more times with all his strength. He must have been someone important or a close acquaintance.
Just then, light, quick steps sounded nearby on the stairs. Someone else was coming. Raskolnikov hadn’t heard them before.
“You don’t mean there’s nobody home?” the newcomer called out, cheerfully, to the first visitor, who was still yanking the bell. “Good evening, Koch.”
“He sounds pretty young,” thought Raskolnikov.
“Who the heck knows? I’ve almost broken the lock,” Koch answered. “But how do you know me?”
“Why, the other day I beat you three times in a row at billiards at Gambrinus’.”
“Oh!”
“So they’re not home? That’s weird. It’s really annoying, too. Where could the old woman have gone? I came on business.”
“Yeah, I have business with her too.”
“Well, what now? I guess we have to go back. Ugh! And I was hoping to get some money!” the young man groaned.

“I guess we have to give up. But why did she set the meeting for now? She arranged for me to come. It’s out of my way. And where the heck could she have gone? She never leaves this place, her legs are bad, and now, all of a sudden, she goes for a walk!”
“Should we ask the porter?”
“What?”
“Where she went and when she’ll be back.”
“Hmm... Damn it!... Maybe we should ask... But you know she never goes anywhere.”
He tugged at the door handle again.
“Forget it. There’s nothing to be done. We have to go!”
“Wait!” the young man suddenly cried. “Do you see how the door shakes when you pull it?”
“Well?”
“That means it’s not locked, but hooked from the inside! Can you hear the hook?”
“Well?”

“Don’t you get it? That means someone is at home. If they were all out, they’d lock the door from the outside with the key, not hook it from inside. See, you hear the hook clanking? To use the hook, someone has to be inside. So they’re in there, but they’re not opening the door!”
“You’re right!” Koch said, surprised. “What are they doing in there?” He started shaking the door hard.
“Hold on!” the young man said. “Don’t pull at it! Something’s wrong… You’ve been ringing and pulling, and still no one opens! So either they’ve both fainted or…”
“What?”
“Here’s what. Let’s get the porter to wake them up.”
“Alright.”
Both of them started down the stairs.
“Wait. You stay here while I go get the porter.”
“Why?”
“Just do it.”
“Okay.”
“I’m studying law, you know! It’s obvious—totally obvious—something’s wrong here!” the young man said, and ran downstairs.

Koch stayed. He softly pressed the bell, which gave a single tinkle, then thoughtfully played with the handle, pulling and letting go, making sure it was only hooked. Then, breathing hard, he bent down to look through the keyhole, but the key was stuck in the lock on the inside, so he couldn’t see anything.

Raskolnikov stood gripping the axe, almost delirious. He was getting ready to fight if they broke in. While they knocked and talked, he kept thinking about just ending it and yelling at them through the door. Sometimes, he even wanted to curse at them, to mock them since they couldn’t get in! “Just hurry up!” he thought.
“What the heck is he doing?…” Time was passing—one minute, then another—and still no one came. Koch started to get restless.
“What the heck?” he suddenly yelled, annoyed, and, giving up on his guard duty, he too went downstairs, his heavy boots thumping on the steps. The noise faded away.
“Oh my God! What am I supposed to do?”
Raskolnikov unhooked the door, opened it—no sound. Without thinking, he walked out, closed the door behind him as best he could, and went downstairs.
He'd only gone down three flights when he heard a loud voice below—where could he go? There was nowhere to hide. He was just about to go back to the old woman’s flat.
“Hey! Stop him! Catch him!”
Someone burst out of a flat below, yelling, and raced down the stairs, shouting at the top of his lungs.
“Mitka! Mitka! Mitka! Mitka! Mitka! Get him!”

The shouts ended in a scream; the last sounds came from the yard; then it was quiet. But at that exact moment, several men started noisily climbing the stairs, talking fast and loud—three or four of them. He recognized the young man’s voice: “Hey!”

Filled with despair, Raskolnikov walked straight toward them, thinking, “Whatever happens, happens!” If they stopped him, he was done for; if they let him pass, he was lost too, because they’d remember his face. They were almost on him—just one flight away—when suddenly, he was saved! Just a few steps away on the right, there was an empty apartment with the door wide open—the painters had been working there and had just left, probably the same ones who’d just run downstairs, shouting. The floor was freshly painted, and in the middle of the room was a pail and a broken pot with paint and brushes. In a split second, he darted inside and hid behind the wall, just in time; the men reached the landing. Then they kept going upstairs, talking loudly. Raskolnikov waited, then tiptoed out and hurried down the stairs.
No one was on the stairs or in the entrance. He hurried through the gateway and turned left onto the street.

He knew, absolutely knew, that right then they were at the old woman’s apartment, shocked to find the door unlocked, since he’d just hooked it. By now, they were looking at the bodies, and soon they would realize the murderer had just been there, hiding somewhere, and had escaped. They’d probably guess he’d hidden in the empty flat while they were going upstairs. But he couldn’t walk too fast, even though the next corner was still about a hundred yards away. Should he slip through another gate and hide in a random street? No, hopeless! Should he throw away the axe? Take a cab? Hopeless—no way out!

Finally, he reached the corner. He turned, barely able to walk. Now he was halfway to safety, and he knew it—there were lots of people here, and he could disappear into the crowd. But he was so weak from everything that had happened that he could barely move. Sweat poured down his face and neck. “Wow, that guy’s really been running!” someone shouted when he reached the canal.

He was barely aware of himself now, and the farther he went, the worse he felt. But he remembered that when he got to the canal, he panicked because there weren’t many people, so he felt more exposed. Even though he was about to collapse, he took a long detour to get home from a different direction.

He wasn’t really conscious as he walked through his house’s gateway. He was already on the stairs when he remembered the axe. He had a serious problem now: he had to put it back without being seen. He didn’t even think that maybe it would have been better to just ditch the axe somewhere else later. But he got lucky—the porter’s room was closed but not locked, so the porter was probably home. But Raskolnikov was so out of it that he just walked in. If the porter had asked, “What do you want?” he might have just handed him the axe. But the porter was gone, so he put the axe back under the bench and covered it with the wood, just like before. He didn’t see anyone else on the way to his room; the landlady’s door was closed. When he got to his room, he threw himself on the sofa, just as he was—not sleeping, but sinking into complete blankness. If anyone had come in, he would have jumped up and screamed. His head was full of scattered, chaotic thoughts, but he couldn’t focus on any of them, no matter how hard he tried…

Raskolnikov lay there for a long time. Every so often, he half woke up and realized it was late, but he didn’t bother to get up. Eventually, he noticed the sky getting lighter—it was almost morning. He was lying on his back, still groggy and dizzy. Suddenly, loud, desperate voices shouted from the street below. He heard these same drunken shouts every night after two o’clock, but this time, they woke him up completely.
“Oh! The drunks are leaving the bars,” he thought. “It’s past two!” With a jolt, he sprang up from the sofa, as if someone had yanked him.
“What? Past two o’clock?”
He sat back down—and in that instant, everything came back to him. All of it. The memories hit him like a flash of lightning.

For a moment, he thought he was losing his mind. An icy chill ran through him, but it was really the fever he’d had since before he fell asleep. He started shaking so badly his teeth chattered and his whole body trembled. He opened his door and listened—everything in the building was silent. He stared at himself and his messy room, confused about how he’d made it home last night without locking the door, and how he’d just collapsed on the sofa fully dressed, not even removing his hat. The hat had fallen to the floor beside his pillow.
“If anyone had come in, what would they think? That I was drunk, but...”

He rushed to the window. There was enough daylight now to see, so he quickly checked himself from head to toe, searching his clothes for any evidence. But that wasn’t good enough. Still shivering, he started to take off all his clothes and checked every piece again, turning over every thread and scrap. Not trusting himself, he searched three times.

He found almost nothing—no stains, no marks—except for one spot, where some thick, dried drops of blood were clinging to the ragged edge of his trousers. He grabbed a big pocketknife, cut off the frayed threads, and checked again. There didn’t seem to be anything else.

Suddenly, he remembered—the purse and the things he’d stolen from the old woman’s box were still in his pockets! He hadn’t even thought to take them out or hide them—not even when he was checking his clothes. Now what? He quickly yanked them all out, dumping everything on the table and turning his pocket inside out to make sure nothing was left. He carried the pile to the corner, where the wallpaper at the bottom of the wall was peeling and hanging in tatters. He stuffed everything into the hole under the loose wallpaper. “It’s in! Everything is hidden, even the purse!” he thought, standing up and staring blankly at the bulging hole. But suddenly, a wave of horror crashed over him. “Oh God!” he whispered desperately. “What’s wrong with me? Is this really hidden? Is that how you hide things?”
He had never planned to hide jewelry or small objects—he had only thought about hiding money, so he hadn’t bothered to prepare a proper hiding place.
“And now, now, what am I even happy about?” he thought. “Is this really hiding anything? I’m losing my mind—completely!”

Exhausted, he sank onto the sofa, and was immediately shaken by another round of violent shivering. Without thinking, he reached for his old, ragged student’s winter coat, which was still warm, and pulled it over himself. Again, he slipped into a half-sleep, drifting into feverish dreams. He lost consciousness.
Barely five minutes had passed before he jumped up again, immediately lunging for his clothes in a panic.
“How could I fall asleep again and not finish? Wait— I didn’t take the loop off the armhole! I forgot! That’s such obvious evidence!”
He tore the noose off, quickly cut it into pieces, and shoved the scraps under his pillow with his bed linens.

“Bits of torn cloth can’t make anyone suspicious, no matter what happens. I think so, I think so, at least!” he muttered, standing in the middle of the room. With painful effort, he looked around again—at the floor, the walls, everywhere—trying to make sure he hadn’t missed anything. The feeling that his mind, his memory, and even his most basic thinking were all failing him was torture.
“Is it starting already? Is this my punishment catching up with me? It is!”
The frayed threads he’d cut from his trousers were lying right in the middle of the floor, where anyone could see them!
“What’s wrong with me!” he cried out in panic.

Then a weird idea hit him: maybe all his clothes were covered in blood, maybe there were obvious stains, but he just couldn’t see them because his mind was breaking down. Suddenly, he remembered there had been blood on the purse, too. “Oh! Then my pocket must be stained, since I put the wet purse in there!”
In a second, he turned the pocket inside out and—yes!—there were blood stains on the lining!

“So my mind isn’t completely gone—I still have some sense and memory, since I figured that out myself,” he thought, relieved, even triumphant. “It’s just the fever, a moment of madness.” He tore the whole lining out of the left pocket of his trousers. Just then, sunlight hit his left boot, and he noticed his sock poking out—it looked like there were stains on it! He ripped off his boots—traces, for sure! The tip of the sock was soaked with blood; he must have stepped in the pool by accident. “But what do I do with the sock, rags, and pocket now?”
He gathered everything up in his hands and stood in the middle of the room.

“In the stove? But if there’s a search, they’d check the stove first. Burn them? But what would I use to burn them? I don’t even have matches. No, I’d better go outside and throw them away somewhere. Yes, I’ll throw them away,” he repeated, sitting down on the sofa again, “right away, this minute, without waiting…”
But his head drooped onto the pillow instead. The freezing shivers took over again, and he pulled the coat over himself once more.

For hours, he couldn’t stop thinking that he needed to get up “right now, this instant, and get rid of everything—just to get it out of sight, to be done with it, now, now!” Several times he tried to stand up from the sofa, but couldn’t.
Finally, he was truly woken by loud banging on his door.

“Open up! Are you dead or alive? He just keeps sleeping in here!” yelled Nastasya, pounding her fist on the door. “He snores here for days like a dog! A real dog, he is. Open up, I tell you! It’s past ten o’clock.”
“Maybe he’s not home,” said a man’s voice.
“Oh, that’s the porter… What does he want?”
Raskolnikov sat up on the sofa. His heart was pounding so hard it hurt.
“Then who could have locked the door?” snapped Nastasya. “Now he’s even started locking himself in! As if anyone would want to steal anything from him! Open up, you idiot, wake up!”
“What do they want? Why is the porter here? They must know. Should I resist, or open the door? Whatever happens…”
He half stood up, bent forward, and undid the latch.
His room was so tiny he could unlock the door without getting off the bed. Yes—it was the porter and Nastasya standing there.
Nastasya stared at him strangely. He glared back at the porter, trying to look tough and unafraid. The porter, without a word, held out a gray folded paper sealed with bottle wax.
“A notice from the office,” he said, handing over the paper.
“From what office?”
“A summons to the police office, obviously. You know which one.”
“To the police?... What for?...”
“How should I know? They called you, so you go.”
The porter looked at him carefully, glanced around the room, and left.
“He’s really sick,” Nastasya said, still staring at Raskolnikov. The porter turned his head for a second. “He’s had a fever since yesterday,” she added.

Raskolnikov didn’t answer. He just held the paper, not opening it. “Don’t bother getting up,” Nastasya said kindly, seeing him trying to put his feet on the floor. “You’re sick, so don’t rush. What’s that in your hand?”

He looked and saw he was holding the rags he’d cut from his trousers, the bloody sock, and the torn pocket lining. He must have fallen asleep holding them. Later, he remembered that, half-awake and feverish, he’d clutched them tightly as he drifted off again.
“Look at all these rags he’s hugging in his sleep, like they’re some kind of treasure…”
Nastasya burst out laughing, almost hysterically.

Instantly, he shoved everything under his coat and stared at her hard. Even though he couldn’t think clearly, it hit him that no one would act like that if he were about to be arrested. “But… the police?”
“You should have some tea! Want some? I’ll bring what’s left.”
“No… I’m going, I’ll go right now,” he muttered, forcing himself to stand.
“You’ll never make it down the stairs!”
“Yes, I will.”
“Suit yourself.”
She left, following the porter out.
Right away, he hurried to the light to inspect the sock and rags.

“There are stains, but they’re not that obvious—they look dirty and faded already. No one would notice unless they were looking for it. Nastasya didn’t see anything, thank God!” Then, shaking, he broke the seal on the notice and read it over and over until he understood: it was just an ordinary summons to appear at the district police station at half-past nine that day.
“But why? Nothing like this ever happens to me! I have nothing to do with the police! Why today?” he thought in total panic. “God, just let it be over soon!”
He dropped to his knees to pray, but then burst out laughing—not at the idea of prayer, but at himself.
He started getting dressed in a hurry. “If I’m doomed, I’m doomed, I don’t care! Should I put this sock on?” he wondered suddenly. “If I wear it, it’ll get dirtier and the stains will disappear.”
But as soon as he put it on, he yanked it off again in disgust and horror. Then, realizing he had no other socks, he picked it up and put it back on—and again, he laughed.
“It’s all just rules, just how people look at things,” he thought for a split second, the idea barely touching his mind while he shuddered. “There, I’ve got it on! I actually put it on!”
But right away, the laughter turned to despair.

“No, this is too much…” he thought. His legs were shaking. “From fear,” he muttered. His head spun and ached with fever. “It’s a trick! They want to lure me there and trip me up,” he thought as he went out to the stairs. “The worst part is I’m half-crazy… I might blurt out something stupid…”

On the stairs, he remembered he was leaving everything hidden in the wall just as it was. “They’ll probably search my room while I’m gone,” he thought, stopping suddenly. But he was so hopeless and miserable right now that he just shrugged and kept going. “Just get it over with!”

In the street, the heat was unbearable again; it hadn’t rained in days. There was more dust, bricks, and stink from the shops and bars. Drunks, Finnish peddlers, and beat-up carriages clogged the street. The sunlight hurt his eyes, and his fever made his head spin, like it always did when he stepped outside on a bright day.
When he reached the turn into the street, he looked down it in dread… at the house… and quickly looked away.
“If they question me, maybe I’ll just tell them everything,” he thought as he neared the police station.

The police station was about a quarter mile away. It had recently moved to the fourth floor of a new building. He’d only been to the old office once, a long time ago. He turned in at the gate and saw a set of stairs on the right, with a peasant carrying a book going up. “That must be the house-porter. So the office is here,” he thought, starting up the stairs. He didn’t want to ask anyone for directions.
“I’ll go in, fall to my knees, and confess everything…” he imagined as he reached the fourth floor.

The staircase was steep, narrow, and soaked with dirty water. The kitchens from the apartments opened onto the stairs and stayed open all day, making the heat and smell unbearable. Porters hurried up and down with books under their arms, along with policemen and people of all sorts. The office door was wide open, peasants waited inside, and the heat and smell of fresh paint and old oil in the newly decorated rooms were sickening.

After waiting a bit, he decided to move into the next room. All the rooms were small and low-ceilinged. His impatience drove him forward. No one paid attention to him. In the second room, some clerks were writing. They looked as poor as he did and a little odd. He went up to one.
“What do you want?”
He showed the clerk the notice he’d received.
“You’re a student?” the man asked, glancing at the paper.
“Yes, I used to be.”
The clerk looked at him without any interest at all. He was an especially scruffy-looking guy who seemed lost in his own thoughts.
“No point trying to get anything out of him—he doesn’t care about anything,” thought Raskolnikov.
“Go in there to the head clerk,” the man said, pointing to the farthest room.

He went into that room—the fourth one. It was small and crowded with people, dressed a little better than those outside. There were two women; one, poorly dressed and in mourning, sat at the table opposite the chief clerk, writing what he told her. The other, a large, heavy woman with a purplish-red blotchy face, dressed up with a huge brooch, stood nearby, apparently waiting. Raskolnikov handed his notice to the head clerk, who glanced at it, said, “Wait a minute,” and kept dealing with the woman in mourning.
Raskolnikov breathed easier. “It can’t be that!”
Slowly, he started to feel more confident; he forced himself to stay calm.
“One dumb mistake, some little slip-up, and I could give myself away! Ugh… it’s so stuffy in here,” he thought. “I feel dizzy… and my brain is foggy…”

He felt a terrible storm inside—he was terrified of losing control. He tried to grab onto some random thought, anything to focus on, but couldn’t manage it. Still, the head clerk fascinated him; he kept thinking he might be able to read something in his face.

The head clerk was very young, about twenty-two, with a dark, expressive face that looked older than it was. He was fashionably dressed and clearly cared about his appearance, with his hair parted in the middle, shiny and neat, wearing several rings and a gold watch chain. He even spoke a few words of French to a foreigner in the room, and did it fairly well.
“Luise Ivanovna, you can sit down,” he said casually to the fancy, purple-faced woman, who was still standing as if afraid to take a seat, though there was a chair right next to her.

“Ich danke,” she said, and with a soft rustle of silk, sat down. Her light blue dress with white lace spread out around the table like a balloon and took up half the room. She smelled strongly of perfume. But she was clearly embarrassed about taking up so much space and smelling so strong; her smile was both bold and nervous at the same time.

The woman in mourning finally finished and stood up. Suddenly, an officer strode in, swinging his shoulders with a cocky walk. He tossed his cap on the table and sat in an easy chair. The big fancy lady jumped up and started bowing and curtsying like crazy, but the officer ignored her completely, and she didn’t dare sit down again. He was the assistant superintendent—he had reddish mustaches sticking out sideways and tiny features that just looked smug. He shot an annoyed look at Raskolnikov; Raskolnikov’s clothes were so shabby, but his attitude didn’t match his appearance. Raskolnikov had accidentally stared at him for too long, which seemed to offend him.
“What do you want?” the officer shouted, surprised that a guy dressed like a beggar didn’t shrink under his stare.
“I was summoned… I got a notice…” Raskolnikov stammered.
“For a debt, from the student,” the head clerk said quickly, tearing himself away from his papers. “Here!” He tossed Raskolnikov a document and pointed to a spot. “Read that!”
“A debt? What debt?” thought Raskolnikov. “So… it’s not about… that.”
He trembled with joy. He felt sudden, overwhelming relief—a huge weight off his shoulders.
“And what time were you told to come, sir?” the assistant superintendent yelled, sounding even more annoyed. “You were supposed to come at nine, and now it’s twelve!”
