“The notice was only brought to me fifteen minutes ago,” Raskolnikov replied loudly, not looking at him. To his own surprise, he felt angry, and it actually felt good. “And I’m sick with fever, but I came anyway.”
“Don’t shout!”
“I’m not shouting, I’m talking quietly. You’re the one shouting. I’m a student, and I won’t let anyone yell at me.”
The assistant superintendent was so furious he could barely get words out. He jumped up from his chair.
“Be quiet! You’re in a government office. Don’t be rude, sir!”
“You’re in a government office too,” snapped Raskolnikov, “and you’re smoking and shouting, so you’re disrespecting everyone here.”
He felt a strange satisfaction at saying this.
The head clerk looked at him with a smile. The angry assistant superintendent was clearly thrown off.

“That’s none of your business!” the officer finally shouted, way too loud. “Just make the declaration we need. Show him, Alexandr Grigorievitch. There’s a complaint against you! You don’t pay your debts! What a great guy you are!”
But Raskolnikov wasn’t even listening anymore; he grabbed the paper, desperate to understand. He read it once, then again, but still didn’t get it.
“What is this?” he asked the head clerk.

“It’s for collecting a debt—an IOU. You either pay it, with all the fees and expenses, or you give a written statement saying when you’ll pay, and promise not to leave the city or sell or hide your property. The creditor has the right to sell your stuff or take other legal action.”
“But I don’t owe anyone money!”

“That’s not our problem. Here—an IOU for 115 roubles, properly signed, due for payment, has been brought to us by the widow of Assessor Zarnitsyn, who passed it on to Mr. Tchebarov. So you’re summoned.”
“But she’s my landlady!”
“So what if she is?”

The head clerk looked at him with a mix of pity and triumph, like he was watching a newbie get his first taste of trouble. But Raskolnikov didn’t care about the IOU or the debt now—why worry about that? He stood, read, listened, and even asked questions, but all on autopilot. The feeling of safety, the belief that he’d escaped something much worse, was all he could feel right now—no thoughts about the future or doubts, just pure, instinctive relief. But right then, chaos broke out in the office. The assistant superintendent, still angry at Raskolnikov and wanting to show off, suddenly turned on the fancy lady, who had been staring at him with a silly smile ever since he arrived.

“You shameful woman!” he suddenly yelled at the top of his lungs. (The woman in mourning had already left.) “What happened at your place last night? Another disgrace! You’re a scandal to the whole street—fighting and drinking again. Do you want to go to jail? I’ve warned you ten times, and now you do it again, again, you… you…!”

Raskolnikov dropped the paper and stared in shock at the fancy lady as the officer shouted at her. But soon he understood and actually found the scene entertaining. He listened with barely hidden laughter… all his nerves were on edge.
“Ilya Petrovitch!” the head clerk began anxiously, but stopped, knowing from experience that nothing could stop the furious assistant except maybe physical force.

At first, the fancy lady trembled in front of the angry officer. But strangely, the more he yelled, the more pleasant and charming she tried to look, smiling at him in a way that was both flirty and nervous. She fidgeted and bowed over and over, waiting for a chance to speak—and finally, she got it.

“There was no noise or fighting in my house, Mr. Captain,” she rattled off, speaking Russian well but with a thick German accent, “and no scandal. It was your officer who came in drunk, and I’m telling the truth, Mr. Captain, I’m not to blame. Mine is an honorable house, Mr. Captain, and I always hate scandal. But he showed up tipsy and wanted three more bottles, and then he started playing the piano with his foot—not proper at all in a respectable house. He broke the piano, bad manners, and I told him so. Then he grabbed a bottle and started hitting people. I called the porter, Karl, and the officer punched him in the eye; he punched Henriette in the eye, too, and slapped me five times. So ungentlemanly in an honorable house, Mr. Captain, and I screamed. Then he opened the window over the canal, stood in it squealing like a little pig—such a disgrace! The idea of squealing out the window into the street! Fie! And Karl dragged him back by his coat, and yes, he tore his coat. Then the officer said we had to pay him fifteen roubles for damages. And I did pay him, Mr. Captain, five roubles for his coat. He’s a terrible guest, caused all the trouble. ‘I’ll expose you,’ he said, ‘I’ll write to the newspapers about you.’”
“So he was a writer?”
“Yes, Mr. Captain, and what a rude guest in an honorable house…”
“Enough! I already told you—”
“Ilya Petrovitch!” the head clerk said meaningfully.
The assistant glanced at him; the head clerk shook his head just a little.

“So listen, most respectable Luise Ivanovna, and this is your last warning,” the officer continued. “If there’s another scandal in your honorable house, I’ll lock you up myself, as they say nicely. Do you hear? So a writer, an author, took five roubles for his coat in an ‘honorable house’? What a crowd, these writers!”

He shot a contemptuous look at Raskolnikov. “There was another scandal in a restaurant recently. A writer ate and wouldn’t pay; ‘I’ll write a satire about you,’ he said. And last week, one cursed out a civil servant’s family on a steamer. And another one got thrown out of a candy shop. That’s what authors are like—writers, students, town criers… Ugh! Get out of here! I’ll come check on you myself one day. You’d better behave! Got it?”

Luise Ivanovna bowed to everyone as she hurried to the door, but she bumped into a good-looking officer with a friendly face and big blond whiskers—the district superintendent, Nikodim Fomitch. She quickly bowed again and with tiny, careful steps, fluttered out of the office.
“Thunder and lightning again—a hurricane!” Nikodim Fomitch said politely to Ilya Petrovitch. “You’ve blown up again! I heard it on the stairs!”

“Well, so what?” Ilya Petrovitch replied coolly, swinging his shoulders as he walked to another table. “Here, look—an author, or at least a student, won’t pay his debts, signed an IOU, refuses to leave his room, and people are always complaining about him. And now he’s even protesting my smoking! He acts like a jerk, just look at him. Here’s the man himself—very impressive, isn’t he?”

“Poverty isn’t a crime, my friend, but we know you blow up easily. Maybe you got offended and went too far yourself,” said Nikodim Fomitch, turning kindly to Raskolnikov. “But you’re wrong—he’s a good guy, I promise, just explosive! He gets worked up fast, but then it’s over. Underneath, he’s got a heart of gold! In the regiment, they called him the Explosive Lieutenant…”
“And what a regiment it was!” cried Ilya Petrovitch, clearly pleased at the teasing, though still sulky.

Suddenly, Raskolnikov wanted to say something nice to everyone. “Excuse me, Captain,” he said, turning to Nikodim Fomitch, “please understand my situation... I’m sorry if I was rude. I’m a poor student, sick and worn out (worn out, that’s the word). I’m not studying now because I can’t support myself, but I’ll get money soon… I have a mother and sister out in the provinces—they’ll send me some and I’ll pay. My landlady is a good woman, but she’s so angry that I lost my tutoring jobs and haven’t paid rent for four months that she won’t even send up my dinner… and I don’t get this IOU at all. She’s asking me to pay her with it. How can I? Please judge for yourselves…”
“But that’s not our job, you know,” the head clerk interrupted.

“Yes, yes, I know. But let me explain…” Raskolnikov went on, still mainly talking to Nikodim Fomitch, but trying to include Ilya Petrovitch, too, though the latter pretended to be busy with paperwork and ignored him. “I’ve lived with her for almost three years and, at first… well, I’ll admit it—I promised to marry her daughter, just a verbal promise… She was a girl… I liked her, though I wasn’t in love… It was a silly, youthful thing. Anyway, because of that, my landlady trusted me with credit, and I was careless… very careless…”
“Nobody wants all these personal stories, sir, we’re busy,” Ilya Petrovitch said, with a hint of triumph. But Raskolnikov cut him off, suddenly struggling to get the words out.

“But please, let me explain how it happened… I know it’s unnecessary, but… About a year ago, the girl died of typhus. I kept living there, and when my landlady moved to her new place, she told me—very kindly—that she still trusted me, but would I sign an IOU for 115 roubles, the whole debt. She said if I gave her that, she’d trust me forever and never—never, she said—use the IOU unless I could pay her. And now, when I’ve lost my jobs and have nothing to eat, she sues me. What do you say to that?”
“All these sad stories aren’t our business,” Ilya Petrovitch interrupted harshly. “Just give us a written promise. As for your love life and tragedies, that’s not our concern.”
“Come on… that’s a little harsh,” muttered Nikodim Fomitch, sitting and starting to write. He seemed a bit ashamed.
“Write!” said the head clerk to Raskolnikov.
“Write what?” Raskolnikov grumbled.
“I’ll tell you what to write.”

Raskolnikov thought the head clerk was treating him more coldly and rudely after his story, but strangely, he suddenly stopped caring what anyone thought. If he’d thought about it, he’d have been surprised he’d spoken like that just a minute ago. Where had those feelings come from? Now, even if the room were full of his closest friends instead of police, he wouldn’t have a word for them—he felt totally empty. A dark, crushing feeling of loneliness and distance settled on him. It wasn’t the humiliation of pouring his heart out, nor the clerk’s mean reaction, that made him feel this way. It was something entirely new—he just sensed that he could never appeal to these people again, for anything—not even if they were his own family. He’d never felt anything like this before, and it was the worst feeling he’d ever known.
The head clerk started dictating the usual statement: that Raskolnikov couldn’t pay, would do so later, wouldn’t leave town or sell his things, and so on.
“But you can barely write, you can hardly hold the pen,” the head clerk said, looking at Raskolnikov curiously. “Are you sick?”
“Yeah, I’m dizzy. Keep going.”
“That’s it. Sign it.”
The head clerk took the paper and turned to someone else.

Raskolnikov handed back the pen, but instead of getting up, he put his elbows on the table and held his head in his hands. It felt like someone was hammering a nail into his skull. Suddenly, a wild idea popped into his head: get up, walk over to Nikodim Fomitch, and confess everything that happened yesterday—then go with him back to his room and show him the things hidden in the wall. The urge was so strong he actually got up to do it. “Shouldn’t I think for a second?” flashed through his mind. “No, better to just get it over with.” But he froze on the spot. Nikodim Fomitch was talking excitedly with Ilya Petrovitch, and Raskolnikov overheard:

“It’s impossible—they’ll both be released. For one thing, the whole story doesn’t add up. Why would they call the porter if they did it? To report themselves? Or as a trick? No, that’s too clever! Plus, Pestryakov, the student, was seen at the gate by both porters and a woman as he went in. He had three friends with him, who left only at the gate, and he asked the porters for directions right in front of them. Would he do that if he’d planned a crime? And Koch, he spent half an hour at the silversmith’s downstairs before going up to the old woman, and left at exactly a quarter to eight. Now think…”
“But how do you explain this? They said they knocked and the door was locked, but three minutes later, when they came back with the porter, the door was open.”

“Exactly! The murderer must have been inside and bolted the door. They would’ve caught him for sure if Koch hadn’t gone looking for the porter, too. The killer must have used that time to sneak downstairs and slip past everyone. Koch keeps saying, ‘If I’d been there, he would have jumped out and killed me with his axe.’ He’s so scared he’s planning a thanksgiving service—ha, ha!”
“And no one saw the murderer?”
“Easy to miss him—the place is a total madhouse,” said the head clerk, who was listening in.
“It’s clear, very clear,” Nikodim Fomitch repeated eagerly.
“No, it’s not clear at all,” Ilya Petrovitch argued.
Raskolnikov picked up his hat and headed for the door, but he didn’t make it…

When he came to, he found himself sitting in a chair, someone supporting him on the right, another person standing on his left holding a yellowish glass of water, and Nikodim Fomitch standing in front of him, watching him closely. Raskolnikov stood up.
“What’s this? Are you sick?” Nikodim Fomitch asked sharply.
“He could barely hold the pen when he signed,” said the head clerk, leaning back and getting back to work.

“Have you been sick long?” Ilya Petrovitch called from his desk, where he’d gone back to his papers. Of course, he’d come to check when Raskolnikov fainted, but he’d gone back to his spot as soon as Raskolnikov came to.
“Since yesterday,” Raskolnikov muttered.
“Did you go out yesterday?”
“Yes.”
“Even though you were sick?”
“Yes.”
“What time?”
“Around seven.”
“And where did you go, may I ask?”
“Along the street.”
“Short and clear.”
Raskolnikov, pale as a sheet, answered sharply and quickly, never looking away from Ilya Petrovitch’s stare.
“He can barely stand. And you…” Nikodim Fomitch began.
“Doesn’t matter,” Ilya Petrovitch said, in a strange way.
Nikodim Fomitch wanted to object, but caught the head clerk’s intense look and fell silent. The room went quiet—it felt odd.
“Alright then,” Ilya Petrovitch finished, “we won’t keep you.”
Raskolnikov left. As he did, he heard eager conversation starting up behind him, with Nikodim Fomitch’s voice standing out. Outside, his dizziness vanished completely.
“A search—they’re going to search my room, right away,” he muttered to himself, hurrying home. “Those brutes! They know.”
His old terror came crashing back over him.
“What if they’ve already searched my room? What if I walk in and find people going through my stuff?”
But when he got to his room, it was empty. No one had come in. Even Nastasya hadn’t touched anything. But still—how could he have left all those things hidden in the hole?

He rushed to the corner, slipped his hand under the wallpaper, pulled out the stolen items, and stuffed them into his pockets. There were eight things in total: two small boxes with earrings or something like that—he barely looked; then four little leather cases; a chain, just wrapped in newspaper; and something else that looked like a medal or decoration. He hid them in different pockets of his coat and pants, trying to keep them out of sight. He grabbed the purse too. Then he hurried out, leaving his door wide open. He moved quickly, determined, even though he felt exhausted and shaky. He was scared someone might start chasing him any minute, so he had to hide every trace before that happened. He needed to get rid of everything while he still had the energy and presence of mind. But where should he go?

He’d already decided: “Throw it all in the canal, let the water hide the evidence. That’ll be the end of it.” He’d made up his mind when he was half-delirious during the night, thinking he should just get up and do it right away. But actually getting rid of the loot turned out to be much harder. He wandered along the bank of the Ekaterininsky Canal for more than half an hour, looking at the steps down to the water, but he couldn’t do it. There were always people around—rafts with women washing clothes, boats tied up, people everywhere. Anyone on the bank could see him, and it would look suspicious for someone to go down, stop, and throw something into the water. Plus, what if the boxes floated instead of sinking? They probably would. Even just walking around, he felt like everyone was watching him. “Is it real, or am I just being paranoid?” he wondered.

Suddenly it occurred to him that the Neva River might be a better option. There would be fewer people there, less chance of being seen, and it was farther away. He couldn’t believe he’d wasted half an hour stuck on his first idea, all because he’d thought of it while he was sick and not thinking straight. He realized he was getting more and more absent-minded and forgetful—he really needed to hurry.

He started walking toward the Neva along V—— Prospect, but then another idea popped into his head. “Why the Neva? Wouldn’t it be better to go somewhere far away, like the Islands, and hide the stuff in the woods or under a bush? Maybe even mark the spot?” Even though he wasn’t thinking clearly, this seemed like a good plan. But he wouldn’t get the chance. As he left V—— Prospect and headed toward the square, he noticed on the left a passageway between two walls leading into a courtyard. On the right was a long, plain, four-story house; on the left, a wooden fence ran for about twenty paces, then turned sharply. It was a deserted, fenced-off area full of trash and junk. At the end, he could see the corner of a low, dirty stone shed—probably part of a workshop, maybe for building carriages or carpentry. The whole place was black with coal dust. “This is the perfect spot,” he thought. Not seeing anyone around, he slipped in and noticed by the entrance a big sink, probably for workers or cab drivers. Above it, someone had chalked “Standing here strictly forbidden.” Even better—it wouldn’t look strange for him to be there. “I can dump everything here and get out fast!”

Glancing around again, with his hand already in his pocket, he spotted a huge rough stone leaning against the outer wall between the entrance and the sink. It must have weighed sixty pounds. The other side of the wall was a busy street—he could hear people going by, but they couldn’t see him unless someone came in suddenly. He had to act fast.

He bent down, grabbed the top of the stone with both hands, and with all his strength, flipped it over. There was a small hollow underneath. He quickly dumped everything into it, with the purse landing on top, and still there was space left. He turned the stone back so it looked just like before, though maybe sitting a little higher. Then he scraped dirt around the edges and pressed it down with his foot. No one would notice.

He left and walked into the square. Suddenly he felt a wave of almost unbearable relief, just like he’d felt at the police station. “I’ve hidden all the evidence! Who’d ever think to look under that stone? It’s probably been there since the building went up and will stay there for years. Even if someone finds it, who’d connect it to me? It’s over! No clues!” He started laughing—a weird, thin, silent laugh that kept going as he crossed the square. But as he reached K—— Boulevard, where he’d seen that girl two days before, the laughter stopped. Other thoughts crept in. The idea of passing that bench where he’d sat thinking after the girl left made him feel sick, and he really didn’t want to see that mustached policeman he’d given twenty copecks to. “To hell with him!”
He walked on, looking around angrily and distractedly. All his thoughts seemed to circle around one central point, and he felt like, for the first time in two months, he was now face-to-face with it.

“Damn it!” he thought suddenly, in a burst of anger. “If this is happening, then let it happen. Forget this ‘new life’! God, how stupid this all is!... And what lies I told today! How disgustingly I acted with that miserable Ilya Petrovitch! But that’s all pointless! Why should I care about them or about how I acted? That’s not even the problem! That’s not it at all!”
Suddenly he stopped. A new, simple question popped into his mind, and it completely confused and upset him.

“If I really did all this on purpose, with a clear goal, then how come I never even looked inside the purse? I don’t even know what was in it, and yet I put myself through all this, sinking this low. And I was ready to throw it all into the water without even seeing what I’d stolen... how does that make sense?”

Yes, that was true, all of it. But he’d known it before—it wasn’t a new question for him, even when he made the decision so quickly, as if it had to be that way. He realized it had already been decided yesterday, when he was bent over the box, pulling out the jewelry cases. Yes, that’s how it was.

“It’s because I’m really sick,” he decided grimly. “I’ve been worrying and stressing so much, I don’t even know what I’m doing.... Yesterday, the day before, all this time, I’ve been worrying myself sick.... I’ll get better, and then I’ll stop worrying.... But what if I never get better? God, I’m so tired of all this!”

He kept walking, not stopping to rest. He desperately wanted something to distract him, but he didn’t know what to do or even try. A new, overpowering feeling was taking over—a huge, almost physical disgust for everything around him, a stubborn, angry sort of hatred. Everyone he saw disgusted him—their faces, the way they moved, everything. If anyone had spoken to him, he felt like he might have spit at them or even bitten them....

Suddenly he stopped as he reached the bank of the Little Neva, near the bridge to Vassilyevsky Island. “Wait, Razumihin lives here, in this building,” he realized. “Did I come here on purpose, or did I just end up here by accident? Doesn’t matter, I told him two days ago I’d visit the day after, so I will! Besides, I really can't go any farther.”
He went up to Razumihin’s room on the fifth floor.

Razumihin was at home in his attic apartment, busy writing, and opened the door himself. They hadn’t seen each other in four months. Razumihin wore a ragged old dressing gown, slippers on bare feet, looking messy and unshaven. He looked surprised.
“Is that you?” he asked. He checked out Raskolnikov’s shabby clothes, then whistled. “Wow, you look even worse off than me! Sit down, you must be exhausted.”
When Raskolnikov collapsed onto the battered old sofa—worse than his own—Razumihin immediately noticed he looked seriously ill.
“You’re really sick, you know that?” Razumihin said, feeling his pulse. Raskolnikov pulled his hand away.
“It doesn’t matter,” he said. “I came because... I’m not teaching any lessons now. I thought I wanted to... but I really don’t.”
“Are you sure you’re not delirious?” Razumihin asked, watching him carefully.
“No, I’m not.”

Raskolnikov got up from the sofa. Climbing the stairs, he hadn’t thought about actually seeing Razumihin face to face. Now, all at once, he realized that was the last thing he wanted right now. He felt a surge of anger at himself as soon as he entered Razumihin’s room.
“Goodbye,” he said suddenly, heading to the door.
“Wait, wait! What’s wrong with you?”
“I don’t want to,” Raskolnikov said, again pulling his hand away.
“Then why the heck did you come? Are you crazy or something? This is almost insulting! I’m not letting you just leave like that.”

“Fine, I came because you’re the only person I know who might help me... at least to start with... because you’re kinder than anyone—well, smarter, I mean, and can judge things... but now I see I don’t want anything. You hear me? Nothing at all... nobody’s help... nobody’s pity. I’m on my own. That’s it. Leave me alone.”

“Hold on a second, you idiot! You’re acting like a total lunatic. Do whatever you want, I don’t care. I’m not teaching any lessons either, but there’s this bookseller, Heruvimov—he’s better than lessons. He’s doing his own kind of publishing, putting out science books, and they sell like crazy! The titles alone are worth the money! You always said I was an idiot, but honestly, there are bigger idiots out there. Now he’s pretending to be all ‘progressive,’ but he doesn’t have a clue. Of course I encourage him. I’ve got two chapters of a German book—it’s total nonsense—debating ‘Is woman a human being?’ and it ‘proves’ that she is. Heruvimov wants to publish it as a big statement about women’s rights; I’m translating it. He’ll stretch these two and a half chapters into six, we’ll slap a huge title on it and sell it for half a rouble. He pays me six roubles per chapter, so I’ll get about fifteen for the whole thing, and I’ve already got six in advance. After this, we’re doing a book about whales, and then a bunch of boring scandals from the second part of Les Confessions—somebody told Heruvimov that Rousseau was like Radishchev. Of course I don’t correct him—why bother! So, do you want to translate the second chapter of ‘Is woman a human being?’ If you do, here’s the German text, pens, and paper—all set up for you. Take three roubles; since I’ve already got six in advance, three are yours for your part. When you finish, you get another three. And don’t think I’m doing you a favor—actually, I thought you could help me as soon as you walked in. For one, my spelling is terrible, and sometimes I get lost in German and just make things up. At least it’ll be an improvement—though who knows, maybe not. So, will you take it?”

Raskolnikov silently took the German pages and the three roubles, and walked out without a word. Razumihin stared after him, shocked. But when Raskolnikov got to the next street, he turned back, climbed Razumihin’s stairs, put the German article and the money back on the table, and left again, still without saying a word.
“Are you out of your mind?” Razumihin finally yelled, losing his temper. “What is this, some kind of joke? You’re going to drive me crazy too... why did you even come to see me, damn it?”
“I don’t want... the translation,” Raskolnikov mumbled from the stairs.
“Then what the hell do you want?” Razumihin shouted after him. Raskolnikov kept going down in silence.
“Hey! Where are you living?”
No answer.
“Fine, whatever! Forget you!”

But Raskolnikov was already in the street. On the Nikolaevsky Bridge, something happened that snapped him out of his daze. A coachman, after yelling at him a few times, hit him hard on the back with his whip for almost stumbling under the horses’ feet. The pain made Raskolnikov furious—he ran to the railing (for some reason, he’d been walking right in the middle of the bridge, in traffic). He clenched his teeth angrily. He heard people laughing, of course.
“Serves him right!”
“Must be a pickpocket.”
“Pretending to be drunk, probably, and getting under the wheels on purpose; then you have to answer for him.”
“That’s a regular scam, that’s what it is.”

While he stood at the railing, still angry and confused, rubbing his back and watching the carriage drive away, he suddenly felt someone shove money into his hand. He looked—it was an old woman in a kerchief and goatskin shoes, with a girl (probably her daughter) wearing a hat and holding a green umbrella.
“Take it, my good man, for Christ’s sake.”
He took it, and they moved on. It was a twenty-copeck coin. Judging by how he looked, they probably thought he was a beggar, and the coachman’s blow had made them feel sorry for him.

He closed his hand around the coin, walked about ten steps, then turned to face the Neva, looking toward the palace. The sky was clear, and the water looked almost bright blue—a rare sight in the Neva. The cathedral dome, which looked best from this bridge, was shining in the sun, and every detail was visible in the clear air. The pain from the whip faded, and he forgot about it; now his mind was filled with a strange, uneasy thought. He stood there, staring into the distance. This spot was familiar—when he’d been a university student, he’d often stopped here on his way home, staring at this amazing view, always feeling a weird, mysterious emotion. But it left him strangely cold; this beautiful scene seemed empty and dead to him. He always wondered why he felt that way, but never figured it out. Now he remembered those old doubts, and it seemed odd that he’d stopped at the same spot again, like he thought he could go back to his old thoughts and feelings—things that had mattered to him just recently. It was almost funny, but it hurt too. His old life, his old ideas, his old problems and theories, all seemed far away now, like they were disappearing. He felt as if he were flying upward, leaving everything behind. Suddenly, he noticed the coin in his hand. He opened his fist, stared at it, then threw it into the water. Then he turned and went home. It felt like, in that moment, he’d cut himself off from everyone and everything.

By the time he got home, evening was coming. He must have been walking for six hours. He couldn’t remember how or where he’d wandered. He undressed, shivering all over, lay down on the sofa, pulled his coat over himself, and immediately blacked out....
It was getting dark when he woke up to a terrifying scream. God, what a scream! He’d never heard anything so awful—such wild, desperate howling, wailing, sobbing, blows, and cursing.

He never could have imagined such violence, such madness. Panicked, he sat up in bed, almost fainting from fear. But the fighting and shouting only got worse. To his shock, he recognized his landlady’s voice. She was screaming and crying for help—someone was beating her brutally on the stairs. The attacker’s voice was harsh and full of rage, almost a croak; he was yelling too, quickly and angrily. Suddenly, Raskolnikov shivered—he recognized that voice. It was Ilya Petrovitch. Ilya Petrovitch was here, beating the landlady! He was kicking her, smashing her head against the steps—you could tell from the sounds, the cries, the thuds. Was the world upside down? He could hear people running from every floor and staircase, voices shouting, doors slamming. “But why? How could this be?” he kept thinking, starting to believe he’d gone insane. But it all sounded too real! And soon, they’d come for him next, “because it must be... about that... about yesterday.... God!” He wanted to lock his door, but he couldn’t move... and it wouldn’t help anyway. Terror gripped his heart, freezing and torturing him.... Finally, after about ten minutes, the chaos began to die down. The landlady was still moaning and crying; Ilya Petrovitch was still cursing... but then he stopped too. “Did he leave? God!” Yes, now the landlady was leaving, still weeping, and her door slammed. The crowd on the stairs started heading back to their rooms, talking, arguing, shouting, then whispering. There must have been a lot of them—almost everyone in the building. “But, God, how could this happen? Why did he come here?”

Raskolnikov collapsed on the sofa, exhausted, but couldn’t close his eyes. For half an hour, he lay there in unbearable terror like he’d never known before. Suddenly, a bright light flashed into his room. Nastasya came in with a candle and a plate of soup. She looked him over carefully, saw he was awake, put the candle on the table, and started laying out what she’d brought—bread, salt, a plate, and a spoon.
“You haven’t eaten since yesterday, I bet. You’ve been wandering all day and you’re burning up with fever.”
“Nastasya... why were they beating the landlady?”
She looked at him closely.
“Who beat the landlady?”
“Just now... half an hour ago, Ilya Petrovitch, the assistant superintendent, on the stairs.... Why was he hurting her like that, and... why was he here?”
Nastasya stared at him, silent and frowning, for a long time. Her look made him uneasy, even scared.
“Nastasya, why aren’t you saying anything?” he asked timidly, his voice weak.
“It’s the blood,” she finally said softly, almost to herself.
“Blood? What blood?” he mumbled, going pale and turning toward the wall.
Nastasya kept looking at him without answering.
“No one beat the landlady,” she finally said firmly.
He stared at her, barely breathing.
“But I heard it... I wasn’t asleep... I was sitting up,” he said, even more timidly. “I listened for a long time. The assistant superintendent came... everyone ran out onto the stairs.”
“No one’s been here. That’s just the blood rushing in your ears. When it’s all blocked up, you start imagining things.... Will you eat something?”
He didn’t answer. Nastasya still stood over him, watching.
“Give me something to drink... Nastasya.”
She went downstairs and came back with a white earthenware jug of water. He only remembered swallowing one sip of the cold water and spilling some on his neck. After that, everything faded away.

Even while he was sick, Raskolnikov wasn’t completely unconscious. He drifted in and out of feverish dreams—sometimes he was confused, sometimes half-aware. Later, he remembered a lot of it. Sometimes, he felt like a crowd of people surrounded him, arguing about him and wanting to take him somewhere. Other times, he was all alone in the room, with people peeking in through a crack in the door, frightened of him. They threatened him, whispered together, laughed, and made fun of him. He often saw Nastasya by his bed, and there was another person too, someone he felt he knew well, but he couldn’t remember who it was. That bothered him so much it made him want to cry. Sometimes he thought he’d been lying there for a month; other times, it felt like it was all happening in a single day. But he couldn’t really remember any of it clearly, and yet every moment he felt like there was something important he’d forgotten. He obsessed over trying to remember, groaned, got angry, or was suddenly terrified for no reason. Now and then, he tried to get up and run away, but someone always held him back, and he’d collapse again, helpless and confused. Finally, he came back to full consciousness.

It happened around ten in the morning. On sunny days, the sunlight would shine into the room at that time, making a bright stripe on the right wall and the corner by the door. Nastasya was standing next to him, along with a stranger who stared at him curiously. The stranger was a young man with a beard, dressed in a short, fitted coat, looking a bit like a messenger or delivery guy. The landlady was peeking through the half-open door. Raskolnikov sat up.
"Who’s that, Nastasya?" he asked, pointing at the young man.
"Hey, look at that! He’s himself again," she said.
"He is himself," repeated the stranger.

The landlady, realizing he was awake, shut the door and left. She was always nervous and tried to avoid conversations. She was about forty, actually looked pretty good, plump, with black eyes and eyebrows, friendly because she was so easygoing and lazy, but ridiculously shy.
"Who... are you?" Raskolnikov said to the man. But just then, the door swung open, and Razumihin came in, ducking because he was so tall.
"What a tiny place this is!" he exclaimed. "I keep bumping my head. You call this a room? So you’re awake, brother? I just heard from Pashenka."
"He just woke up," said Nastasya.
"Just woke up," echoed the stranger, smiling.
"And who are you?" Razumihin asked the man sharply. "I’m Vrazumihin, at your service—not Razumihin like everyone calls me, but Vrazumihin, student and gentleman. And he’s my friend. And you are?"
"I’m the messenger from our office, from the merchant Shelopaev. I’m here on business."

"Please, sit down." Razumihin sat on the other side of the table. "Good thing you woke up, brother," he said to Raskolnikov. "You barely ate or drank anything for four days. We had to feed you tea with a spoon. I brought Zossimov to see you twice. Remember Zossimov? He checked you out and said it wasn’t anything serious—just something getting to your head. He called it nerves from not eating properly, said you need more bread and veggies, but you'll be fine. Zossimov is a great guy! He’s getting famous. Anyway, I won’t keep you," he said to the messenger. "What’s your business? This is the second time someone’s come from the office; last time it was another guy, and I talked to him. Who came before?"
"That was the day before yesterday, I think, if you don’t mind me saying, sir. That was Alexey Semyonovitch; he works with us."
"He seemed smarter than you, don’t you think?"
"Yes, sir, he’s higher up than me."
"Right, go on."

"At your mother’s request, through Afanasy Ivanovitch Vahrushin—maybe you’ve heard of him—a payment is being sent to you from our office," the man said, looking at Raskolnikov. "If you’re clear-headed, I have thirty-five roubles to give you, since Semyon Semyonovitch got instructions from Afanasy Ivanovitch, who got them from your mother, just like before. Do you know him, sir?"
"Yeah, I remember... Vahrushin," Raskolnikov said, sounding dreamy.
"See, he knows Vahrushin!" Razumihin shouted. "He’s in his right mind! And you seem sensible too. Good to hear some sense for a change."

"That’s the man—Vahrushin, Afanasy Ivanovitch. And as your mother asked, he sent you money again, just like last time, and told Semyon Semyonovitch a few days ago to give you thirty-five roubles, hoping for better times soon."
"That ‘hoping for better times’ is the best part you’ve said, but ‘your mother’ isn’t bad either. So, what do you think? Is he all there?"
"He’s fine, as long as he can sign this form."
"He can scribble his name. Do you have the book?"
"Yes, here it is."
"Give it here. Okay, Rodya, sit up. I’ll hold you. Take the pen and just write ‘Raskolnikov’ for him. Because right now, brother, money is sweeter than candy."
"I don’t want it," said Raskolnikov, pushing the pen away.
"You don’t want it?"
"I won’t sign it."
"How can you refuse to sign for it?"
"I don’t want... the money."
"Don’t want the money! Come on, that’s just crazy, I tell you. Don’t worry," he said to the messenger, "he gets like this sometimes. But we’ll help him out—just take his hand and he’ll sign. Here."
"I can come back later."
"No, no. No need to bother you. You’re an understanding man.... Come on, Rodya, don’t keep him waiting," and Razumihin got ready to hold Raskolnikov’s hand for real.
"Wait, I’ll do it myself," Raskolnikov said, taking the pen and signing his name.
The messenger counted out the money and left.
"Bravo! Now, brother, are you hungry?"
"Yes," Raskolnikov replied.
"Is there any soup?"
"Some from yesterday," Nastasya said, still standing there.
"With potatoes and rice in it?"
"Yes."
"I know it by heart. Bring the soup and make us some tea."
"Alright."
Raskolnikov watched all this in total confusion, feeling a heavy, strange fear. He decided to stay quiet and see what would happen. "I think I’m not hallucinating. I think this is real," he thought.

A couple minutes later, Nastasya brought in the soup and said the tea would be ready soon. She set the table with two spoons, two plates, salt, pepper, mustard for the beef, and so on. The table hadn’t looked this nice in a long time. The tablecloth was clean.
"It wouldn’t be a bad idea if Praskovya Pavlovna sent up a couple of bottles of beer. We could finish them," Razumihin said.
"You’re something else," Nastasya muttered, but left to do what he asked.

Raskolnikov still stared around, tense and confused. Meanwhile, Razumihin sat down next to him on the sofa, awkwardly like a big bear, put his left arm around Raskolnikov’s head—even though Raskolnikov could sit up himself—and with his right hand gave him spoonfuls of soup, blowing on each so it wouldn’t be too hot. The soup was just warm, though. Raskolnikov gulped down one spoonful, then a second, then a third. After a few more, Razumihin suddenly stopped and said he should check with Zossimov about giving him more.
Nastasya came in with two bottles of beer.
"And do you want tea?"
"Yes."

"Go on, Nastasya, bring us some tea. We can have tea without a doctor’s permission. But here’s the beer!" Razumihin moved back to his chair, pulled the food in front of him, and started eating like he hadn’t eaten in days.

"You know, Rodya, I have dinner here like this every day now," he mumbled with his mouth full. "It’s all thanks to Pashenka, your landlady. She loves doing things for me. I don’t ask, but I don’t say no, either. And here’s Nastasya with the tea. She’s quick. Nastasya, want some beer?"
"Stop your nonsense!"
"How about some tea then?"
"I’ll have a cup of tea, maybe."
"Pour it out. Wait, I’ll pour it myself. Sit down."

He poured two cups, left his food, and sat back on the sofa. Again, he put his left arm around Raskolnikov’s head, lifted him up, and fed him tea by the spoonful, blowing on every spoonful like it was the key to getting Raskolnikov well. Raskolnikov didn’t say anything or fight, even though he was strong enough to sit up and could have held his own cup or spoon—maybe even walked around. For some reason, though, he decided to hide how strong he really was and just act weak, so he could listen and figure out what was going on. Still, he felt disgusted. After a dozen spoonfuls of tea, he pushed away the spoon, let his head drop back on the pillow, and lay there. He noticed the pillows were now real, soft, and had clean cases.
"Pashenka should give us some raspberry jam today so we can make him raspberry tea," Razumihin said, going back to his chair and digging into his food and beer.
"And where’s she supposed to get raspberries for you?" Nastasya asked, balancing a saucer and sipping tea through a lump of sugar.

"She’ll get them at the shop, of course. You see, Rodya, a lot has happened while you’ve been out of it. When you disappeared without an address, I was so mad I decided to track you down and teach you a lesson. I started the very same day. I ran all over the place trying to find you! I’d forgotten where this apartment was, and I never really knew it anyway, just remembered your old place was at the Five Corners, Harlamov’s house. I kept searching for Harlamov’s, but it turned out to be Buch’s house instead. It’s funny how you mix up names! I got so frustrated I went to the address office the next day, and believe it or not, they found you in two minutes! Your name’s right in their book."
"My name?"

"Of course! But while I was there, they couldn’t even find a General Kobelev. Anyway, once I found your place, I got to know everything about you—everything, brother. Nastasya can tell you. I met Nikodim Fomitch, Ilya Petrovitch, the house-porter, Mr. Zametov, Alexandr Grigorievitch at the police office, and, last but not least, Pashenka herself. Nastasya knows…"
"He’s charmed her," Nastasya said with a sly smile.
"Why don’t you put sugar in your tea, Nastasya Nikiforovna?"
"You’re too much!" Nastasya burst out laughing. "I’m not Nikiforovna, but Petrovna," she added, still giggling.
"I’ll remember that. Anyway, brother, I was about to shake things up around here, but Pashenka won me over. I didn’t expect her to be so... nice. What do you think?"
Raskolnikov didn’t answer, but still stared at him, worried.
"And really, she’s everything you could want," Razumihin went on, not bothered by the silence.
"Oh, you sly dog!" Nastasya burst out laughing again, clearly enjoying the conversation.

"It’s too bad you didn’t handle things right from the start, brother. You should’ve approached her differently. She’s really unpredictable. But we’ll talk about her later... How did things get so bad that she stopped sending you meals? And that IOU? You must have been crazy to sign it. And that marriage promise when her daughter, Natalya Yegorovna, was alive?... I know all about it! But I get that's a sensitive subject, and I’m an idiot, so forgive me. But honestly, Praskovya Pavlovna isn’t as silly as she seems at first."
"No," Raskolnikov mumbled, turning away but deciding he’d better keep the conversation going.

"She isn’t, right?" Razumihin said, happy to get any answer. "But she’s not super smart either, huh? She’s just so unpredictable! Sometimes I don’t know what to make of her. She must be forty, though she says thirty-six—and sure, she can say whatever she wants. But I swear I judge her on an intellectual, almost philosophical level. There’s some strange connection between us, like algebra, or something! I don’t get it! But never mind that. Since you’re not a student anymore, lost your tutoring jobs and clothes, and her daughter’s gone, she doesn’t have to treat you like family. When you hid away and stopped talking to her, she decided to get rid of you. She’d wanted to for a while, but didn’t want to lose the IOU, since you told her your mother would pay."
"It was low of me to say that... My mother is nearly broke herself... and I lied so I could keep my room... and get food," Raskolnikov said loudly and clearly.

"Yeah, it was smart, actually. But then Mr. Tchebarov, a businessman, showed up. Pashenka would never have done anything herself—she’s too shy—but this guy wasn’t shy at all. First thing, he asked, ‘Can you cash in the IOU?’ Answer: sure, because you have a mother who’d give up her whole pension for you, and a sister who’d do anything for you. That’s what he was counting on.... Why are you so startled? I know all your business now, my friend—it’s not for nothing you were so open with Pashenka when you might have married her daughter. I say this as a friend.... But listen, an honest, sensitive man is open; a businessman just listens and then tries to eat you alive. Anyway, she gave the IOU to Tchebarov as payment, and he immediately demanded the cash. When I heard, I wanted to yell at him too, to clear my conscience, but by that time I’d made peace with Pashenka. I promised to stop the whole thing and said you’d pay. I stood up for you, brother. Get it? We called Tchebarov, threw him ten roubles, and got the IOU back. Here—she trusts your word now. Here it is, I even tore it up."
Razumihin put the torn note on the table. Raskolnikov looked at him, turned to the wall, and didn’t say a word. Even Razumihin felt a little awkward.
"I see, brother," he said after a moment, "I’ve been an idiot again. I thought I’d cheer you up, but I’ve probably just annoyed you."
"Was it you I didn’t recognize when I was delirious?" Raskolnikov asked after a pause, not turning his head.
"Yeah, and you got really angry about it, especially when I brought Zametov one day."
"Zametov? The head clerk? Why?" Raskolnikov turned quickly and stared at Razumihin.

"What’s wrong? Why are you worried? He wanted to meet you because I told him all about you.... How else do you think I found out so much? He’s a great guy, brother, really good... in his own way. We’re friends now—see each other almost every day. I moved to this neighborhood, you know. Just moved in, actually. I’ve even been with him to Luise Ivanovna’s a couple times.... Remember Luise, Luise Ivanovna?"
"Did I say anything strange when I was delirious?"
"Oh, you definitely did! You were out of your mind."
"What did I talk about?"
"What didn’t you talk about? Just normal delirious stuff.... Anyway, brother, I have to get going. Time to work." He got up and grabbed his cap.
"What did I talk about?"

"Man, you don’t give up! Are you afraid you spilled some secret? Don’t worry—you didn’t say anything about a countess. But you did talk a lot about a bulldog, about earrings and chains, about Krestovsky Island, about some porter, and about Nikodim Fomitch and Ilya Petrovitch, the assistant superintendent. And you were really obsessed with your sock. You kept whining, ‘Give me my sock.’ Zametov searched your whole room looking for socks, and with his fancy, ring-covered fingers, he finally gave you a ragged sock. That calmed you down, and for the next day you just held on to it; we couldn’t get it away from you. It’s probably still under your quilt right now. Oh, and you begged for fringe for your trousers. We tried to figure out what you meant, but couldn’t. Now, to business! Here’s thirty-five roubles; I’ll take ten and give you an account later. I’ll let Zossimov know too, even though he should have been here already—it’s almost noon. And Nastasya, check in often while I’m out to see if he needs anything. I’ll tell Pashenka what’s needed myself. Bye!"

"He calls her Pashenka! What a sly one!" Nastasya said as he left. She couldn’t resist running downstairs after him, desperate to hear what he’d say to the landlady. She was clearly fascinated by Razumihin.

As soon as she left, Raskolnikov threw off the covers and jumped out of bed like a madman. He’d waited impatiently for everyone to leave so he could get to work. But what was he supposed to do? Now that he was alone, he couldn’t remember.

"God, just tell me—do they know about it or not? What if they know and are just pretending, making fun of me while I’m sick, and then they’ll come in and say it was discovered ages ago and they only... What am I supposed to do now? That’s what I’ve forgotten—forgotten on purpose; just a minute ago I remembered."

He stood in the middle of the room, looking around in misery. He went to the door, opened it, listened—but that wasn’t what he needed. Suddenly, like he remembered something, he ran to the corner where there was a hole in the wall, poked around in it, but that wasn’t it either. He checked the stove, digging through the ashes—the ragged ends of his pants and the cloth he’d cut from his pocket were still there, just as he’d left them. No one had searched. Then he remembered the sock Razumihin had mentioned. There it was, under the quilt on the sofa, but it was so dirty and dusty that Zametov couldn’t have found anything on it.

"Wait, Zametov! The police station! And why was I called to the police station? Where’s the notice? Wait—that was before. I looked at my sock back then, too, but now... now I’ve been sick. But why did Zametov come? Why did Razumihin bring him?" he muttered, helplessly sitting down again. "What does it mean? Am I still delirious, or is this real? I think it’s real.... Oh, I remember: I have to escape! I need to run away. Yes, I must, I must escape! Yes... but where? And where are my clothes? No boots. They took them! They hid them! I get it! Oh, here’s my coat—they missed that! And here’s money on the table, thank God! And here’s the IOU... I’ll take the money and find another place to stay. They won’t find me!... But the address office? They’ll find me; Razumihin will find me. Better to run away completely... far away... to America, and let them do whatever they want! And take the IOU... it could be useful there.... What else should I take? They think I’m sick! They don’t know I can walk, ha-ha-ha! I could see in their eyes that they know everything! If only I could get downstairs! But what if they have someone watching—policemen! What’s this, tea? Oh, and there’s beer left, half a bottle, cold!"

He grabbed the bottle, which still had a glass of beer left, and drank it down, like he was putting out a fire inside him. But in a minute, the beer went to his head, and a pleasant little shiver ran down his back. He lay down and pulled the quilt over himself. His sick, confused thoughts drifted apart, and soon he felt a soft, gentle drowsiness wash over him. He snuggled into the pillow, wrapped himself up in the soft, warm quilt that had replaced his old ragged coat, sighed, and fell into a deep, healing sleep.
He woke up when someone came in. He opened his eyes and saw Razumihin standing in the doorway, not sure whether to come in. Raskolnikov sat up quickly and stared at him, trying to remember something.
"Oh, you’re awake! There you are! Nastasya, bring the package!" Razumihin shouted down the stairs. "I’ll give you the bill in a minute."
"What time is it?" Raskolnikov asked, looking around nervously.
"You had a great sleep, brother—it’s almost evening, nearly six. You slept more than six hours."
"Wow! Did I really?"

"Why not? It’s good for you. What’s the rush? Are you meeting someone? We have plenty of time. I’ve been waiting for you for three hours; I’ve checked on you twice and you were still sleeping. I went to see Zossimov twice, but he wasn’t home—not that it matters, he’ll show up. I was out on my own business, too. I moved today, with my uncle. My uncle lives with me now. But that’s not important—let’s get to business. Give me the package, Nastasya. We’ll open it in a second. How are you feeling, brother?"
"I’m fine, I’m not sick. Razumihin, have you been here long?"
"I told you, I’ve been waiting three hours."
"No, before that."
"What do you mean?"
"How long have you been coming here?"
"I told you all this morning. Don’t you remember?"
Raskolnikov thought about it. The morning felt like a dream. He couldn’t remember alone, so he looked at Razumihin, confused.

"Hmm," Razumihin said. "He’s forgotten. I thought you weren’t yourself earlier. Now you’re better after your nap.... You really do look better. Great! Anyway, let’s get to business. Look here, my boy."
He started unwrapping the package, obviously interested.
"Believe me, brother, this means a lot to me. We need to get you back on your feet. Let’s start at the top. See this cap?" he said, pulling out a decent but ordinary cap. "Let me try it on you."
"Later," said Raskolnikov, waving him off.

"Come on, Rodya, don’t fight it. Later will be too late, and I’ll be up all night worrying—I bought it by guess, without measuring you. It fits perfectly!" he crowed, putting it on. "A good hat is the first step to looking respectable. Tolstyakov, a friend of mine, always has to take off his old hat in public because he’s embarrassed by it, and people think he’s just super polite. Look, Nastasya, here’s two hats: this old thing"—he held up Raskolnikov’s battered hat, which for some reason he called the Palmerston—"or this beauty! Guess the price, Rodya! What do you think, Nastasya?"
"Twenty copecks, no more, I bet," Nastasya answered.

"Twenty copecks! You’re kidding. These days you’d cost more than that—eighty copecks! And only because it’s been worn. Plus, they’ll give you another one for free next year if this one wears out. I swear! Now, for the United States of America, as we called them in school. I’m proud of these trousers," and he showed off a pair of light, gray wool pants. "No holes, no stains, and totally decent, even if a little worn. There’s a matching vest, too, very stylish. And the fact that they’re worn makes them softer—see, Rodya, the key to getting by is sticking to the right season. If you don’t demand asparagus in January, you save money; same goes for clothes. It’s summer, so I bought summer stuff. You’ll need heavier things in autumn, and these will be worn out by then anyway. Guess how much? Two roubles, twenty-five copecks! And if you wear them out, you get another suit for free! They only do that at Fedyaev’s; if you buy once, you’re set for life because you’ll never go back by choice. Now for the boots. They’re a bit used, but should last a couple months—they’re foreign-made, good leather. The secretary from the English Embassy sold them last week—he wore them six days but needed cash. Price: one and a half roubles. A deal, right?"
"But what if they don’t fit?" Nastasya said.

"Not fit? Just look!" and he pulled out Raskolnikov’s old, broken boot, still covered in dried mud. "I didn’t go empty-handed—they sized these from this monster. We all did our best. And about your shirts, your landlady took care of that. Here are three—hemp, but with a nice front. So, let’s add it up: eighty copecks for the cap, two roubles twenty-five for the suit—three roubles five copecks. A rouble and a half for the boots—so four roubles fifty-five copecks. Five roubles for the shirts—so nine roubles fifty-five copecks. Forty-five copecks left in change. So, Rodya, you’re all set: new clothes, and your coat will do for now. That’s the benefit of buying from Sharmer’s! For socks and other stuff, that’s up to you—we’ve got twenty-five roubles left. And don’t worry about Pashenka or paying for your room. She’ll trust you. Now, let me help you change your shirt—you’ll feel better."
"Leave me alone! I don’t want to!" Raskolnikov snapped. He’d listened to Razumihin’s joking about the clothes with disgust.

"Come on, brother, don’t tell me I did all that walking for nothing," Razumihin insisted. "Nastasya, don’t be shy, help me," and despite Raskolnikov’s protests, they changed his shirt. Raskolnikov flopped back on the pillows and was silent for a minute or two.
"I’ll never get rid of them," he thought. "What money did you buy all this with?" he asked at last, staring at the wall.
"Money? With your own—the cash the messenger brought from Vahrushin, from your mother. Don’t you remember?"
"I remember now," Raskolnikov said after a long, sullen pause. Razumihin looked at him, frowning and worried.
Just then, the door opened and a tall, heavy man walked

Zossimov was a tall, heavyset guy with a pale, puffy, clean-shaven face and straight, light-blond hair. He wore glasses and had a thick gold ring on his chubby finger. He was twenty-seven. He dressed in a stylish, loose light gray coat and summer trousers—everything about him was neat, fashionable, and spotless. His shirt was perfectly clean, and his watch chain was thick and flashy. He moved slowly and acted relaxed, even a bit casual, but you could tell he thought highly of himself, even though he tried to hide it. People found him boring, but everyone admitted he was good at his job.
"I’ve already been to see you twice today, man. Look, he’s finally woken up," Razumihin announced.
"I see, I see. So, how are you feeling now, hmm?" Zossimov said to Raskolnikov, watching him closely. He sat down at the end of the sofa and made himself comfortable.
"He’s still really down," Razumihin continued. "We just changed his sheets, and he almost started crying."
"That’s normal. You could have waited if he didn’t want to... His pulse is great. Still have a headache?"

"I’m fine, I’m perfectly fine!" Raskolnikov said firmly, sounding annoyed. He sat up on the sofa and glared at them with bright eyes, but then immediately fell back onto the pillow and turned to face the wall. Zossimov kept a close eye on him.
"Good... He’s getting better," Zossimov said lazily. "Has he eaten anything?"
They told him what Raskolnikov had eaten and asked what else he could have.

"He can have pretty much anything... soup, tea... But no mushrooms or cucumbers, and probably not meat either—but you know that already," Zossimov said. He and Razumihin exchanged glances. "No more medicine. I’ll check on him again tomorrow. Maybe even later today... but we’ll see."
"Tomorrow evening I’m taking him for a walk," Razumihin said. "We’re going to the Yusupov garden, and then to the Palais de Cristal."
"I wouldn’t bother him at all tomorrow, but... maybe just a little, we’ll see how he is," Zossimov replied.

"Ugh, what a pain! I have a house-warming party tonight. It’s just around the corner. Couldn’t he come? He could just lie on the sofa. You’re coming, right?" Razumihin asked Zossimov. "Don’t forget, you promised."
"Sure, but I’ll come a bit later. What’s the plan?"
"Oh, nothing fancy—tea, vodka, herrings. There’ll be a pie... just our friends."
"And who’s coming?"
"Almost all are neighbors from around here, mostly new friends, except my old uncle—but he’s new too, just got into Petersburg yesterday on business. We only meet every five years."
"What does he do?"

"He’s been stuck his whole life as a district postmaster—lives off a tiny pension. He’s sixty-five, not much to talk about... but I like him. Porfiry Petrovitch, the head of the Investigation Department, is coming too... But you know him."
"Is he related to you too?"
"Very distant relative. But why are you frowning? Is it because you argued once? Are you not coming because of that?"
"I couldn’t care less about him."
"Even better. Anyway, there’ll be some students, a teacher, a government clerk, a musician, an officer, and Zametov."
"Tell me, honestly, what do you or he"—Zossimov nodded at Raskolnikov—"have in common with Zametov?"
"Oh, you and your principles! You always go by your rules, never just do what you want. I just care if someone’s a good guy, that’s all. Zametov’s a great guy."
"Even if he takes bribes?"

"Well, so what if he does? I don’t care," Razumihin snapped irritably. "I’m not saying I admire him for it. I’m just saying he’s a decent person in his own way! But if you look at everyone from every angle, are there really many good people left? I probably wouldn’t be worth a baked onion myself... maybe not even with you added on."
"That’s too cheap; I’d give two for you."

"And I wouldn’t give more than one for you. Enough with your jokes! Zametov’s basically just a kid. I can mess with him, and you have to encourage him, not push him away. You never help someone by pushing them away, especially a young guy. You have to be extra careful with them. Man, you ‘progressive’ types just don’t get it. You hurt yourselves by always putting others down... But if you want to know, we actually do have something in common."
"I’d like to know what that is."
"It’s all about a house painter... We’re helping him out of a jam! Though actually, there’s nothing to worry about anymore. It’s super obvious. We’re just pushing things along."
"A painter?"
"Didn’t I tell you about it? I only told you the start—about the old pawnbroker’s murder. Well, the painter got tangled up in it..."
"Oh, I heard about that murder before, and was pretty interested... partly... for some reason... I read about it in the news too..."
"Lizaveta was killed, too," Nastasya suddenly blurted out, looking at Raskolnikov. She’d been standing by the door, listening the whole time.
"Lizaveta," Raskolnikov mumbled, barely audible.
"Lizaveta, the one who sold old clothes. Didn’t you know her? She used to come here. She even mended a shirt for you once."

Raskolnikov turned to the wall and started staring at a messy white flower with brown lines on the dirty, yellow wallpaper. He focused on counting the petals, the scallops, and the lines. His arms and legs felt numb, as if they weren’t even there. He didn’t try to move, just kept his eyes fixed on the flower.
"But what about the painter?" Zossimov interrupted Nastasya’s talk, clearly annoyed. She sighed and fell silent.
"He was accused of the murder," Razumihin continued, getting heated.
"Was there actually any evidence against him?"

"Evidence? Ha! It was barely evidence, and that’s what we have to prove. It was just like when they blamed those guys Koch and Pestryakov at first. Ugh, it’s all handled so stupidly, it makes me sick, even if it’s not my business! Pestryakov might come tonight... By the way, Rodya, you already heard about this before you got sick—the day before you fainted at the police station while they were talking about it."
Zossimov looked at Raskolnikov with curiosity. Raskolnikov didn’t move.
"Honestly, Razumihin, you’re such a busybody," Zossimov commented.

"Maybe, but we’re still gonna help him," Razumihin shouted, slamming his fist on the table. "The worst part isn’t the lying—you can forgive lying, it sometimes leads to the truth. The worst part is when they lie and then believe their own lies. I respect Porfiry, but... What made them suspect Koch and Pestryakov at first? The door was locked, and when they came back with the porter, it was open. So they decided Koch and Pestryakov must be murderers! That was their reasoning!"
"Don’t get so worked up; they just held them for questioning—they had no choice... And, by the way, I met that guy Koch. He used to buy stuff people never picked up from the old woman, right?"

"Yeah, he’s a scammer. He buys up bad debts too. It’s his thing. But forget about him! You know what bugs me? It’s how stuck-in-the-past and lazy their whole process is... And this case could be a way to show a new method. You can figure out the real killer just by the psychological clues. ‘We have facts,’ they say. But facts aren’t everything—half of it is how you understand them!"
"So can you interpret them, then?"
"At least I can’t stay quiet when I feel like I could help, if only... Anyway, do you know all the details?"
"I’m waiting to hear about the painter."

"Oh, right! Here’s what happened: Early on the third day after the murder, while they were still messing with Koch and Pestryakov—who had already explained everything they did and were clearly innocent—something unexpected happened. A peasant named Dushkin, who runs a bar across from the building, brought a jeweler’s box with some gold earrings to the police and told a long story. ‘The day before yesterday, just after eight,’—notice the day and time!—‘a house painter, Nikolay, who’d already stopped by that day, brought me this jewelry box and asked for two roubles for it. When I asked where he got it, he said he found it in the street. I didn’t ask more.’ That’s Dushkin’s story. ‘I gave him a rouble—figured if he didn’t pawn it with me, he’d just pawn it somewhere else and spend it on booze, so it might as well stay with me. If anything turned up, I’d give it to the police.’ Of course, that’s a lie—Dushkin’s a pawnbroker and buys stolen goods, and he wouldn’t give up a thirty-rouble trinket unless he was scared. But anyway, back to Dushkin’s story. ‘I’ve known Nikolay Dementyev since he was a kid; we’re both from the same place—Zaraïsk, both Ryazan men. Nikolay isn’t a drunk, but he does drink, and I knew he was painting in that building with Dmitri, who’s from our village too. As soon as he got the rouble, he changed it, had a couple drinks, took his change, and left. I didn’t see Dmitri with him then. The next day I heard someone had killed Alyona Ivanovna and her sister, Lizaveta, with an axe. I knew them, and right away I got suspicious about the earrings, since the old woman lent money on pawned things. I went to the building and started asking around quietly. First, I asked, “Is Nikolay here?” Dmitri told me Nikolay had gone off somewhere, came home at dawn drunk, stayed ten minutes, and left again. Dmitri didn’t see him again and was finishing the job alone. And their painting job was on the same floor as the murder, the second floor. After hearing that, I didn’t say anything to anyone’—that’s Dushkin’s story—‘but I looked into the murder as much as I could and went home feeling even more suspicious. At eight this morning’—the third day, remember—‘I saw Nikolay come in, not totally drunk, but not sober either—he could understand what was said to him. He sat down and didn’t speak. Only one stranger was there, someone I knew was asleep on a bench, and our two boys were around. “Have you seen Dmitri?” I asked. “No, I haven’t,” he said. “And you haven’t been here either?” “Not since the day before yesterday,” he said. “Where did you sleep last night?” “In Peski, with the Kolomensky guys.” “Where did you get those earrings?” I asked. “Found them in the street,” and he said it kind of weirdly; he wouldn’t look at me. “Did you hear what happened that night, at that same time, on that staircase?” I said. “No,” he answered, “I hadn’t heard,” but he was listening hard, his eyes staring, and he turned white as a ghost. I told him all about it and he grabbed his hat and started to get up. I tried to keep him there. “Wait, Nikolay,” I said, “won’t you have a drink?” I signaled the boy to block the door and came out from behind the bar; but Nikolay dashed out and ran down the street. I haven’t seen him since. At that point, I was sure—he was guilty, no doubt...’"
"Sounds like it," Zossimov said.

"Wait! Let me finish. Of course, they searched everywhere for Nikolay; they held Dushkin and searched his place; Dmitri was arrested too, and the Kolomensky guys as well. The day before yesterday they found Nikolay in a bar at the edge of town. He’d gone there, taken off his silver cross, and traded it for a drink. A few minutes later, the barmaid went out to the cowshed, and through a crack in the wall saw Nikolay in the next stall making a noose from his sash, standing on a block, and trying to hang himself. She screamed, people ran in. ‘So that’s what you’re up to!’ they said. ‘Take me,’ he said, ‘to such-and-such police officer. I’ll confess everything.’ They took him to the station—here, actually—with guards. So, they questioned him: How old are you? ‘Twenty-two,’ and so on. Then: ‘When you were working with Dmitri, did you see anyone on the stairs at that time?’ ‘Maybe people were going up and down, but I didn’t notice.’ ‘Did you hear anything—any noise?’ ‘Nothing special.’ ‘Did you hear, Nikolay, that on the same day the widow and her sister were murdered and robbed?’ ‘I didn’t know anything about it. I only heard from Afanasy Pavlovitch the day before yesterday.’ ‘Where did you find the earrings?’ ‘On the pavement.’ ‘Why didn’t you go to work with Dmitri that day?’ ‘Because I was drinking.’ ‘Where were you drinking?’ ‘Oh, at such-and-such place.’ ‘Why did you run from Dushkin’s?’ ‘Because I was really scared.’ ‘What were you afraid of?’ ‘That I’d be blamed.’ ‘How could you be scared if you weren’t guilty?’ And get this, Zossimov—they actually asked him exactly that way! I know because it was repeated to me word for word! What do you think of that?"
"Well, anyway, that’s some pretty strong evidence."

"I’m not talking about the evidence, I’m talking about that question—they’re so sure of themselves. Anyway, they kept pressing him and finally he confessed: ‘I didn’t find it in the street, but in the apartment where I was painting with Dmitri.’ ‘How did that happen?’ ‘Well, Dmitri and I painted there all day, and just as we were finishing up, Dmitri took a brush and wiped paint on my face, then ran off with me chasing him. I chased him, yelling, and at the bottom of the stairs we ran right into the porter and a couple of gentlemen—I don’t remember how many. The porter cursed at us, the other porter cursed too, and the porter’s wife came out and yelled at us, too; then a man came in with a lady and he cursed us too, because Dmitri and I were blocking the way. I grabbed Dmitri’s hair and pulled him down, started wrestling him, and he grabbed my hair too, and we both started wrestling. But we were just horsing around, not mad, just goofing off. Then Dmitri ran off into the street and I chased him but didn’t catch him, so I came back to the apartment alone to pack up my stuff. I started gathering my things, waiting for Dmitri, when in the hallway by the door, I stepped on the box. I saw it wrapped up in paper. I unwrapped it, saw there were some little hooks, opened them, and there were the earrings inside....’"
"Behind the door? Lying behind the door? Behind the door?" Raskolnikov suddenly shouted, staring at Razumihin in terror, and slowly sat up on the sofa, supporting himself with his hand.
"Yeah... why? What’s wrong? What is it?" Razumihin asked, getting up from his seat too.
"Nothing," Raskolnikov answered weakly, turning to face the wall. Everyone fell silent for a bit.
"He must have just woken up from a dream," Razumihin finally said, looking at Zossimov for confirmation. Zossimov just shook his head slightly.
"Well, go on," Zossimov said. "What happened next?"

"What next? As soon as Nikolay saw the earrings, he forgot all about Dmitri and everything else, grabbed his cap, and ran to Dushkin’s, where he got a rouble. He lied, saying he found them in the street, and then went off drinking. He keeps repeating the same story about the murder: ‘I know nothing, I didn’t hear about it until the day before yesterday.’ ‘Why didn’t you go to the police sooner?’ ‘I was scared.’ ‘Why did you try to hang yourself?’ ‘From anxiety.’ ‘What anxiety?’ ‘That I’d be accused.’ That’s the whole story. And what do you think the police decided from that?"
"Well, there’s no need to guess. That’s a clue, at least—it’s something. Would you just let the painter go?"
"Now they’re sure he’s the killer. No doubts at all."

"That’s ridiculous. You’re upset. But what about the earrings? You’ve got to admit, if the earrings from the old lady’s box ended up with Nikolay on the same day and hour, there’s got to be a reason. That means a lot in a case like this."

"How did they get there? How did they get there?" Razumihin cried. "You’re a doctor, you study people, you should see what kind of guy Nikolay is from the story. Can’t you tell right away he’s telling the plain truth? The earrings got into his hands exactly how he said—they were on the floor, and he picked them up."
"The plain truth! But didn’t he admit he lied at first?"

"Listen to me—really listen! The porter, Koch, Pestryakov, the other porter, the porter’s wife, the woman in the porter’s lodge, and the man Kryukov who’d just gotten out of a cab and came into the entry with a lady—eight or ten witnesses in all—agree that Nikolay was wrestling Dmitri on the ground, beating him, while Dmitri grabbed Nikolay’s hair and beat him too. They were blocking the hallway, getting yelled at by everyone while they, like little kids (that’s exactly what the witnesses said), rolled around, screamed, fought, and laughed with ridiculous faces, then chased each other into the street. Now pay attention—the bodies upstairs were still warm when they were found! If they, or even just Nikolay, had killed those women and stolen the jewelry, would they really have started acting like that—laughing, goofing off, attracting attention—right after murdering two people? And there are a dozen witnesses who saw it!"
"It is strange! It’s impossible, really, but..."

"No, man, no ‘buts.’ And if the fact that Nikolay had the earrings right after the murder seems like strong evidence against him—even though his story makes sense and shouldn’t count against him much—you have to consider the facts that prove he’s innocent, especially since they’re impossible to deny. And do you really think our legal system would accept, or even be able to accept, this fact—just because of a psychological impossibility—as definite proof to break down the evidence against him? No, they won’t, because they found the jewelry box and Nikolay tried to hang himself, ‘which he couldn’t have done unless he felt guilty.’ That’s what gets me, you see!"
"Okay, I get that you’re worked up! Wait a second, I forgot to ask: how do they know the box came from the old woman?"
"That’s been proven," Razumihin said reluctantly, frowning. "Koch recognized the jewelry box and gave the owner’s name, and the owner proved it was his."
"That’s bad. Now, another thing. Did anyone see Nikolay at the exact time Koch and Pestryakov were first going upstairs? Any evidence about that?"

"Nobody saw him," Razumihin answered, annoyed. "That’s the worst part. Koch and Pestryakov didn’t notice them when they went up either, but their testimony wouldn’t have been worth much anyway. They said the apartment door was open and there must have been work going on, but they didn’t pay attention and couldn’t remember if there were actually workers there."
"Hm!... So the only thing helping the defense is that they were wrestling and laughing. That’s a pretty strong argument, but... How do you explain what happened?"

"How do I explain it? It’s obvious—at least, where to look for the answer is obvious, and the jewelry box points to it. The real killer dropped those earrings. He was upstairs, locked inside, when Koch and Pestryakov knocked. Koch, like an idiot, didn’t wait at the door, so the murderer slipped out and ran down too; he had no other way out. He hid in the apartment while Nikolay and Dmitri had just run out. He waited there until the coast was clear, then calmly went downstairs at the exact moment Dmitri and Nikolay ran into the street and there was no one in the entry; maybe someone saw him but didn’t notice. Tons of people go in and out. The killer must have dropped the earrings from his pocket while hiding behind the door and didn’t realize it, since he had other things on his mind. The jewelry box proves he was there. That’s my explanation."
"Too clever! Really, you’re overthinking it. That’s too much."
"Why? Why do you say that?"

The man who walked in wasn’t young. He looked stiff and important, with a sour, suspicious face. He stopped in the doorway and stared around with obvious shock and even some rudeness, as though he couldn’t believe what kind of place he’d entered. He looked around Raskolnikov’s tiny, cramped room, acting as if the whole place offended him. Then he looked hard at Raskolnikov himself, who was lying on the dirty, torn-up sofa, messy, in pajamas, hair wild, and staring right back. After that, the man studied Razumihin, who was sitting nearby, scruffy and unshaven, but meeting his stare confidently. No one said a word for a couple minutes; the silence was tense and awkward. Realizing that his attitude wouldn’t get him anywhere in this shabby room, the visitor tried to appear a little friendlier, though he still sounded strict as he clearly asked Zossimov:
“Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov, a student, or was a student?”
Zossimov started to answer, but Razumihin beat him to it.
“He’s right there on the sofa! What do you want?”
Razumihin’s blunt “what do you want” seemed to throw the fancy man off. He started to reply to Razumihin, but changed his mind and turned back to Zossimov.
“This is Raskolnikov,” Zossimov mumbled, nodding at him. He yawned widely, stuck his hand in his vest pocket, pulled out a huge gold watch, checked the time, and then slowly put it away.

Raskolnikov didn’t say anything, just lay there on his back, staring at the stranger without really understanding who he was. Now that he’d turned away from the weird flower pattern on the wallpaper, his face was pale and twisted with pain, like someone who’d just gone through a terrible ordeal. But as the stranger stood there, Raskolnikov started to get curious, then suspicious, and finally a little scared. When Zossimov said, “This is Raskolnikov,” he suddenly sat up on the couch and, with a shaky but challenging voice, said:
“Yes, I’m Raskolnikov! What do you want?”
The visitor looked him over and announced, very seriously:
“Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin. I hope you’ve at least heard of me?”
But Raskolnikov, who had been expecting something completely different, just stared at him blankly, as if he’d never heard the name Pyotr Petrovitch before in his life.
“You mean to say you really haven’t heard anything yet?” Luzhin asked, looking embarrassed.

Instead of answering, Raskolnikov sank back into the pillow, put his hands behind his head, and stared up at the ceiling. Luzhin looked upset. Zossimov and Razumihin stared at him even harder, and Luzhin started to look awkward and lost.
“I had assumed,” he stammered, “that a letter sent over ten days—maybe two weeks ago...”
“Hey, why are you standing in the doorway?” Razumihin broke in. “If you have something to say, sit down. Nastasya, can you make space? Here’s a chair, come on in!”

Razumihin pushed his chair back, making a small gap between himself and the table, and waited, a bit squished, for the visitor to squeeze through. Luzhin had no choice and made his way in, bumping and hurrying, and finally sat down, looking nervously at Razumihin.

“There’s no need to be nervous,” Razumihin said. “Rodya’s been sick for five days and out of his mind for three, but he’s getting better now and eating again. That’s his doctor, who just checked him. I’m Rodya’s friend, also a former student, and I’m taking care of him. So don’t mind us, just do what you came to do.”
“Thank you. But am I not disturbing the patient?” Luzhin asked Zossimov.
“N-no,” Zossimov mumbled. “You might even entertain him.” He yawned again.

“He’s been awake for a while, since this morning,” Razumihin added, sounding casual and friendly enough that Luzhin finally relaxed a little—maybe because this scruffy guy had said he was a student, too.
“Your mother,” Luzhin began.
“Ahem!” Razumihin coughed loudly. Luzhin looked at him, confused.
“It’s okay, go on.”
Luzhin shrugged.
