“Your mother started a letter to you while I was visiting her. I waited a few days after getting here before coming to see you, just to make sure you already knew the news. But now, to my surprise...”
“I know, I know!” Raskolnikov suddenly snapped, sounding annoyed. “So you’re the fiancé? I know, that’s enough!”
This time, Luzhin was definitely offended, but he kept quiet and tried to figure out what was happening. There was a brief silence.

Meanwhile, Raskolnikov, now turned a little toward Luzhin, started studying him as if he hadn’t really looked at him before, or as if something new had caught his attention. He sat up on purpose to look more closely. There was definitely something about Luzhin’s look that fit with being called “the fiancé” so bluntly. For one thing, he looked like he’d spent his first days in the city getting himself perfectly dressed for meeting his future bride—not that there was anything wrong with that. Even the way Luzhin proudly showed off his new clothes could be forgiven, since he was supposed to be the fiancé. All his clothes were straight from the tailor, but almost too new and too carefully chosen. Even his new, stylish round hat seemed like part of his “I’m engaged” outfit—he held it with extra care. Luzhin had fancy lavender gloves (real Louvain ones), but instead of wearing them, he just carried them in his hand to show them off. His clothes were mostly light, cheerful summer colors: a nice fawn-colored jacket, thin light trousers, a matching vest, crisp new shirt, and a white tie with pink stripes. The funny thing was, all of it actually looked pretty good on him. His face, which was still handsome and looked younger than his actual forty-five years, was framed by thick, dark sideburns and a shiny, clean-shaven chin. Even his hair, though graying and obviously styled at the barber’s, didn’t look silly or fake. If there was something off-putting about Luzhin’s appearance, it wasn’t his looks or his clothes, but something else in his expression. After looking Luzhin over without any politeness, Raskolnikov gave him a wicked smile, lay back on his pillow, and stared at the ceiling again.
But Luzhin toughened up and decided to ignore their weird behavior.

“I’m very sorry to find you like this,” he said, making himself speak. “If I’d known you were sick, I would have come sooner. But you know how business is. I’ve got important legal work in the Senate, not to mention other things you can imagine. Your mother and sister should be here any minute.”
Raskolnikov moved, looking like he wanted to say something, his face suddenly more animated. Luzhin stopped, waited, but when Raskolnikov said nothing, he continued:
“...Any minute now. I’ve found a place for them to stay when they arrive.”
“Where?” Raskolnikov asked weakly.
“Very close by, in Bakaleyev’s house.”
“That’s on Voskresensky Street,” Razumihin added. “There are two floors of rooms owned by a merchant named Yushin; I’ve been there myself.”
“Yes, those rooms...”
“It’s a terrible place—dirty, smelly, and kind of sketchy. Bad things have happened there, and all sorts of weird people live there. I was there once about some scandal. But it’s cheap...”

“Of course, I couldn’t find all that out, since I’m new to Petersburg,” Luzhin replied stiffly. “But the two rooms are very clean, and it’s only for a little while... I’ve already rented our permanent apartment,” he said to Raskolnikov, “and I’m getting it fixed up. Meanwhile, I’m squeezed in with my friend Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov, at Madame Lippevechsel’s place; he’s the one who told me about Bakaleyev’s house...”
“Lebeziatnikov?” Raskolnikov said slowly, like he was trying to remember something.
“Yes, Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov, he works for the Ministry. Do you know him?”
“Yes... no,” Raskolnikov replied.

“Sorry, I thought you might, since you asked. I was once his guardian.... He’s a nice young guy and pretty modern-thinking. I like meeting young people; you learn a lot from them.” Luzhin glanced around, hoping for interest.
“What do you mean?” asked Razumihin.

“In really important ways,” Luzhin replied, clearly happy with the question. “See, I haven’t been to Petersburg in ten years. We hear about new ideas and changes in the provinces, but you see things much more clearly here. I think you learn the most by watching young people, so I’m glad to be here...”
“Glad about what?”
“That’s a big question. Maybe I’m wrong, but I think I see clearer thinking, more criticism, more practicality...”
“That’s true,” Zossimov chimed in.

“Nonsense! There’s nothing practical about it,” Razumihin snapped. “Real practicality is hard to find; it doesn’t just fall from the sky. For two hundred years, we’ve been cut off from real life. Sure, there are new ideas and a desire to do good, but it’s all kind of childish, and though there’s some honesty, there are tons of crooks, too. But practicality? Real practicality means having your act together.”

“I don’t agree,” Luzhin replied, clearly enjoying the debate. “People make mistakes, but that just shows they’re passionate and affected by their environment. If not much progress has been made, it’s only because there hasn’t been much time. I won’t even get into resources. Personally, I think some progress has happened already. New ideas and works are replacing our old, dreamy authors. Literature is more mature, and lots of harmful old prejudices have been thrown out and laughed at. Basically, we’ve cut ourselves off from the past forever, and I think that’s huge...”
“He memorized all that just to show off!” Raskolnikov said suddenly.
“What?” Luzhin asked, not catching what he said. Raskolnikov didn’t answer.
“It’s all true,” Zossimov quickly jumped in.

“Isn’t it?” Luzhin continued, giving Zossimov a friendly look. Then, turning to Razumihin, he added with a bit of pride and superiority—he almost said “young man”—“You have to admit there’s progress, especially in science and economics...”
“That’s just the usual stuff.”

“No, it’s not just the usual!” Luzhin said, maybe a little too fast. “Before, if someone said, ‘love your neighbor,’ what happened? You’d split your coat in half and both end up cold. Like the Russian saying, ‘Chase two rabbits and you catch neither.’ Now science says, love yourself first, because everything in life is based on self-interest. If you take care of yourself, you keep your coat whole. Economics says that the more people manage their own affairs well, the more everyone benefits. So by getting rich for myself, I’m actually helping others too—not by charity, but because progress raises everyone up. It’s a simple idea, but it took a long time to reach us because of old-fashioned feelings. Really, it shouldn’t be that hard to see...”

“Sorry, I’m not that smart,” Razumihin interrupted sharply. “So let’s drop it. I started this conversation for a reason, but after three years of hearing the same old talk, I’m sick of it—it makes me cringe when people go on like that. I get you want to show what you know, and that’s fine. I just wanted to see what kind of person you are, because a lot of shady people have gotten involved in ‘progress’ lately and twisted everything for themselves, dragging the whole cause through the mud. That’s enough!”
“Excuse me, sir,” Luzhin said stiffly, clearly insulted. “Are you seriously suggesting that I...”
“Oh, come on, of course not!... That’s enough,” Razumihin said, turning away from Luzhin to talk with Zossimov again.
Luzhin was smart enough to accept that. He decided to leave in a minute or two.
“I hope,” he said to Raskolnikov, “that after you recover, and because of our family connection, we can get to know each other better... Most important, I hope you get well soon...”
Raskolnikov didn’t even look at him. Luzhin started to get up.
“One of her customers must have killed her,” Zossimov said flatly.
“No doubt,” Razumihin agreed. “Porfiry isn’t saying what he thinks, but he’s questioning everyone who pawned things with her.”
“He’s questioning them?” Raskolnikov asked out loud.
“Yeah. So what?”
“Nothing.”
“How’s he finding them all?” Zossimov asked.
“Koch gave some names, others are on the pledge tickets, and some came forward on their own.”
“The killer must have been clever and experienced! So bold! So calm!”

“Actually, I don’t think so,” Razumihin interrupted. “That’s what’s confusing everyone. I’m sure he wasn’t clever or experienced, and this was probably his first crime! If you think about it, it looks like luck is all that saved him—and luck can do anything. He probably didn’t even plan things out! Look how he did it: he took cheap jewelry, stuffed his pockets, rummaged through her stuff—and meanwhile, they found fifteen hundred roubles and banknotes in a box in her dresser! He didn’t know how to rob; he only managed to kill. I’m telling you, it was his first crime; he panicked. He escaped more by accident than by smarts!”

“You’re talking about the old pawnbroker murder, right?” Luzhin asked Zossimov. He was standing, holding his hat and gloves, but before leaving, he wanted to sound smart and make a good impression. His pride got the better of him.
“Yes. You’ve heard about it?”
“Oh, yes, since I’m in the area.”
“Do you know the details?”

“Not really, but there’s something about the case that interests me—the whole question, actually. Besides the fact that crime has gone up among the poor in the last five years, there’s also more crime among the upper classes. You hear about students robbing the mail, people in good positions forging banknotes, and just recently in Moscow, a whole gang was caught making fake lottery tickets—one of the leaders was a history professor! And our secretary was murdered abroad for who knows what reason. And if this pawnbroker was killed by someone from a higher class—since peasants don’t pawn gold jewelry—what does that say about the decay of the ‘civilized’ part of society?”
“There are a lot of economic changes,” Zossimov commented.
“Why is that?” Razumihin jumped in. “Maybe it’s because we’re just not practical.”
“What do you mean?”

“When the professor in Moscow was asked why he was making fake notes, he said, ‘Everyone’s getting rich somehow, so I want to get rich quickly too.’ I don’t remember the exact words, but basically, he wanted money without waiting or working! We’re used to having everything done for us, to getting help all the time. Then, when the big moment came,[*] everyone showed their true colors.”
[*] The footnote says this refers to the emancipation of the serfs in 1861.
“But what about morals? Principles and such...”
“Why do you care?” Raskolnikov cut in suddenly. “It fits with your theory!”
“My theory?”
“Yeah, if you take your idea to its logical end, it means people can kill others...”
“Really!” Luzhin protested.
“No, that’s not right,” Zossimov added.
Raskolnikov lay there, pale, his upper lip twitching, breathing hard.
“There’s a limit to everything,” Luzhin said, acting superior. “Economic theories don’t encourage murder, and you just have to imagine...”

“And is it true,” Raskolnikov suddenly interrupted again, his voice shaking with anger and a sort of twisted pleasure in insulting Luzhin, “that you told your fiancée... right after she agreed to marry you... that what you liked most... was that she was poor... because it’s better to raise a wife out of poverty, so you can control her completely and always remind her you’re her savior?”

“Come on,” Luzhin shouted angrily, his face bright red. “Twisting my words like that! Let me assure you, the story you heard, or rather, the story someone told you, is totally false. And I... I think I know who... in short... this accusation... your mother... She’s a good woman, but a bit too dreamy and romantic. Still, I never thought she’d misunderstand and twist things so wildly.... And really... really...”
“Listen,” Raskolnikov said, sitting up on his pillow and staring at Luzhin with sharp, blazing eyes. “Listen to me.”
“What?” Luzhin stood still, looking back angrily. There was a long pause.
“If you ever... mention a single word... about my mother again... I’ll throw you down the stairs!”
“What’s wrong with you?” Razumihin shouted.

“So that’s how it is?” Luzhin turned pale and bit his lip. “Let me tell you, sir,” he said, trying hard to keep calm but breathing heavily, “from the moment I met you, you were hostile to me, but I stayed to learn more. I could forgive a lot in a sick man and a relative, but you... after this, never again...”
“I’m not sick,” Raskolnikov yelled.
“That’s even worse...”
“Get lost!”

But Luzhin was already on his way out, squeezing past the table and chair; this time Razumihin stood up to let him pass. Luzhin didn’t look at anyone or even nod to Zossimov, who had been trying to signal him to leave Raskolnikov alone. He left, lifting his hat to keep it from getting crushed as he ducked out the door—even the way he walked away showed how insulted he felt.
“How could you—how could you?” Razumihin said, shaking his head in confusion.

“Leave me alone—just leave me alone, all of you!” Raskolnikov shouted wildly. “Will you ever stop torturing me? I’m not afraid of you! I’m not afraid of anyone, not now! Go away! I want to be alone, alone, alone!”
“Let’s go,” Zossimov said to Razumihin, nodding toward the door.
“But we can’t just leave him like this!”
“Let’s go,” Zossimov repeated firmly, heading out. Razumihin paused, then hurried to catch up.
“It might be worse if we don’t listen to him,” Zossimov said as they went downstairs. “He shouldn’t be upset.”
“What’s wrong with him?”

“He needs some kind of positive shock, that’s what would help! He was better earlier.... You know he’s got something weighing on his mind. Some fixed idea stuck there.... I’m really worried; I’m sure of it!”
“Maybe it’s that guy, Pyotr Petrovitch. From what he said, he’s going to marry Raskolnikov’s sister, and Raskolnikov got a letter about it just before he got sick....”
“Yeah, curse that man! He might have messed up everything. But did you notice, Raskolnikov doesn’t care about anything, except he gets really worked up about the murder?”
“Yes, yes,” Razumihin agreed, “I noticed that too. He’s interested and scared. The day he was sick at the police station, it shocked him so much he fainted.”
“Tell me more about that tonight, and I’ll tell you something later. He really interests me! I’ll come check on him again in half an hour.... There’s no danger of infection, though.”
“Thanks! I’ll wait with Pashenka and keep an eye on him through Nastasya....”
Left alone, Raskolnikov looked at Nastasya with frustration and misery, but she still lingered.
“Won’t you have some tea now?” she asked.
“Later! I’m tired! Leave me alone.”
He turned sharply to face the wall; Nastasya finally left.

As soon as Nastasya left, Raskolnikov got up, locked the door, opened the package Razumihin had brought earlier, and started getting dressed. Strangely, he suddenly felt completely calm—none of his recent fever or fear remained. For the first time, he was at peace, moving with purpose as if he knew exactly what he was doing. “Today, today,” he whispered to himself. He realized he was still weak, but his intense focus made him feel strong and confident. He also hoped he wouldn’t collapse in the street. Once he was dressed in all new clothes, he stared at the money on the table, thought for a moment, then put it in his pocket—twenty-five roubles. He also grabbed all the small change left over from what Razumihin had spent on the clothes. Quietly, he unlocked the door, slipped out, went downstairs, and peeked into the kitchen. Nastasya was busy with the landlady’s samovar and didn’t notice him. No one would have expected him to go out. A minute later, he was out on the street.

It was almost eight o’clock and the sun was setting. The air was just as hot and suffocating as before, but Raskolnikov breathed it in eagerly, even though it stank and was full of dust. His head spun a little; a wild energy flashed in his feverish eyes and pale, thin face. He had no idea where he was going—he just knew one thing: “it has to end today, once and for all, right now. I’m not coming home without ending it, because I can’t go on like this.” How exactly would he end it, or with what? He didn’t know, and he didn’t want to think about it. Thinking only made things worse. All he felt was that something had to change, “one way or another,” he kept telling himself with desperate confidence.

Out of habit, he walked his usual route toward the Hay Market. On the street outside a little general store, a dark-haired young man was playing a barrel organ, grinding out a sad song, while a fifteen-year-old girl stood on the pavement and sang along. She wore an old, faded dress, a cape, and a straw hat with a bright feather, all pretty shabby. Her voice was strong but rough from singing on the streets, and she was hoping for a coin from the store. Raskolnikov joined a couple of listeners, took out a five-copeck coin, and gave it to the girl. She stopped singing in the middle of a high note, shouted at the organ grinder, “Let’s go,” and they both moved on to the next shop.
“Do you like street music?” Raskolnikov asked a middle-aged man who was standing nearby. The man looked at him, surprised and confused.

“I really like hearing singing with a street organ,” Raskolnikov said, his tone oddly serious for such a simple topic. “I especially like it on cold, dark, damp autumn evenings—when it’s wet and there’s no wind and the street lamps shine through the snow. You know what I mean?”
“I don’t know... Excuse me...” muttered the man, obviously freaked out by Raskolnikov’s question and weird attitude. He quickly crossed the street to get away.

Raskolnikov kept walking and soon reached the corner of the Hay Market, where the huckster and his wife had spoken with Lizaveta before—but they weren’t there now. Recognizing the place, he stopped, looked around, and asked a young guy in a red shirt who was staring at a grain shop.
“Isn’t there a man who runs a booth here with his wife?”
“Lots of people run booths here,” the young man replied, glancing at Raskolnikov with barely hidden annoyance.
“What’s his name?”
“Whatever name he was baptized with.”
“Aren’t you from Zaraïsk, too? Which province?”
The young man looked Raskolnikov over again.
“It’s not a province, sir, it’s a district. Forgive me, sir!”
“Is that a tavern up there?”
“Yeah, it’s a restaurant. There’s billiards, and you’ll even find princesses there... la-la!”

Raskolnikov crossed the square. In that corner, a thick crowd of peasants was gathered. He pushed his way into the middle, looking at their faces. He felt a strange urge to talk to people. But the peasants ignored him, busy shouting in their own groups. He stood there for a while, thinking, then turned right toward V.

He had often walked down that little street, which bent at an angle from the market to Sadovy Street. Lately, whenever he felt down, he’d been drawn to wander around this part of town, hoping it would make him feel even worse.

Now he walked along, his mind blank. That area was full of big buildings, all rented out as bars and cheap restaurants. Women kept darting in and out, bareheaded and in their house-clothes. Some stood in groups on the pavement, especially near the bright entrances to the party places on the lower floors. From one of these, loud music, singing, guitar strumming, and shouting spilled out into the street. A bunch of women hung around the door—some on the steps, some standing, some sitting on the pavement, all talking. A drunk soldier, smoking a cigarette, staggered past them, swearing as if he’d forgotten where he was going. Two beggars were fighting, and a man who was dead drunk lay sprawled across the road. Raskolnikov joined the crowd of women, who talked in rough, raspy voices. They were bareheaded, wearing cotton dresses and goatskin shoes. Some were as old as forty, some as young as seventeen, almost all with black eyes.

Raskolnikov felt strangely drawn to the music and loud noise coming from the bar below. Someone inside was dancing wildly, stomping his heels in time to the guitar and a high, thin voice singing a cheerful tune. Raskolnikov listened with gloomy curiosity, leaning down at the entrance and peeking in from the sidewalk.
“Oh, my handsome soldier
Don’t beat me for nothing,”
sang the thin voice. Raskolnikov was suddenly obsessed with figuring out what the song was, as if it were the most important thing in the world.
“Should I go in?” he wondered. “They’re laughing—probably drunk. Should I get drunk too?”
“Why don’t you come in?” one of the women asked. Her voice was still pretty and less rough than the others; she was young and actually not bad-looking—the only one in the group like that.
“Hey, she’s pretty,” he said, straightening up and looking at her.
She smiled, clearly pleased with the compliment.
“You’re not bad yourself,” she told him.
“He sure is skinny!” another woman said in a deep voice. “Did you just get out of the hospital or something?”
“They’re all general’s daughters, I guess, but every one of them’s got a snub nose,” joked a tipsy peasant in a loose coat, smirking. “Look how happy they are.”
“Get out of here!”
“I’ll go, darling!”
He rushed down into the bar. Raskolnikov continued on his way.
“Hey, mister!” the young woman called after him.
“What?”
She hesitated.
“I’d love to spend an hour with you, kind sir, but I’m a little shy right now. Give me six copecks for a drink, will you?”
Raskolnikov handed her the first coin he found—fifteen copecks.
“Wow, what a nice gentleman!”
“What’s your name?”
“Ask for Duclida.”
“That’s just too much,” one of the women said, shaking her head at Duclida. “How can you ask like that? I’d die of shame...”

Raskolnikov looked curiously at the speaker. She was a thirty-year-old woman, her face pocked and bruised, her upper lip swollen. She spoke quietly and seriously. “Where was it,” Raskolnikov thought, “that I read about someone about to be executed who said, an hour before his death, that if he could live on a high rock, on a tiny ledge, with the ocean and darkness and storms all around, but just enough room to stand—he’d rather live forever like that than die at once? Just to live, to live, to live! Life, no matter what!... How true! God, it’s true! People are such rotten creatures... and it’s just as rotten to call them rotten for it,” he added to himself a moment later.

He went into another street. “Ah, the Palais de Cristal! Razumihin was just talking about the Palais de Cristal. Wait, what did I want again? Oh right, the newspapers... Zossimov said he’d seen it in the papers. Do you have the papers?” he asked as he stepped into a surprisingly clean and spacious restaurant with several rooms, though it was mostly empty. Two or three people were drinking tea, and further in, four men were drinking champagne. Raskolnikov thought one of them might be Zametov, but he couldn’t tell for sure from here. “So what if it is?” he thought.
“Do you want some vodka?” the waiter asked.
“Bring me some tea and the newspapers—the old ones from the last five days. I’ll tip you.”
“Yes, sir, here’s today’s. No vodka?”
The waiter brought the tea and old newspapers. Raskolnikov sat down and started going through them.

“Ugh, just the usual news. An accident on some stairs, a shopkeeper burned up from drinking too much, a fire in Peski... another fire in Petersburg... and another... and another... Ah, here it is!” He finally found what he was looking for and began to read. The words swam before his eyes, but he read it all and then searched the next papers for updates. His hands shook with nerves as he turned the pages. Suddenly, someone sat down beside him. He looked up—it was Zametov, the chief clerk, looking just the same as before: rings on his fingers, a watch chain, slicked-back curly hair, a stylish vest, a shabby coat, and a not-so-clean shirt. He was in a good mood, smiling widely, his dark face flushed from the champagne.
“What, you’re here?” Zametov said, surprised, as if he’d known Raskolnikov forever. “Razumihin told me just yesterday you were unconscious. How strange! Did you know I came to see you?”
Raskolnikov had expected Zametov to come over. He set aside the papers and faced him, a smile on his lips, but with an impatient, almost irritated look.

“I know you did,” Raskolnikov answered. “I heard about it. You looked for my sock... And you know Razumihin is crazy about you? He says you went with him to Luise Ivanovna’s place—you know, the woman you tried to help, the one you winked at the Explosive Lieutenant for, but he didn’t get it. Remember? How could he not get it? It was obvious, wasn’t it?”
“He’s such a hothead!”
“The lieutenant?”
“No, your friend Razumihin.”
“You must have a fun life, Mr. Zametov—free entry to all the best places. Who’s been pouring you champagne now?”
“We were just... having a drink together. Listen to you, ‘pouring it into me!’”

“As a tip! You get something out of everything!” Raskolnikov laughed. “It’s all good, my friend,” he added, patting Zametov on the shoulder. “I’m not mad at you—just joking around, like your workman said when he was wrestling Dmitri, about the old woman’s case...”
“How do you know about that?”
“Maybe I know more than you think.”
“You’re acting really strange... I think you’re still sick. You shouldn’t be out.”
“Oh, do I seem strange to you?”
“Yeah. What are you doing, reading the papers?”
“Yes.”
“There’s a lot about the fires.”

“No, I’m not reading about the fires.” Raskolnikov gave Zametov a mysterious look and a twisted, mocking smile. “No, not about the fires,” he repeated, winking. “But admit it, you’re dying to know what I am reading?”
“Not really. Mind if I ask—why do you keep...?”
“Tell me, you’re an educated man, right?”
“I got to the sixth grade at the gymnasium,” Zametov replied, sounding a bit proud.

“Sixth grade! Oh, my sparrow! With your fancy hair and rings—you’re a man of the world. Ha! What a charming boy!” Raskolnikov suddenly burst out laughing right in Zametov’s face. Zametov took a step back, more shocked than offended.
“Wow, you really are strange!” Zametov said, now totally serious. “I keep thinking you’re still out of it.”
“I’m delirious? You’re the one making stuff up, sparrow! So I’m strange and curious to you, huh?”
“Yes, really curious.”
“Want to know what I was reading? What I was looking for? See how many papers I made them bring me? Suspicious, right?”
“So, what is it?”
“You’re all ears?”
“What do you mean, ‘all ears’?”

“I’ll explain later, but for now, my friend, I declare—no, better yet, I confess—no, that’s not it; I’ll make a statement and you can take it down. I was reading, searching here...” He squinted his eyes and paused. “I came here on purpose to look for news about the murder of the old pawnbroker woman,” he finally whispered, leaning in close to Zametov’s face. Zametov stared back without moving. Later, Zametov would remember how strange it was that they sat in silence for a full minute, just staring at each other.
“So what if you were reading about it?” Zametov finally blurted out, confused and annoyed. “What’s that to me? So what?”
“The same old woman,” Raskolnikov continued in a whisper, ignoring Zametov, “the one you were talking about at the police station, remember, when I fainted. Do you get it now?”
“What do you mean? Get what?” Zametov replied, almost scared.

Raskolnikov’s serious face suddenly broke into the same strange laugh as before, as if he couldn’t help himself. In a flash, he remembered standing with the axe behind the door, the latch shaking, the men cursing outside—and he suddenly wanted to shout at them, mock them, stick out his tongue, just laugh and laugh!
“You’re either crazy or...” Zametov started, but stopped short, as if a wild idea had suddenly hit him.
“Or what? Come on, say it!”
“Nothing,” Zametov snapped, getting angry. “This is all nonsense!”

They were both silent. After that burst of laughter, Raskolnikov grew thoughtful and sad. He leaned on the table, resting his head in his hand, as if he forgot Zametov was even there. The silence dragged on.
“Why don’t you drink your tea? It’s getting cold,” Zametov said.

“Tea? Oh, right...” Raskolnikov sipped his tea, took a bite of bread, and then, suddenly remembering Zametov, pulled himself together. At the same moment, his mocking look returned. He started drinking tea again.
“There have been a bunch of crimes like this lately,” Zametov said. “I just read in the Moscow News that a whole gang of counterfeiters got caught. It was like a club—they even made fake tickets!”
“Oh, that was ages ago! I read about it a month back,” Raskolnikov answered calmly. “So you think they’re criminals?” he added, smiling.
“Of course they’re criminals.”

“Them? They’re just kids, idiots, not criminals! Imagine fifty people meeting up for something like that—what a dumb plan! Even three would be too many. Then they have to trust each other more than themselves! One guy gets drunk and blabs, and it all falls apart. They even hired random people to swap the fake money—why trust a stranger? Let’s say these idiots manage to pull it off and each makes a million. Then what? They’re stuck with each other forever! You might as well hang yourself right away. And they didn’t even know how to change the notes—the guy who tried took five thousand roubles, but his hands were shaking. He counted the first four thousand, but didn’t even count the fifth—he just stuffed the money in his pocket and ran. Of course, people got suspicious. The whole thing collapsed because of one fool. Makes sense, right?”
“His hands shook?” Zametov said. “Yeah, I believe that. It’s possible. Sometimes you just can’t handle it.”
“Can’t handle what?”
“Could you do it? No, I couldn’t. For a hundred roubles, I wouldn’t risk going into a bank with fake notes—they’re trained to spot fakes! No way. Could you?”
Raskolnikov suddenly wanted to stick his tongue out again. Shivers ran down his spine.

“I’d do it differently,” Raskolnikov began. “Here’s how I’d change the notes: I’d count the first thousand three or four times, back and forth, checking every note. Then I’d move on to the second thousand, count half, hold a fifty-rouble note up to the light, turn it, check again, say, ‘I’m worried—a relative of mine lost twenty-five roubles on a fake note the other day,’ and tell the whole story. Then I’d start the third thousand, but say, ‘No, wait, I think I made a mistake in the second thousand, I’m not sure.’ I’d go back, check, then when I finished, I’d take one note from the fifth and one from the second thousand, check them in the light, ask to change them, and make the clerk so nervous he’d just want to get rid of me. After I left, I’d come back and ask for an explanation. That’s how I’d do it.”

“Wow, that’s insane!” Zametov laughed. “But that’s just talk. I bet if it came to actually doing it, you’d mess up. Even the most desperate, experienced criminal can’t always rely on himself—let alone you or me. Take the murder of that old woman in our district. Whoever did it was desperate, took a huge risk in daylight, only escaped by a miracle—but his hands shook, too. He couldn’t even steal the stuff, he freaked out. That’s obvious from the...”
Raskolnikov looked offended.
“Obvious? Then why haven’t you caught him yet?” he snapped at Zametov.
“We will catch him.”
“Who, you? Do you really think you could catch him? That’s tough! You think if a man had no money, then suddenly starts spending, he must be the guy. Any kid could fool you!”

“But that’s what they always do,” Zametov replied. “Someone commits a smart murder, risks everything, and then goes drinking in a bar. They get caught spending the money—they’re not all as clever as you. You wouldn’t go drinking, right?”
Raskolnikov frowned and stared at Zametov.
“You seem to really enjoy this. Want to know how I’d act in that situation too?” he asked, annoyed.
“I’d really like to,” Zametov answered, growing serious. His words and look were getting a bit too intense.
“A lot?”
“A lot!”

“Fine then. Here’s what I’d do,” Raskolnikov began, leaning close and whispering so Zametov actually shivered. “I’d take the money and jewels, walk out, and go straight to some deserted place with fences around it where no one goes—like a kitchen garden or something. I’d already have picked out a big stone, one that’s been there since the house was built. I’d lift the stone—there’s always a hole under it—and hide the money and jewels in there. Then I’d roll the stone back so it looked just the same, stomp it down, and walk away. I wouldn’t touch it for a year, maybe two, maybe three. Let them search—there’d be no trace.”

“You’re insane,” Zametov whispered, scooting away from Raskolnikov, whose eyes were glittering and face had gone pale, his upper lip twitching. Raskolnikov bent in as close as possible; his lips moved, but no sound came. This lasted for half a minute—he knew what he was doing, but couldn’t stop. The terrible words were about to burst out, just like the trembling latch on that door.
“And what if it was me who killed the old woman and Lizaveta?” he suddenly said—and then realized what he’d just done.
Zametov stared at him, turning as white as the tablecloth, his face twisted in a weird smile.
“Could it be true?” he whispered. Raskolnikov glared at him.
“Admit it, you believed me, didn’t you?”
“Not at all! I believe it even less now,” Zametov said quickly.
“I’ve caught you, sparrow! So you did believe it before, if now you believe it even less?”
“Not at all,” Zametov insisted, clearly embarrassed. “Were you just trying to scare me with all that?”

“You don’t believe it? Then what were you talking about behind my back at the police station? And why did the Explosive Lieutenant question me after I fainted? Hey, waiter!” he yelled, getting up and grabbing his cap, “how much do I owe?”
“Thirty copecks,” the waiter hurried up to say.

“And here’s twenty copecks for vodka. See how much money I have!” He held out his shaking hand to Zametov, showing off his red and blue notes. “Twenty-five roubles. Where did I get it? And these new clothes? You know I didn’t have a cent. You probably even questioned my landlady. Well, that’s enough! Enough talking! See you!”

He left, trembling all over with a wild, half-happy, half-tortured feeling. Yet he was gloomy and exhausted, his face twisted as if after a seizure. Any shock or strong feeling woke him up, but he lost all strength again as soon as it passed.
Zametov stayed there for a long time, lost in thought. Without meaning to, Raskolnikov had changed his mind about something important—he’d made up his mind for good.
“Ilya Petrovitch is an idiot,” Zametov decided.

Raskolnikov had barely opened the restaurant door when he nearly walked right into Razumihin on the steps. They didn’t notice each other until they almost crashed. They stood for a second, staring each other up and down. Razumihin was shocked, then real anger flashed in his eyes.

“So here you are!” he shouted. “You ran away from your bed! I’ve been looking for you everywhere—even up in the attic. I almost beat Nastasya because of you. And here you are after all. Rodya! What’s going on? Tell me the truth! Confess! Do you hear me?”
“It means I’m sick of all of you and I want to be alone,” Raskolnikov replied calmly.
“Alone? You can barely walk, you’re pale as a ghost, and gasping for air! Idiot!... And what were you doing in the Palais de Cristal? Tell me right now!”
“Let me go,” Raskolnikov said, trying to walk past. That was too much for Razumihin: he grabbed Raskolnikov’s shoulder.
“Let you go? You dare tell me that? Do you know what I’ll do? I’ll pick you up, tie you in a bundle, carry you home, and lock you up!”

“Listen, Razumihin,” Raskolnikov said quietly, staying calm, “can’t you see I don’t want your kindness? Why do you insist on helping someone who... hates it, who feels like it’s a burden? Why did you come looking for me when I got sick? Maybe I wanted to die. Didn’t I tell you today you were making things worse for me, that I was... sick of you? You seem to enjoy torturing people! I swear, your help is slowing down my recovery because it keeps irritating me. You saw how Zossimov just left to avoid bothering me. Leave me alone too, please! What right do you have to keep me by force? Can’t you see I’m in my right mind now? How can I convince you not to smother me with your kindness? Maybe I’m ungrateful, maybe I’m mean—just let me be, for God’s sake! Let me be, let me be!”
He started off calm, almost enjoying how sharp his words were, but ended up panting and ranting, just like he’d been with Luzhin.
Razumihin stood there a moment, thought, and let go of Raskolnikov’s shoulder.

“Well, go to hell then,” he said quietly, almost thoughtfully. “Wait,” he yelled as Raskolnikov tried to leave. “Listen. Let me tell you, you’re all a bunch of dramatic, fake idiots! If you have a problem, you obsess over it like a hen on an egg. And you copy each other even in that! None of you have any real life in you! You’re all made of ointment and water instead of blood. I don’t believe in any of you! The first thing you all do is act less human than possible! Stop!” he yelled again as Raskolnikov started to leave, “hear me out! I’m having a house-warming party tonight, I bet everyone’s already arrived, but I left my uncle to welcome them. If you weren’t such a fool, Rodya, you’d come over instead of wandering the streets! If you’re already out, fine! I’ll give you a comfy chair, my landlady has one—a cup of tea, some company... Or you can lie on the sofa—anyway, you’d be with us. Zossimov will be there too. Will you come?”
“No.”

“Nonsense!” Razumihin yelled, losing patience. “How do you know? You can’t predict yourself! You know nothing... I’ve fought with people and gone back to them a thousand times... You feel bad and go back, that’s normal! So remember, Potchinkov’s house, third floor...”
“Razumihin, I believe you’d let anyone beat you, just because you’re so nice.”
“Beat me? Who? I’d twist their nose off just for trying! Potchinkov’s house, 47, Babushkin’s flat...”
“I’m not coming, Razumihin.” Raskolnikov turned and walked away.
“I bet you will!” Razumihin shouted after him. “I won’t know you if you don’t! Wait—is Zametov in there?”
“Yes.”
“Did you see him?”
“Yes.”
“Talk to him?”
“Yes.”
“What about? Ugh, never mind. Potchinkov’s house, 47, Babushkin’s flat, remember!”
Raskolnikov kept walking and turned the corner onto Sadovy Street. Razumihin watched him go, then waved and went back to the house—but stopped at the stairs.

“Damn it,” he muttered almost out loud. “He talked normally, but... I’m an idiot! Even crazy people talk normal sometimes! That’s exactly what Zossimov was worried about.” He tapped his forehead. “What if... How could I let him wander off alone? He might drown himself... What a mistake! I can’t.” He rushed back to catch up with Raskolnikov, but Raskolnikov was already gone. With a curse, Razumihin hurried to the Palais de Cristal to talk to Zametov.

Raskolnikov walked straight to X—— Bridge, stopped in the middle, and leaned both elbows on the rail, staring out over the city. After leaving Razumihin, he felt so weak he could barely make it there. He wished he could sit or lie down right there in the street. Bending over the water, he stared blankly at the last bit of sunset, the row of darkening houses, a distant attic window still glowing in the sun, and the dark water. The water caught his attention. Suddenly, red spots flashed before his eyes, the houses seemed to move, people, carriages, canal banks—all blurred and danced. Then, he snapped to attention, shocked by a horrible sight. Standing beside him was a tall woman with a scarf on her head, her face long, yellow, and wasted, her eyes red and sunken. She stared straight ahead, but clearly didn’t see anyone. Suddenly, she put her right hand on the rail, swung her right leg, then her left, over the edge, and jumped into the canal. The filthy water swallowed her, but a second later, she floated back up, her head and legs in the water, her skirt ballooning up behind her.
“A woman’s drowning! A woman’s drowning!” dozens of voices shouted. People rushed to the banks, the bridge filled with spectators pressing in behind Raskolnikov.
“Oh no, it’s our Afrosinya!” a woman wailed nearby. “Please, someone save her! Pull her out!”

“A boat, a boat!” people shouted. But there was no need; a policeman ran down the steps, threw off his coat and boots, and jumped in. She was floating close by, so he grabbed her clothes with one hand, held a pole his partner handed him with the other, and they pulled her out right away. They laid her on the stone pavement. Soon she woke up, sat up, and started sneezing and coughing, stupidly trying to wipe her wet dress. She didn’t say a word.

“She’s drunk out of her mind,” cried the same woman nearby. “Last time she tried to hang herself, we had to cut her down. I just ran to the shop and left my girl watching her—now this! We live nearby, second house from the end, see over there...”

The crowd started to leave, though the police stayed by the woman. Someone mentioned the police station. Raskolnikov watched, feeling weirdly numb and indifferent. He was disgusted. “No, that’s disgusting... water... not good enough,” he muttered to himself. “Nothing will come of it,” he added. “No point waiting. What about the police station...? And why isn’t Zametov there? The station’s open till ten...” He turned away from the rail and looked around.

“Fine then!” he said firmly. He left the bridge and walked toward the police station. His heart felt empty. He didn’t want to think. Even his depression had faded—there was nothing left of the energy he’d started out with, the urge to “end it all.” Now he just felt nothing.

“Well, it’s a way out,” he thought, walking slowly and aimlessly along the canal. “At least I’ll end it, since I want to... but is it really a way out? What does it matter? There’ll be that tiny ledge—ha! But what an end! Is it really the end? Do I tell them or not? Ugh, I’m tired! Wish I could just sit or lie down! The stupidest part is how dumb this all is. But I don’t care! What ridiculous ideas come into my head.”

To reach the police station, he just had to go straight and take the second left. It was only a short walk. But at the first turn, he stopped, thought for a minute, then turned onto a side street, going two blocks out of his way—maybe to stall, maybe for no reason. He stared at the ground as he walked; then it felt like someone whispered in his ear. He looked up and realized he was standing right at the gate of the house. He hadn’t passed it or even been near it since that night. Some weird, irresistible feeling drew him in. He went through the gate, took the first entrance on the right, and started climbing the familiar stairs to the fourth floor. The narrow, steep stairs were very dark. He stopped on each landing and looked around with curiosity. On the first landing, the window frame was missing. “That wasn’t like that then,” he thought. Here was the second-floor flat where Nikolay and Dmitri had worked. “It’s shut and freshly painted. For rent.” Then the third floor, then the fourth. “Here!” He was surprised to find the door wide open, and men’s voices inside. He hadn’t expected that. After a moment’s hesitation, he went up and walked in. The apartment was being renovated; workers were inside. This surprised him; he’d imagined everything would be just as he’d left it, maybe even the bodies on the floor. But now there were bare walls, no furniture. It felt odd. He walked to the window and sat on the windowsill. Two young workmen were there, one much younger than the other, hanging new wallpaper with lilac flowers to replace the old, dirty yellow paper. For some reason, this annoyed Raskolnikov terribly. He stared at the new paper with dislike, almost sorry that everything had changed. The workers were in a hurry to leave, barely noticing him, talking as they packed up. Raskolnikov folded his arms and listened.

“She came to me this morning,” the older one was saying, “really early, all dressed up. ‘Why are you so fancy?’ I said. ‘I want to look good for you, Tit Vassilitch!’ Can you believe it? She was dressed like something out of a fashion book!”
“What’s a fashion book?” the younger one asked, clearly taking the older guy as an expert.

“It’s a bunch of colored pictures they send to the tailors here every Saturday from abroad, to show people how to dress—men and women. The men usually wear fur coats, and for the women, the ruffles are beyond belief.”
“There’s nothing you can’t find in Petersburg,” the younger guy said, impressed, “except a father and mother—everything else is here!”
“Except them, everything’s here, my boy,” the older one replied wisely.

Raskolnikov stood up and walked into the other room, where the chest, bed, and dresser used to be. Without furniture, it seemed tiny. The wallpaper was the same, with a mark in the corner where the icons had been. He looked at it, then went to the window. The older worker glanced at him sideways.
“What do you want?” he asked suddenly.

Instead of replying, Raskolnikov went into the hallway and pulled the bell. It rang with the same cracked sound. He rang it a second, then a third time, listening and remembering. The hideous, terrifying feeling he’d had then started coming back, stronger each time. He shuddered, but somehow enjoyed it.
“Well, what do you want? Who are you?” the workman shouted, coming out. Raskolnikov stepped back inside.
“I want to rent an apartment,” he said. “I’m looking around.”
“It’s not the right time to look at rooms at night! You should come with the porter.”
“The floors have been washed—will they be painted?” Raskolnikov continued. “No blood left, huh?”
“What blood?”
“From the old woman and her sister—they were killed here. There was a huge pool right there.”
“But who are you?” the worker asked, unsettled.
“Who am I?”
“Yes.”
“You want to know? Come to the police station, I’ll tell you.”
The workers stared at him in disbelief.
“We’re late, we have to go. Come on, Alyoshka. Let’s lock up,” the older worker said.
“Fine, let’s go,” Raskolnikov replied indifferently. He led the way down. “Hey, porter!” he called in the gateway.
At the entrance, several people were standing around, watching passersby: the two porters, a peasant woman, a man in a long coat, and a few others. Raskolnikov went right up to them.
“What do you want?” one of the porters asked.
“Have you been to the police station?”
“I just came from there. What do you want?”
“Is it open?”
“Of course.”
“Is the assistant there?”
“He was there a while. What do you want?”
Raskolnikov didn’t answer, just stood there, lost in thought.
“He went to look at the flat,” the older worker said, stepping forward.
“Which flat?”

“The one we’re working in. ‘Why did you wash away the blood?’ he says. ‘There was a murder here, and I want to rent it.’ Then he started ringing the bell, almost broke it. ‘Come to the police station,’ he says. ‘I’ll tell you everything there.’ He wouldn’t leave us alone.”
The porter frowned and stared at Raskolnikov, confused.
“Who are you?” he shouted, trying to sound intimidating.

“I’m Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov, a former student. I live in Shil’s house, not far from here, flat Number 14. Ask the porter, he knows me.” Raskolnikov said this in a lazy, dreamy voice, not turning around, just staring into the dark street.
“Why did you go to the flat?”
“To look at it.”
“What’s there to see?”
“Take him straight to the police station,” the man in the long coat said sharply.
Raskolnikov looked at him over his shoulder and replied in the same slow, lazy voice:
“Let’s go.”
“Yeah, take him,” the man repeated, sounding more sure of himself. “Why did he go in there, what’s he thinking, huh?”
“He’s not drunk, but who knows what’s wrong with him,” one of the workers muttered.
“But what do you want?” the porter shouted again, getting really angry now. “Why are you hanging around?”
“Afraid of the police station, eh?” Raskolnikov mocked.
“Afraid? Why are you hanging around?”
“He’s a crook!” shouted the peasant woman.
“Why waste time talking to him?” the other porter yelled, a big man with keys at his belt. “Get out of here! He’s a crook, no doubt. Get going!”
And grabbing Raskolnikov by the shoulder, he shoved him out onto the street. Raskolnikov stumbled, but caught himself, looked at the crowd silently, and walked away.
“Strange guy,” said the worker.
“There are a lot of weird people these days,” the woman added.
“You should’ve just taken him to the police station,” said the man in the long coat.
“Better to leave him be,” decided the big porter. “He wants trouble, but once you take him in, you’ll never get rid of him. We know his type.”

“Should I go or not?” Raskolnikov wondered, standing in the middle of the intersection, looking around like he was waiting for a sign. But there was only silence, as dead as the stones under his feet—dead to him, at least. Suddenly, at the end of the street, a couple hundred yards away, he saw a crowd and heard shouting. There was a carriage in the middle, a light shining in the street. “What’s that?” Raskolnikov turned toward the crowd. He felt drawn to everything, and even smiled coldly when he recognized it, because he’d already decided to go to the police station, knowing this would all be over soon.

A fancy carriage was stopped in the middle of the street, pulled by two lively gray horses. No one was sitting inside. The coachman had climbed down and was standing nearby, holding the horses by their reins. A crowd of people surrounded the scene, with police officers at the front. One policeman was shining his lantern on something lying near the carriage’s wheels. Everyone was talking loudly and excitedly. The coachman looked upset and kept repeating:
“What a disaster! Oh God, what a disaster!”

Raskolnikov pushed through the crowd as far as he could and finally managed to see what everyone was staring at. On the ground lay a man who had been run over, unconscious and covered in blood. His clothes were shabby, but he didn’t look like a worker. Blood streamed from his head and face, which were bruised, swollen, and horribly disfigured. It was clear he was seriously hurt.

“Dear God!” wailed the coachman. “What else could I do? I wasn’t going fast, and I shouted at him! Everyone saw I was just driving normally. The man was staggering all over, clearly drunk. I called out once, twice, three times, and pulled the horses back, but he fell right under their feet! Maybe he did it on purpose, or he was just that drunk. The horses got scared and jumped, he screamed, and that made them panic even more. That’s how it happened!”
“That’s exactly how it was,” someone in the crowd agreed.
“He shouted, it’s true, he called out three times,” another person said.
“Three times, we all heard it,” a third voice chimed in.

But the coachman didn’t seem too scared or upset. The carriage obviously belonged to someone important who was waiting for it, so the police were nervous about causing any trouble. Their main concern now was to get the hurt man to the police station and the hospital. No one knew his name.
Meanwhile, Raskolnikov managed to get closer and bent down over the injured man. The lantern’s light suddenly fell on his face, and Raskolnikov recognized him.

“I know him! I know who he is!” Raskolnikov called out, moving to the front. “He’s a retired government clerk, Marmeladov. He lives nearby in Kozel’s house. Hurry, get a doctor! I’ll pay for it, see?” He pulled money from his pocket and showed it to the policeman. He was shaking with anxiety.

The police were relieved to have found out who the victim was. Raskolnikov gave them his own name and address and begged them, as if Marmeladov was his own father, to carry the unconscious man home right away.

“It’s just three houses away,” he said eagerly. “The house is owned by Kozel, a rich German. Marmeladov was probably coming home drunk; I know him, he’s a heavy drinker. He has a family—a wife, kids, a daughter. If you take him to the hospital, it’ll take too long. There’s probably a doctor in the building. I’ll pay, I promise! At least at home, they can look after him right away. He might die before you get him to the hospital.” He slipped something into the policeman’s hand. But it was all handled properly, and help was closer here. They lifted the injured man, and some bystanders offered to help.
Kozel’s house was only about thirty yards away. Raskolnikov walked behind, carefully supporting Marmeladov’s head and showing them the way.
“This way! Take him up the stairs head first. Turn around, that’s it! I’ll pay you, I promise,” he muttered.

Katerina Ivanovna, Marmeladov’s wife, was pacing her tiny room, as she always did when she had a spare moment. She walked from the window to the stove and back, arms folded over her chest, talking to herself and coughing. Lately, she talked more and more to her oldest daughter, Polenka, a ten-year-old who didn’t understand everything, but knew her mother needed her. Polenka watched her intently with big, clever eyes, trying her best to look like she understood. Right now, Polenka was undressing her little brother, who had been sick all day and was getting ready for bed. The boy sat very still on a chair, waiting for his shirt to be taken off so it could be washed at night. His face was serious and silent; his legs stretched straight out, heels together, toes pointing out.

He listened quietly to his mother speaking to his sister, sitting perfectly still with his lips pushed out and his eyes wide open—just like little boys do when being undressed for bed. A younger girl, dressed in little more than rags, stood nearby, waiting for her turn. The door to the stairs was open, hoping to let out some of the tobacco smoke that drifted in from the other rooms and triggered terrible coughing fits in sickly Katerina Ivanovna. She looked even thinner than she had the week before, and her cheeks were flushed with fever.

“You wouldn’t believe it, Polenka,” she said, pacing the room, “what a happy, fancy life we had in my father’s house before this drunk ruined me—and ruined all of you! My father was an army colonel, almost a governor! Visitors used to say, ‘Colonel Ivan Mihailovitch, we look at you as our governor!’ When I—” she stopped to cough hard, “oh, this awful life,” she cried, clutching her chest, “when I—at the last ball at the marshal’s—Princess Bezzemelny saw me. She blessed me when your father and I got married, Polenka! She asked, ‘Isn’t that the pretty girl who danced the shawl dance at the party?’ (You must fix that tear, take your needle and mend it like I showed you, or tomorrow—cough, cough, cough—he’ll make it worse,” she struggled to say.) “Prince Schegolskoy, a fancy court man, had just come from Petersburg, he danced the mazurka with me and wanted to propose the next day. But I politely told him my heart belonged to someone else—your father, Polya. My father was furious. Is the water ready? Give me the shirt and stockings! Lida,” she called to the youngest, “you’ll have to do without your undershirt tonight—put out your stockings, I’ll wash them together. Why isn’t that drunken fool home yet? He’s worn his shirt to rags! I’d wash everything at once and be done with it. Oh, dear! (Cough, cough, cough!) Again! What’s this?” she cried, noticing people crowding into the hallway, carrying someone into her room. “What’s going on? What are they bringing in? Oh, God!”
“Where should we put him?” asked the policeman, looking around after they’d carried the bloody, unconscious Marmeladov inside.
“On the sofa! Lay him down with his head this way,” Raskolnikov directed.
“Run over in the street! Drunk!” someone shouted from the hallway.
Katerina Ivanovna turned pale and struggled to breathe. The children were terrified. Little Lida screamed, ran to Polenka, and clung to her, shaking.
After laying Marmeladov down, Raskolnikov rushed to Katerina Ivanovna.

“Please, try to stay calm, don’t panic!” he said quickly. “He was crossing the street and got run over, but he’ll wake up. I told them to bring him here—I’ve been here before, remember? He’ll be okay, I promise! I’ll pay for everything!”
“This time he’s done it for real!” Katerina Ivanovna cried hopelessly and rushed to her husband.

Raskolnikov immediately noticed that she wasn’t the kind of woman to faint easily. She quickly put a pillow under Marmeladov’s head—something no one else thought of—then started undressing and checking him. She kept her cool, biting her quivering lips and holding back the cries that wanted to burst out.
Meanwhile, Raskolnikov got someone to run for a doctor. It turned out there was a doctor just a couple of doors away.

“I’ve sent for a doctor,” he kept reassuring Katerina Ivanovna. “Don’t worry. I’ll pay. Do you have any water? And a napkin or towel—anything, quickly.... He’s hurt, but he’s not dead, believe me. We’ll see what the doctor says!”

Katerina Ivanovna ran to the window, where a big clay basin full of water sat on a broken chair in the corner, ready for her to wash her family’s clothes that night. She washed at night at least twice a week, sometimes more, because they barely had any spare clothes. Katerina Ivanovna couldn’t stand dirt, so she’d rather exhaust herself at night, washing and hanging the laundry to dry by morning, than see her family dirty. She tried to lift the basin for Raskolnikov but nearly dropped it. He had already found a towel, though, soaked it, and began cleaning the blood off Marmeladov’s face.

Katerina Ivanovna stood nearby, breathing heavily and holding her hands to her chest. She needed help herself. Raskolnikov began to worry he’d made a mistake bringing Marmeladov here. The policeman also hesitated.
“Polenka!” Katerina Ivanovna called, “run to Sonia, quickly! If she’s not home, leave a message that her father’s been run over and she should come here right away. Go, Polenka! Put on your shawl.”
“Run as fast as you can!” the little boy suddenly shouted from his chair, then went back to sitting silently, his heels stuck out and his eyes wide.

Meanwhile, the room was so packed with people you could hardly move. The policemen all left except one, who tried for a while to clear out the strangers who kept coming in from the stairs. Almost all of Madame Lippevechsel’s boarders had come in from the other rooms; first crowding the doorway, then spilling into the room. Katerina Ivanovna was furious.

“Can’t you let him die in peace?” she yelled at the crowd. “Is this a show for you to stare at? And with cigarettes, too! (Cough, cough, cough!) You might as well keep your hats on.... And there’s one of you with your hat inside!... Get out! At least have some respect for the dead!”

Her coughing cut her off—but her angry words had an effect. The boarders, who seemed to be a little afraid of Katerina Ivanovna, squeezed out into the hallway, though they still felt that strange curiosity everyone gets at the scene of an accident, even when they care about the person.
Voices could be heard outside, talking about the hospital and saying they shouldn’t make a scene here.

“No business to die here!” Katerina Ivanovna shouted and rushed to the door to yell at them, but instead came face-to-face with Madame Lippevechsel, the landlady, who had just heard about the accident and barged in to take charge. She was a cranky and quarrelsome German woman.
“Oh my God!” she cried, wringing her hands. “Your husband—drunk—trampled by horses! He needs to go to the hospital! I’m the landlady!”

“Amalia Ludwigovna, please remember what you’re saying,” Katerina Ivanovna answered sharply (she always acted superior to the landlady, just to remind her “who’s boss”—even now, she couldn’t help herself). “Amalia Ludwigovna...”
“I have already told you not to call me Amalia Ludwigovna; you must call me Amalia Ivanovna.”

“You are not Amalia Ivanovna, you’re Amalia Ludwigovna, and I am not one of your silly flatterers like Mr. Lebeziatnikov, who’s laughing behind the door right now—” (a laugh and a shout of “They’re at it again!” came from the hall) “so I’ll always call you Amalia Ludwigovna, even if I don’t know why you hate that name. You can see for yourself what’s happened to Semyon Zaharovitch—he’s dying. Please close the door and don’t let anyone else in! Let him die in peace! Or I’ll have to tell the Governor-General about your behavior tomorrow. The prince knew me as a girl; he remembers Semyon Zaharovitch and has helped him before. Everyone knows Semyon Zaharovitch had many friends and supporters, whom he left behind out of pride because of his drinking problem. But now—” (she pointed at Raskolnikov) “a generous young man has come to help us. He’s well-off and well-connected, and Semyon Zaharovitch has known him since he was a child. So don’t worry, Amalia Ludwigovna...”

She spoke faster and faster, but a coughing fit cut her off. Just then, Marmeladov came to and groaned. She ran over to him. Marmeladov opened his eyes and stared blankly at Raskolnikov, who was leaning over him. His breathing was slow and painful, blood leaking from his mouth, sweat on his forehead. He didn’t seem to recognize Raskolnikov and looked around nervously. Katerina Ivanovna gazed at him with a sad but stern face; tears trickled down her cheeks.
“Oh God! His chest is crushed! He’s bleeding so much,” she said in despair. “We need to get his clothes off. Turn over a little, Semyon Zaharovitch, if you can,” she pleaded.
Marmeladov recognized her.
“A priest,” he croaked.
Katerina Ivanovna went to the window, leaned her head against the frame, and cried out in despair:
“Oh, this cursed life!”
“A priest,” the dying man said again after a short pause.

“They’ve gone to get one,” Katerina Ivanovna called to him. He relaxed and was quiet. He looked for her with sad, nervous eyes; she came back and stood by his pillow. He seemed to calm down a bit, but not for long.
Soon his eyes rested on little Lida, his favorite, who was shaking in the corner as if having a seizure, staring at him with her big, wondering eyes.
“A-ah,” he breathed out toward her, reaching for words.
“What is it now?” Katerina Ivanovna snapped.
“Barefoot, barefoot!” he gasped, staring at the child’s bare feet.
“Be quiet,” Katerina Ivanovna said irritably. “You know why she has no shoes.”
“Thank God, here’s the doctor,” Raskolnikov said with relief.

The doctor entered—a neat, precise little old German man who looked around suspiciously. He went up to Marmeladov, felt his pulse, checked his head, and with Katerina Ivanovna’s help unbuttoned the bloody shirt, exposing Marmeladov’s chest. It was crushed and cut, several ribs broken on the right, and on the left, just over the heart, was a huge, ugly black-and-yellow bruise—a kick from a horse’s hoof. The doctor frowned. The policeman explained that Marmeladov had been dragged by the wheel for thirty yards down the street.
“It’s a miracle he’s still conscious,” the doctor whispered to Raskolnikov.
“What do you think?” Raskolnikov asked.
“He’ll die very soon.”
“Is there really no hope?”
“Not a chance. He’s almost gone... His head is badly injured, too... Hm... I can bleed him if you want, but it won’t help. He’ll die in five or ten minutes.”
“Then bleed him, just in case.”
“If you wish... but I warn you, it’s pointless.”

Just then, more footsteps sounded. The crowd in the hallway parted, and a priest—a small, gray-haired old man—appeared carrying the sacrament. A policeman had gone for him right after the accident. The doctor stepped aside for the priest, and Raskolnikov asked the doctor to stay a bit longer. The doctor shrugged but stayed.

Everyone stepped back. The confession was quick. Marmeladov probably didn’t understand much; he could only mumble. Katerina Ivanovna took little Lida, lifted her son from the chair, knelt by the stove, and made the children kneel in front of her. The little girl still shook, but the boy knelt with bare knees, crossing himself carefully and bowing to touch the floor, which seemed to make him happy. Katerina Ivanovna bit her lips, holding back tears, and prayed too, now and then pulling the boy’s shirt straight or covering the girl’s shoulders with a scarf she grabbed from the chest without getting up. Meanwhile, the door to the inner rooms opened again as curious people peered in. In the hallway, the crowd from all the apartments on the stairs grew thicker and thicker, but no one dared come inside. The scene was lit by a single stub of candle.

Just then, Polenka squeezed through the crowd at the door. She came in, out of breath from running, took off her scarf, looked for her mother, walked up to her and whispered, “She’s coming, I met her in the street.” Her mother made her kneel down next to her.

Timidly and quietly, a young girl slipped in through the crowd. She looked strange in this bleak, poor room full of death and misery. She, too, wore rags, but her outfit was decorated with cheap, flashy accessories that made her shame obvious. Sonia stopped in the doorway, dazed, barely aware of anything. She forgot about her old, bright silk dress with its silly long train, her huge hoop skirt that filled the doorway, her light shoes, the parasol she’d brought even though it was night, and the silly straw hat with its bright red feather. Under the tilted hat was a pale, frightened face with parted lips and wide, terrified eyes. Sonia was small, thin, and eighteen, with light hair and beautiful blue eyes. She stared at the bed and the priest, breathing hard from running. Finally, she overheard whispers around her and took a step into the room, still sticking close to the door.
The priest finished his service. Katerina Ivanovna went to her husband. The priest turned to say some comforting words to her before leaving.
“But what am I supposed to do with these children?” she interrupted sharply, pointing to them.
“God is merciful; look to Him for help,” the priest began.
“Oh, He’s merciful—but not to us.”
“That’s a sin to say, madam,” the priest said, shaking his head.
“And isn’t this a sin?” Katerina Ivanovna yelled, pointing to her dying husband.
“Maybe those who accidentally caused the accident will pay you something, at least for his lost wages.”

“You don’t get it!” Katerina Ivanovna shouted, waving her hand angrily. “Why should they pay me? He was drunk and threw himself under the horses! What wages? He only ever brought misery. He drank everything away—he stole from us for drink, ruined their lives and mine for drink! Thank God he’s dying! That’s one less mouth to feed!”
“You must forgive in the hour of death. That’s a sin, madam. Such feelings are very wrong.”

Katerina Ivanovna was busy with Marmeladov—giving him water, wiping blood and sweat from his face, fixing his pillow. She only turned to the priest for a moment to answer him. Now she snapped at him, almost frantic.

“Oh, Father! That’s easy for you to say! Forgive? If he hadn’t been run over, he’d have come home drunk, his only shirt filthy and torn, and passed out. Then I’d be up all night washing his rags and the kids’ clothes, drying them by the window, and as soon as morning came, I’d be darning them. That’s my life! What’s the use of talking about forgiveness? I’ve already forgiven enough!”

A terrible, hollow cough stopped her. She pressed a handkerchief to her mouth and showed it to the priest, her other hand on her chest. The cloth was covered in blood. The priest bowed his head and said nothing.

Marmeladov was dying now; he didn’t take his eyes off Katerina Ivanovna’s face as she bent over him. He tried to say something, moving his tongue with difficulty and mumbling, but Katerina Ivanovna, realizing he wanted to ask her forgiveness, cut him off:
“Be quiet! There’s no need! I know what you want to say!” The sick man fell silent, but at that moment his wandering eyes drifted to the doorway and saw Sonia.
Until then, he hadn’t noticed her—she was standing in the shadowy corner.
“Who’s that? Who’s that?” he suddenly said in a thick, hoarse voice, panicked, turning his eyes in horror toward the door where his daughter stood, trying to sit up.
“Lie down! Lie down!” Katerina Ivanovna shouted.

With surprising strength, he managed to prop himself up on his elbow. He stared at Sonia for a long moment, not recognizing her at first—he had never seen her dressed like this. Suddenly he realized it was his daughter, crushed and ashamed in her gaudy, humiliating outfit, waiting quietly to say goodbye to her dying father. His face twisted in pain.

“Sonia! Daughter! Forgive me!” he cried, trying to reach out to her, but lost his balance and fell off the sofa, face-down on the floor. They rushed to pick him up and put him back on the couch; but he was dying. Sonia, with a soft cry, ran to him, hugged him, and didn’t move. He died in her arms.
“He got what he wanted,” Katerina Ivanovna cried, seeing her husband dead. “Now what? How am I supposed to bury him? What will I feed the kids tomorrow?”
Raskolnikov went over to Katerina Ivanovna.

“Katerina Ivanovna,” he began, “last week your husband told me his whole story.... He spoke about you with so much respect and love. From the day I heard how devoted he was to all of you, especially to you, I felt like we were friends. Please let me help now, to pay my debt to my dead friend. Here are twenty roubles, I think—and if that helps you, then... I’ll come again, I promise—maybe even tomorrow. Goodbye.”

He quickly left the room, pushing through the crowd to the stairs. But in the hallway he bumped into Nikodim Fomitch, who had come after hearing about the accident to give orders himself. They hadn’t seen each other since the scene at the police station, but Nikodim Fomitch recognized him right away.
“Oh, it’s you?” Nikodim Fomitch asked.

“He’s dead,” Raskolnikov replied. “The doctor and priest came, everything was done properly. Please don’t upset the poor woman too much—she’s already sick. Try to cheer her up if you can... you’re a good person, I know...” he added with a smile, looking him in the eye.
“But you’re covered in blood,” Nikodim Fomitch said, noticing fresh stains on Raskolnikov’s vest in the lamp light.
“Yes... I’m covered in blood,” Raskolnikov answered, in a strange way. Then he smiled, nodded, and walked downstairs.

He went down slowly, feverish but not noticing it, completely caught up in a sudden, powerful feeling of life and strength welling up inside him. It was like a person on death row who suddenly gets a pardon. Halfway down the stairs, the priest passed him on his way out; Raskolnikov let him go, exchanging a silent nod. He was just reaching the last steps when he heard someone running behind him. Someone caught up—it was Polenka. She was running after him, calling, “Wait! Wait!”

He turned. She was at the bottom of the stairs and stopped a step above him. A faint light shone from the yard. Raskolnikov could see her small, thin but pretty face, looking up at him with a bright, childish smile. She’d come after him with a message and was clearly happy to deliver it.
“What’s your name?... and where do you live?” she asked quickly, out of breath.
He put both hands on her shoulders and looked at her with a kind of wonder. He didn’t know why, but it made him happy just to look at her.
“Who sent you?”
“Sister Sonia sent me,” she said, still smiling even more brightly.
“I knew it was Sonia that sent you.”
“Mama sent me too... When Sonia told me to go, Mama came over and said, ‘Run fast, Polenka.’”
“Do you love Sonia?”
“I love her more than anyone,” Polenka answered very seriously, her smile fading a little.
“And will you love me?”

Instead of answering, she leaned toward him, lips out to kiss his cheek. Suddenly her skinny arms hugged him tight, her head rested on his shoulder, and she began to cry softly, pressing her face against him.

“I feel sorry for Father,” she said a moment later, lifting her tear-streaked face and wiping her eyes. “It’s all just bad luck now,” she added suddenly, with the serious tone children use when they want to sound grown up.
“Did your father love you?”

“He loved Lida most,” she said, very seriously, without smiling, sounding just like an adult. “He loved her because she’s little and sick. He always brought her presents. But he taught us to read—me grammar and Bible, too,” she said with pride. “Mama never said anything, but we knew she liked it, and Father knew it too. Mama wants to teach me French, because it’s time for my education.”
“And do you know your prayers?”

“Of course! We learned them a long time ago. I say mine to myself because I’m a big girl now, but Kolya and Lida say theirs out loud with Mama. First the ‘Ave Maria,’ then another prayer: ‘Lord, forgive and bless Sister Sonia,’ and then another, ‘Lord, forgive and bless our second father.’ Our first father is dead, and this is our new one, but we pray for both.”
“Polenka, my name is Rodion. Pray for me sometimes too. Just ‘and Thy servant Rodion,’ that’s all.”
“I’ll pray for you all my life,” the girl promised passionately; then, smiling again, she hugged him warmly once more.

Raskolnikov told her his name and address, and promised to visit the next day. The child left, completely delighted with him. It was after ten when he reached the street. Five minutes later, he was standing on the bridge, at the spot where the woman had jumped in.

“That’s enough,” he said firmly and with pride. “I’m done with fears, nightmares, and ghosts! Life is real! Haven’t I just lived it now? My life didn’t end with that old woman! Heaven to her—and now, enough, leave me alone! It’s time for reason, light, will, and strength. Now we’ll see! Let’s test my strength!” he added, almost daring the darkness. “And I was willing to live in a box!

“I’m weak right now, but... I think my sickness is over. I knew it would end as soon as I went out. By the way, Potchinkov’s house is just a few steps away. I really should go see Razumihin, even if it wasn’t so close—let him win his bet! Let’s do something nice for him, too—why not? Strength, that’s what you need, you can’t get anything without it, and you only get it by being strong—that’s what people don’t get,” he said, feeling proud and confident, and walked away from the bridge, though his steps were still shaky. He felt more and more sure of himself, as if he were turning into a new person with every step. He had no idea what had brought on this change—he just suddenly felt that he could live, that there was still life left for him, that his life hadn’t ended with the old woman’s. Maybe he was jumping to conclusions, but he didn’t care.
“But I did ask her to remember ‘Thy servant Rodion’ in her prayers,” he suddenly thought. “Well, that was... just in case,” he added, and laughed at himself. He was in a great mood.

He easily found Razumihin; the new tenant was already known at Potchinkov’s, and the porter led him right up. Halfway upstairs, he could hear lots of voices and lively conversation. The door was wide open on the landing; he could hear people exclaiming and talking. Razumihin’s room was pretty big, and there were about fifteen people inside. Raskolnikov stopped in the entry, where two of the landlady’s servants were busy behind a screen with samovars, bottles, plates, and dishes of pies and snacks from the landlady’s kitchen. Raskolnikov sent for Razumihin. He ran out, delighted. Right away, it was obvious he’d been drinking a lot, and though Razumihin never got truly drunk, this time he was definitely tipsy.

“Listen,” Raskolnikov said quickly, “I just came to tell you that you won your bet, and that you never know what can happen. I can’t come in; I’m so weak I’ll fall down at any minute. So good night and goodbye! Come see me tomorrow.”
“You know what? I’ll walk you home. If you say you’re weak, you need—”
“And your guests? Who’s the curly-haired one who just peeked out?”

“Him? Who knows! Maybe a friend of uncle’s, or maybe he just showed up uninvited... I’ll leave Uncle with them, he’s very useful—too bad I can’t introduce you now. But forget them! They won’t even notice I’m gone and I need some fresh air. You showed up just in time—two more minutes and I’d have started a fight! They’re talking such nonsense... you wouldn’t believe what people will say! Though, why not? We talk nonsense too, don’t we? Let them—it’s how people learn!... Hold on, I’ll get Zossimov.”
Zossimov greeted Raskolnikov eagerly; he seemed especially interested in him and soon looked pleased.
“You must go to bed right away,” he said, checking Raskolnikov as best he could. “And take this medicine tonight. Will you take it? I got it ready a while ago... a powder.”
“Two if you want,” Raskolnikov replied. He took the medicine right away.
“It’s good you’re taking him home,” Zossimov told Razumihin. “We’ll see how he is tomorrow. He’s much better today—a big improvement since this afternoon. You learn something new every day...”

“Do you know what Zossimov whispered to me on the way out?” Razumihin blurted as soon as they were outside. “I won’t tell you everything, brother, because they’re idiots. Zossimov told me to get you talking on the way and then tell him about it, because he thinks you’re... crazy or close to it. Can you believe it? First, you’re three times smarter than he is; second, if you’re not crazy, who cares what he thinks; and third, that beefy surgeon is obsessed with mental illnesses, and what made him think that about you was your talk with Zametov today.”
“Zametov told you all about it?”

“Yeah, and I’m glad he did. Now I get it, and so does Zametov. Well, Rodya... the thing is... I’m a little drunk right now... but it doesn’t matter... the point is, this idea was just forming in their heads... you get it? No one wanted to say it out loud because it’s ridiculous, and since they arrested that painter, the whole idea has vanished. But why are they such fools? I gave Zametov a piece of my mind at the time—just between us, brother; don’t let on you know. I noticed he’s sensitive about it; it happened at Luise Ivanovna’s. But today, today it’s all clear. Ilya Petrovitch started it! He took advantage of your fainting at the police station, but now he’s embarrassed; I know he is...”
Raskolnikov listened eagerly. Razumihin was drunk enough to talk without holding back.
“I fainted then because it was so stuffy and the smell of paint,” Raskolnikov said.

“No need to explain! And it wasn’t just the paint—the fever’s been building for a month; Zossimov says so! But you wouldn’t believe how crushed that boy is now! ‘I’m not worth his little finger,’ he says—yours, he means. He has good qualities sometimes, brother. But the lesson you gave him at the Palais de Cristal today—that was perfect! You scared him so much, he almost had a fit! You almost convinced him that all that nonsense was true, and then you just—stuck out your tongue at him: ‘Well, what do you think of that?’ It was brilliant! He’s crushed, wiped out! I wish I’d been there! He really wanted to see you. Porfiry wants to meet you, too...”
“Ah!... him too... but why did they think I was mad?”

“Oh, not really mad. I must have said too much, brother. What got to him was that only that topic seemed to interest you. Now, knowing all the circumstances, it makes sense; and it fits with your illness... Sorry, I’m a little drunk, brother. But forget him, he’s obsessed with mental illness. Don’t worry about it...”
They were silent for a moment.

“Listen, Razumihin,” Raskolnikov began, “I’ll be honest: I was just at a deathbed, a clerk who died... I gave them all my money... and besides, I was just kissed by someone who, even if I’d killed someone, would still...
