Actually, I saw someone else there... with a bright red feather... but I’m talking nonsense; I’m really weak, hold me up... we’ll be at the stairs soon...”
“What’s wrong? What’s wrong with you?” Razumihin asked, worried.
“I’m a little dizzy, but that’s not the point. I feel so sad, so sad... like a woman. Look, what’s that? Look!”
“What is it?”
“Don’t you see? There’s a light in my room, see? Through the crack...”
They were already at the bottom of the last flight of stairs, near the landlady’s door, and they could see from below that there was a light in Raskolnikov’s attic room.
“Weird! Maybe it’s Nastasya,” Razumihin said.
“She’s never in my room at this hour—she must be asleep by now, but... I don’t care! Goodbye!”
“What do you mean? I’m coming with you, we’ll go in together!”
“I know we’re going in together, but I want to shake your hand and say goodbye right here. So, shake—goodbye!”
“What’s wrong, Rodya?”
“Nothing... come on... you’ll be my witness.”
They started up the stairs, and Razumihin suddenly thought maybe Zossimov was right after all. “Ah, I’ve upset him with my babbling!” he muttered to himself.
As they reached the door, they heard voices coming from inside.
“What’s going on?” Razumihin called. Raskolnikov was the first to open the door. He flung it open wide and froze in shock.

His mother and sister were sitting on his sofa—they had been waiting for him for an hour and a half. Why hadn’t he expected them, even though he’d been told that they’d be arriving soon, just that day? They had spent the whole time asking Nastasya questions. She had told them everything. The two women were frantic with worry after hearing about his “running off” that day, sick and, as they understood from Nastasya, half-delirious! “Dear God, what had happened to him?” Both had been crying, both were terrified during that hour and a half.

A cry of joy and excitement greeted Raskolnikov as he entered. Both women rushed to him. But he stood there like he was dead; a sudden, unbearable feeling hit him like lightning. He couldn’t even raise his arms to hug them. His mother and sister hugged and kissed him, laughing and crying. He took a step, swayed, and collapsed in a faint.
Panic, cries, groans... Razumihin, who was at the doorway, rushed in, scooped Raskolnikov up in his strong arms, and in a moment had him lying on the sofa.
“It’s nothing, nothing!” he told the mother and sister. “Just a faint, that’s all! The doctor just said he’s much better, that he’s almost well! Water! See, he’s coming around, he’s already okay!”
And grabbing Dounia’s arm so hard he almost dislocated it, he made her lean down to see that Raskolnikov was “all right again.”

Raskolnikov stood up shakily and sat down on the sofa. He waved a tired hand at Razumihin, signaling him to stop the flood of awkward, comforting words he was giving to his mother and sister. Raskolnikov took both their hands and stared at them in silence for a minute or two. His mother, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, was frightened by the look on his face. It showed deep pain, but also something cold and almost crazy. Tears started running down her cheeks.
Avdotya Romanovna (Dounia) looked pale, and her hand shook in her brother’s grasp.
“Go home… with him,” Raskolnikov said in a weak, broken voice, nodding at Razumihin. “Goodbye until tomorrow. Tomorrow everything… When did you get here?”
“This evening, Rodya,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna answered. “The train was terribly late. But, Rodya, I absolutely cannot leave you now! I’ll stay the night here, right by your side…”
“Don’t torture me!” Raskolnikov said, waving her off irritably.
“I’ll stay with him,” Razumihin insisted. “I won’t leave him for a second. Forget my guests! They can complain all they want. My uncle can handle them.”
“How can I ever thank you!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna began, squeezing Razumihin’s hands, but Raskolnikov interrupted again.
“I can’t have it! I can’t!” he said, more and more agitated. “Don’t make it worse! Enough, just go... I can’t take it!”
“Come on, Mom, let’s at least leave the room for a minute,” Dounia whispered, upset. “We’re upsetting him, it’s obvious.”
“Can’t I even look at him after three years?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna sobbed.
“Wait,” Raskolnikov stopped them again. “You keep interrupting and I can’t think straight… Have you seen Luzhin?”
“No, Rodya, but he knows we’ve arrived. We heard, Rodya, that Pyotr Petrovitch was kind enough to visit you today,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna added, a bit nervously.
“Yeah… he was so kind… Dounia, I told Luzhin I’d throw him down the stairs and told him to get lost…”
“Rodya, what are you saying! You can’t mean…,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna gasped, but stopped and looked at Dounia.

Dounia watched her brother carefully, waiting to see what he’d say next. Both she and her mother had already heard something about the argument from Nastasya, as much as she could explain, and they were confused and worried.
“Dounia,” Raskolnikov said, forcing the words out, “I don’t want you marrying Luzhin. Tomorrow, as soon as you can, you need to refuse him. I don’t want to ever hear his name again.”
“Good heavens!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried.
“Brother, think about what you’re saying!” Dounia started to protest, but stopped herself. “Maybe you shouldn’t talk about this now; you must be exhausted,” she said gently.

“You think I’m out of my mind? No… You’re marrying Luzhin for me. But I won’t let you make that sacrifice. Write him a letter tonight, break it off… Let me read it in the morning, and that’ll be the end of it!”
“I can’t do that!” Dounia said, hurt. “What right do you have—?”
“Dounia, you’re being too quick, calm down, tomorrow…” her mother said, trying to stop the argument. “Let’s just go for now!”

“He’s raving,” Razumihin said, a little drunk, “or else how would he dare! Tomorrow he’ll forget all this nonsense… But he really did kick Luzhin out today. That’s true. Luzhin was furious. He tried to act smart but left with his tail between his legs…”
“So it’s true?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna gasped.
“Goodbye until tomorrow, brother,” Dounia said kindly. “Let’s go, mother… Goodbye, Rodya.”

“Do you hear me, Dounia?” Raskolnikov called after them, using the last of his strength. “I’m not crazy—this marriage is shameful. I can be a scoundrel, but you mustn’t—one in the family is enough… and even if I am a scoundrel, I won’t accept a sister who’d do this. It’s me or Luzhin! Go now…”

“You’re out of your mind! Tyrant!” Razumihin shouted. But Raskolnikov didn’t answer—maybe he couldn’t. He collapsed onto the sofa and turned to face the wall, completely worn out. Dounia glanced at Razumihin; her dark eyes sparkled, and Razumihin actually flinched from her look.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna was left standing, overwhelmed.
“Nothing can make me leave,” she whispered desperately to Razumihin. “I’ll find somewhere to stay… just take Dounia home.”

“You’ll ruin everything,” Razumihin whispered back impatiently. “At least let’s step into the hallway. Nastasya, bring a light! Listen,” he continued in a half-whisper as they reached the stairs, “earlier today, he almost attacked the doctor and me! Even the doctor had to back off so he wouldn’t freak out more. I stayed downstairs, but Raskolnikov got dressed and slipped out right away. If you upset him now, he’ll run off again, maybe hurt himself…”
“What are you saying?”

“And Dounia can’t stay alone in your lodgings. Do you realize where you’re staying? That jerk Pyotr Petrovitch couldn’t find you a better place? Look, I’ve had a bit to drink, that’s why I’m swearing, don’t mind me…”
“But I’ll go to the landlady here,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna insisted. “I’ll beg her for a spot for Dounia and me for the night. I can’t leave Rodya like this, I just can’t!”

They were talking right outside the landlady’s door, with Nastasya holding a light from a step below. Razumihin was unusually worked up. When he brought Raskolnikov home earlier, he’d been a bit too talkative, but now, though he was tipsy, his mind was clear and his excitement had only grown. He grabbed both ladies by the hands, explaining his reasons for everything, squeezing their hands tightly every time he made a point. He stared at Dounia without any sense of manners. Sometimes they tried to pull their hands away, but he just held on tighter. If they had told him to jump off the staircase, he would have done it without a second thought for their sake. Pulcheria Alexandrovna found him odd and his grip a little painful, but she was too worried about Rodya to care. Dounia, not easily scared, was still a bit alarmed by the fiery look in Razumihin’s eyes, but she trusted Nastasya’s stories about him enough not to run away. Besides, now it seemed too late to escape. Ten minutes later, though, she felt much better. Razumihin’s real personality always showed up quickly, no matter what mood he was in, so people soon knew what to expect from him.

“You can’t go to the landlady, that’s ridiculous!” Razumihin exclaimed. “If you stay, you’ll just drive him crazy, even though you’re his mother. Who knows what might happen then! Here’s my plan: Nastasya will stay with him now, and I’ll walk you both home—you can’t go out alone at night in Petersburg, it’s dangerous. But it’ll be fine! Then I’ll rush right back and, I promise, in fifteen minutes I’ll bring you news about how he is, if he’s asleep, and so on. Then, listen! I’ll hurry home—my friends are all drunk there, but I’ll fetch Zossimov, the doctor looking after Rodya. He’s not drunk, never is! I’ll drag him here, first to Rodya, then to you, so you’ll get two reports—one from the doctor himself! If anything’s wrong, I swear I’ll bring you here myself. If all’s well, you go to bed, and I’ll stay in the hallway, and Zossimov will sleep at the landlady’s, just in case. Which is better for Rodya: you or a doctor? So let’s go! And don’t even think about the landlady; she’d never take you. She’s jealous—really, of Dounia, and you too… She’s a very strange woman! But so am I… Never mind! Come on! Do you trust me? Tell me, do you trust me or not?”
“Let’s go, mother,” Dounia said. “He’ll do what he says. He already saved Rodya, and if the doctor really stays nearby, what could be better?”
“You see, you get me! Because you’re an angel!” Razumihin cried in delight. “Let’s go! Nastasya! Run upstairs and stay with him, with a lamp. I’ll be back in fifteen minutes.”

Pulcheria Alexandrovna still wasn’t totally convinced, but she didn’t object anymore. Razumihin took both women by the arm and led them downstairs. He still made her nervous—he seemed capable and kind, but could he really keep his promise? He didn’t seem very stable…

“Ah, I see you think I’m out of it,” Razumihin said, reading her mind as they walked along the street, his long strides making it hard for the women to keep up. He didn’t notice, though. “Nonsense! Yes, I’m drunk, but not from alcohol. It’s seeing you two that’s made me dizzy… But don’t mind me! Don’t pay attention, I’m rambling, I’m not good enough for you… I’ll dump a couple of buckets of water over my head once I’ve taken you home, and I’ll be fine… If only you knew how much I love you both! Don’t be angry, don’t laugh! You can be mad at anyone, but not me! I’m Rodya’s friend, so I’m your friend too. I want to be… I had a feeling… Last year, for a moment… well, it doesn’t matter, you seem to have just fallen from heaven. I probably won’t sleep all night… Zossimov was worried earlier that Rodya might go crazy… That’s why we can’t upset him.”
“What did you say?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried, startled.
“Did the doctor really say that?” Dounia asked, alarmed.

“Yes, but it’s not true, not at all. He gave Rodya some medicine—a powder, I saw it—and then you both arrived… Actually, it would’ve been better if you came tomorrow. It’s good we left him alone. In an hour Zossimov himself will tell you everything. He’s not drunk! And I won’t be either… I only got drunk because they dragged me into some stupid argument! I promised myself I’d never argue again! They talk such nonsense. I almost ended up fighting! I left my uncle to host. Would you believe, they argue that people shouldn’t be themselves, but as different as possible! They call that progress. And not even their own ideas, just stuff they heard from others…”
“Listen!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna tried to interrupt, but it only made him talk more.

“What do you think?” Razumihin practically shouted. “You think I’m mad at them for talking nonsense? Not at all! I love it when people talk nonsense. That’s what makes us human! By making mistakes, we find the truth. I make mistakes, so I’m a man! You can’t find the truth without making a bunch of mistakes first, maybe a hundred or more. And that’s fine! But the thing is, we don’t even make our own mistakes! If you talk your own nonsense, I’ll love you for it. It’s better to be wrong in your own way than right in someone else’s. Then you’re a real person; otherwise, you’re just a bird. Truth won’t run away, but life can get cramped. And what are we doing now? In science, ideas, inventions, everything—we’re still like little kids in school. We just live off other people’s ideas, that’s what we’re used to! Am I right, am I right?” He squeezed the women’s hands as he spoke.
“Oh, goodness, I don’t know,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said helplessly.
“Yes, yes… though I don’t agree with you on everything,” Dounia added honestly—and yelped, because he squeezed her hand so hard.

“You say yes—after that, you… you…” Razumihin burst out, “you’re a fountain of goodness, sense, and perfection. Give me your hand… both of you! I want to kiss your hands right here, on my knees…” He actually knelt down on the sidewalk, which was luckily empty at the moment.
“Stop it, please, what are you doing?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried, very embarrassed.
“Get up, get up!” Dounia said, laughing, though she was also a little disturbed.

“Not until you let me kiss your hands! There, done! Now I’ll get up and we’ll keep going. I’m an idiot, I know; I’m not worthy of you, and I’m drunk… I’m ashamed… I don’t deserve to love you, but every decent man should honor you! And I just did. And look, here are your lodgings, and for that alone Rodya was right to kick out Pyotr Petrovitch. How dare he put you in a place like this! What a scandal! Do you know the kind of people who live here? And you’re supposed to marry him? You’re really engaged to him? Well, then, your fiancé is a jerk.”
“Excuse me, Mr. Razumihin, you’re forgetting…” Pulcheria Alexandrovna began.

“Yes, yes, you’re right, I forgot myself. I’m sorry,” Razumihin apologized quickly. “But you can’t be mad at me for speaking so honestly! I mean every word, not because… uh, never mind! Anyway, we all saw today that he’s not like us. Not because he had his hair done, or tried to act smart, but because he’s a sneak, a cheapskate, and a clown. That’s obvious. Do you think he’s clever? No, he’s a fool. Is he a match for you? No way! Do you see, ladies?” He stopped suddenly as they climbed the stairs. “Even though my friends are all drunk, they’re honest, and even though we talk a lot of nonsense, we’ll figure things out eventually. We’re on the right path, but Pyotr Petrovitch isn’t. I may have called them names, but I respect them all… except maybe Zametov, I like him, he’s just a puppy; and that big guy Zossimov, he’s honest and knows his stuff. But enough, let’s move on. I know this building, I’ve been here before—there was some trouble at Number 3… Which room are you in? Eight? Lock your door for the night. Don’t let anyone in. I’ll be back in fifteen minutes with news, and half an hour later with Zossimov, you’ll see! Goodbye, I’m off.”
“Oh my goodness, Dounia, what’s going to happen?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said, turning anxiously to her daughter.

“Don’t worry, mother,” Dounia said, taking off her hat and coat. “God has sent this man to help us, even if he did come from a party. We can trust him, I’m sure. And think of all he’s done for Rodya already…”
“Oh, Dounia, who knows if he’ll really come back! How could I leave Rodya?… And our meeting was so different from what I imagined! He seemed so cold, like he didn’t even want to see us…”
Tears filled her eyes.
“No, it’s not that, mother. You didn’t notice because you were crying. He’s just really sick—that’s all it is.”

“Ah, this illness! What will happen? And did you hear how he talked to you, Dounia?” the mother said, looking nervously at her daughter, trying to guess her feelings. She was already half comforted by Dounia defending her brother, which meant she’d forgiven him. “I’m sure he’ll see things differently in the morning,” she added, hoping for reassurance.

“And I’m sure he’ll say the same thing tomorrow… about that,” Dounia said firmly. And there was nothing more to say, as Pulcheria Alexandrovna was too scared to keep arguing. Dounia came over and kissed her. Her mother hugged her tightly without a word, then sat down to wait anxiously for Razumihin’s return, watching her daughter pace the room with her arms folded, deep in thought. Dounia always paced like this when she was thinking, and her mother never dared interrupt her at those moments.

Razumihin, of course, seemed ridiculous with his sudden drunken crush on Dounia. But aside from his strange behavior, plenty of people would have understood if they saw Dounia just then, walking back and forth, serious and thoughtful. Dounia was very beautiful—tall, graceful, strong, and confident, though she moved with real gentleness. Her face looked a lot like her brother’s, but even more beautiful. Her hair was dark brown, a bit lighter than Raskolnikov’s, and her almost black eyes could look proud, but sometimes incredibly kind. She was pale, but in a healthy way, and her face practically glowed. Her mouth was small, with a slightly jutting lower lip and chin—the only imperfect thing about her face, but it made her look even more unique, almost noble. She usually looked serious, but when she smiled or laughed, her whole face lit up. It’s no wonder that someone like Razumihin, a big, honest, open-hearted guy who’d never met anyone like her (and who wasn’t quite sober), would fall for her instantly. Plus, he saw her first when she was glowing with love for her brother. Later, he saw her lips tremble with anger at Raskolnikov’s harsh words—and that sealed his fate.

Razumihin had actually been right when he blurted out on the stairs that Praskovya Pavlovna, Raskolnikov’s odd landlady, would be jealous of both Pulcheria Alexandrovna and Dounia because of him. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was forty-three, but still had traces of her old beauty, and looked much younger than her age. That’s often true for women who keep a kind spirit and warm heart as they get older. Her hair was going grey and thin, wrinkles had formed around her eyes, and her cheeks were hollow from worry, but her face was still lovely. She looked like Dounia, just twenty years older and without the jutting lip. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was emotional, but not overly sentimental, timid and willing to bend—but only up to a point. She could tolerate a lot, even things that went against her beliefs, but there was a line of honesty and principle she would never cross.
Exactly twenty minutes after Razumihin left, there were two quick, quiet knocks at the door: he was back.

“I won’t come in, I don’t have time,” he said quickly when the door opened. “He’s sleeping like a log, peaceful and quiet. God willing, he’ll sleep for ten hours. Nastasya’s with him; I told her not to leave until I come back. Now I’m off to get Zossimov. He’ll report to you, and then you should really get some sleep; you look exhausted.”
And he dashed away down the hallway.
“What a capable and… devoted young man!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna exclaimed, thrilled.
“He seems wonderful,” Dounia agreed warmly, and went back to pacing the room.

Nearly an hour later, they heard footsteps in the hallway and another knock at the door. This time, both women waited calmly, trusting Razumihin’s promise. He really had managed to bring Zossimov along. Zossimov had agreed right away to leave the party and go to Raskolnikov’s, but he was suspicious about meeting the ladies, not sure what Razumihin was up to in his excited state. But as soon as he saw that they were expecting him almost like a hero, his pride was satisfied. He stayed just ten minutes and left Pulcheria Alexandrovna completely reassured and grateful. He spoke kindly but with the seriousness of a young doctor in an important consultation, never talking about anything else or acting too familiar with the women. He noticed Dounia’s beauty as soon as he entered, but tried not to look at her during his visit, speaking only to Pulcheria Alexandrovna. This made him feel very pleased with himself. He said the patient was doing well, and explained that Raskolnikov’s illness was partly due to his rough living situation, and partly from mental strain—“a mix of different worries, troubles, ideas…” and so on. Noticing how closely Dounia listened, Zossimov went on about this. When Pulcheria Alexandrovna nervously asked if Raskolnikov might be insane, Zossimov smiled calmly and said his words had been exaggerated; yes, the patient had a fixed idea, maybe something like an obsession—which Zossimov was studying in his medical work—but reminded her that until today, Raskolnikov had been delirious. He also said that having his family here would help his recovery, as long as there were no more shocks. Then he stood up, bowed politely, received their thanks and goodbyes, and even got a spontaneous handshake from Dounia. He left feeling very proud of himself.
“We’ll talk tomorrow; go to bed now!” Razumihin said as he followed Zossimov out. “I’ll be here first thing in the morning with an update.”
“That Avdotya Romanovna is a real beauty,” Zossimov said, almost licking his lips as they stepped outside.
“Beauty? Did you say beauty?” Razumihin roared, then lunged at Zossimov and grabbed him by the collar, pressing him against the wall. “If you ever dare… Do you hear me? Do you hear?” he shouted.
“Let me go, you drunken idiot,” Zossimov coughed. When Razumihin let him go, Zossimov started laughing loudly. Razumihin just stood there, lost in gloomy thought.
“Of course, I’m a fool,” he said, as dark as a thundercloud, “but you’re no better.”
“No, not at all. I’m not thinking about anything like that,” Zossimov replied.
They walked in silence for a while, and only when they neared Raskolnikov’s place did Razumihin speak again, sounding anxious.

“Listen,” he said, “you’re a great guy, but you’ve got some bad habits. You’re a bit of a mess—lazy, spoiled, and you don’t deny yourself anything, which makes you kind of dirty. You’ve gotten so lazy, I don’t know how you’re still a good, even devoted, doctor. You—a doctor—sleep on a feather bed, but still get up at night for your patients! In three or four years, you’ll stop even that… But never mind! Tonight, you’re staying in the landlady’s flat here (it took a lot of convincing!), and I’ll be in the kitchen. So here’s your chance to get to know her… But it’s not what you think! There’s nothing going on, I swear…”
“But I don’t think that!”
“She’s got modesty, silence, shyness—a kind of old-fashioned virtue… and yet she’s sighing and melting for you. Help me out, will you? She’s really quite nice… I’ll owe you, I’ll do anything…”
Zossimov laughed harder than ever.
“Wow, you’ve really got it bad! But what am I supposed to do with her?”

“It won’t be that hard. Talk about anything, as long as you sit with her. You’re a doctor, maybe try to cure her of something. I swear you won’t regret it. She has a piano; I play a little. I have a song, a real Russian one: ‘I shed hot tears.’ She loves the real thing—and that’s how it all started. Now you’re the main act, a maestro, a Rubinstein… I promise, you’ll enjoy it!”
“Did you make her some kind of promise? Like, marriage or something?”
“Nothing, nothing like that! She’s not that sort at all… Tchebarov tried that…”
“Well then, just leave her alone!”
“But I can’t just drop her like that!”
“Why not?”
“I just can’t, that’s all! There’s something that draws me in.”
“Then why did you get her hopes up?”

“I didn’t! Maybe I was the one who got hooked. But honestly, she wouldn’t care if it was you or me, as long as someone sat with her, sighing. I can’t explain it… Look, you’re good at math, right? Try teaching her calculus—seriously, I mean it. It’ll be the same to her. She’ll just stare at you and sigh for a whole year. I once talked to her for two days straight about the Prussian House of Lords (you have to talk about something)—she just sighed and sweated! And don’t talk about love—she’s too shy for that—but just act like you can’t leave her side, and that’s enough. It’s actually really nice; you can read, sit, nap, write—whatever. You could even try a kiss, if you’re careful.”
“But what do I want with her?”

“Ugh, you don’t get it! You two are made for each other! I’ve often thought so… You’ll end up together eventually, so what’s the difference if it’s now or later? There’s something special here—it’s like the end of the world, a safe harbor, the center of everything, the best pancakes, the evening samovar, soft sighs and warm shawls, hot stoves to sleep on—as cozy as death, but you’re still alive. The best of both! Okay, I’m talking nonsense—it’s late! Listen, sometimes I wake up at night, so I’ll check on him. But there’s really no need, he’s fine. You don’t need to worry, but if you want, you can look in on him too. But if you notice anything—delirium or fever—wake me up right away. But there shouldn’t be anything…”

Razumihin woke up the next morning at eight, feeling worried and serious. He was facing a bunch of new and unexpected problems. He’d never thought he’d wake up feeling like this. He remembered every detail from the day before and realized something completely new had happened to him, something he’d never experienced before. But at the same time, he knew that the dream that had filled his mind was totally impossible—so much so that he felt embarrassed even thinking about it. He quickly tried to focus on the more practical problems left over from that “cursed day.”

The worst memory from yesterday was how he’d acted “badly and meanly.” Not only because he’d gotten drunk, but also because he’d taken advantage of the young woman’s situation to insult her fiancé out of stupid jealousy, even though he knew almost nothing about their relationship or about the man himself. What right did he have to judge him so quickly? No one had asked for his opinion! Did he really believe someone like Avdotya Romanovna would marry a bad man just for money? There must be something good about him. The apartment? But how could he know what it was really like? He was just furnishing a place... Ugh, it was all so pathetic! And blaming the alcohol was even worse. “In wine there’s truth,” and all the ugly stuff in his jealous heart had come out! How could someone like Razumihin ever dare to dream about someone like her? Who was he compared to her—him, the noisy, drunken fool from last night? It was ridiculous to even imagine! Razumihin blushed hard just thinking about it, and suddenly remembered how he’d joked last night on the stairs about the landlady being jealous of Avdotya Romanovna... that was just too much. He slammed his fist on the kitchen stove, hurting his hand and knocking a brick loose.

“Of course,” he muttered to himself a minute later, feeling ashamed, “of course, none of these awful things can ever be fixed... so there’s no point even thinking about it. I just have to go see them and do what I have to do... without saying anything, not even asking for forgiveness... because it’s all over now!”

Still, as he got dressed, he was more careful with his clothes than usual. He only had one suit—if he’d had another, he probably wouldn’t have worn it. “I’d have made sure not to.” But either way, he couldn’t just show up looking like a slob; he had no right to make people uncomfortable, especially when they needed his help and actually wanted to see him. He brushed his clothes thoroughly. His shirt was always clean; he was especially careful about that.

That morning he washed himself really well—he got some soap from Nastasya, and cleaned his hair, neck, and especially his hands. When he thought about whether to shave his scruffy chin (Praskovya Pavlovna had some great razors from her late husband), he angrily decided not to. “Just leave it! If I shave, they’ll think I did it to impress them... That’s exactly what they’d think! No way!”

“The worst thing is, I’m so rough and messy; I act like I live in a bar,” he thought. “And even if I do have some good qualities, what’s there to brag about? Everyone should act decent—and more than that... And still (he remembered) I’ve done things... not exactly wrong, but still... And some of the thoughts I’ve had, hmm... How can I even compare myself to Avdotya Romanovna? Forget it! Fine, then—I’ll just keep being messy and rude, like I don’t care! I’ll be even worse!”
He was having this kind of inner argument with himself when Zossimov, who had spent the night in Praskovya Pavlovna’s parlor, came in.
Zossimov was heading home and wanted to check on his patient first. Razumihin told him that Raskolnikov was sleeping soundly. Zossimov said not to wake him and promised to come back around eleven.
“If he’s still here,” he added. “Honestly! If you can’t keep track of your patients, how are you supposed to help them? Do you know if he’s going to them, or if they’re coming here?”

“They’re coming here, I think,” said Razumihin, understanding what Zossimov was getting at, “and they’ll probably talk about family stuff. I’ll get out of the way. You, as the doctor, have more reason to be here than I do.”
“But I’m not their priest; I’ll just come and go. I’ve got plenty of other things to do besides looking after them.”

“There’s one thing that bothers me,” Razumihin said, frowning. “On the way home I talked a lot of nonsense to him while I was drunk... all kinds of things... and I told him you were worried he... might go crazy.”
“You told the ladies that too.”
“I know it was stupid! You can smack me if you want! Did you really think that?”

“No way, that’s just nonsense! How could I seriously think that? You yourself called him obsessed when you dragged me to him... and yesterday we just made things worse—you did, at least, with your story about the painter; what a lovely topic, when he might have been obsessed with that very thing! If I’d known what happened at the police station, and that some jerk... had insulted him with this suspicion! Hmm... I wouldn’t have let that topic come up yesterday. People like that always take the smallest thing and turn it into a huge problem... and they think their wild ideas are totally real... As far as I’m concerned, it was Zametov’s story that actually cleared up half the mystery. I mean, I know a case where a hypochondriac, a forty-year-old man, cut the throat of an eight-year-old boy just because he couldn’t stand the kid’s jokes at dinner! And with Raskolnikov, you’ve got his shabby clothes, that rude police officer, the fever, and the suspicion! All that piling up on a guy who’s half-crazy with worry and has this touchy pride! That could easily set off an illness. Well, whatever!... And by the way, that Zametov is a decent guy, but... he really shouldn’t have said all that last night. He talks way too much!”
“But who did he tell it to? Just us, right?”
“And Porfiry.”
“So what?”
“Oh, and do you have any influence over them—his mother and sister? Tell them to be careful with him today....”
“They’ll be fine,” Razumihin replied, sounding a bit annoyed.
“Why does he hate this Luzhin guy so much? He’s got money, and she doesn’t seem to dislike him... and I guess they’re totally broke, right?”
“Why do you care?” Razumihin snapped. “How should I know if they have any money? Ask them yourself if you want to find out....”

“Jeez, you can be such an idiot sometimes! You’re still not over last night’s wine.... Goodbye; thank Praskovya Pavlovna for letting me stay. She locked herself in, didn’t answer when I said good morning through the door; she was up at seven, took the samovar into her room from the kitchen. I wasn’t even allowed to see her....”

Exactly at nine, Razumihin arrived at Bakaleyev’s house where the ladies were staying. Both women were waiting anxiously—they’d been up since seven or even earlier. He came in looking gloomy, bowed awkwardly, and immediately felt mad at himself for it. He hadn’t expected what happened next: Pulcheria Alexandrovna rushed at him, grabbed both his hands, and almost kissed them. He glanced shyly at Avdotya Romanovna, but her proud face showed so much gratitude and respect (instead of the sarcasm and hidden dislike he’d feared) that it made him even more uncomfortable than if she’d been angry. Luckily, there was something to talk about, and he quickly changed the subject.

When she heard that everything was going well and that Rodya was still sleeping, Pulcheria Alexandrovna said she was glad, because “there’s something we really, really need to talk about first.” Then came questions about breakfast and an invitation to eat with them—they’d waited for him. Avdotya Romanovna rang for the waiter, who turned out to be dirty and ragged, and the tea was served in such a messy way that the ladies were embarrassed. Razumihin complained about the place, but remembering Luzhin, stopped and felt relieved when Pulcheria Alexandrovna started asking him question after question.

For forty-five minutes, he talked, constantly interrupted by their questions, and managed to tell them all the most important things he knew about Raskolnikov’s life in the past year, finishing with a detailed story about his illness. He left out some things that were better left out, especially what happened at the police station. They listened eagerly, and when he thought he was done and had answered everything, he realized they thought he’d barely started.
“Tell me, tell me! What do you think...? Sorry, I still don’t know your name!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna interrupted quickly.
“Dmitri Prokofitch.”

“I’d really, really like to know, Dmitri Prokofitch... what he’s like now, I mean, what does he like or dislike? Is he always so irritable? Can you tell me what he hopes for, or what he dreams about? Who influences him these days? In short, I’d just like...”
“Mother, how can he answer all that at once?” said Dounia.
“Oh my, I never expected to find him like this, Dmitri Prokofitch!”

“Naturally,” Razumihin replied. “I don’t have a mother, but my uncle visits every year and almost never recognizes me, even though he’s smart; and you’ve been apart for three years, which is a long time. What can I say? I’ve known Rodion for a year and a half; he’s moody, gloomy, proud, and lately—and maybe for a long time—he’s been suspicious and a bit odd. He’s got a good heart and a noble nature. He doesn’t like to show his feelings, and would rather do something hurtful than open up. Sometimes, though, he’s not just gloomy, he’s plain cold and acts like nothing matters; it’s like he keeps switching between two personalities. Sometimes he’s extremely closed off! He says he’s so busy but then lies in bed doing nothing. He doesn’t make jokes—not because he can’t, but like he thinks it’s a waste of time. He never really listens to what people say. He doesn’t care about what interests others. He thinks a lot of himself, and maybe he’s right. Well, what else? I think you being here will really help him.”
“God grant it does,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said, upset by what she’d just heard about Rodya.

At last, Razumihin dared to look more directly at Avdotya Romanovna. He’d looked at her a few times while talking, but only for a second before looking away. Avdotya Romanovna sat at the table, listening closely, then stood and paced with her arms folded and lips pressed together, occasionally asking a question without stopping. She had the same habit as Raskolnikov—not always listening. She wore a thin dark dress and a white, see-through scarf. Razumihin quickly noticed how poor they must be. If Avdotya Romanovna had been dressed like a queen, he wouldn’t be afraid of her, but because she was dressed so simply and he could see how hard up they were, he felt even more awkward and afraid of saying or doing the wrong thing—which was tough for someone already lacking confidence.

“You’ve told us a lot about my brother’s character... and you were fair about it. I’m glad. I thought you’d be uncritically devoted to him,” Avdotya Romanovna said with a smile. “I think you’re right—he does need a woman’s care,” she added thoughtfully.
“I didn’t say that; but maybe you’re right, only...”
“Only what?”
“He doesn’t love anyone and maybe he never will,” Razumihin said flatly.
“You mean he can’t love?”

“You know, Avdotya Romanovna, you’re a lot like your brother—in almost every way!” he blurted out, surprising even himself, but then remembered what he’d just said about her brother and turned bright red, feeling very embarrassed. Avdotya Romanovna couldn’t help laughing when she saw him.

“Maybe you’re both wrong about Rodya,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said, slightly annoyed. “I’m not talking about our current problem, Dounia. What Pyotr Petrovitch wrote in this letter and what you and I thought might be wrong, but you can’t imagine, Dmitri Prokofitch, how moody and unpredictable he is. I never knew what he’d do, even when he was fifteen. And I’m sure he could do something now that nobody else would ever think of doing... For example, do you know how, a year and a half ago, he shocked me and nearly gave me a heart attack with his idea of marrying that girl—what was her name—his landlady’s daughter?”
“Did you hear about that?” asked Avdotya Romanovna.

“Do you think—” Pulcheria Alexandrovna went on emotionally, “Do you think my tears, my begging, my sickness, the thought that I might die from grief, or our poverty would have stopped him? No, he would have calmly ignored all that. And it’s not because he doesn’t love us!”
“He’s never mentioned that to me,” Razumihin replied carefully. “But I did hear a bit from Praskovya Pavlovna herself, and she’s not a gossip. What I heard was definitely strange.”
“And what did you hear?” both women asked at once.

“Well, nothing special. I only heard that the wedding, which didn’t happen because the girl died, was something Praskovya Pavlovna didn’t want. They say the girl wasn’t pretty—in fact, some people say she was ugly... and she was sick... and a little strange. But she must have had some good qualities, or else it doesn’t make sense.... She had no money, and he wouldn’t have cared about her money anyway.... But it’s always hard to judge these things.”
“I’m sure she was a good girl,” Avdotya Romanovna said simply.

“God forgive me, but I was actually glad when she died. Though now I don’t know which would have made the other more miserable—him or her,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna finished. Then she started carefully asking Razumihin about what had happened with Luzhin the previous day, hesitating and often glancing at Dounia, who was clearly annoyed. This bothered Pulcheria Alexandrovna more than anything else. Razumihin explained what happened in detail, but this time added his own opinion: he openly blamed Raskolnikov for purposely insulting Pyotr Petrovitch, not excusing him because he was sick.
“He planned it before he got sick,” he added.
“I think so too,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna agreed sadly. Still, she was surprised to hear Razumihin speak so carefully and even respectfully about Pyotr Petrovitch. Avdotya Romanovna noticed it too.
“So that’s what you think of Pyotr Petrovitch?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna couldn’t help asking.

“I can’t think anything else about your daughter’s future husband,” Razumihin replied firmly and warmly, “and I’m not just being polite, but... simply because Avdotya Romanovna willingly chose to marry him. If I spoke so rudely about him last night, it’s because I was disgustingly drunk and... actually crazy; yes, crazy, I totally lost my head... and I’m ashamed of it this morning.”
He blushed and stopped talking. Avdotya Romanovna also blushed but didn’t say anything. She hadn’t spoken at all since they started talking about Luzhin.
Without her daughter’s support, Pulcheria Alexandrovna clearly didn’t know what to do. Finally, hesitating and glancing at Dounia, she admitted something was worrying her a lot.
“You see, Dmitri Prokofitch,” she started. “I want to be completely honest with Dmitri Prokofitch, right, Dounia?”
“Of course, mother,” said Avdotya Romanovna firmly.

“It’s like this,” she said quickly, like just being allowed to say it made her feel lighter. “Very early this morning we got a note from Pyotr Petrovitch replying to our letter about our arrival. He promised to meet us at the station, but instead sent a servant with the address and directions, saying he’d come see us this morning. But this morning, this note arrived. You’d better read it yourself; there’s a part that’s really bothering me... you’ll see, and... please tell me what you honestly think, Dmitri Prokofitch! You know Rodya better than anyone, and no one can advise us as well as you can. Dounia made up her mind right away, but I’m still not sure, and I’ve been waiting for your opinion.”
Razumihin opened the note, dated the night before, and read:

“Dear Madam, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, I’m sorry to say that because of unexpected problems I couldn’t meet you at the train station; instead, I sent someone trustworthy to help. I also won’t be able to see you tomorrow morning because of urgent Senate business and because I don’t want to intrude while you’re reuniting with your son and Avdotya Romanovna with her brother. I will visit you at your lodgings tomorrow evening at exactly eight o’clock, and I must ask—very seriously—that Rodion Romanovitch not be present, since he insulted me badly when I visited him yesterday, and also because I need to discuss something important with you directly. If Rodion Romanovitch is there despite my request, I’ll have to leave right away and that will be your responsibility. I believe that, even though he was so ill when I saw him, he recovered enough to go out two hours later and might visit you as well. I know this because I saw him myself at the home of a drunk man who was run over and died, where he gave the man’s daughter—a girl with a bad reputation—twenty-five roubles for the funeral, which surprised me, knowing how hard you worked to get that money. Please give my special regards to your esteemed daughter, Avdotya Romanovna, and accept the respect of
“Your humble servant,
“P. LUZHIN.”

“What should I do now, Dmitri Prokofitch?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna began, almost in tears. “How can I ask Rodya not to come? Yesterday he begged us to refuse Pyotr Petrovitch, and now we’re told not to let Rodya in! If he hears, he’ll come on purpose, and... what will happen then?”
“Follow Avdotya Romanovna’s decision,” Razumihin said calmly, right away.

“Oh dear! She says... I don’t even know what she means, she won’t explain! She says it’s best—no, not best, but absolutely necessary that Rodya be here at eight o’clock and that they must meet.... I didn’t even want him to see the letter; I wanted to keep him away with your help... because he gets so upset.... Besides, I don’t understand what this dead drunk man and his daughter have to do with anything, or how he could have given her all that money... which...”
“Which you worked so hard to save, mother,” Avdotya Romanovna interrupted.

“He wasn’t himself yesterday,” Razumihin said thoughtfully. “If you only knew what he did at a restaurant yesterday, though there was some sense in it too.... Hmm! He did mention something last night about a dead man and a girl as we walked home, but I didn’t get it.... But last night, I myself...”

“The best thing, mother, is for us to go to him, and then we’ll be able to decide what to do. Besides, it’s getting late—oh my, it’s past ten,” she said, glancing at a beautiful gold watch on a thin Venetian chain around her neck, which didn’t match her shabby clothes at all. “A present from her fiancé,” thought Razumihin.
“We must go, Dounia, we must go,” her mother cried, flustered. “He’ll think we’re still angry after yesterday, since we’re coming so late. Oh my goodness!”

As she spoke, she hurriedly put on her hat and coat; Dounia, too, got ready. Her gloves, Razumihin noticed, weren’t just worn out—they had holes in them. But even though they were so obviously poor, the two ladies had a special dignity, the kind you see in people who know how to wear old clothes with pride. Razumihin looked at Dounia with respect and felt proud to be walking with her. “The queen who mended her stockings in prison,” he thought, “must have looked even more queenly then than at fancy banquets.”
“Oh God!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna exclaimed, “I never thought I’d be scared to see my own son, my dear, dear Rodya! I’m scared, Dmitri Prokofitch,” she added, looking at him nervously.
“Don’t be scared, mother,” said Dounia, kissing her. “Better to trust him.”
“Oh, I do trust him, but I haven’t slept all night,” said the poor woman.
They went out into the street.

“You know, Dounia, when I dozed off this morning, I dreamed of Marfa Petrovna... she was all in white... she came up to me, took my hand, and shook her head at me—so sternly, like she was blaming me.... Is that a bad sign? Oh dear! Dmitri Prokofitch, you don’t know, but Marfa Petrovna’s dead!”
“No, I didn’t know; who is Marfa Petrovna?”
“She died suddenly; and imagine...”
“Later, mom,” Dounia said. “He doesn’t know who Marfa Petrovna is.”

“Oh, you don’t know? I thought you must know all about us. Sorry, Dmitri Prokofitch, I don’t know what I’m thinking these days. I really see you as a guardian angel for us, so I figured you knew everything already. I feel like you’re family.... Please don’t be upset with me for saying that. Oh, what happened to your right hand? Did you hurt it?”
“Yeah, I bruised it,” Razumihin mumbled, delighted.

“I talk too much from the heart sometimes, Dounia always tells me off for it.... But honestly, what a tiny place he lives in! I wonder if he’s awake? Does his landlady really call this a room? Listen, you said he doesn’t like to show his feelings, so maybe I’ll bother him with my... emotional outbursts? Please tell me, Dmitri Prokofitch, how should I act? I’m so anxious, you know.”
“Don’t ask him too many questions if you see him frown; don’t ask too much about his health; he doesn’t like that.”
“Ah, Dmitri Prokofitch, it’s so hard to be a mother! But here are the stairs.... What a terrible staircase!”
“Mother, you’re so pale, don’t upset yourself,” said Dounia, hugging her. Then, with shining eyes, she added, “He should be happy to see you, and you’re worrying yourself so much.”
“Wait, I’ll go ahead and see if he’s awake.”
The ladies slowly followed Razumihin, who went ahead. When they reached
“He’s doing really well, totally fine!” Zossimov said cheerfully as they walked in.

Zossimov had arrived about ten minutes earlier and was sitting in his usual spot on the sofa. Raskolnikov was in the opposite corner, fully dressed, clean, and neatly combed—something he hadn’t bothered with in a while. The room quickly filled up with people, but Nastasya managed to slip in behind everyone and stayed to listen.

Raskolnikov really was almost back to normal compared to yesterday, but he was still pale, tired, and looked gloomy. He seemed like someone who’d been through something terrible. His eyebrows were tense, his lips pressed together, and his eyes looked feverish. He barely spoke and seemed like he was only talking because he had to. Even his movements were restless.

The only thing missing was a sling or a bandage to make him look like he’d broken something. His pale, sad face lit up for a second when his mother and sister walked in, but that just made him look like he was in even more pain instead of just tired. The brightness quickly faded, but the suffering stayed. Zossimov, watching his patient like an eager young doctor, noticed that Raskolnikov didn’t seem happy to see his family—more like he was bracing himself for another hour of torture. Almost every part of the conversation seemed to poke at something sensitive for him. Still, Zossimov was impressed by how well Raskolnikov hid his feelings, since yesterday he'd gotten upset over the smallest things.

“Yes, I can see I’m almost well now,” Raskolnikov said, giving his mother and sister a welcoming kiss that made Pulcheria Alexandrovna light up. “And I’m not just saying that like I did yesterday,” he added to Razumihin, giving his hand a friendly squeeze.

“Yes, it’s amazing how much better he is today,” Zossimov said, happy to see the ladies, since he’d struggled to keep a conversation going with Raskolnikov for ten minutes before. “If he keeps this up, in three or four days he’ll be back to how he was a month—or even two or three months—ago. This has been building up for a while, hasn’t it? Come on, admit it—it might be your own fault?” he asked, smiling carefully, like he was worried about upsetting him.
“Maybe,” Raskolnikov replied coldly.

“I think your recovery totally depends on you,” Zossimov went on, sounding more enthusiastic. “Now that you can actually talk, I want to remind you to avoid the main things that made you sick in the first place. If you do that, you’ll be fine. If not, things might get worse. I don’t know exactly what those things are, but you must. You’re smart—you’ve probably noticed it yourself. I think your problems started when you left university. You need to stay busy, have a goal, maybe go back to studying. That would help.”
“Yes, yes, you’re absolutely right... I’ll hurry and go back to university, and then everything will be fine...”

Zossimov had partly started giving advice to impress the women, but he was a bit confused when he noticed Raskolnikov’s face showed clear sarcasm for a moment. It was gone in a second. Pulcheria Alexandrovna started thanking Zossimov right away, especially for visiting them the night before.
“Wait, he saw you last night?” Raskolnikov asked, sounding surprised. “So you didn’t sleep after your trip?”
“Oh, Rodya, it was only until two in the morning. Dounia and I never go to bed before two at home.”

“I don’t know how to thank him either,” Raskolnikov continued, suddenly frowning and looking down. “Even forgetting about payment—forgive me for mentioning it,” he said to Zossimov, “I honestly don’t know why you’re giving me all this special attention! I just don’t get it... and... and... it actually bothers me, since I don’t understand. I’m just being honest.”

“Don’t get upset.” Zossimov forced a laugh. “Think of it this way—you’re my first real patient. When doctors start out, we get really attached to our first patients, almost like they’re our own children. Some of us even fall in love with them. And, honestly, I don’t have many patients yet.”
“I’m not even talking about him,” Raskolnikov added, pointing at Razumihin, “even though all I’ve done is trouble him and insult him.”
“What nonsense are you saying! Are you in a sentimental mood today or something?” Razumihin shouted.

If Razumihin had been more observant, he would have noticed that Raskolnikov wasn’t being sentimental at all—actually, it was the opposite. But Avdotya Romanovna (Dounia) noticed and watched her brother closely and nervously.

“As for you, Mother, I don’t even know what to say,” he continued, like he was repeating something from memory. “It’s only today I’ve started to realize how worried you must have been yesterday, waiting for me.”

After saying this, he suddenly reached out his hand to his sister and smiled silently. For a second, there was real, honest feeling in his smile. Dounia noticed it immediately and squeezed his hand, feeling happy and thankful. It was the first time he’d spoken to her since their argument the day before. Their mother’s face lit up with joy at this silent but obvious reconciliation. “That’s what I love about him,” Razumihin muttered to himself, turning in his chair, “he has these moments.”

“And he does it all so well,” his mother thought. “He’s so generous, and he solved everything with Dounia so simply—just by holding out his hand and looking at her like that... And his eyes, his whole face—he’s even better looking than Dounia... But, oh, his clothes—he’s dressed so terribly! Even Vasya, the delivery boy at Afanasy Ivanitch’s shop, dresses better! I just want to hug him... cry over him—but I’m scared... Oh, he’s so strange! He seems kind, but I’m afraid! Why am I afraid...?”

“Oh, Rodya, you wouldn’t believe,” she suddenly burst out, hurrying to answer him, “how unhappy Dounia and I were yesterday! Now that everything’s okay and we’re happy again—I can tell you. We ran here straight from the train to see you, and that woman—oh, here she is! Good morning, Nastasya!—she told us you were in bed with a high fever and had run away from the doctor, and people were looking for you all over. You can’t imagine how we felt! I kept thinking about Lieutenant Potanchikov, your father’s friend—you don’t remember him, Rodya—who ran out in a fever and fell into the well in the courtyard, and they couldn’t get him out until the next day. Of course, we imagined the worst. We were about to go look for Pyotr Petrovitch to help us... Because we were totally alone,” she added sadly, stopping herself, remembering it was risky to mention Pyotr Petrovitch, even though “we’re happy again now.”
“Yeah, yeah... It’s really annoying...” Raskolnikov muttered, but he looked distracted and wasn’t really paying attention, and Dounia stared at him, confused.
“What else was I going to say?” He tried to remember. “Oh, right; Mother, and you too, Dounia, please don’t think I didn’t plan to come see you today and was just waiting for you to visit me first.”
“What are you saying, Rodya?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried, surprised.
“Is he just answering us out of duty?” Dounia wondered. “Is he making up with us like it’s a ritual or something he memorized?”
“I just woke up and planned to come to you, but my clothes delayed me. I forgot to ask her—Nastasya—to wash the blood out yesterday... I just got dressed.”
“Blood? What blood?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked, panicked.
“Oh, it’s nothing—don’t worry. Yesterday, when I was wandering around, kind of out of it, I ran into a guy who’d been run over... a clerk...”
“Out of it? But you remember everything!” Razumihin interrupted.
“That’s true,” Raskolnikov answered carefully. “I remember every detail, but I still can’t really explain why I did it, went there, or said what I did.”
“That happens a lot,” Zossimov chimed in. “People can do things perfectly, even cleverly, but the reason behind it is all mixed up because of their illness—it’s like being in a dream.”
“Maybe it’s good if they think I’m almost crazy,” Raskolnikov thought.
“But healthy people act like that sometimes, too,” Dounia said, looking nervously at Zossimov.

“There’s some truth to that,” Zossimov replied. “Honestly, all of us act a little crazy sometimes—the only difference is that the sick are just a bit more so. A truly normal person almost doesn’t exist. Out of thousands, maybe you’d find one.”
When Zossimov casually used the word “madman,” everyone frowned.
Raskolnikov seemed lost in thought, not even listening, with a strange smile on his pale lips. He was still deep in his own mind.
“So, what happened to the guy who was run over? I interrupted you!” Razumihin asked quickly.

“What?” Raskolnikov snapped back to reality. “Oh... I got blood on me helping to carry him home. By the way, Mom, I did something really dumb yesterday. I was basically out of my mind. I gave away all the money you sent me... to his wife for the funeral. She’s a widow now, dying of tuberculosis, poor thing... three little kids, starving... nothing in the house... and a daughter, too... Maybe you would’ve given it yourself if you’d seen them. But I had no right to do it, I know, especially since you need the money. To help others, you have to have the right, or else, well, “Crevez, chiens, si vous n’êtes pas contents”—die like dogs if you’re not happy. That’s right, isn’t it, Dounia?”
“No, it’s not,” Dounia answered firmly.

“Ha! So you have your own ideals,” he muttered, looking at her almost angrily and smirking. “I should’ve thought of that... That’s good for you, better for you. If you have a line you won’t cross, you’ll be unhappy; if you cross it, maybe you’ll be even more unhappy... Anyway, that’s all nonsense,” he added irritably, annoyed at himself. “I just wanted to say I’m sorry, Mom,” he finished, short and sharp.
“That’s enough, Rodya, I’m sure everything you do is good,” his mother said happily.
“Don’t be too sure,” he replied, twisting his mouth into a grim smile.
Silence followed. The whole conversation felt awkward, and so did the silence, and even the making up and forgiving—all of it was uncomfortable for everyone.
“It’s like they’re scared of me,” Raskolnikov thought, glancing at his mother and sister. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was definitely getting more nervous the longer she stayed quiet.
“But when I wasn’t with them, I thought I loved them so much,” flashed through his mind.
“Rodya, did you know Marfa Petrovna is dead?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna suddenly blurted out.
“Marfa Petrovna? Who?”
“Oh, goodness—Marfa Petrovna Svidrigailov. I wrote you so much about her.”
“Ah, right! Now I remember... So she’s dead! Really?” he perked up, suddenly more interested. “What did she die of?”

“It happened so suddenly,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna hurried to answer, encouraged by his interest. “On the very day I sent you that letter! Can you believe it, they say that awful man might be the reason she died. They say he beat her terribly.”
“Were things really that bad between them?” he asked, turning to his sister.

“Not at all. Actually, it was the opposite. He was always patient and considerate with her. In fact, during their seven years together, he always gave in to her, maybe too much. But suddenly, he just lost his patience.”
“Then he couldn’t have been that awful if he behaved for seven years. Are you defending him, Dounia?”
“No, no, he’s terrible! I can’t imagine anyone worse!” Dounia answered, almost shivering, frowning and lost in thought.

“It happened in the morning,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna continued quickly. “Right after, she ordered the horses to take her to town after lunch. She always did that when there was trouble. She ate a really good meal, they say...”
“After being beaten up?”

“That was her routine; and right after lunch, so she wouldn’t be late, she went to the bathhouse... She was in treatment—taking cold spring baths every day—and as soon as she got in the water, she suddenly had a stroke!”
“Not surprising,” said Zossimov.
“Did he really beat her that badly?”
“Why does that matter!” Dounia interrupted.
“Hmm. But, Mom, I don’t know why you want to talk about this kind of gossip,” Raskolnikov said, sounding irritated even though he didn’t mean to.
“Oh, my dear, I don’t know what else to talk about,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna blurted out.
“Why, are you all afraid of me?” he asked, forcing a smile.
“It’s true,” said Dounia, looking him straight in the eyes. “Mother was making the sign of the cross out of fear as we came up the stairs.”
His face twitched, like he was fighting something inside.

“Oh, Dounia! Don’t say that—don’t make him angry, Rodya... Why did you say that, Dounia?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna pleaded, overwhelmed. “On the train, I was dreaming about seeing you, talking about everything together... I was so happy, I didn’t even notice the trip! But what am I saying? I’m happy now... You shouldn’t, Dounia... I’m happy now—just to see you, Rodya...”
“Hush, Mom,” he muttered, embarrassed, not looking at her but squeezing her hand. “We’ll have time to talk about everything soon!”

As he said this, a wave of confusion and paleness swept over him. That horrible feeling he’d had lately came back, cold and intense. Once again, it hit him that he’d just told a huge lie—he would never be able to talk honestly about anything, ever again. The pain of that thought was so sharp, he nearly lost himself. He stood up, not looking at anyone, and headed for the door.
“What are you doing?” Razumihin yelled, grabbing his arm.
He sat down again, looking around silently. Everyone stared at him, confused.
“Why is everyone so quiet?” he suddenly shouted. “Say something! Why just sit here? We get together and sit in silence... Come on, talk about something—anything!”
“Thank God; I was afraid he was about to have another episode like yesterday,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said, crossing herself.
“What’s wrong, Rodya?” Dounia asked, distrustfully.
“Oh, nothing! I just remembered something,” he replied, and suddenly started laughing.
“Well, if you remembered something, that’s good!... I was starting to think...” Zossimov muttered, getting up. “I should be going. I’ll drop by again if I can...” He said goodbye and left.
“What a nice man!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said.

“Yes, very nice, smart, well-educated,” Raskolnikov suddenly said, speaking faster and livelier than before. “I can’t remember where I met him before I got sick... I think I’ve seen him somewhere... And this is a good guy, too,” he nodded at Razumihin. “Do you like him, Dounia?” he asked, and for some reason, laughed.
“Very much,” Dounia answered.
“Ugh, you’re such a jerk!” Razumihin protested, blushing furiously, and stood up. Pulcheria Alexandrovna smiled a little, but Raskolnikov laughed out loud.
“Where are you going?”
“I have to go.”
“No, you don’t. Stay. Zossimov left, so you have to stay. Don’t go. What time is it? Is it noon? That’s a nice watch, Dounia. But why is everyone quiet again? I’m the only one talking.”
“It was a present from Marfa Petrovna,” Dounia said.
“And it was expensive!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna added.
“Wow! It’s huge! Doesn’t look like a woman’s watch.”
“I like that kind,” Dounia said.
“So it’s not from her fiancé,” Razumihin thought, feeling way happier than he should.
“I thought Luzhin gave it to her,” Raskolnikov said.
“No, he hasn’t given Dounia any gifts yet.”
“Ah! Do you remember, Mom, I was once in love and wanted to get married?” he suddenly said, looking at his mother, who was thrown off by the sudden topic change.
“Yes, dear.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna exchanged glances with Dounia and Razumihin.

“Hmm, what should I say? I don’t remember much. She was always sick,” he went on, looking dreamy and staring at the floor. “She liked giving money to the poor, always dreaming of becoming a nun, and once she started crying when we talked about it. Yes, yes, I remember now. She wasn’t pretty at all. I don’t know why I liked her—maybe because she was always ill. If she’d been lame or hunched over, I’d probably have liked her even more,” he said with a dreamy smile. “Yeah, I guess it was just spring fever.”
“No, it wasn’t just because of spring fever,” said Dounia warmly.
He stared at his sister, but didn’t seem to hear or understand her. Then, lost in thought, he stood up, went to his mother, kissed her, and sat back down.
“You still love her?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked, touched.

“Her? Now? Oh, no... That’s all in the past... it feels like another world. And everything here seems far away too.” He looked at them carefully. “You—I feel like I’m looking at you from a thousand miles away... but who knows why we’re even talking about this! What’s the point?” he added, annoyed, and started biting his nails, falling silent again.
“Rodya, your place is so awful! It’s like a tomb,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna suddenly said, breaking the heavy silence. “I’m sure this place is half the reason you’re so depressed.”
“My place,” he replied, sounding bored. “Yeah, the place had a lot to do with it... I thought so, too... But, Mom, what you just said is really strange,” he added, laughing in a weird way.

If he’d had to spend much longer with his mother and sister, after three years apart, having this kind of close talk—but not really being able to talk about anything real—it would’ve been too much for him. But there was something he had to settle that day, and he remembered it now as a way out.

“Listen, Dounia,” he began, serious and cold, “I’m sorry for yesterday, but I still have to say: it’s either me or Luzhin. If I’m a scoundrel, then you shouldn’t be. One is enough. If you marry Luzhin, I’ll stop thinking of you as my sister.”
“Rodya, Rodya! You’re saying the same thing as yesterday,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried sadly. “And why do you call yourself a scoundrel? I can’t stand it. You said the same yesterday.”

“Brother,” Dounia answered firmly, just as coldly. “You’re making a mistake. I thought about it last night and figured it out. You think I’m sacrificing myself for someone else, but I’m not. I’m marrying for me—because life is hard for me. Yes, I hope I can help my family, but that’s not the main reason...”
“She’s lying,” he thought, biting his nails angrily. “Too proud to admit she wants to do it for others! So proud! Even their love feels like hate... I... hate them all!”

“Actually,” Dounia went on, “I’m marrying Pyotr Petrovitch because I think he’s the lesser evil. I plan to do everything he expects, so I’m not tricking him. Why did you just smile?” She blushed, and her eyes flashed with anger.
“Everything?” he asked, grinning bitterly.
“Within limits. The way Pyotr Petrovitch proposed showed me exactly what he wants. Maybe he thinks too highly of himself, but I hope he respects me too... Why are you laughing again?”

“And why are you blushing again? You’re lying, Dounia. You’re just being stubborn to stand up against me... You can’t respect Luzhin. I’ve met him. So you’re selling yourself for money, and in any case, you should be ashamed—at least you can blush about it.”

“That’s not true. I’m not lying,” Dounia fired back, losing her composure. “I wouldn’t marry him if I didn’t believe he respected me. I wouldn’t do it if I didn’t believe I could respect him. And I’ll have proof today... and such a marriage isn’t as awful as you say! And anyway, if I really were doing something terrible, is it fair for you to demand heroism from me that maybe you don’t have yourself? That’s just controlling. If I hurt anyone, it’s only myself... I’m not killing anyone. Why are you looking at me like that? Why do you look so pale? Rodya, what’s wrong?”
“Oh no! You made him faint,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried.

“No, no, it’s nothing. Just dizzy—not fainting. You’re obsessed with fainting. So, what was I saying? Oh, right. How will you get proof today that you can respect him and that he... respects you, like you said. Did you mean today?”
“Mother, show Rodya Pyotr Petrovitch’s letter,” Dounia said.
With shaking hands, Pulcheria Alexandrovna handed him the letter. He took it, looking very interested, but before opening it, he looked at Dounia with a surprised expression.
“This is strange,” he said slowly, as if he’d just thought of something new. “Why am I making such a big deal out of this? What’s the point? Marry whoever you want!”

He said it almost to himself, but out loud, and stared at his sister, puzzled. Finally, he opened the letter and read it carefully—twice. Pulcheria Alexandrovna looked extra anxious, and everyone expected something big.

“What surprises me,” he finally said, handing the letter back to his mother but not talking to anyone in particular, “is that he’s a business man, a lawyer, and he’s so full of himself, but he writes like he’s not educated at all.”
They all looked shocked. They’d expected something completely different.
“But they all write like that,” Razumihin said suddenly.
“You read it?”
“Yeah.”
“We showed him, Rodya. We... asked his opinion just now,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna admitted, embarrassed.
“That’s just legal language,” Razumihin explained. “Court documents sound like that even today.”
“Legal? Yes, it’s the usual business talk—not too dumb, but not really smart either—just business speak.”
“Pyotr Petrovitch doesn’t hide that he had a basic education. He’s actually proud he made it on his own,” Dounia said, sounding a little insulted by Raskolnikov’s tone.

“Well, if he’s proud of it, that’s fine. You seem offended, Dounia, that I’m only making a silly comment about his letter, and think I’m trying to annoy you with small stuff. Actually, I think it matters. For example, he says ‘blame yourselves’ very clearly, and then threatens to leave if I show up. That’s basically a threat to abandon you both if you don’t do what he wants, and to leave you here after calling you to Petersburg. What do you think? Would we get mad at Razumihin, or Zossimov, or one of us, if they wrote like that?”
“No,” Dounia answered, sounding more lively. “I could see it was clumsy, and maybe he just doesn’t know how to write... you’re right, brother. I didn’t expect...”

“It sounds legal, and maybe harsher than he meant. But I have to be honest. There’s one part in the letter—a mean little lie about me. I gave the money last night to the widow, a sick woman, not ‘pretending it was for the funeral,’ but for the actual funeral, and not to the daughter—who has a bad reputation, and whom I only met last night—but to the widow. I think he just wants to stir up trouble between us. It’s obvious what he’s trying to do, even if he tries to hide it behind legal talk. He’s smart, but being smart isn’t enough to act right. To me, it shows the kind of person he is... and I don’t think he really respects you. I’m telling you this just to warn you, because I really want what’s best for you...”
Dounia didn’t reply. She’d already made up her mind. She was just waiting for the evening.
“So what are you going to do, Rodya?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked, more worried than ever by his sudden, businesslike tone.
“What do you mean?”
“Pyotr Petrovitch wrote that you’re not to be with us this evening, and that he’ll leave if you come. So... are you coming?”
“That’s really

At that moment, the door quietly opened and a young girl stepped inside, looking around nervously. Everyone turned to stare at her, surprised and curious. At first, Raskolnikov didn’t recognize her. It was Sofya Semyonovna Marmeladov—Sonya. He had seen her just the day before, but then she had been in a very different situation and outfit, so he remembered her differently. Now she looked like a shy, modest girl, really young—almost a kid—with gentle manners and an open but scared face. She wore a plain old dress and an out-of-style, worn hat, but was still carrying a parasol. When she realized the room was full of people, she wasn’t just embarrassed—she was almost paralyzed with shyness, like a little kid who wants to run away. She even looked like she might leave. “Oh… it’s you!” Raskolnikov said, very surprised, suddenly feeling awkward himself. He remembered that his mother and sister knew, from Luzhin’s letter, about “some young woman with a bad reputation.” He had just been standing up for Sonya, saying he’d only met her the night before, and now here she was. He also realized he hadn’t actually argued against calling her “notorious.” All these thoughts flashed through his mind, but as he looked at her, he saw how truly humiliated she was, and suddenly felt sorry for her. When she started to back away in fear, it hurt him.
“I wasn’t expecting you,” he said quickly, giving her a look that made her pause. “Please, sit down. You must be here from Katerina Ivanovna. Wait—not there. Sit here…”

As Sonya came in, Razumihin—who was sitting in one of Raskolnikov’s three chairs by the door—got up to make space. At first, Raskolnikov pointed to the sofa where Zossimov had been sitting, but realizing that was his bed and maybe too personal, he quickly offered Sonya Razumihin’s chair instead.
“You sit here,” he said to Razumihin, moving him over to the sofa.

Sonya sat down, almost trembling with fear, and glanced shyly at the two women. She could hardly believe she was sitting next to them. The idea scared her so much that she jumped up again and, totally confused, turned to Raskolnikov.

“I… I… just came for a minute. I’m sorry for bothering you,” she started in a shaky voice. “I’m here from Katerina Ivanovna, she had no one else to send. She asked me to beg you… to come to the service… tomorrow morning… at Mitrofanievsky… and then… to our place… to her… she wanted me to beg you, please…” Sonya stammered, then stopped, unable to continue.

“I’ll try, of course, really, I will,” Raskolnikov replied. He stood up, but he too was fidgety and couldn’t finish his sentence. “Please, sit down,” he said suddenly. “I want to talk to you. Maybe you’re in a hurry, but please, can you give me just two minutes?” He pulled up a chair for her.

Sonya sat down again and, still shaking, glanced quickly and nervously at the two women before dropping her eyes. Raskolnikov’s pale face turned red, a shiver ran through him, and his eyes seemed to burn.
“Mother,” he said firmly, “this is Sofya Semyonovna Marmeladov, the daughter of Mr. Marmeladov, the man who was run over yesterday—the one I was just telling you about.”

Pulcheria Alexandrovna squinted a little at Sonya, even though she was embarrassed by Rodya’s intense look. She couldn’t help herself. Dounia stared seriously at Sonya’s face, studying her with confusion. Sonya tried to look up after being introduced, but was even more embarrassed.
“I wanted to ask,” Raskolnikov said quickly, “how things went yesterday. Did the police bother you?”
“No, everything was fine… it was obvious what caused his death… they didn’t bother us… only the other tenants are angry.”
“Why?”
“Because the body stayed so long. It’s hot now, so today they’ll move it to the cemetery chapel until tomorrow. At first Katerina Ivanovna didn’t want to, but now she sees it’s necessary…”
“So, today?”
“She asks you to come to the church tomorrow for the service, and then to the lunch after.”
“She’s having a funeral lunch?”
“Yes… just a small one… She also told me to thank you very much for helping us yesterday. Without you, we wouldn’t have had anything for the funeral.”
Suddenly her lips and chin started to tremble, but she managed to control herself and looked down again.

While they talked, Raskolnikov watched her closely. She had a thin, pale little face, not exactly pretty, with a sharp nose and chin. But her blue eyes were so honest and kind that you couldn’t help but like her. Even though she was eighteen, she looked even younger—almost like a kid. Some of her gestures made her seem even more childlike, sometimes almost in a funny way.
“But how can Katerina Ivanovna manage with so little money? Is she really planning a funeral lunch?” Raskolnikov pressed, keeping the conversation going.

“The coffin and everything will be plain, so it won’t cost much. Katerina Ivanovna and I worked it out so there’ll be enough left. She really wants it that way. You know, for her it’s some comfort… that’s just how she is…”
“I understand… of course… but why do you keep looking around my room like that? My mother just said it looks like a tomb.”

“You gave us everything yesterday,” Sonya suddenly whispered, her voice loud and fast, and again she looked down in embarrassment. Her lips and chin trembled again. She had noticed right away how poor Raskolnikov’s room was, and now she just blurted it out. The room fell silent. There was a special look in Dounia’s eyes, and even Pulcheria Alexandrovna looked kindly at Sonya.

“Rodya,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said, standing up, “we’ll have dinner together, of course. Come on, Dounia… And you, Rodya, should go for a walk, then rest before you come see us… I’m afraid we’ve worn you out…”
“Yes, yes, I’ll come,” he said, jumping up, “but I have something to take care of.”
“But surely you’ll eat with us?” Razumihin said, surprised at Raskolnikov. “What do you mean?”
“Yes, yes, I’ll be there… of course! You stay here a minute. You don’t need him right now, do you, Mother? Or am I taking him away from you?”
“Oh, no, not at all. And Dmitri Prokofitch, will you please join us for dinner?”
“Please do,” Dounia added.
Razumihin bowed, glowing with happiness. For a moment, everyone felt awkward.
“Goodbye, Rodya—or rather, see you soon. I don’t like saying goodbye. Goodbye, Nastasya. Oh, I said it again!”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna wanted to say something to Sonya too, but it didn’t really come out, and she left the room in a flutter.

But Dounia waited her turn, and as she followed her mother out, she gave Sonya a polite, thoughtful bow. Sonya quickly and nervously did a little curtsy. Her face was full of discomfort, as if Dounia’s kindness made her feel even worse.
“Dounia, see you soon,” Raskolnikov called in the hallway. “Give me your hand.”
“I already did. Did you forget?” Dounia said, turning to him warmly but a bit awkwardly.
“Doesn’t matter, give it again.” He squeezed her hand tightly.
Dounia smiled, blushed, pulled her hand away, and left looking happy.
“Well, that went well,” Raskolnikov said to Sonya, turning back to her with a sudden brightness. “God give peace to the dead—those still living have to go on. Isn’t that right?”
Sonya was surprised by his sudden cheerful look. He stared at her for a few moments in silence. The whole story of her dead father flashed through his mind…

“Oh, Dounia,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said as soon as they were outside, “I actually feel relieved after leaving—I’m more at ease. Who would have thought, yesterday on the train, that I’d be glad about that?”
“I’m telling you again, Mother, he’s still very sick. Don’t you see? Maybe he’s worried about us. We have to be patient, and a lot can be forgiven.”

“Well, you weren’t very patient!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna snapped, jealous. “You know, Dounia, looking at you two—you’re just like him, not just in looks but in spirit. You’re both so gloomy, both stubborn and quick-tempered, both proud but generous… He can’t really be selfish, can he? Oh, when I think what might happen tonight, my heart just sinks!”
“Don’t worry, Mother. Whatever happens, happens.”
“Dounia, just imagine what a situation we’re in! What if Pyotr Petrovitch calls off the engagement?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna blurted out, not thinking.
“Then he’s not worth much if he does,” Dounia answered sharply, with contempt.

“We did well to leave,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna interrupted quickly. “He seemed in a hurry about something. If he goes out, maybe the fresh air will help—his room is so stuffy… But where can you get fresh air in this city? Even the streets feel like closed rooms. Goodness, what a city! Wait—move over, they’re carrying something. Oh, it’s a piano! Look how they push!… I’m really worried about that young woman, too.”
“What young woman, Mother?”
“Why, that Sofya Semyonovna, who was just there.”
“Why?”
“I just have a bad feeling, Dounia. Maybe you think it’s silly, but as soon as she walked in, I felt like she was the main reason for all this trouble…”
“That’s nonsense!” Dounia snapped, annoyed. “Your feelings don’t mean anything here, Mother! He only met her the night before, and he didn’t even recognize her when she came in.”

“Well, you’ll see… She worries me; you’ll see, you’ll see! I was so scared. She stared at me with those eyes. I could barely sit still when he introduced her—do you remember? It’s so strange, but Pyotr Petrovitch wrote about her like that, and Rodya introduces her to us—to you! He must think a lot of her.”
“People write all sorts of things. We were gossiped about too, remember? I’m sure she’s a good girl, and it’s all just rumors.”
“I hope you’re right!”
