“And Pyotr Petrovitch is just a nasty liar,” Dounia said sharply.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna was crushed; they didn’t talk anymore.
“Let me tell you what I want,” Raskolnikov said, pulling Razumihin over to the window.
“Then I’ll go tell Katerina Ivanovna you’re coming,” Sonya said quickly, getting ready to leave.

“Wait a minute, Sofya Semyonovna. No secrets here. You’re not in the way. I just want to ask you a couple more things. Listen!” He suddenly turned back to Razumihin. “You know… what’s his name… Porfiry Petrovitch?”
“Of course! He’s a relative. Why?” Razumihin said, interested.
“Isn’t he in charge of that case… you know, the murder? You mentioned it yesterday.”
“Yes… well?” Razumihin’s eyes got wide.

“He’s looking for people who pawned stuff, and I have some things there, too—just little things: a ring my sister gave me when I left home, and my father’s silver watch. They’re not worth more than five or six roubles together… but they mean a lot to me. So what should I do now? I don’t want to lose them, especially the watch. I was really nervous just now that Mother might ask about it, when we talked about Dounia’s watch. That’s all we have from Father. It would make her sick if it went missing. You know how moms are. So what do you think? I know I should have told the police, but maybe it’s better to go straight to Porfiry? It might get sorted faster. Mother could ask about the watch before dinner.”
“Definitely not the police. Go straight to Porfiry!” Razumihin shouted, suddenly excited. “Great! Let’s go now. He’s nearby. We’ll find him for sure.”
“Alright, let’s go.”
“He’ll be so happy to meet you. I’ve talked about you to him before. I even mentioned you yesterday. Let’s go. So you knew the old woman? That’s it! It’s all working out… Oh, yes, Sofya Ivanovna…”
“Sofya Semyonovna,” Raskolnikov corrected. “Sofya Semyonovna, this is my friend Razumihin, he’s a good guy.”
“If you need to go now…” Sonya began, still not looking at Razumihin and even more uncomfortable.
“Let’s go,” Raskolnikov decided. “I’ll come see you today, Sofya Semyonovna. Just tell me where you live.”
He wasn’t exactly embarrassed, but seemed rushed and avoided looking at her. Sonya gave her address, blushing as she did. They all left together.
“Don’t you lock your door?” Razumihin asked as they went down the stairs.
“Never,” said Raskolnikov. “I keep meaning to buy a lock, but it’s been two years. People who don’t need locks are lucky,” he joked to Sonya. They all stopped in the gateway.
“Do you turn right, Sofya Semyonovna? By the way, how did you find me?” he added, sounding like he wanted to say something else. He wanted to look into her soft, clear eyes, but it was hard.
“You gave your address to Polenka yesterday.”
“Polenka? Oh, right—Polenka, the little girl. She’s your sister? Did I give her my address?”
“Did you forget?”
“No, I remember.”

“I had heard my father talk about you… but I didn’t know your name, and he didn’t either. So today, after I learned your name, I just asked, ‘Where does Mr. Raskolnikov live?’ I didn’t know you only had a room too… Goodbye, I’ll tell Katerina Ivanovna.”

Sonya was really glad to finally leave; she hurried away, looking down, desperate to get out of sight. She rushed the twenty steps to the corner, wanting to be alone so she could think about every word and detail. She’d never felt anything like this before. Without really understanding it, she felt like a whole new world was opening up. She suddenly remembered—Raskolnikov was coming to see her today, maybe even right now!
“Just not today, please, not today!” she kept muttering to herself like a little kid scared of something. “Oh no, to my room… he’ll see… oh, no!”

She was so distracted that she didn’t notice a stranger who was following her. He had started following her from the gateway. When Razumihin, Raskolnikov, and Sonya stopped to say goodbye, this man—who was just passing by—stopped when he heard Sonya ask about “Mr. Raskolnikov.” He quickly but carefully checked out all three, especially Raskolnikov, then looked back at the house. He tried not to seem interested, but slowed down, as if waiting for something. He was watching Sonya; he saw they were splitting up and that she was heading home.
“Home? Where? I’ve seen that face somewhere,” he thought. “I need to find out.”

At the corner he crossed the street, glanced back, and saw Sonya coming the same way, not noticing anything. She turned the corner; he followed on the other side. After about fifty steps, he crossed over again, caught up, and walked just a few yards behind her.

He was a man of about fifty, pretty tall and broad-shouldered, with a slight stoop. He was nicely dressed, clearly someone with money. He carried a fancy cane, which he tapped as he walked, and wore spotless gloves. His face was wide and kind of pleasant, with high cheekbones and a healthy color you didn’t see much in Petersburg. His blond hair was thick, with just a little gray, and his beard was even lighter. His blue eyes looked cold and thoughtful, and his lips were very red. He looked much younger than fifty—he was in great shape for his age.

When Sonya reached the canal, they were the only ones on the sidewalk. He noticed how lost in thought she was. When she got to her building, Sonya turned in; the man followed, looking a bit surprised. In the courtyard, she turned to the right. “Ha!” the stranger muttered, climbing the stairs after her. It was only then that Sonya noticed him. She reached the third floor, walked down the hall, and rang the bell at No. 9. The door had “Kapernaumov, Tailor” written in chalk. “Ha!” the stranger said again, surprised at the coincidence, and rang next door at No. 8. The doors were just a few yards apart.
“So you live at Kapernaumov’s,” he said, looking at Sonya and laughing. “He fixed a vest for me yesterday. I’m staying right nearby at Madame Resslich’s. How funny!” Sonya looked at him closely.
“We’re neighbors,” he went on cheerfully. “I just got to town two days ago. Goodbye for now.”
Sonya didn’t answer; the door opened and she slipped inside. For some reason, she felt embarrassed and uneasy.
On the way to Porfiry’s, Razumihin was clearly excited.
“That’s great, brother,” he said more than once, “I’m glad! I’m really glad!”
“What’s he so happy about?” Raskolnikov wondered.
“I didn’t know you pawned things at the old lady’s too. And… was it a while ago? I mean, when were you there last?”
“What a simple, honest guy he is,” Raskolnikov thought.

“When was it?” Raskolnikov stopped to think. “It was two or three days before she died, I think. But I’m not going to get my stuff back now,” he added quickly, pretending to care a lot about the things. “I’ve only got a silver rouble left… after last night’s stupid fever!”
He made a point of saying “fever.”

“Yes, yes,” Razumihin agreed right away—though it wasn’t clear what he was agreeing with. “So that’s why you… were stuck… and you kept talking about rings or chains in your fever! Yes, yes… it all makes sense now.”
“Wow! That story must’ve spread. Here’s this guy who’d do anything for me, and he’s just happy he finally knows why I was talking about rings in my fever! They’re all obsessed with it.”
“Will we find him?” he asked suddenly.

“Oh yes,” Razumihin replied quickly. “He’s a good guy, you’ll see. A little awkward, but I mean that in a different way. He’s very polite, but he has his own way of thinking… He’s smart, really smart, but he likes to joke around. He doesn’t believe much, questions everything, likes to mess with people, or really, just make fun. He’s old-school, looks at every detail… but he knows his stuff, for sure. Last year he solved a murder case no one else could. And he’s really excited to meet you!”
“Why is he so eager?”

“Oh, it’s not exactly that… You see, since you’ve been sick, I’ve talked about you a few times… So when he heard you were a law student who couldn’t finish school, he said, ‘What a shame!’ So I figured, from everything, not just that… Yesterday Zametov… you know, Rodya, I said some dumb stuff to you on the way home yesterday, when I was drunk… I hope you didn’t take it too seriously.”
“What? That they think I’m crazy? Maybe they’re right,” he said, forcing a smile.
“No, no… I mean, well… And all that other stuff, it was just me being drunk and talking nonsense.”
“Then why bring it up? I’m so tired of all this!” Raskolnikov burst out, sounding more annoyed than he really was.
“I know, I know, I get it. It’s embarrassing to even talk about.”
“If you’re embarrassed, then stop talking about it.”
They both fell silent. Razumihin was almost giddy, and Raskolnikov noticed it with irritation. He was also worried about what Razumihin had just said about Porfiry.

“I’ll have to act all serious in front of him too,” Raskolnikov thought, heart pounding, turning pale. “And I have to do it naturally. But maybe the most natural thing is to do nothing at all. But then, maybe that would look weird… Oh well, we’ll see soon enough. Is it good to go or not? The moth flies to the flame. My heart’s pounding—this is bad!”
“It’s this grey house,” Razumihin said.

“The most important thing—does Porfiry know I was at the old woman’s place yesterday, asking about the blood? I need to find out as soon as I get inside, see it in his face. If not… Well, I’ll find out, even if it ruins me.”
“Hey, brother,” he suddenly said to Razumihin, grinning, “I’ve noticed all day that you seem really excited. Isn

Raskolnikov walked into the room, barely able to keep from bursting out laughing again. Right behind him came Razumihin, looking even more awkward than usual—his face was bright red and he looked both embarrassed and angry, like he couldn’t decide if he should hide or shout. He really did look pretty ridiculous, which only made Raskolnikov want to laugh more. Without waiting for anyone to introduce him, Raskolnikov bowed to Porfiry Petrovitch, who was standing in the middle of the room, clearly wondering what was going on. Raskolnikov shook Porfiry’s hand, still fighting to keep a straight face and say his name. But as soon as he managed to look serious, he glanced at Razumihin again—almost by accident—and just couldn’t help it: he started laughing for real, the harder he tried to stop, the worse it got. Razumihin’s furious reaction to this “outburst” only made the whole thing seem more genuine and funny. Razumihin, maybe on purpose, made it even funnier.
“You idiot! You devil!” Razumihin shouted, swinging his arm and accidentally smacking a little round table with an empty tea-glass on it. Everything fell off and crashed.
“Why smash the furniture, gentlemen? That’s property of the state, you know,” Porfiry Petrovitch joked cheerfully.

Raskolnikov was still laughing, his hand in Porfiry’s, but he was trying not to take it too far and waited for a good moment to stop. Razumihin, now totally embarrassed by knocking over the table and breaking the glass, stared gloomily at the mess, cursed under his breath, and turned sharply to the window, standing there with his back to everyone, scowling so fiercely he couldn’t possibly be seeing anything outside. Porfiry laughed and seemed like he could keep laughing, but was also clearly waiting for an explanation. Zametov had been sitting in a corner but stood up when they entered. He was smiling, but looked surprised and maybe even a little doubtful about the whole scene, especially at Raskolnikov, as if he couldn’t believe what he was watching. Raskolnikov didn’t like seeing Zametov there—it put him on edge.
“I’ll have to remember that,” Raskolnikov thought quickly. Then, pretending to be embarrassed, he started, “Excuse me, please—Raskolnikov.”
“Not at all, it’s a pleasure to meet you... and you made quite an entrance!” Porfiry Petrovitch said. “But is your friend not even going to say good morning?” he nodded toward Razumihin.
“Honestly, I don’t know why he’s so mad at me,” Raskolnikov said. “All I did was tease him on the way here that he looked like Romeo—and I proved it! That’s all, really.”
“Jerk!” Razumihin snapped, still not turning away from the window.
“There must be a serious reason for that kind of fury,” Porfiry laughed.

“Oh, you sly lawyer! Forget it, all of you!” Razumihin suddenly burst out laughing himself. He walked over to Porfiry, his face now much brighter, as if nothing had happened. “Enough! We’re all fools. Let’s get to business. This is my friend, Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov. First, he’s heard of you and wanted to meet you, and second, he has a bit of business with you. Wait, Zametov—what are you doing here? Have you two met before? Known each other long?”
“What’s going on here?” Raskolnikov wondered, uneasy.
Zametov looked a bit surprised, but not much.
“We met yesterday at your place,” he said, acting casual.
“Well, that saves me the trouble then! He’s been begging me to introduce him to you all last week. But you and Porfiry met without me. Where’s your tobacco?”

Porfiry Petrovitch was wearing a dressing gown, a very clean shirt, and slippers that looked worn out. He was about thirty-five, short and pretty chubby, and had a round, clean-shaven face, with his hair cut short. The back of his head stuck out a bit. His soft, round face was a weird yellowish color, but his expression was lively and a little sarcastic. He might have seemed friendly, except his eyes—almost white eyelashes, always blinking, and watery. Those eyes didn’t match his soft, almost womanly body, giving him a much more serious look than you’d expect at first.

As soon as Porfiry heard Raskolnikov had business with him, he asked him to sit on the sofa, and sat down at the other end himself, waiting for Raskolnikov to explain. He listened with this intense, overly serious attention that made Raskolnikov feel awkward—especially since he thought the matter was barely worth talking about. Still, Raskolnikov explained the situation clearly and briefly, and was so satisfied with his own explanation that he managed to check Porfiry out while talking. Porfiry didn’t take his eyes off Raskolnikov even once. Razumihin, sitting at the same table, listened closely, looking from one to the other with almost too much interest.
“Idiot,” Raskolnikov cursed to himself.

“You’ll need to inform the police,” Porfiry said in a business-like way, “that after hearing about the murder, you want to let the lawyer in charge know these items belong to you, and that you’d like to get them back... or... well, they’ll write to you about it.”

“That’s just it,” Raskolnikov said, trying to sound embarrassed, “Right now I’m really short on money... even a small amount is too much for me. I just wanted to say the things are mine for now, and that when I have the money...”

“That’s fine,” said Porfiry coldly, not really caring about Raskolnikov’s money problems. “If you want, you can write directly to me, saying you’ve heard about the situation, claim your property, and ask for it back...”
“On a regular piece of paper?” Raskolnikov cut in eagerly, interested in how much this would cost him.

“Yes, just plain paper,” Porfiry replied, suddenly giving Raskolnikov a strange, almost mocking look—he squinted and seemed to wink. Or maybe Raskolnikov just imagined it, because it was only for a second. Still, he was almost sure Porfiry had winked at him, for some unknown reason.
“He knows,” flashed through Raskolnikov’s mind in a split second.

“Sorry to bother you about such small stuff,” Raskolnikov went on, a bit thrown off. “The things are only worth five roubles, but they really matter to me because of who they’re from. I was honestly scared when I heard...”
“That’s why you looked so shocked when I told Zossimov that Porfiry was asking about everyone who had left things with her!” Razumihin said, clearly wanting to make a point.
This was unbearable. Raskolnikov shot him a look, his eyes flashing with anger, but quickly got control of himself.

“Are you making fun of me, brother?” he said, pretending to be annoyed. “I probably do seem kind of obsessed with this junk, but don’t think I’m greedy. These two things mean a lot to me. I told you—the silver watch isn’t worth anything, but it’s the only thing left from my father. You can laugh, but my mother is here,” he turned to Porfiry, “and if she found out,” then back to Razumihin, making his voice shake, “that the watch was lost, she’d be heartbroken! You know how women are!”
“No way! That’s not what I meant at all! Not even close!” Razumihin yelled, upset.
“Was that too much? Was that believable? Did I overdo it?” Raskolnikov wondered, feeling jittery. “Why did I even bring up women?”
“Oh, your mother is with you?” Porfiry asked.
“Yes.”
“When did she arrive?”
“Last night.”
Porfiry paused, like he was thinking about something.
“Your things wouldn’t have been lost anyway,” he said calmly and coldly. “I’ve been expecting you to come here for a while.”

As if it didn’t matter, he handed the ashtray to Razumihin, who was dropping cigarette ash all over the carpet. Raskolnikov shivered, but Porfiry didn’t seem to notice—he was still focused on Razumihin’s cigarette.
“Wait, you were expecting him? Did you know he’d pawned things there?” Razumihin asked.
Porfiry turned to Raskolnikov.
“Your ring and watch were wrapped together, and your name and the date you left them were written clearly on the paper in pencil...”
“Wow, you’re really observant!” Raskolnikov said, forcing a smile and trying hard to look Porfiry in the eye, but failing. Suddenly he added,
“It’s just, I figured there were a lot of pawned things. It must be hard to remember them all... but you remember them so well, and... and...”
“Stupid! Weak!” he thought. “Why did I say that?”
“But we know everyone who’s left things, and you’re the only one who hasn’t come forward,” Porfiry answered, his voice carrying a hint of sarcasm.
“I haven’t been feeling well.”
“I heard that too. I heard you were really upset about something. You still look pale.”

“I’m not pale at all... I’m perfectly fine,” Raskolnikov snapped, suddenly rude and angry, his mood shifting fast. His anger was bubbling up and he knew it. “I’m going to give myself away, acting like this,” flashed through his mind. “Why are they toying with me?”

“Not well!” Razumihin interrupted. “What a joke! He was unconscious and babbling all day yesterday. Would you believe it, Porfiry, the minute we turned our backs, he got dressed, even though he could barely stand, and disappeared somewhere until midnight, totally out of it! Can you believe that? Incredible!”
“Really out of his mind? You don’t say!” Porfiry shook his head, almost like a woman.
“Nonsense! Don’t believe it! Actually, you don’t believe it anyway,” Raskolnikov let slip angrily. But Porfiry didn’t seem to notice his strange words.

“But how could you even leave the house if you weren’t out of your mind?” Razumihin pressed. “Why did you go out? What was the point? And why sneak around? Were you thinking straight when you did it? Now that you’re safe, I can ask honestly.”

“I was just totally sick of them yesterday.” Raskolnikov turned to Porfiry with a defiant smile. “I ran away from them to rent a room where they couldn’t find me, and I had a lot of money with me. Mr. Zametov over there saw it. Tell me, Mr. Zametov, was I sane or crazy yesterday? Settle our argument.”
Raskolnikov wanted to strangle Zametov right then—he hated his look and silence.
“In my opinion, you talked sensibly and even cleverly, but you were very irritable,” Zametov replied dryly.
“And Nikodim Fomitch told me today,” Porfiry added, “that he saw you very late last night at the place of a man who’d been run over.”

“And there,” Razumihin put in, “weren’t you crazy then? You gave your last bit of money to the widow for the funeral. If you wanted to help, give fifteen or twenty roubles, but keep at least three for yourself. But you gave away the whole twenty-five at once!”

“Maybe I found a treasure somewhere and you don’t know about it. That’s why I was generous yesterday.... Mr. Zametov knows about my treasure! Sorry for taking up half an hour of your time with such nonsense,” he said to Porfiry, his lips trembling. “We’re boring you, right?”
“Oh no, not at all! If you only knew how interesting you are to me! I love to watch and listen... I’m really glad you finally showed up.”
“But you could at least offer us some tea! My throat’s dry,” Razumihin burst out.
“Great idea! Maybe we’ll all join you. Would anyone like... something stronger before tea?”
“Get out of here!”
Porfiry left the room to order tea.
Raskolnikov’s mind was spinning. He was furious.

“The worst part is they’re not even hiding it anymore! They’re not trying to be polite! If you didn’t know me, why did you talk to Nikodim Fomitch about me? They don’t care if I know they’re watching me like a pack of dogs. It’s like they’re spitting in my face,” he thought, shaking with rage. “Just hit me already—stop toying with me like a cat with a mouse. It’s not even polite, Porfiry, but maybe I won’t let it go! Maybe I’ll just stand up and tell you the truth to your faces, and you’ll see how much I despise you.” He could barely breathe. “But what if I’m just imagining things? What if I’m wrong, and I’m just getting mad because I’m inexperienced? Maybe it’s all unintentional. Their words are normal, but there’s something about the way they say them.... Why did he say ‘With her’ so directly? Why did Zametov say I spoke ‘cleverly’? Why do they use that tone? And Razumihin is sitting here, totally clueless! That idiot never notices anything! Am I getting a fever again? Did Porfiry wink at me earlier? That’s stupid! Why would he wink? Are they trying to rattle my nerves or just mess with me? Either it’s my imagination or they know everything! Even Zametov is rude now... Or is he? He’s changed somehow. I knew he would! He feels at home here, and this is my first time. Porfiry doesn’t even treat him like a guest, sits with his back to him. They’re obviously in this together, against me! They were definitely talking about me before we got here. Do they know about the apartment? If only they’d get to the point! When I said I left to rent an apartment, he let it slide.... That might come in handy later. ‘Delirious,’ yeah right... ha! He knows about last night! But he didn’t know my mother had arrived! The old woman wrote the date in pencil! You’re wrong—you won’t catch me! There’s no proof, just guesses! Bring out your evidence! Even the apartment isn’t evidence, just my ‘delirium.’ I know what to say to them.... Do they know about the apartment? I’m not leaving without finding out. Why did I even come here? But if I’m angry now, maybe that’s a clue! Idiot, why am I so irritable? Or maybe that’s good—play the sick guy.... He’s testing me. He’s going to try to trap me. Why did I come?”
All this raced through his mind in an instant.
Porfiry Petrovitch came back quickly, suddenly acting more cheerful.
“That party yesterday, brother, really messed up my head... I’m all out of sorts,” he said to Razumihin, laughing.
“Was it interesting? I left when it was just getting good. Who won the argument?”
“Oh, nobody, of course. They went off on endless questions, just talking in circles.”
“Just imagine, Rodya, the stuff we argued about yesterday! Whether crime even exists! I told you, we argued nonstop.”
“What’s so strange about that? It’s a common topic,” Raskolnikov replied, sounding casual.
“But that’s not exactly how the question was asked,” Porfiry said.

“True, not exactly,” Razumihin agreed quickly, getting excited as usual. “Listen, Rodion, tell us what you think—I really want to hear it! I was arguing like crazy with them and wanted you to help. I told them you were coming.... It started with socialist ideas. You know the theory: crime is just a protest against how bad society is and nothing else—no other cause allowed!”
“You’ve got it wrong,” Porfiry cut in, looking almost amused and glancing at Razumihin, which only made Razumihin more heated.
“Nothing else is allowed!” Razumihin shot back, getting worked up.

“No, I’m not wrong. I can show you their pamphlets. To them, it’s always ‘the influence of the environment,’ nothing else. That means, if society was set up right, there would be no crime—everyone would be perfect in an instant, no more protests, just like that. They ignore human nature. They actually think some genius can design a system that’ll turn everyone good at once, faster than people actually change in real life! That’s why they hate history—‘It’s all just ugly and dumb,’ they say, and explain it all away as stupidity. They don’t like real life; they want a world that’s dead, like it’s made of rubber, not alive, no will, nothing that might rebel! In the end, it comes down to building walls and planning rooms in some perfect community! The community is all set, but people aren’t ready for it—it’s like burying people before they’re dead! You can’t just logic your way around human nature. Logic only has a few options, but real life has millions! Chop away a million problems and just focus on comfort—that’s their answer! It’s so simple you don’t have to think at all. That’s the secret to life in two pages!”

“Now he’s off on a rant! Somebody stop him!” Porfiry laughed. “Can you imagine, Raskolnikov? Six people arguing like that last night, and they started with punch! But you’re wrong—environment does explain a lot about crime, believe me.”
“Oh, sure, but tell me this: a forty-year-old man abuses a ten-year-old girl—was it his environment that made him do it?”
“Well, technically, it did,” Porfiry replied, suddenly serious. “A crime like that could be blamed on environment.”

Razumihin was almost shouting. “Oh, if you want, I’ll prove your white eyelashes are because the Ivan the Great bell tower is 250 feet high, and I’ll do it clearly, step by step, and even make it sound liberal! Want to bet?”
“Deal! Let’s hear how you’ll prove that!”

“He’s always joking, curse him!” Razumihin said, jumping up and waving his arms. “What’s the point of arguing with you? He just does it to mess with people—Raskolnikov, you don’t know him! He took their side last night just to make them look stupid. The things he said! And they loved it! He can keep it up for weeks. Last year he convinced us he was becoming a monk—kept it up for two months. Not long ago he said he was getting married, everything ready. He even bought new clothes! We all congratulated him—but there was no bride, nothing! It was all pretend!”
“No, you’re wrong! I already had the clothes. It was the new clothes that made me think of playing the trick.”
“Are you really that good at pretending?” Raskolnikov asked, sounding bored.

“You wouldn’t have guessed, would you? Wait, I’ll fool you too. Ha! But seriously, all this talk about crime and environment reminds me of something you wrote that I read a couple of months ago. ‘On Crime’... or something like that. It was in the Periodical Review.”
“My article? In the Periodical Review?” Raskolnikov said, surprised. “I did write about a book six months ago after leaving university, but I sent it to the Weekly Review.”
“But it was published in the Periodical.”
“The Weekly Review shut down, so that’s why it wasn’t printed back then.”
“Right, but when the Weekly Review closed, it merged with the Periodical, so your article was printed there two months ago. Didn’t you know?”
Raskolnikov hadn’t known.
“Hey, maybe you can get paid for it! You live so cut off, you don’t even know what’s happening to you. It’s true, I swear.”
“Good job, Rodya! I didn’t know either!” Razumihin exclaimed. “I’ll go to the reading-room today and get the issue. Two months ago? Doesn’t matter, I’ll find it. Why didn’t you tell us?”
“How did you find out it was mine? It’s only signed with an initial.”
“I just found out by accident the other day from the editor—I know him.... I was really interested.”
“I analyzed, if I remember right, the psychology of criminals before and after the crime.”

“Yes, and you said that committing a crime always comes with sickness. Very original, but... that wasn’t the part that interested me. What caught my eye was an idea at the end—though you only hinted at it. You suggested there are some people who, not just able, but have the right to break laws and commit crimes, and that the law doesn’t apply to them.”
Raskolnikov smiled a little at how Porfiry exaggerated and twisted his idea.
“What? You mean a right to commit crimes? Not because of environment?” Razumihin asked, sounding uneasy.

“No, not exactly because of environment,” Porfiry replied. “In his article, he says people are divided into ‘ordinary’ and ‘extraordinary.’ Ordinary people have to obey the law—because they’re ordinary. But extraordinary people have the right to break any law, just because they’re extraordinary. That was your idea, wasn’t it?”
“What do you mean? That can’t be right,” Razumihin muttered, confused.
Raskolnikov smiled again. He immediately saw what they were getting at and decided to play along.

“That’s not exactly what I argued,” he began calmly, “but you’ve described it pretty well—maybe even perfectly.” (He almost enjoyed admitting it.) “The only difference is, I never said extraordinary people must break the law. I just hinted that an extraordinary person has the right—not legally, but in their conscience—to go beyond... certain boundaries if it’s necessary to carry out their idea (sometimes for the good of all humanity). You said my article wasn’t clear; well, I’ll try to explain. I believe if Kepler or Newton couldn’t have made their discoveries public except by sacrificing one, a dozen, or a hundred people, Newton would have had the right—even the duty—to do so for the sake of humanity. But that doesn’t mean Newton could just kill people or steal every day. I also wrote that all—well, lawmakers and leaders like Lycurgus, Solon, Muhammad, Napoleon, etc.—were all criminals in a way, because they broke the old laws and sometimes didn’t stop at bloodshed, even of innocent people defending the old ways. It’s amazing how most of these great people caused a lot of bloodshed. Basically, I think all great men, or even those just a little unusual, are criminals—more or less. Otherwise, they’d never get out of the normal rut, and they can’t stand to stay in that rut, and I don’t think they should. There’s nothing new about that—people have said it a thousand times. As for dividing people into ordinary and extraordinary, I admit it’s kind of random, but it’s just to make my point: people are naturally divided into two types: the ordinary (who just keep life going), and the ones with talent to say something new. There are loads of sub-divisions, but you can usually tell the difference. The first group, generally, are conservative and obey the law; they like being controlled, and I think that’s their purpose—nothing shameful about it. The second group break the law; they’re destroyers, depending on how far they can go. Their crimes are all different, but usually they want to destroy the current world for a better one. If one of them has to step over a dead body for their idea, they can find a reason in their conscience for doing it—depending on the size of the idea. That’s all I meant about the right to crime in my article. Don’t worry, though—the masses almost never accept this right, so they punish or hang the extraordinary, which is fair enough for their job. But then, the next generation puts those same people on a pedestal. The first group are people of the present, the second are for the future. The first maintain the world, the second move it forward. Both have equal rights to exist. Actually, everyone is equal in my book—vive la guerre éternelle—until the New Jerusalem, of course!”
“So you believe in the New Jerusalem, do you?”
“I do,” Raskolnikov answered firmly. While saying this, and during his whole speech, he stared at one spot on the carpet.
“And... do you believe in God? Sorry if I’m being nosy.”
“I do,” Raskolnikov said again, looking up at Porfiry.
“And... do you believe that Lazarus really came back from the dead?”
“I... I do. Why are you asking all this?”
“You believe that literally?”
“Literally.”
“Really?... I’m just curious, sorry. But back to the topic—these people aren’t always executed. Some, actually...”
“Succeed in their lifetime? Oh yeah, some do.”
“And then they start executing others?”
“If they have to; most of the time they do. That’s a pretty clever comment.”

“Thanks. But tell me—how do you tell who’s extraordinary and who’s ordinary? Are there signs at birth? I just feel like it should be clearer. Sorry, it’s just the worry of a regular law-abiding citizen, but couldn’t they wear a special uniform or something? Like, what if someone from the first group thinks they’re from the second and starts ‘removing obstacles,’ as you said?”
“Oh, that happens a lot! That’s even cleverer than your last joke.”
“Thanks.”

“No need to thank me. But the mistake only happens with the first group, the ordinary ones. Even though they’re usually obedient, a lot of them, for fun, imagine they’re advanced or ‘destroyers,’ and jump into the ‘new movement’—honestly believing it. Meanwhile, the truly new people are often missed or even thought of as old-fashioned. Still, I don’t think it’s a big problem—they never get far. Sometimes they might need a good smack to remind them of their place, but even that’s not really needed—they punish themselves, since they’re so conscientious: sometimes they publicly confess and do things to make up for it. So, really, there’s nothing to worry about. It’s just how nature works.”

“Well, you’ve made me feel better about that. But here’s another thing—are there a lot of these extraordinary people who have the right to kill? I’m ready to respect them, but isn’t it scary if there are a lot?”

“You don’t need to worry about that either,” Raskolnikov replied in the same tone. “People with new ideas—those who can say anything new at all—are super rare. One thing’s certain: all these grades and kinds of people must follow some law of nature. That law isn’t known yet, but I’m sure it exists, and one day we’ll find out. Most people are just material, only around to eventually, somehow, produce someone with real independence—maybe one in a thousand. One in ten thousand, maybe. The real geniuses—one in a million, and the greatest of all maybe one in many billion. I have no idea how it works, but there must be a rule, not just luck.”
“Wait, are you two joking?” Razumihin finally broke in, frustrated. “You’re just playing with each other. Are you serious, Rodya?”

Raskolnikov looked up, his face pale and almost sad, but didn’t answer. Porfiry’s open, persistent, even rude sarcasm seemed weird to Razumihin, especially compared to Raskolnikov’s quiet, mournful look.

“Well, if you really mean this... You’re right that none of this is new, we’ve all read or heard it a thousand times. But what’s really your own, and actually scares me, is that you say conscience can approve of bloodshed, and you say it with such passion.... That, I think, is the main idea of your article. But justifying bloodshed by conscience is, to me, even scarier than the law justifying it....”
“You’re right, it is scarier,” Porfiry agreed.
“You must be exaggerating! There must be a mistake—I'll read it myself. You can’t really believe that! I’ll read it.”
“That’s not all in the article, it’s just hinted at,” Raskolnikov said.

“Yes, yes,” Porfiry said, unable to sit still. “Your attitude to crime is clear to me now, but... sorry to bother you (I’m really embarrassed to keep pushing), but even though you calmed my worry about the two groups mixing, there are still real-life things that worry me! What if some guy, or even a teenager, thinks he’s a future Lycurgus or Muhammad, and starts ‘removing obstacles’... he has some big plan and needs money, so he tries to get it... you see?”
Zametov suddenly burst out laughing from his corner. Raskolnikov didn’t even look at him.
“I have to admit,” he went on calmly, “that this does happen. The vain and foolish, especially young people, often fall into that trap.”
“Exactly—so then what?”

“So what?” Raskolnikov smiled. “That’s not my fault. It’s always been that way, always will be. He just said (he nodded at Razumihin) that I justify bloodshed. But society is well protected—prisons, police, punishments. There’s no need to worry. Just catch the criminal.”
“And what if we do catch him?”
“Then he gets what he deserves.”
“You’re very logical. But what about his conscience?”
“Why do you care about that?”
“Just out of humanity.”
“If he has a conscience, he’ll suffer for his mistake. That’s his punishment—along with prison.”
“But what about the real geniuses,” Razumihin asked, frowning, “the ones with the right to kill? Shouldn’t they suffer for the blood they spill?”

“Why ‘should’? It’s not about permission or rules. He’ll suffer if he feels sorry for his victim. Pain and suffering always come with a big mind and a deep heart. The truly great people, I think, have a lot of pain on earth,” he added dreamily, not like he’d been talking before.
He looked up, gave them all a serious look, smiled, and picked up his cap. Compared to how he’d acted when he came in, he was too quiet now—and he felt it. Everyone stood up.

“Well, you can scold me, be angry if you want,” Porfiry started again, “but I can’t resist. Let me ask one little question (I know I’m bothering you). Just one idea I want to mention so I don’t forget it.”
“Fine, say your idea,” Raskolnikov said, standing still, pale and serious.

“Well, you see... I don’t really know how to put this.... It’s more of a psychological thing.... When you wrote your article, you must have, heh, imagined yourself—even a little—as an ‘extraordinary’ person, someone bringing a new idea.... Isn’t that right?”
“Maybe,” Raskolnikov answered, sounding contemptuous.
Razumihin shifted in his seat.
“And if that’s true, could you, if life was hard or you wanted to help humanity, bring yourself to break the rules? Like, would you rob and murder?”
And again Porfiry winked with his left eye and laughed silently, just like before.
“If I did, I definitely wouldn’t tell you,” Raskolnikov replied, sounding proud and defiant.
“No, I asked just because of your article, from a literary point of view...”
“Ugh! How obvious and rude!” Raskolnikov thought, disgusted.
“Just so you know,” he answered dryly, “I don’t see myself as a Muhammad or a Napoleon, or anyone like that, and since I’m not one of them, I can’t say what I’d do.”
“Oh, come on, doesn’t everyone in Russia think he’s a Napoleon these days?” Porfiry said, sounding way too familiar.
Something in his tone was different—almost revealing.
“Maybe it was one of these future Napoleons who took care of Alyona Ivanovna last week?” Zametov blurted out from his corner.

Raskolnikov didn’t say a word. He stared hard at Porfiry. Razumihin was frowning darkly—he finally seemed to notice something was going on. He looked angrily around. There was a long, uncomfortable silence. Raskolnikov turned to leave.

“Leaving already?” Porfiry said pleasantly, holding out his hand with extra politeness. “Very glad to have met you. And about your request, don’t worry—just write as I told you, or even better, come see me yourself in a day or two... actually, come tomorrow at eleven. We’ll sort it out; we’ll talk. Since you’re one of the last, maybe you can tell us something,” he finished, putting on his friendliest face.
“You want to interrogate me officially?” Raskolnikov shot back sharply.

“Oh, no, not at all. You misunderstand. I just don’t want to miss anything, see... I’ve talked to everyone who had pawned things. I got statements from some, and you’re the last.... Oh, and by the way,” he said, acting suddenly delighted, “I just remembered—what was I thinking?” He turned to Razumihin. “You were talking my ears off about that Nikolay... I know, I know,” he said to Raskolnikov, “the guy’s innocent, but what can we do? We had to question Dmitri too.... Here’s the thing: when you went up the stairs, it was after seven, right?”
“Yes,” Raskolnikov answered, feeling weird even as he said it—he didn’t have to answer.

“So when you went upstairs between seven and eight, did you see an apartment open on the second floor? There were two workmen, or at least one, painting. Did you see them? It’s really important for them.”

“Painters? No, I didn’t see any,” Raskolnikov replied slowly, acting like he was searching his memory—while actually he was desperately trying to figure out where the trap was and not miss anything. “No, I didn’t see them, and I don’t think I noticed any open apartment.... But on the fourth floor,” (he realized the trap and felt proud), “I remember now, someone was moving out of the apartment across from Alyona Ivanovna’s.... I remember clearly—some movers were carrying out a sofa and squeezed me against the wall. But painters... no, I don’t remember any painters, and I don’t think there was any open apartment, no.”

“Wait, what are you talking about?” Razumihin suddenly shouted, as if he just realized something. “The painters were working on the day of the murder, and he was there three days before! Why are you asking him?”

“Oops! I messed up!” Porfiry slapped his forehead. “This case is driving me mad!” He turned to Raskolnikov, sounding apologetic. “It would be great for us to know if anyone saw the painters between seven and eight, so I thought you could tell us.... I got mixed up.”
“Then you should be more careful,” Razumihin said grimly.
The last words were spoken in the hallway. Porfiry Petrovitch saw them out, being extra polite.
They walked out into the street, both looking gloomy and upset, not saying a word for a while. Raskolnikov took a deep breath.
“I don’t buy it, I just can’t!” Razumihin said, trying to argue against Raskolnikov’s points, looking totally confused.

They were almost at Bakaleyev’s apartment now, where Pulcheria Alexandrovna and Dounia (Raskolnikov’s mother and sister) had been waiting for them for quite a while. Razumihin kept stopping on their walk, getting really worked up as they talked openly about everything for the first time.
“Then don’t believe it,” Raskolnikov replied with a cold, careless smile. “You never notice anything, but I was paying attention to every single word.”

“You’re just suspicious. That’s why you analyze everything… hmm… okay, I admit, Porfiry did act weird, and that jerk Zametov was even stranger! You’re right, there was definitely something off about him—but why? What’s the reason?”
“He changed his mind since last night.”
“No, the opposite! If they really believed that stupid idea, they’d hide it, play their cards close, and try to catch you later. But instead, they acted shameless and careless.”

“If they had real evidence—or even just a good reason to suspect me—they would’ve tried to hide it and watch for more clues. They’d probably have searched me already. But they’ve got nothing. It’s all just a theory, nothing solid. So, they try to throw me off with boldness. Maybe Porfiry is annoyed he doesn’t have any proof and just blurted things out. Or maybe he has some plan… he seems smart. Maybe he wanted to scare me by acting like he knew more than he does. They have their own way of thinking. But honestly, explaining this is disgusting. Let’s stop.”

“And it’s insulting! I get how you feel. But now that we’re talking honestly (and I’m glad we finally are), I’ll admit I noticed their attitude a while ago. Only little hints—suggestions—but still, why even hint? How dare they? What proof do they have? Just imagine! Just because a poor student, messed up by poverty and depression, on the edge of a really bad fever (don’t forget that), suspicious, proud, hasn’t talked to anyone properly in six months, dressed in rags and worn-out boots, gets stuck dealing with rude policemen, and then suddenly gets hit with an old debt, a new landlord, a sweltering hot day, a packed crowd, talk about a murder where he was seen just before, and all that while starving—of course he might faint! And that’s what they’re using against you! Ridiculous! I know it’s annoying, but if I were you, Rodya, I’d laugh at them—or better, spit in their faces, again and again. I’d punch back every way I could and put an end to it. Don’t let it get you down. It’s shameful!”
“He actually put that pretty well,” Raskolnikov thought to himself.
“Curse them, but what about the interrogation tomorrow?” he said bitterly. “Do I really have to explain myself to them? I already regret talking to Zametov at the restaurant yesterday…”
“Forget it! I’ll go see Porfiry myself. I’ll get the truth out of him—he’s like family, he has to tell me what’s really going on! And as for Zametov…”
“Finally, he gets it,” thought Raskolnikov.

“Wait!” Razumihin shouted, grabbing Raskolnikov’s shoulder again. “Hold on! You’re wrong. I’ve thought it through. You’re wrong! You say Porfiry’s question about the workmen was a trap. But if you really had done it, would you have said you saw the painters and the workmen? No way! You wouldn’t admit that, even if you saw it. Who would confess against themselves?”
“If I had done it, I probably would’ve said I saw the workmen and the flat,” Raskolnikov answered, sounding reluctant and disgusted.
“But why would you say something that hurts your own case?”

“Because only peasants, or people who have no idea how interrogations work, deny everything flat-out. Anyone with a bit of sense will admit the obvious facts they can’t escape, but then come up with a different explanation, or twist things to make them look harmless. Porfiry probably guessed I’d answer like that, say I saw the workmen to sound believable, and then invent some excuse.”

“But he could’ve told you right away that the workmen weren’t even there two days before, so you’d have to have been there on the day of the murder at eight in the morning. That way he’d catch you on a small detail.”
“Exactly, that’s what he was hoping for—that I’d answer too quickly without thinking, and forget that the workmen couldn’t have been there two days before.”
“But how could you forget something like that?”

“That’s easy. Clever people often get caught on simple things like that. The smarter someone is, the less they expect to trip up on something so basic. The smarter you are, the simpler the trap that’ll catch you. Porfiry’s no fool, trust me.”
“Then he’s a total trickster, if that’s true!”

Raskolnikov couldn’t help laughing. But at the same time, he was surprised by how honest he was being, and how eager he was to explain all this—even though up until now he’d talked with nothing but gloom and reluctance, obviously just because he had to.

“I’m actually starting to enjoy some of this!” he thought to himself. But almost immediately, he grew anxious, as if some new, frightening thought had hit him out of nowhere. The feeling kept getting stronger as they reached Bakaleyev’s door.
“Go in without me!” Raskolnikov said suddenly. “I’ll be back soon.”
“Where are you going? We’re already here.”
“I can’t help it… I’ll come in half an hour. Just tell them that.”
“Say what you want, I’m coming with you.”

“You just want to torture me, too!” Raskolnikov yelled, his eyes full of pain and anger so sharp that Razumihin let his hands drop. He stood on the steps for a while, glaring after Raskolnikov, who was storming off toward his own place. Finally, Razumihin clenched his fists, swore to squeeze the truth out of Porfiry that very day, and went upstairs to calm down Pulcheria Alexandrovna, who was getting nervous about how long they’d been gone.

When Raskolnikov got home, his hair was sweaty and he was breathing hard. He quickly climbed the stairs, went into his room (which was unlocked), and locked it behind him. Then, in a panic, he rushed to the corner—to the hiding spot under the wallpaper where he’d stashed the stolen things. He stuck his hand in and spent several minutes feeling around every crack and crease. Finding nothing, he stood up and took a deep breath. On his way to Bakaleyev’s, he’d suddenly worried that maybe something—a chain, a pin, or even a scrap of paper with the old woman’s handwriting—had slipped out and gotten stuck somewhere, and that it might turn up later as evidence against him.

He stood there, lost in thought, a strange, embarrassed half-smile on his lips. Finally, he grabbed his cap and quietly left the room. His thoughts were all mixed up. He wandered out through the gateway, barely paying attention.
“Hey, here he is!” shouted a loud voice.
Raskolnikov looked up.

The porter was standing at the door to his tiny room, pointing out Raskolnikov to a short, workman-looking guy in a long coat and vest, who looked a bit like a woman from a distance. He was bent over, his greasy cap pulled down, and his wrinkled, saggy face made him look over fifty. His small, squinty eyes were buried in fat, and he stared out grimly and grumpily.
“What is it?” Raskolnikov asked, walking over to the porter.
The man glanced up at him from under his brows, staring carefully and slowly. Then, without saying a word, he turned and walked out the gate into the street.
“What’s going on?” Raskolnikov called after him.
“That guy was asking if a student lived here—he mentioned your name and asked who you rent from. I saw you coming and pointed you out, and then he just left. Weird.”
The porter looked a little puzzled, but not much, and after a moment he just went back into his room.

Raskolnikov ran after the stranger and quickly spotted him walking steadily along the other side of the street, staring at the ground as if deep in thought. Raskolnikov caught up, but for a while just walked behind him. Finally, he moved up to walk beside him and looked at his face. The man noticed him but only glanced quickly, then looked down again. They walked side by side in silence for about a minute.
“You were asking about me… at the porter’s?” Raskolnikov finally said, his voice oddly quiet.
The man didn’t answer; he didn’t even look at him. They kept walking in silence.
“Why did you… come ask for me… and then say nothing? What’s this about?”
Raskolnikov’s voice cracked and he could barely get the words out.
The man finally raised his eyes and shot a dark, threatening look straight at Raskolnikov.
“Murderer,” he said suddenly, in a low but clear voice.

Raskolnikov kept walking next to him. His legs suddenly felt weak, a cold chill ran down his back, and for a second his heart seemed to stop—then started pounding like crazy. They walked about a hundred steps like that, side by side, silent.
The man didn’t look at him again.
“What do you mean… what is… Who’s a murderer?” Raskolnikov mumbled, barely louder than a whisper.
“You’re the murderer,” the man said, even clearer and stronger this time, with a smile full of hatred and satisfaction. He looked Raskolnikov right in the eyes, which were pale and shocked.

They reached a crossroads. The man turned left without looking back. Raskolnikov stood there staring after him. He watched the man look back at him from about fifty steps away. Raskolnikov couldn’t see clearly, but thought the man was still wearing that cold, triumphant, hateful smile.

With slow, shaky steps and legs that could barely hold him up, Raskolnikov made his way back to his tiny room, feeling frozen all over. He took off his cap and put it on the table, then stood there for ten minutes, not moving. Finally, he fell onto the sofa, groaning weakly, and stretched out. He lay there for half an hour.

He didn’t really think about anything. Bits and pieces of thoughts drifted through his mind—faces from his childhood, or people he’d met just once, the church bell tower in V., a billiard table in a restaurant, officers playing, the smell of cigars in a smoky shop, a tavern, a dark back staircase covered in dirty water and eggshells, church bells ringing somewhere far away… The images spun through his mind like a whirlwind. Some he tried to hold on to, but they slipped away. He felt a weight inside him, but it wasn’t unbearable—sometimes, it even felt a little comforting. He was still shivering, but even that felt almost nice.

He heard Razumihin’s hurried footsteps. Raskolnikov closed his eyes and pretended to be asleep. Razumihin opened the door and stood there, hesitating, then crept softly into the room and leaned over the sofa. Raskolnikov heard Nastasya whisper:
“Don’t wake him! Let him sleep. He can eat later.”
“You’re right,” Razumihin replied. They both quietly left and shut the door. Another half hour passed. Raskolnikov opened his eyes, rolled onto his back, and put his hands behind his head.

“Who is that guy? Who was that man who came out of nowhere? Where was he, what did he see? He must have seen everything, that’s obvious. But where was he at the time? Why did he only just show up now? And how could he have seen? Is it even possible? Hm…” Raskolnikov shivered, feeling cold. “And the jewelry box that Nikolay found behind the door—how could that happen? Another clue? You miss one tiny detail and it becomes a mountain of evidence! Even a fly could have seen it! Is that really possible?” He suddenly felt disgusted by how weak he was. “I should have known I’d end up like this,” he thought with a bitter smile. “And how could I, knowing myself, ever dare to pick up an axe and spill blood? I should have known all along… But I did know!” he whispered in despair. Sometimes his thoughts just stopped and went nowhere.

“No, people like that aren’t made of flesh. The real ‘great men’—the ones who are allowed to do anything—storm cities, cause massacres, lose armies in Egypt, waste half a million men in Moscow, and then just make a joke about it. After they die, people build altars to them, and suddenly anything is allowed for them. No, those people aren’t human—they’re like statues made of bronze!”

Suddenly, a weird random thought almost made him laugh. Napoleon, pyramids, Waterloo, and a skinny old pawnbroker woman with a red trunk under her bed—what a crazy mix for Porfiry Petrovich to figure out! How could anyone make sense of it all? It’s so ridiculous. “A Napoleon hiding under an old lady’s bed! Ugh, disgusting!”

Sometimes he felt like he was going crazy. He got worked up and feverish. “The old woman doesn’t matter,” he thought, all mixed up. “Maybe killing her was a mistake, but that’s not the point! She was just a sickness… I was in too much of a hurry to cross the line. I didn’t kill a person, I killed a theory! I killed the idea, but I couldn’t actually go through with it… I was only able to kill. And it looks like I wasn’t even good at that… Theory? Why was Razumihin trashing the socialists? They’re hardworking, practical people; ‘happiness for everyone’ is all they care about. No, I only live once, and I’ll never get another chance; I don’t want to wait for ‘everyone’s happiness.’ I want to live for myself, or not at all. I couldn’t just walk past my starving mother and keep my money, waiting for ‘happiness for all.’ I’m putting my little brick into the wall of happiness for everyone, and that’s supposed to make my heart peaceful. Ha! Why did you let me slip through your fingers? I only live once; I want… Ugh, I’m just a bug, nothing more,” he added, suddenly laughing like a madman. “Yes, I’m definitely a bug,” he continued, latching onto the idea and obsessing over it with a kind of twisted pleasure. “First, because I can even think about it. Second, because for a month I’ve been bothering God, saying that I didn’t do it for myself, but for some noble reason—ha! Third, because I wanted to do it in the fairest way possible, weighing and measuring everything. Of all the bugs, I picked the most useless one, and I only wanted to take exactly what I needed for my first step, no more (the rest would have gone to a monastery, just like she wanted—ha!). And what really proves I’m a total bug,” he added, grinding his teeth, “is that I’m probably even worse than the bug I killed, and I knew all along I’d call myself that after it was over. Is there anything more horrible? How pathetic! How low! I get why the ‘prophet’ with his sword on his horse says, ‘God commands and the world must obey!’ He’s right when he fires a cannon into a crowd and doesn’t bother to explain! It’s your job to obey, trembling world, not to have wishes, because that’s not for you!… I’ll never, ever forgive the old woman!”
His hair was sweaty, his lips dry and trembling, and his eyes stared up at the ceiling.

“Mother, sister—how I loved them! Why do I hate them now? Yes, I hate them, I feel it physically, I can’t stand them near me… I went up to my mom and kissed her, I remember… Hugging her, thinking if she only knew… should I tell her? Maybe I will… She must be just like me,” he added, forcing himself to think, almost delirious. “Oh, how I hate the old woman now! I’d kill her again if she came back to life! Poor Lizaveta! Why did she have to walk in?… It’s weird, though, why don’t I ever think about her, like I didn’t even kill her? Lizaveta! Sonia! Poor gentle souls, with kind eyes… Dear women! Why don’t they cry? Why don’t they scream? They just give everything up… their eyes are so soft and gentle… Sonia, Sonia! Sweet Sonia!”

He blacked out; it seemed odd to him that he couldn’t remember how he got outside. It was late evening, twilight, and the full moon was shining brighter and brighter; the air felt heavy. The streets were crowded; workers and business people were heading home, others were out for a walk; everything smelled of dust, concrete, and dirty water. Raskolnikov walked along, sad and anxious; he knew he’d come out with some urgent purpose, but couldn’t remember what it was. Suddenly he stopped and saw a man on the other side of the street, waving him over. He crossed to him, but as soon as he did, the man turned and walked away, head down, as if he’d never signaled. “Wait, did he actually signal to me?” Raskolnikov wondered, but he tried to catch up. When he got close, he recognized him and was scared; it was the same stooped man in the long coat. Raskolnikov followed him at a distance, heart pounding; they turned down a side street; the man still didn’t look back. “Does he know I’m following?” Raskolnikov thought. The man went into a big house’s entrance. Raskolnikov hurried up, hoping to see if the man would look back or wave. In the courtyard, the man did look back and seemed to beckon again. Raskolnikov followed him into the yard, but the man was gone. He must have gone up the first staircase. Raskolnikov rushed after him, hearing slow, steady footsteps two flights up. The staircase felt strangely familiar. He reached the first floor window; moonlight poured in. Then he climbed to the second floor. Wait, this was the apartment where the painters worked… why didn’t he recognize it right away? The footsteps above had stopped. “He must have stopped or is hiding.” He reached the third floor—should he go on? The silence was terrifying… but he kept going. His own footsteps made him nervous. It was so dark! The man must be hiding somewhere. Ah! The apartment was wide open; he hesitated, then went inside. The hall was pitch dark and empty, like everything had been moved out; he crept into the living room, filled with moonlight. Everything was just as before: the chairs, the mirror, the yellow sofa, the paintings. A huge, copper-red moon stared through the windows. “It’s the moon making everything so weird, so mysterious,” Raskolnikov thought. He stood and waited, heart beating harder with every second of silence. Suddenly, he heard a sharp crack, like something breaking, then silence again. A fly buzzed at the window. Then he noticed in the corner, between the window and a little cupboard, something like a cloak hanging. “Why is that cloak here?” he wondered. “It wasn’t here before…” He walked over and sensed someone was hiding behind it. Cautiously, he moved the cloak and found the old woman, bent over on a chair so he couldn’t see her face, but it was definitely her. He stood over her. “She’s scared,” he thought. He quietly grabbed the axe and hit her once, then again on the head. But weirdly, she didn’t move—like she was made of wood. He got scared, bent lower to see her face, but she bent her head even more. He crouched all the way down and tried to look up at her face. When he finally did, he froze in horror: the old woman was sitting there laughing, shaking with soundless giggles, trying her hardest not to let him hear. Suddenly, he thought the bedroom door opened a little and heard laughter and whispering inside. He went wild, swinging the axe at the old woman’s head again and again, but with each blow, the laughter and whispers grew louder, and the old woman just shook with silent laughter. He tried to run, but the hallway was packed with people, doors flung open, heads everywhere on the stairs and landings, all staring at him in silence, waiting. His heart squeezed tight, his legs felt glued to the floor, he couldn’t move… He tried to scream—and woke up.
He gasped for breath—but the dream stuck with him: his door flew open and a man he’d never seen before stood there, watching him closely.
Raskolnikov barely opened his eyes, then quickly shut them again. He lay still on his back.
“Am I still dreaming?” he wondered, and peeked through his lashes; the stranger was still there, standing in the same place, watching him.

The man quietly stepped into the room, closed the door behind him, walked to the table, paused, still staring at Raskolnikov, and then sat down on a chair next to the sofa. He set his hat on the floor, leaned on his cane, and rested his chin on his hands—clearly ready to wait as long as needed. From Raskolnikov’s quick glances, the man looked middle-aged, heavyset, with a full, light-colored beard.

Ten minutes passed. It was still light out, but getting dark. The room was completely silent. No sounds from the stairs. Only a big fly buzzing at the window. Finally, Raskolnikov couldn’t stand it anymore. He suddenly sat up on the sofa.
“Alright, just tell me what you want.”
“I knew you weren’t really asleep, just faking it,” the stranger answered, almost amused. “Arkady Ivanovich Svidrigailov—allow me to introduce myself...”
“Am I still dreaming?” Raskolnikov wondered again.
He stared carefully and suspiciously at the unexpected visitor.
“Svidrigaïlov! That’s impossible! It can’t really be you!” he finally said aloud, totally confused.
The visitor didn’t seem at all surprised by Raskolnikov’s outburst.

“I’m here for two reasons. First, I wanted to meet you personally—I’ve heard a lot about you, and it was all very interesting and flattering. Second, I’m hoping you might help me with something that concerns your sister, Avdotya Romanovna. Without your support, she probably won’t even let me near her, since she’s prejudiced against me. But if you help—"
“You’re wrong about that,” Raskolnikov interrupted.
“Did they just arrive yesterday, may I ask?”
Raskolnikov didn’t answer.

“It was yesterday, I know. I only arrived the day before. Anyway, Rodion Romanovitch, I don’t feel I need to defend myself, but can you tell me what crime I actually committed in all this, speaking honestly and reasonably?”
Raskolnikov just kept staring at him in silence.

“That I harassed a helpless girl in my own house and ‘insulted her with my disgusting proposals’—is that it? (I know what you’re thinking.) But if you just accept that I’m human too, and can be attracted to someone or fall in love (which you can’t control), then it all makes sense. The question is, am I a monster, or am I a victim myself? And what if I am a victim? When I asked the woman I loved to run away with me to America or Switzerland, maybe I really did respect her and thought I was helping us both be happy! Passion controls reason, you know; maybe I was hurting myself more than anyone else!”
“But that’s not the point,” Raskolnikov cut in, sounding disgusted. “Whether you’re right or wrong, we just don’t like you. We want nothing to do with you. The door’s over there. Leave!”
Svidrigaïlov suddenly burst into laughter.
“You... you’re tough to fool!” he said, laughing openly. “I hoped I’d be able to get around you, but you figured me out right away!”
“But you’re still trying to get around me!”

“So what? So what?” Svidrigaïlov cried, still laughing. “This is what the French call ‘fair play’—just a harmless little trick! Anyway, you interrupted me. As I was saying, none of this unpleasantness would have happened except for what happened in the garden. Marfa Petrovna—"
“People say you got rid of Marfa Petrovna too, didn’t you?” Raskolnikov cut in harshly.

“Oh, you heard that too? Of course you would.... But as for your question, I really have nothing to worry about there. My conscience is clear. The doctors said it was apoplexy—she went swimming right after a heavy meal and a bottle of wine, so it couldn’t have been anything else. Still, on the train here, I kept thinking: did I somehow help cause that disaster, maybe by upsetting her? But no, even that’s not possible.”
Raskolnikov laughed.
“I’m surprised you even care about it!”

“What are you laughing at? Just think, I only hit her twice with a switch—didn’t even leave a mark... don’t think I’m a total jerk; I know it was horrible of me and all that, but honestly, Marfa Petrovna probably even liked my, let’s call it, ‘passion.’ She had already made a huge drama about your sister’s story; for three days she wouldn’t leave the house, and everyone was sick of her reading that letter (you heard about the letter). Then, suddenly, those two switches—what luck! Her first reaction was to order the carriage. And you know, sometimes women are actually happy to be insulted, even if they pretend to be angry. It happens to everyone; actually, most people secretly like to be insulted, have you noticed? But especially women. You could even say it’s their favorite pastime.”
At one point, Raskolnikov thought about just getting up and leaving to end this conversation. But he was curious, and maybe a bit cautious, so he stayed for a moment longer.
“Do you like fighting?” he asked, trying to sound casual.

“Not really,” Svidrigaïlov replied calmly. “Marfa Petrovna and I barely ever fought. We got along pretty well, and she was always happy with me. In our seven years together, I only used the whip twice (not counting a third, kind of weird incident). The first time was two months after we got married, right after we moved to the country. The second was recently, the one we’re talking about. Did you really think I was such a monster, some old-school tyrant? Ha! By the way, do you remember a few years ago, when a nobleman—I forget his name—was shamed all over the newspapers for beating a German woman on a train? Remember? That was the year of that big public reading, ‘The Egyptian Nights’—the dark eyes, you know! Ah, those golden days! Well, I don’t feel sorry for that guy, honestly. Some people are so irritating, you can’t blame anyone for losing control. No one ever thought about it that way back then, but really, that’s a more human point of view, don’t you think?”
Svidrigaïlov burst out laughing again. Raskolnikov could see that this was a man with a strong purpose, and that he was good at hiding it.
“I guess you haven’t talked to anyone in a while?” he asked.
“Almost no one. Surprised I can adapt so easily?”
“No, I’m just surprised you’re so adaptable.”

“Because I’m not offended by your rude questions? Is that it? But why get offended? You asked, I answered,” Svidrigaïlov replied with surprising simplicity. “Honestly, there’s not much I care about anymore, especially now—I’ve got nothing to do.... You can think I’m just trying to get something from you, especially since I said I wanted to talk to your sister. But really, I’m just bored. The last three days, especially, have been dull, so I’m happy to see you.... Don’t get mad, Rodion Romanovitch, but you seem pretty strange yourself. There’s something off about you, you know, not just now, but in general.... All right, all right, I’ll stop, don’t glare at me! I’m not as bad as you think.”
Raskolnikov looked at him darkly.
“Maybe you’re not a bad person at all,” he said. “In fact, I think you know how to act like a gentleman, or at least pretend to.”
“I don’t really care about anyone’s opinion,” Svidrigaïlov replied, dryly, with a hint of pride. “So why not be rude when it’s convenient? Especially if it comes naturally,” he added, laughing again.
“But I’ve heard you have plenty of friends here. They say you’re ‘well connected.’ So what do you want with me, unless you have some specific reason?”

“It’s true, I have friends here,” Svidrigaïlov admitted, dodging the real question. “I’ve seen a few already in the last three days, or they’ve seen me. That’s normal. I’m well dressed, not poor; the freeing of the serfs didn’t hurt me—my wealth is in forests and meadows. My income hasn’t dropped. But I haven’t gone to see anyone—I got sick of them a long time ago. Three days here and I haven’t called on a single person.... What a city! How did it even get here? It’s just full of officials and students. There’s a lot I didn’t notice eight years ago, when I last visited.... Now my only hope is in anatomy, honestly!”
“Anatomy?”
“As for clubs, Dussauts, parades, or ‘progress’—well, they can all go on without me,” he continued, ignoring the question. “And who wants to be a card cheat, anyway?”
“Wait, were you a card cheat?”

“How could I help it? Back then, there was a whole group of us, all high society—poets, landowners, gentlemen. Actually, in Russian society, the people with the best manners are often the ones who’ve been beaten up, have you noticed? I got worse living out in the country. At one point I even landed in debtor’s prison, thanks to a shady Greek from Nezhin. Then Marfa Petrovna saved me; she paid him thirty thousand silver pieces (I owed seventy thousand). We got married and she took me to the country like I was treasure. She was five years older than me, and she loved me a lot. I stayed in the country for seven years straight. And all that time, she kept the IOU over my head, so if I ever tried anything, I’d be trapped! And she would have done it! Women don’t see anything wrong with that.”
“If it wasn’t for that, would you have left her?”

“I don’t know. It wasn’t really the IOU that kept me. I didn’t want to go anywhere else. Marfa Petrovna actually suggested I travel, because I was bored, but I’ve traveled before, and it just made me miserable. No reason—just the sunrise, the Bay of Naples, the sea—you see it and feel sad. The worst part is, it’s real sadness! No, it’s better at home. Here, you can always blame someone else and excuse yourself. Maybe I would’ve gone to the North Pole instead, because I’m a bad drunk and hate drinking, but there’s nothing else to do. I tried it. By the way, I heard Berg is going up in a big balloon from the Yusupov Garden next Sunday, and he’ll take paying passengers. Is it true?”
“Would you go up in the balloon?”
“Me?... No, no,” Svidrigaïlov mumbled, looking lost in thought.
“Is he serious? Is he joking?” Raskolnikov wondered.

“No, the IOU didn’t keep me there,” Svidrigaïlov continued, thinking aloud. “It was my own choice to stay, and almost a year ago, on my name-day, Marfa Petrovna gave me back the IOU and even gave me a large sum of money. She was rich, you know. ‘See how I trust you, Arkady Ivanovitch’—that’s what she actually said. You don’t believe me? But I managed the estate well, the neighbors know me. I even ordered books. At first, Marfa Petrovna approved, but later she was afraid I’d read too much.”
“You seem to miss Marfa Petrovna a lot?”
“Miss her? Maybe. Actually, maybe I do. By the way, do you believe in ghosts?”
“Ghosts?”
“Yeah, ordinary ghosts.”
“Do you believe in ghosts?”
“Maybe not, just to please you.... I wouldn’t say no, exactly.”
“Have you seen any, then?”
Svidrigaïlov looked at him in a strange way.
“Marfa Petrovna likes to visit me,” he said, twisting his mouth into a weird smile.
“What do you mean, ‘she likes to visit you’?”

“She’s come three times. The first was the day of her funeral, an hour after she was buried, just before I left to come here. The second was the day before yesterday, at dawn, at the Malaya Vishera train station. The third time was two hours ago, in my room. I was alone.”
“Were you awake?”
“Wide awake. Every time. She comes in, talks for a minute, and leaves by the door—always the door. I can almost hear her.”
“Why did I feel like something like this must be happening to you?” Raskolnikov suddenly said.
At the same time, he was surprised at himself for saying it. He was very agitated.
“What! You thought that?” Svidrigaïlov asked, amazed. “Really? Didn’t I say we had something in common?”
“You never said that!” Raskolnikov snapped, heatedly.
“Didn’t I?”
“No!”
“I thought I did. When I came in and saw you lying there with your eyes closed, pretending, I thought, ‘This is the guy.’”
“What do you mean—‘the guy’? What are you talking about?” Raskolnikov shouted.
“What do I mean? Honestly, I’m not sure myself,” Svidrigaïlov muttered, sounding genuinely confused.
For a minute, they sat in silence, staring at each other.
“This is ridiculous!” Raskolnikov suddenly yelled, annoyed. “What does she say when she comes to you?”

“She? You won’t believe it, but she talks about the silliest things—and people are strange—it makes me angry. The first time, I was tired from the funeral and the lunch afterward. I was finally alone, lit a cigar, started thinking—she came in through the door. ‘You’ve been busy today, Arkady Ivanovitch, you forgot to wind the dining-room clock,’ she said. I’d wound that clock every week for seven years, and if I forgot, she always reminded me. The next day I left for here. At dawn at a train station, I was half-asleep, drinking coffee. I looked up and there was Marfa Petrovna, sitting next to me with a deck of cards. ‘Want your fortune told for the trip, Arkady Ivanovitch?’ She was great at telling fortunes. I’ll never forgive myself for not asking her to do it. I ran away, scared, and the train bell rang anyway. Today, after a terrible dinner, I was sitting and smoking, and suddenly there she was again, dressed up in a new green silk dress with a long train. ‘Good day, Arkady Ivanovitch! How do you like my dress? Aniska can’t make one like this.’ (Aniska was a dressmaker from the country, one of our old serf girls trained in Moscow, a pretty girl.) She spun around to show it off. I stared at the dress, then at her face. ‘Why do you bother coming to me about such silly things, Marfa Petrovna?’ ‘Goodness, you never want me to bother you about anything!’ she said. Just to tease her I said, ‘I want to get married, Marfa Petrovna.’ ‘That’s just like you, Arkady Ivanovitch. It doesn’t look good to start looking for a bride right after you’ve buried your wife. And if you could at least choose well, but I know it won’t make you or her happy—you’ll just be laughed at by decent people.’ Then she left, and her dress rustled as she went. Isn’t that silly?”
“Or maybe you’re just making this up?” Raskolnikov said.
“I rarely lie,” Svidrigaïlov replied thoughtfully, seeming not to notice the rude question.
“Have you ever seen ghosts before?”

“Y-yes, once, six years ago. I had a serf, Filka; just after he was buried, I accidentally called out, ‘Filka, my pipe!’ He came in and went to the cupboard for my pipes. I sat there, thinking, ‘He’s doing this to get back at me,’ because we’d had a huge argument before he died. ‘How dare you come in here with a hole in your sleeve?’ I said. ‘Go away, you rascal!’ He turned and left, and never came back. I never told Marfa Petrovna. I wanted to have a prayer service for him, but I was embarrassed.”
“You should see a doctor.”

“I know I’m not well, you don’t have to tell me, though I don’t know what’s wrong. But I bet I’m five times stronger than you. I wasn’t asking if you believe people can see ghosts, but whether you believe ghosts really exist.”
“No, I don’t believe it!” Raskolnikov snapped angrily.

“What do people usually say?” Svidrigaïlov muttered, as if talking to himself, looking away and bowing his head. “They say, ‘You’re sick, so what you see isn’t real, it’s just imagination.’ But that’s not logical. I agree ghosts only appear to sick people, but that just means they can only show themselves to the sick, not that they don’t exist.”
“That’s nonsense,” Raskolnikov said irritably.

“No? You don’t think so?” Svidrigaïlov continued, looking at him carefully. “But what about this idea: ghosts are like bits and pieces from other worlds, the start of them. A healthy person wouldn’t see them, because they belong to this world and are supposed to live only in it. But once someone gets sick, as soon as their body isn’t working normally, they can feel the possibility of another world; and the sicker you are, the closer you get to that other world, so that when you die you just step straight into it. I thought about that a long time ago. If you believe in an afterlife, you could believe that too.”
“I don’t believe in an afterlife,” Raskolnikov said.
Svidrigaïlov sat there, lost in thought.
“But what if it’s just spiders or something like that over there?” he suddenly said.
“He’s insane,” Raskolnikov thought.

“People always imagine eternity as something huge, beyond understanding. But why does it have to be huge? What if it’s just a little room, like a dirty bathhouse in the country, with spiders in every corner—and that’s all eternity is? Sometimes I imagine it that way.”
“Is that really the best, the most comforting thing you can imagine?” Raskolnikov cried, feeling disturbed.
“Best? How do we know, maybe that is fair. Actually, it’s what I would have made it,” Svidrigaïlov replied, with a vague smile.
That terrible answer sent a chill through Raskolnikov. Svidrigaïlov looked up at him and suddenly started laughing.

“Just think,” he said, “half an hour ago we’d never met, we thought of each other as enemies, there are unresolved issues between us—and now we’re off talking about the meaning of life! Wasn’t I right that we’re two of a kind?”
“Please,” Raskolnikov said irritably, “tell me why you really came here... and... I’m in a hurry, I want to leave.”
“Of course, of course. Your sister, Avdotya Romanovna, is marrying Mr. Luzhin, Pyotr Petrovitch, right?”
“Can you not mention my sister or say her name? I don’t know how you even dare talk about her in front of me, if you actually are Svidrigaïlov.”
“But I came to talk about her; how can I not mention her?”
“Fine, talk, but make it quick.”

“I’m sure you have your own view of Mr. Luzhin, who’s related to me through my wife, even if you’ve only met him briefly or just heard about him. He’s not good enough for Avdotya Romanovna. I think she’s sacrificing herself for her family, and not thinking of her own happiness. From what I’ve heard, I thought you’d be glad if the engagement could be broken off without losing anything. Now that I’ve met you, I’m sure of it.”
“This is all very childish... Actually, it’s just plain rude of you,” Raskolnikov replied.

“You mean I have my own agenda. Don’t worry, Rodion Romanovitch, if I were just looking out for myself, I wouldn’t be so upfront. I’m not stupid. I’ll admit something a bit odd: earlier, when I was defending my feelings for Avdotya Romanovna, I called myself a victim. But now, honestly, I don’t feel any love—not even a little. It’s strange, because I really did feel something before...”
“You were just bored and acting out,” Raskolnikov interrupted.
“I definitely am bored and bad, but your sister is so impressive that even I was struck by her. But now I see it was all nonsense.”
“Have you realized that for long?”
