“I started to feel it earlier, but I was certain two days ago, right when I got to Petersburg. In Moscow, I still thought I was coming here to ask for her hand and beat out Luzhin.”
“Sorry to interrupt; please get to the point. I’m in a hurry, I want to leave...”

“Of course. When I got here, and decided on a certain... journey, I wanted to sort out a few things first. I left my children with an aunt; they’re well taken care of and don’t need me. I took only what Marfa Petrovna gave me last year; that’s enough. Excuse me, I’m getting to the point. Before my journey, I want to deal with Mr. Luzhin. It’s not that I hate him, but he’s the reason I fell out with Marfa Petrovna—she arranged this marriage. I want to see Avdotya Romanovna, with your help and maybe while you’re there, to explain that she’ll only get hurt by marrying Luzhin. Then, to apologize for everything, I want to give her ten thousand roubles to help her break off the engagement, which I think she’d do if she saw a way out.”
“You’re definitely crazy,” Raskolnikov said—not angry, just shocked. “How can you talk like that?”

“I knew you’d shout at me. But I’m not rich, and this ten thousand roubles is completely free—I don’t need it at all. If Avdotya Romanovna doesn’t take it, I’ll waste it on something even stupider. That’s the first thing. Second, my conscience is clear; I’m not doing this for any secret reason. You might not believe me, but eventually you and your sister will. The point is, I really did cause your sister, whom I respect, some trouble, and so, feeling truly sorry, I just want— not to pay her back, but to do something good for her, to prove I’m not just a villain. If I had even a tiny bit of self-interest, I wouldn’t be so open about it; and I wouldn’t just offer ten thousand, when I offered her more five weeks ago. Besides, I might soon marry someone else, and that should prove I have no plans for Avdotya Romanovna. And anyway, if she marries Luzhin, she’s still marrying for money, just from a different man. Don’t get mad, Rodion Romanovitch, just think it over calmly.”
Svidrigaïlov himself was extremely calm and relaxed as he said all this.
“Please say no more,” Raskolnikov said. “This is totally out of line.”

“Not at all. So a person can only do harm to others, but even the smallest good deed is blocked by silly rules? That’s ridiculous. If I died and left your sister that money in my will, she wouldn’t refuse it, would she?”
“She probably would.”
“Oh, no, she wouldn’t. But if you refuse, fine, though ten thousand roubles is a very handy thing to have. Either way, please tell Avdotya Romanovna what I said.”
“No, I won’t.”
“Then I’ll have to try to see her myself and bother her.”
“And if I do tell her, will you leave her alone?”
“I really don’t know. I’d really like to see her once more.”
“Don’t count on it.”
“Too bad. But you don’t know me yet. Maybe we’ll become friends.”
“You think we could be friends?”
“Why not?” Svidrigaïlov said, smiling. He stood up and grabbed his hat. “I didn’t mean to bother you, and I came here without planning to... though your face this morning really struck me.”
“Where did you see me this morning?” Raskolnikov asked, uneasy.

“By chance.... I kept thinking you reminded me of myself.... But don’t worry. I’m not pushy; I was fine with card sharks, and I never bothered Prince Svirbey (he’s a distant relative), and I could write about Raphael’s Madonna in Madam Prilukov’s album, and I never left Marfa Petrovna’s side for seven years, and I used to spend the night at Viazemsky’s place in the Hay Market, and maybe I’ll go up in a balloon with Berg.”
“Okay. Are you leaving soon for your journey, may I ask?”
“What journey?”
“The ‘journey’ you mentioned yourself.”

“A journey? Oh, right. I did mention that. Well, that’s a big topic.... If only you knew what you were asking,” he added, suddenly giving a loud, short laugh. “Maybe I’ll get married instead. They’re setting me up.”
“Here?”
“Yes.”
“How did you find time for that?”

“But I really want to see Avdotya Romanovna just once. I ask you, please. Well, goodbye for now. Oh, I almost forgot—tell your sister, Rodion Romanovitch, that Marfa Petrovna left her three thousand roubles in her will. That’s definitely true. Marfa Petrovna arranged it a week before she died, and I was there. Avdotya Romanovna can get the money in two or three weeks.”
“Are you telling the truth?”
“Yes, tell her. Well, goodbye. I’m staying very close by.”
As he left, Svidrigaïlov ran into Razumihin in the doorway.
It was almost eight o’clock. The two young men hurried toward Bakaleyev’s place, trying to get there before Luzhin.
“Who was that guy back there?” Razumihin asked as soon as they were outside.

“That was Svidrigaïlov,” Raskolnikov said. “He’s the landowner whose house my sister worked in as a governess, the one who harassed her. Because he wouldn’t leave her alone, his wife, Marfa Petrovna, fired Dounia. Later, Marfa Petrovna begged Dounia’s forgiveness, and she just died suddenly. We were talking about her this morning. I don’t know why, but I’m scared of Svidrigaïlov. He showed up right after his wife’s funeral. He’s weird, and he’s definitely planning something. We need to protect Dounia from him—that’s what I wanted to warn you about. Do you get it?”
“Protect her? What can he do to Avdotya Romanovna? Still, thank you, Rodya, for telling me. We’ll keep an eye out. Do you know where he’s staying?”
“No idea.”
“Why didn’t you ask? That’s a shame! I’ll find out, though.”
“Did you actually see him?” Raskolnikov asked after a moment.
“Yeah, I saw him. Got a good look.”
“You really saw him? You’re sure?” Raskolnikov pressed.
“Yes, I remember his face exactly. I’d know him anywhere; I’m good with faces.”
They walked in silence for a bit.
“Hmm... all right,” Raskolnikov muttered. “You know, I was starting to think... maybe I imagined the whole thing.”
“What do you mean? I don’t get it.”
“Well, everyone keeps saying I’m crazy,” Raskolnikov went on, forcing a smile. “I was just thinking, maybe I really am losing my mind, and I only saw a ghost.”
“What are you talking about?”
“Who knows? Maybe I really am crazy, and everything that’s happened in the past few days is just in my head.”
“Oh, Rodya, you’re upset again!... But what did Svidrigaïlov say to you? Why did he come?”
Raskolnikov didn’t answer. Razumihin thought for a second.

“Let me tell you what happened with me,” he began. “I went to see you, but you were asleep. Then we had dinner, and after that I went to Porfiry’s place. Zametov was still there. I tried to bring up the topic, but I couldn’t say it right. They just don’t get it—or pretend not to—and they’re not even embarrassed. I pulled Porfiry over to the window to talk privately, but it was pointless. We both looked away. Finally, I shook my fist in his face and told him, as your cousin, I’d smash his head in. He just stared at me, so I swore at him and left. It was stupid. I didn’t say a word to Zametov. At first, I thought I’d messed up, but as I was going downstairs, I had a great idea: why should we even care? Unless you’re actually in danger, what does it matter? Just ignore them! We’ll laugh at them later, and if I were you, I’d confuse them even more. They’ll be so embarrassed in the end! Forget them. We can get back at them when this is over, but for now, let’s just enjoy the joke.”

“I guess so,” Raskolnikov replied. But he thought to himself, What are you going to say tomorrow? Oddly, he’d never wondered until now what Razumihin would think when he found out the truth. As he looked at Razumihin, he realized he barely cared about his story with Porfiry—so much had happened since then.

In the hallway, they ran into Luzhin, who had arrived right at eight and was looking for the right apartment. All three of them went in together, not saying a word to each other. The two young men entered first, while Pyotr Petrovitch (Luzhin) stayed behind a bit to take off his coat, as was polite. Pulcheria Alexandrovna came to greet him at the door, while Dounia went to her brother. Luzhin entered, acting friendly but even more formal than usual, and bowed to the women. Still, he looked like something had upset him and he couldn’t shake it off. Pulcheria Alexandrovna, also a little nervous, quickly told everyone to sit at the round table where the samovar was steaming. Dounia and Luzhin sat across from each other. Razumihin and Raskolnikov faced Pulcheria Alexandrovna, with Razumihin next to Luzhin and Raskolnikov beside his sister.

There was an awkward silence. Pyotr Petrovitch slowly took out a fancy handkerchief that smelled strongly of perfume and blew his nose, trying to look like a kind man who’d been wronged and was determined to get answers. It had crossed his mind in the hallway to keep his coat on and storm out, just to teach the two ladies a harsh lesson and show how serious he was. But he couldn’t go through with it. Besides, he hated not knowing what was going on, and he wanted to get to the bottom of things: if they’d ignored his request so openly, there had to be a reason, and he wanted to find out. He could always punish them later if needed.
“I hope your journey went well,” he asked Pulcheria Alexandrovna in his most proper tone.
“Oh, yes, Pyotr Petrovitch, very well.”
“Glad to hear it. And Avdotya Romanovna, you’re not too tired?”
“I’m young and strong, so I don’t get tired easily. But it was hard for mother,” Dounia replied.
“That’s just how it is! Russian railways are so long. ‘Mother Russia’ is a huge country.... I really wanted to meet you yesterday, but couldn’t. I hope everything went smoothly anyway?”

“Oh, no, Pyotr Petrovitch, it was really difficult,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said quickly, sounding very pointed about it. “If Dmitri Prokofitch hadn’t come to help us—I truly believe God sent him—we would’ve been completely lost. Here he is! Dmitri Prokofitch Razumihin,” she added, introducing him to Luzhin.
“We met yesterday,” Luzhin muttered, shooting a dirty look at Razumihin before scowling and going quiet.

Luzhin was the type of person who acted very polite in public and paid a lot of attention to details, but as soon as something went wrong, he’d get totally flustered and stiff, more like a sack of flour than a real gentleman. Once again, no one spoke; Raskolnikov stayed stubbornly silent, Dounia didn’t want to open up too fast, Razumihin had nothing to say, and Pulcheria Alexandrovna grew anxious again.
“Did you hear Marfa Petrovna died?” she started, grabbing for the main topic she had prepared.
“Yes, I heard. I was told right away. In fact, I came to let you know that Arkady Ivanovitch Svidrigaïlov left for Petersburg immediately after his wife’s funeral. I have reliable sources.”
“To Petersburg? Here?” Dounia asked, alarmed, looking at her mother.
“Exactly, and judging by how quickly he left and everything that happened, he definitely has some plan.”
“Oh no! He won’t leave Dounia alone even here?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried.
“I don’t think you or Avdotya Romanovna have anything to worry about, unless you want to contact him yourselves. Personally, I’m being careful, and I’m already trying to find out where he’s staying.”
“Oh, Pyotr Petrovitch, you have no idea how much you scared me,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna went on. “I’ve only seen him twice, but he terrified me! I’m sure he caused Marfa Petrovna’s death.”

“It’s impossible to know for sure. I have specific information. I won’t argue—he may have pushed events along because of how badly he treated her; but as for his overall character, I totally agree with you. I don’t know if he’s well-off now, or exactly what Marfa Petrovna left him. I’ll find out soon. But I bet if he has any money here in Petersburg, he’ll go right back to his old habits. He’s a complete scoundrel, the worst kind of person. I’m pretty sure Marfa Petrovna, who was unlucky enough to fall for him and pay his debts eight years ago, helped him out in another way, too. Because of her, a criminal case—something violent and crazy, for which he could have gone to Siberia—was covered up. That’s the kind of man he is, if you didn’t know.”
“Oh my God!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna gasped. Raskolnikov listened closely.
“Are you telling the truth? Do you really have good evidence for all this?” Dounia asked, her voice firm.

“I’m only repeating what Marfa Petrovna told me in confidence. Legally, the case wasn’t clear. There was a woman here, Resslich, a foreigner, who lent people small amounts of money and did favors, and Svidrigaïlov had a long and mysterious connection with her. She had a niece, I think, a deaf and mute girl, maybe only fourteen or fifteen, living with her. Resslich hated the girl and hardly gave her enough to eat; she beat her badly. One day, the girl was found hanged in the attic. The official verdict was suicide, and after the investigation, that was the end of it. But later, someone reported that Svidrigaïlov had... abused her. They couldn’t prove it—the tip came from another German woman who wasn’t trustworthy; nothing was reported to the police, thanks to Marfa Petrovna’s money and effort. It all stayed as gossip. But the story matters. You probably heard, Avdotya Romanovna, when you were there, about the servant Philip who died from mistreatment six years ago, before serfdom was ended.”
“Actually, I heard that Philip hanged himself.”
“Right, but what made him, or pushed him, to suicide was Svidrigaïlov’s constant bullying and harshness.”

“I’m not sure about that,” Dounia said coolly. “I just heard he was sort of a gloomy guy, a ‘domestic philosopher,’ as the servants joked, and that he hanged himself partly because Svidrigaïlov mocked him, not because he beat him. When I worked there, Svidrigaïlov treated the servants well, and they actually liked him, though they did blame him for Philip’s death.”

“I see, Avdotya Romanovna, you seem eager to defend him all of a sudden,” Luzhin said, twisting his mouth into an odd smile. “There’s no doubt he’s clever and knows how to charm women—Marfa Petrovna’s story proves that. I only wanted to help you and your mother by warning you, since he’ll probably try something again. Honestly, I’m sure he’ll end up in debtor’s prison again. Marfa Petrovna didn’t plan to leave him anything significant—she wanted to protect her children’s inheritance. If she did leave him anything, it would just be a small amount, nothing that could last a year for a man like him.”
“Pyotr Petrovitch, please,” Dounia said, “let’s stop talking about Mr. Svidrigaïlov. It’s upsetting.”
“He just came to see me,” Raskolnikov said, breaking his silence.
Everyone gasped and turned to look at him. Even Luzhin was surprised.

“It was about an hour and a half ago. He came in while I was asleep, woke me up, and introduced himself,” Raskolnikov continued. “He seemed cheerful and relaxed, and said he hopes we’ll become friends. By the way, Dounia, he really wants to meet you, and asked me to help arrange it. He has a proposal for you—he told me about it. He also said that a week before she died, Marfa Petrovna left you three thousand roubles in her will, Dounia, and you’ll be able to get the money soon.”
“Thank God!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried, crossing herself. “Pray for her soul, Dounia!”
“It’s true!” Luzhin blurted out.
“What else did he say?” Dounia urged Raskolnikov.
“He said he isn’t rich and that the estate went to his children, who are staying with an aunt. He told me he’s living somewhere near me, but I didn’t ask exactly where....”
“But what does he want to propose to Dounia?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked, frightened. “Did he tell you?”
“Yes.”
“What was it?”
“I’ll tell you later.”
Raskolnikov stopped talking and focused on his tea.
Pyotr Petrovitch checked his watch.
“I have a business meeting, so I should get going,” he said, sounding a little annoyed as he started to stand up.
“Don’t go, Pyotr Petrovitch,” Dounia said. “You planned to spend the evening with us, and you said in your letter you wanted to talk with mother.”

“Yes, Avdotya Romanovna,” Luzhin replied, sitting down again but still holding his hat. “I did want to discuss something very important with you and your mother. But since your brother can’t talk openly about Svidrigaïlov’s proposals in front of me, I also can’t talk openly... in front of everyone... about things that are very important to me. Besides, my most urgent request has been ignored....”
Looking hurt, Luzhin went silent.

“The reason my brother is here, even though you asked he not be, is because I insisted,” Dounia said. “You wrote that Rodya insulted you. I think we need to clear that up immediately and make peace. If my brother did insult you, he should and will apologize.”
Pyotr Petrovitch got more serious.
“There are insults, Avdotya Romanovna, that can never be forgotten. There’s a line that shouldn’t be crossed; once it’s crossed, there’s no going back.”

“That’s not really what I meant, Pyotr Petrovitch,” Dounia interrupted, getting impatient. “Please understand, our entire future depends on sorting this out right now. I’m telling you honestly, I can’t see it any other way. If you care about me at all, this needs to be fixed today, no matter how hard it is. And again, if my brother’s to blame, he’ll ask for your forgiveness.”

“I’m surprised you’d put it that way,” Luzhin said, getting more irritated. “I care for you deeply, but that doesn’t mean I have to like every member of your family. Even though I want to marry you, I can’t take on obligations that are...”

“Don’t get so offended, Pyotr Petrovitch,” Dounia interrupted, her voice full of emotion. “Be the reasonable and generous man I always believed you to be. I’ve promised myself to you—I’m your fiancée. Trust me, and believe that I can judge fairly. My asking to be the judge here is just as surprising to my brother as it is to you. When I insisted that he come today after your letter, I didn’t tell him anything about what I planned. If you two can’t make peace, then I’ll have to choose between you—it’s either you or him. That’s how serious this is, for both of you. I don’t want to make the wrong choice, and I can’t afford to. If I have to, I’ll cut ties with my brother for your sake, or with you for his. I want to see if he’s really my brother, and I need to know it; and from you, I want to know if you really care for me, if you respect me, if you’re the right husband for me.”

“Avdotya Romanovna,” Luzhin said stiffly, “your words mean a lot to me; actually, they’re pretty offensive, considering my position as your fiancé. Besides your strange and insulting way of comparing me to an insolent boy, you’re saying you might break your promise to me. You’re putting it as ‘you or him,’ showing how little I matter to you... I can’t just let that go, considering our relationship and everything that’s between us.”
“What!” Dounia exclaimed, her face red. “I put your interests on the same level as what’s been most important in my life, and you’re offended because I don’t value you enough?”
Raskolnikov smirked, Razumihin fidgeted, but Pyotr Petrovitch didn’t accept the criticism. In fact, he seemed to enjoy getting more stubborn and irritated with every word.

“Love for your future husband should outweigh love for your brother,” he said, trying to sound wise. “And I can’t be put on the same level.... Even though I said I wouldn’t talk openly in front of your brother, I’ll now have to ask your mother for an explanation about something very important to my dignity. Your son,” he said, turning to Pulcheria Alexandrovna, “yesterday, in front of Mr. Razsudkin—or... is that the name? Sorry, I forgot your last name,” he nodded to Razumihin, “insulted me by twisting what I said to you in a private conversation over coffee. I said that marrying a poor girl who’s been through hard times is better for the marriage than marrying one who’s always lived in luxury, since it builds character. Your son exaggerated what I said and made me look bad, accused me of bad intentions, and seemed to base it all on what you wrote to him. I’d be grateful, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, if you could clear this up for me and set my mind at ease. Please tell me exactly how you repeated my words in your letter to Rodion Romanovitch.”
“I don’t remember,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna stammered. “I wrote what I understood. I don’t know how Rodya repeated them to you—maybe he exaggerated.”
“He couldn’t have exaggerated unless you put him up to it.”
“Pyotr Petrovitch,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said with dignity, “the fact that Dounia and I didn’t take your words in a bad way is proved by the fact that we’re sitting here right now.”
“Good, mother,” Dounia said approvingly.
“So it’s my fault again,” Luzhin said, sounding hurt.
“Well, Pyotr Petrovitch, you keep blaming Rodion, but you just wrote something untrue about him yourself,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said, getting braver.
“I don’t remember writing anything false.”

“You wrote,” Raskolnikov said sharply, not even looking at Luzhin, “that yesterday I gave money not to the widow of the man who died, which is what actually happened, but to his daughter, whom I only met yesterday. You wrote that just to stir up trouble between me and my family, and you added nasty comments about a girl you don’t even know. That’s just mean slander.”

“Excuse me, sir,” Luzhin said, shaking with anger. “I described your behavior in my letter because your sister and mother asked me how I found you, and what I thought of you. As for what you mentioned, show me one thing that’s false—prove you didn’t throw your money away, and that there aren’t worthless people in that family, no matter how unfortunate they are.”
“As far as I’m concerned, for all your so-called virtues, you’re not worth even the little finger of that poor girl you insult.”
“So you’d let her spend time with your mother and sister?”
“I already have, if you want to know. I had her sit with mother and Dounia today.”
“Rodya!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried. Dounia blushed deeply, Razumihin frowned, and Luzhin smiled with a mocking look.

“You see for yourself, Avdotya Romanovna,” he said, “that it’s impossible for us to agree. I hope this ends the matter once and for all. I’ll leave now, so I don’t interrupt your family time or your talk about secrets.” He stood up and grabbed his hat. “But before I go, I want to ask that you don’t put me in this sort of awkward position again. Especially you, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, since my letter was addressed to you and no one else.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna was a little offended.

“You act like we’re completely under your control, Pyotr Petrovitch. Dounia already told you why your request was ignored—she meant well. But you write as if you’re giving us orders. Are we supposed to treat everything you want as a command? Actually, you should be especially considerate with us now, since we dropped everything and came here relying on you. That means, in a way, we’re in your hands.”

“That’s not exactly true, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, especially now that you’ve just gotten news about Marfa Petrovna’s inheritance—which is pretty convenient, judging by your new attitude,” he added sarcastically.
“From that comment, it sounds like you were counting on us being helpless,” Dounia snapped.

“Well, now I can’t count on that, and I definitely don’t want to stand in the way of your secret talks about Svidrigaïlov’s proposal, which he told your brother about and which, I see, is very exciting for you.”
“Oh my God!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried.
Razumihin couldn’t sit still anymore.
“Aren’t you ashamed, sister?” Raskolnikov asked.
“I am, Rodya,” Dounia said. “Pyotr Petrovitch, please leave,” she told him, white with anger.

Pyotr Petrovitch clearly hadn’t expected things to end this way. He’d always been sure of his power and the others’ helplessness. He couldn’t believe what was happening. His face went pale and his lips shook.
“Avdotya Romanovna, if I walk out that door now, after being dismissed like this, you can be sure I’ll never come back. Think about what you’re doing. I won’t change my mind.”
“How dare you!” Dounia shouted, jumping up. “I don’t want you to come back.”
“What! So that’s it?” Luzhin shouted, still not believing what was happening. “That’s how it is! But do you realize, Avdotya Romanovna, that I could protest?”

“How can you talk to her like that?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said angrily. “What do you have to protest about? What rights do you think you have? Am I supposed to give my Dounia to someone like you? Leave us, now! We’re the ones at fault for agreeing to this in the first place, especially me....”
“But you made a promise to me, Pulcheria Alexandrovna,” Luzhin yelled, almost losing control, “and now you break it and... and besides... I’ve spent money because of this....”
That last complaint was so typical of Pyotr Petrovitch that Raskolnikov, pale with anger and trying to hold it in, couldn’t help but start laughing. But Pulcheria Alexandrovna was furious.

“Expenses? What expenses? Are you talking about our suitcase? But the conductor brought it for free for you. My goodness, we tied you down! What are you thinking, Pyotr Petrovitch? You tied us down, not the other way around!”
“Enough, mother, please stop,” Dounia begged. “Pyotr Petrovitch, please just go.”

“I am going. But one last thing,” Luzhin said, unable to control himself. “Your mother seems to have forgotten that I decided to take you, even after all the gossip about your reputation in town. I ignored what people said and restored your good name. I could have expected some gratitude from you. Now I see I may have made a huge mistake ignoring everyone’s opinion....”
“Does this

The truth was, right up until the last moment, Pyotr Petrovitch (Luzhin) never believed things would end like this. He was always so full of himself, completely sure that two poor and powerless women could never get away from him. His pride and arrogance made this belief even stronger. Luzhin, who had worked his way up from nothing, was obsessed with admiring himself. He thought he was smarter and more capable than almost anyone and sometimes even enjoyed looking at his own reflection when he was alone. But above everything else, he loved his money—the money he’d earned and schemed for. That money made him feel like he was just as good as all the people who used to look down on him.

When Luzhin angrily reminded Dounia that he had chosen her “in spite of the rumors,” he really meant it and honestly felt offended by what he saw as her “shocking ingratitude.” But even when he first proposed, he knew those rumors weren’t true. Marfa Petrovna had told everyone the story was made up, and nobody in town believed it anymore; people actually defended Dounia. Luzhin would have admitted he knew that. Still, he thought he was being heroic by “lifting” Dounia up to his level. When he talked about it to Dounia, he let slip just how proud he was of himself, and he couldn’t understand why everyone else didn’t admire him too. When he visited Raskolnikov, he felt like a hero about to get some well-deserved praise. Now, as he walked down the stairs, he felt deeply wronged and unappreciated.

Dounia was absolutely necessary for him—he couldn’t imagine life without her. For years, he’d dreamed about marriage, but always waited, saving up more money. In secret, he would daydream about marrying a girl who was innocent, poor (she had to be poor), very young, beautiful, well-brought-up and educated, shy, someone who had suffered, and who would always look up to him as her savior—someone who would think he was amazing forever. He’d imagined all kinds of romantic scenes with such a girl after work. And now, finally, his dream was almost real. Dounia had everything he wanted—she was beautiful, educated, and her tough situation had attracted him even more. In Dounia, he found even more than he’d hoped: she had pride, strength, and good manners, maybe even better than his own (he could tell). And he was sure she’d be grateful to him forever for his “heroic” kindness, always humble before him, letting him control everything about her life. Not long ago, after a lot of thinking, he’d even changed his career and was about to start a new business, hoping to enter a higher social class in St. Petersburg. He knew that having a smart, charming wife could help him a lot, making people notice him more. But now, everything was ruined! This sudden breakup felt like a lightning bolt—like some sick joke. He’d just been a little bit bossy, hadn’t even finished speaking, just made a joke—and suddenly it was all over. And yes, in his own way, he did love Dounia; he already felt like she belonged to him in his daydreams—and now she was gone! No, he told himself, tomorrow he’d fix it, smooth things over, settle it all. Most of all, he had to crush Raskolnikov, who had messed everything up. He felt sick when he thought of Razumihin, too, but quickly reassured himself—someone like Razumihin could never compare to him! The only person he was really worried about was Svidrigaïlov. In short, Luzhin had a lot to deal with now....

“No, I’m the one most to blame!” said Dounia, hugging and kissing her mother. “I was tempted by his money, but honestly, Rodya, I never guessed he was such a terrible person. If I’d known sooner, nothing could have tempted me! Please don’t blame me, brother!”
“God has saved us! God has saved us!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna muttered, not quite believing what had just happened.

They all felt relieved, and within five minutes, they were laughing. Only sometimes, Dounia would go pale and frown whenever she remembered what happened. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was surprised to find she was actually glad too—just that morning, she’d thought breaking up with Luzhin would be a disaster. Razumihin was thrilled. He didn’t dare show how happy he was, but inside he was buzzing, like a huge weight had been lifted off his chest. Now he could really dedicate himself to helping them. Anything could happen now! But he was afraid to hope for too much. Raskolnikov, though, just sat in the same spot, looking gloomy and uninterested. Even though he’d wanted Luzhin gone more than anyone, he seemed the least bothered by what had happened. Dounia thought her brother might still be mad at her, and Pulcheria Alexandrovna watched him nervously.
“What did Svidrigaïlov say to you?” Dounia asked, coming closer to Raskolnikov.
“Yes, yes!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna added eagerly.
Raskolnikov lifted his head.
“He wants to give you ten thousand roubles and asks to see you—once, with me there,” Raskolnikov said.
“See her? Absolutely not!” cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna. “And how dare he offer her money!”
Then, in a rather dry voice, Raskolnikov repeated what Svidrigaïlov had said to him, leaving out the part about Marfa Petrovna’s ghost because he didn’t want to get into that.
“What did you tell him?” Dounia asked.

“At first, I said I wouldn’t give any message to you. Then he told me he’d try to see you anyway, even without my help. He insisted his feelings for you were just a passing crush and that now he doesn’t care about you. He also doesn’t want you to marry Luzhin. Honestly, his whole speech was kind of a mess.”
“How do you see him, Rodya? What impression did he leave on you?” Dounia asked.

“Honestly, I don’t really get him,” Raskolnikov admitted. “He offers you ten thousand but says he’s not rich. He says he’s leaving, then forgets he said it ten minutes later. Then he tells me he’s getting married soon, already picked the girl.... He must have some kind of motive, probably a bad one. But if he has a plan, it’s weird that he’s so clumsy about it.... Anyway, I refused the money for your sake, once and for all. Overall, he seemed really odd to me.... You might even think he’s crazy. But maybe he just acts that way. Marfa Petrovna’s death really seems to have shaken him up.”

“God rest her soul,” said Pulcheria Alexandrovna. “I’ll always pray for her! Where would we be without that three thousand she left us, Dounia? It’s like a gift from heaven! Rodya, this morning we only had three roubles left, and Dounia and I were about to pawn her watch, just to keep from borrowing from that man before he offered help.”
Svidrigaïlov’s offer seemed to really disturb Dounia. She stood there, deep in thought.
“He must be up to something terrible,” she whispered to herself, almost shivering.
Raskolnikov noticed how scared she seemed.
“I think I’m going to have to see him again—maybe more than once,” he said to Dounia.

“We’ll keep an eye on him! I’ll track him down!” Razumihin said, full of energy. “I won’t let him out of my sight. Rodya just told me, ‘Take care of my sister.’ Will you let me help too, Avdotya Romanovna?”
Dounia smiled and shook his hand, but she still looked worried. Pulcheria Alexandrovna kept glancing at her nervously, but having the three thousand roubles clearly helped calm her down.
Fifteen minutes later, everyone was deep in conversation. Even Raskolnikov listened for a while, though he didn’t say much. Razumihin was talking the most.

“And why should you leave?” Razumihin said enthusiastically. “What’s there for you in a little town? The important thing is, you’re all together here and you need each other—really need each other, believe me. At least for now.... Let me join you, and I promise we’ll set up something amazing. Listen! I’ll explain my whole plan—it popped into my head this morning before anything happened... Listen, I have an uncle I want you to meet—he’s a good, helpful old guy. He has a thousand roubles saved up, lives on his pension, and doesn’t need that money. He’s actually been begging me to borrow it from him for two years and pay him six percent interest. I know he just wants to help me out. Last year I didn’t need it, but this year I decided I’d borrow it when he visits. If you add another thousand from your three thousand, we’ll have enough to get started—so let’s be partners! And what will we do?”

Then Razumihin started laying out his plan. He explained that most publishers and booksellers have no clue what they’re selling, so they’re usually bad at their jobs, and that good books usually make a profit—sometimes a lot. Razumihin had been dreaming of starting his own publishing company. He’d worked in publishing offices for two years and spoke three European languages well, though, six days ago, he’d told Raskolnikov he was “weak” in German just to convince him to split a translation job and the money. That was a lie, and Raskolnikov had known it.

“Why shouldn’t we take this chance, now that we’ve got the money?” Razumihin said excitedly. “Sure, it’ll be a lot of work, but we’ll work—me, Avdotya Romanovna, Rodya... Some books make great profits these days! The best part is, we’ll know exactly what to translate and publish, and we’ll be learning as we go. I can help—I've got experience. I’ve been dealing with publishers for almost two years, and I know all the ins and outs. You don’t need to be a saint to make money! And listen, I secretly know of two or three books that could easily bring in a hundred roubles just for getting them translated and published. I wouldn’t take five hundred for the idea of one of them! And if I told a publisher, he’d probably hesitate—publishers can be so clueless! As for the business side—printing, paper, sales—just leave it to me. We’ll start small and grow. At the very least, we’ll make a living and get our money back.”
Dounia’s eyes lit up.
“I like your idea, Dmitri Prokofitch!” she said.

“I don’t know anything about this kind of work,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said, “maybe it’s a good plan, but only God knows. It’s all new to us. Of course, we’ll have to stay here for a while, at least.” She glanced at Rodya.
“What do you think, brother?” Dounia asked.

“I think he’s got a great idea,” Raskolnikov answered. “It’s too soon to dream of a big publishing company, but we could definitely publish five or six books and do well. I even know a book myself that would sell for sure. And as for Razumihin running things, there’s no doubt—he knows the business. But we can talk more about it later....”

“Yes!” Razumihin cheered. “Listen, there’s an apartment in this building, owned by the same landlord. It’s separate—not connected to these rooms. It’s furnished, cheap, three rooms. Why not take it for now? I’ll pawn your watch tomorrow to get you some money, and we can get everything set up. You three could live together, and Rodya could stay with you. Wait, Rodya, where are you going?”
“What? Rodya, you’re leaving already?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked, worried.
“Now? At a time like this?” Razumihin exclaimed.
Dounia stared at her brother in disbelief. He was holding his cap, clearly about to leave.

“You’d think you were at my funeral or saying goodbye forever,” he said in a strange way. He tried to smile, but it didn’t really work. “But who knows—maybe this is the last time we’ll see each other...” The thought just slipped out. That’s what he’d really been thinking, and somehow it escaped.
“What’s wrong with you?” his mother cried.
“Where are you going, Rodya?” Dounia asked, her voice sounding odd.
“Oh, I have to...” he said vaguely, as if he wasn’t sure what to say. But his pale face looked determined.

“I wanted to tell you—as I was coming here—I wanted to say, mother, Dounia, it’s better if we separate for a while. I’m sick, I’m not at peace.... I’ll come back later, on my own, when it’s possible. I remember you and love you.... Please leave me alone. I decided this even before... I’m completely sure. No matter what happens to me, whether I fall apart or not, I want to be alone. Forget about me—it’s better for you. Don’t ask about me. When I can, I’ll come or... I’ll send for you. Maybe things will go back to normal, but right now, if you love me, let me go... otherwise I’ll start to hate you, I can feel it.... Goodbye!”
“Oh my God!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried. Both his mother and Dounia were terrified. Razumihin was shocked too.
“Rodya, please, make up with us! Let’s be like we were before!” his poor mother begged.
He turned slowly to the door and walked out. Dounia quickly followed him.
“Brother, what are you doing to mother?” she whispered, her eyes fierce with anger.
He looked at her blankly.
“It’s okay, I’ll come... I’m coming,” he muttered quietly, almost like he wasn’t fully aware of what he was saying, and left the room.
“He’s so selfish and cold-hearted!” Dounia cried.

“He’s not cold-hearted—just out of his mind. He’s not cruel! Can’t you see it? You’re the one being harsh!” Razumihin whispered in her ear, squeezing her hand. “I’ll be right back,” he shouted to their terrified mother, and ran out.
Raskolnikov was waiting for him at the end of the hallway.
“I knew you’d come after me,” he said. “Go back to them—be with them tomorrow and always.... I... maybe I’ll come... if I can. Goodbye.”
And without shaking hands, he walked away.
“But where are you going? What are you doing? What’s wrong with you? How can you just leave like this?” Razumihin stammered, completely lost.
Raskolnikov stopped again.
“Just don’t ask me anything. I have nothing to tell you. Don’t come looking for me. Maybe I’ll come here.... Leave me alone, but don’t leave them. Got it?”

The hallway was dark; they stood near a lamp. For a minute, they stared at each other in silence. Razumihin would remember that moment for the rest of his life. Raskolnikov’s intense, burning eyes seemed to look straight into his soul. Suddenly, Razumihin shivered. Something strange, almost like a secret message, passed between them—an awful, terrible understanding. Razumihin turned pale.
“You get it now?” Raskolnikov said, his face twitching. “Go back, go to them,” he said suddenly, and quickly left the building.

I won’t try to describe how Razumihin went back to the women, comforted them, insisted that Rodya just needed rest, promised Rodya would come every day, begged them not to worry or upset him, and swore he’d watch over Rodya and get him the best doctor possible. From that evening on, Razumihin really became part of their family—as a son and a brother.

Raskolnikov went straight to the house by the canal where Sonia lived. It was an old, green, three-story building. He found the porter and got some vague directions about where Kapernaumov, the tailor, lived. After searching in a corner of the yard, he found the entrance to a dark, narrow staircase, climbed up to the second floor, and ended up in a hallway that wrapped around the whole building, overlooking the yard. As he wandered in the darkness, unsure of which door was Kapernaumov’s, a door just a few steps away opened. He reached out and grabbed it almost without thinking.
“Who’s there?” a woman’s voice asked nervously.
“It’s me... I came to see you,” Raskolnikov replied, stepping into the tiny entryway.
On a broken chair sat a candle in a battered, old copper holder.
“It’s you! Oh my God!” Sonia cried weakly, frozen where she stood.
“Which is your room? This way?” Raskolnikov asked, trying not to look at her, and hurried inside.

A minute later Sonia came in with the candle, set it down, and stood there looking completely flustered, deeply upset, and clearly scared by his sudden visit. Her pale face suddenly turned red and tears filled her eyes... She felt sick, embarrassed, but also happy. Raskolnikov quickly turned away and sat on a chair by the table, taking in the room with a quick look.

The room was big but had a very low ceiling. It was the only room rented out by the Kapernaumovs, whose own rooms were behind a closed door on the left wall. On the right wall was another door, always locked, which led to another apartment. Sonia’s room was shaped oddly, almost like a barn, with walls slanting so that one corner was super sharp and hard to see into without strong light, while the other corner was strangely wide. The room was almost empty: in the right corner was a bed frame, next to it by the door was a chair. A plain wooden table with a blue cloth stood against the same wall, close to the other apartment’s door, with two simple chairs by it. Across from that, near the sharp corner, stood a small, lonely set of drawers. That was all the furniture. The yellow wallpaper was scratched and dirty, black in the corners. It must have been damp and smelly in the winter. Everything screamed poverty—even the bed had no curtain.
Sonia silently watched her guest, who was openly and almost rudely inspecting her room. She started trembling out of fear, as if she was standing in front of a judge who would decide her fate.
“I’m late... It’s eleven, right?” he asked, still not looking up.
“Yes,” Sonia mumbled. “Oh, yes, it is,” she added quickly, as if that could help her somehow. “My landlady’s clock just struck... I heard it myself...”
“I’ve come to see you for the last time,” Raskolnikov said darkly, even though it was his first visit. “I might not see you again...”
“Are you... leaving?”
“I don’t know... maybe tomorrow...”
“So you aren’t coming to see Katerina Ivanovna tomorrow?” Sonia’s voice shook.
“I don’t know. I’ll know in the morning.... But never mind that, I came to say something...”
He looked up at her and suddenly realized he was sitting while she was still standing.
“Why are you standing? Sit down,” he said, his voice suddenly softer and kinder.
She sat down. He looked at her gently, almost with pity.
“You’re so thin! Your hand—it’s almost see-through, like a dead person’s.”
He took her hand. Sonia gave a small, sad smile.
“I’ve always been like this,” she said.
“Even when you lived at home?”
“Yes.”
“Of course you were,” he said suddenly, his face and tone changing again.
He glanced around the room once more.
“You rent this place from the Kapernaumovs?”
“They live through that door?”
“Yes... They have another room like this one.”
“All in one room?”
“Yes.”
“I’d be afraid to sleep here at night,” he said grimly.
“They’re very good people, very kind,” Sonia answered, still a little lost. “All the furniture—everything—belongs to them. And they’re really kind, and their kids often come to see me.”
“They all stutter, don’t they?”

“Yes... He stutters and limps. His wife... she doesn’t exactly stutter, but she can’t speak clearly. She’s very kind. He used to be a house servant. They have seven kids... only the oldest stutters, the rest are just sickly, but they don’t stutter... But how did you hear about them?” she asked, a little surprised.
“Your father told me. He told me all about you... and how you’d go out at six and come back at nine, and how Katerina Ivanovna would kneel by your bed.”
Sonia looked embarrassed.
“I thought I saw him today,” she whispered nervously.
“Who?”
“Father. I was walking on the street, right there on the corner, around ten o’clock, and I thought I saw him walking ahead of me. It looked just like him. I wanted to go to Katerina Ivanovna....”
“You were walking the streets?”
“Yes,” Sonia whispered quickly, looking down, embarrassed again.
“Did Katerina Ivanovna ever beat you?”
“Oh no, what are you saying? No!” Sonia looked almost shocked.
“So you love her?”

“Love her? Of course!” Sonia said desperately, wringing her hands. “Oh, you just don’t understand! She’s like a child... her mind is broken, you see, from all the sorrow. And she used to be so smart, so generous, so kind! You just don’t understand, you really don’t!”

Sonia said this as if she was falling apart, twisting her hands in stress and pain. Her pale face turned red, her eyes full of suffering. Clearly, she was deeply moved and wanted to defend Katerina Ivanovna, or at least explain. You could see endless compassion in her face.

“Beat me! How could she? Good heavens, beat me! And even if she did, what does it matter? You know nothing, nothing about it... She is so unhappy, so very unhappy! And she’s sick... she’s just trying to do the right thing, she’s pure. She really believes the world should be fair and expects it... Even if you tortured her, she wouldn’t do wrong. She just doesn’t see that it’s impossible for everyone to be good, and it makes her mad. She’s like a child. She’s good!”
“So what will happen to you?”
Sonia looked at him, waiting for an answer.
“They’re all your responsibility now, you know. They were before, too... And your father came to you to beg for money for drink. So what’s going to happen now?”
“I don’t know,” Sonia said sadly.
“Will they stay there?”
“I don’t know... They owe money for the room, but today I heard the landlady wants them out, and Katerina Ivanovna says she won’t stay another minute.”
“How is she so brave? Is she depending on you?”

“Oh, no, don’t say that... We’re like one person, we live like that.” Sonia was upset again, almost angry, the way a little bird might get angry. “What else could she do? What could she possibly do?” she asked, getting more upset. “And how she cried today! Her mind is broken, don’t you see? One minute she’s fussing about tomorrow, wanting everything to be perfect—the lunch and all that. Then she’s wringing her hands, coughing up blood, crying, and suddenly she’ll bang her head against the wall in total despair. Then she’ll calm down again. She puts all her hope in you; she says you’ll help her now, and that she’ll borrow some money and go back to her hometown with me and open a boarding school for girls, and I’ll help run it, and we’ll start a wonderful new life. She hugs and kisses me, comforts me, and she really believes in her dreams! You can’t argue with her. And all day she’s been washing, cleaning, mending. She dragged the wash tub into the room with her weak hands and then collapsed on the bed, gasping. This morning we went to buy shoes for Polenka and Lida because theirs are worn out. But we didn’t have nearly enough money. She picked out such pretty little boots—she has such good taste, you don’t know. And in the shop, she burst out crying in front of everyone because she didn’t have enough money. Oh, it was so sad to see her...”
“Well, after all that, I can see why you live like this,” Raskolnikov said with a bitter smile.

“And aren’t you sorry for them? Aren’t you?” Sonia demanded. “I know you gave your last coin even though you hadn’t seen any of it, and if you had, oh, it would have broken your heart! And how many times—I’ve made her cry so many times! Just last week! Yes, me! Just a week before his death. I was cruel! And I’ve done it so many times! Oh, I’ve hated myself for it all day!”
Sonia twisted her hands in pain as she remembered.
“You were cruel?”

“Yes, me. I went to see them,” she said, crying. “Father said, ‘Read something to me, Sonia, my head hurts, read to me, here’s a book.’ He had this book from Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov, who lives there—he always got strange books. And I said, ‘I can’t stay,’ because I didn’t want to read, and I’d only come to show Katerina Ivanovna some collars. Lizaveta, the peddler, sold me some nice, cheap, embroidered collars and cuffs. Katerina Ivanovna loved them; she put them on and looked at herself in the mirror and was so happy. ‘Give them to me, Sonia, please,’ she said. She wanted them so much. But when would she ever wear them? They just reminded her of happier times. She looked at herself, admired herself, even though she has no clothes, nothing for herself, not for years! She never asks for anything, she’s proud, she’d rather give things away. And for once, she asked for something, she wanted those collars so much. But I didn’t want to give them up. ‘What use are they to you, Katerina Ivanovna?’ I said. I shouldn’t have said that! She looked at me with such pain. She was so hurt, not because of the collars, but because I said no. Oh, if only I could take it back, change it, take back those words! But... it’s nothing to you anyway!”
“Did you know Lizaveta, the peddler?”
“Yes... Did you know her?” Sonia asked, surprised.
“Katerina Ivanovna has tuberculosis, bad tuberculosis; she will die soon,” Raskolnikov said after a pause, ignoring her question.
“Oh, no, no, no!”
Sonia grabbed both his hands without realizing, begging him not to say that.
“But it would be better if she died.”
“No, not better, not at all!” Sonia repeated, horrified.
“And the children? What else can you do except take them in yourself?”
“Oh, I don’t know,” Sonia cried, almost in despair, pressing her hands to her head.
Obviously, this idea had occurred to her many times before, and he was only bringing it back up.
“And what if, even now, while Katerina Ivanovna is still alive, you get sick and are taken to the hospital? What happens then?” he pushed, not letting up.
“How could you say that? That can’t happen!”
Sonia’s face twisted in terror.

“Can’t happen?” Raskolnikov said with a cold smile. “You’re not protected from it, are you? What will happen then? They’ll all end up on the street, she’ll cough and beg and bang her head against a wall, like today, and the kids will cry... Then she’ll collapse, get taken to the police station, to the hospital, she’ll die, and the kids...”
“Oh, no... God won’t let it happen!” Sonia burst out, her heart heavy.
She looked at him, hands clasped, silently begging—as if everything depended on him.
Raskolnikov stood up and started pacing the room. A minute passed. Sonia stood with her head and hands drooping, crushed by sadness.
“Can’t you save up? For emergencies?” he asked, suddenly stopping in front of her.
“No,” Sonia whispered.
“Of course not. Have you tried?” he asked, almost mocking.
“Yes.”
“And it didn’t work! Of course not. No surprise.”
He started pacing again. Another minute passed.
“You don’t get money every day?”
Sonia blushed again, more embarrassed than ever.
“No,” she whispered, struggling to get the word out.
“It’ll be the same with Polenka, I bet,” he suddenly said.
“No, no! It can’t, no!” Sonia cried desperately, as if stabbed. “God wouldn’t let something so horrible happen!”
“He lets it happen to others.”
“No, no! God will protect her, God!” she repeated, almost in a frenzy.
“But what if there is no God at all?” Raskolnikov said harshly, then laughed and looked at her.
Sonia’s face changed at once; she trembled. She looked at him with deep pain, tried to say something, but couldn’t speak, and broke down in bitter sobs, hiding her face in her hands.
“You say Katerina Ivanovna’s mind is lost—yours is too,” he said after a short pause.

Five minutes passed. He kept pacing the room, silent, not looking at her. Then he came up to her; his eyes were shining strangely. He put both hands on her shoulders and looked straight into her tearful face. His eyes were wild, burning and sharp, his lips twitching. Suddenly, he bent down, dropped to the floor, and kissed her foot. Sonia jerked away from him like he was crazy. And he really did look insane.
“What are you doing to me?” she whispered, going pale, a sudden pain gripping her heart.
He stood up right away.

“I didn’t bow to you, I bowed to all of humanity’s suffering,” he said wildly, and walked to the window. “Listen,” he added, turning back after a minute. “Just now I told a rude man that he wasn’t worth your little finger... that I honored my sister by having her sit next to you.”
“Oh, you told them that! And in front of her?” Sonia cried, scared. “Sit with me? An honor? But I’m... dishonorable... Why did you say that?”

“It wasn’t because of your shameful situation that I said it, but because of all the pain you’ve suffered. But you are a great sinner, that’s true,” he said seriously, “and your worst sin is that you ruined and betrayed yourself for nothing. Isn’t that horrible? Isn’t it terrible that you live in this misery you hate so much, and deep down you know (if you just opened your eyes) that you’re not really helping anyone by it, not saving anyone? Tell me,” he continued, almost in a frenzy, “how can this shame and misery live side by side with such holy feelings inside you? It would be better, a thousand times better, to just jump into the canal and end it all!”
“But what would happen to them?” Sonia asked weakly, looking at him with pain, but not shocked by his suggestion.

Raskolnikov looked at her strangely. He saw it all in her face; she must have had that thought before, maybe many times, and had seriously thought about ending it all in her despair—so much that now she wasn’t even surprised to hear it from him. She hadn’t even noticed how harsh his words were. (She hadn’t noticed the meaning behind his blame and his odd attitude toward her shame, either, and he realized that.) But he could see how much her painful, humiliating situation had been torturing her for a long time. “What, what,” he wondered, “has kept her from ending it all?” Only then did he realize what those poor orphans and half-crazy Katerina Ivanovna meant to Sonia.

Still, he realized again that, with her personality and the bit of education she had, she couldn’t possibly keep living this way forever. He wondered how she could have stayed in this situation so long without going insane, if she couldn’t bring herself to jump into the canal. He knew Sonia’s case was rare, but sadly not unique. Still, her background and her former life should have made her break down at the very first step along this horrible path. What kept her going—was it really corruption? He saw that all this dirt had only touched her on the surface, and not one drop of true depravity had reached her heart; he could see right through her....
“There are three paths for her,” he thought, “the canal, the madhouse, or eventually sinking into the kind of depravity that makes your heart turn to stone.”
The last option was the most disgusting, but he was a skeptic, he was young, and so he couldn’t help but believe that was the most likely end.

“But is that possible?” he asked himself. “Can someone whose spirit is still so pure really end up in that filth? Has it already started? Has she only been able to bear it because she’s getting used to it? No, no, that can’t be!” he cried, just like Sonia had. “No, what’s kept her from the canal is the thought of sin and those children.... And if she hasn’t gone mad yet... but who says she hasn’t? Is she sane? Can someone talk and think like she does? How can she live so close to the edge and ignore the danger? Does she expect a miracle? She probably does. Isn’t that madness?”
He clung to that thought. He almost liked it better than any other explanation. He started watching her even more closely.
“So you pray a lot, Sonia?” he asked.
Sonia didn’t answer. He stood beside her, waiting.
“What would I be without God?” she whispered quickly, forcefully, glancing at him with sudden shining eyes, squeezing his hand.
“Ah, so that’s it!” he thought.
“And what does God do for you?” he asked, probing.
Sonia was silent for a long time, as if she couldn’t find the words. Her thin chest shook with emotion.
“Be quiet! Don’t ask! You don’t deserve to know!” she suddenly said, looking at him sternly and angrily.
“That’s it, that’s it,” he thought to himself.
“He does everything,” she whispered quickly, looking down again.

“There’s the answer! That explains everything,” he decided, watching her with curiosity, with a new, weird, almost unhealthy interest. He stared at her pale, thin, uneven little face, those gentle blue eyes that could suddenly blaze with fire and determination, her small body still trembling with anger—and it all seemed stranger and stranger. “She’s a religious fanatic!” he thought.
There was a book on the dresser. He’d noticed it before as he paced. Now he picked it up and looked at it. It was the New Testament in Russian. The cover was old, the leather worn out.
“Where did you get this?” he called across the room.
She was still standing, three steps from the table.
“It was brought to me,” she answered reluctantly, not looking at him.
“Who brought it?”
“Lizaveta. I asked her for it.”
“Lizaveta! That’s odd,” he thought.
Sonia seemed stranger and more amazing every minute. He carried the book to the candle and began flipping through it.
“Where’s the story of Lazarus?” he suddenly asked.
Sonia stared hard at the floor and wouldn’t answer. She was standing sideways to the table.
“Where’s the raising of Lazarus? Find it for me, Sonia.”
She glanced at him.
“You’re looking in the wrong place... It’s in the fourth gospel,” she said sternly, still not looking at him.
“Find it and read it to me,” he said. He sat down, leaned his head on his hand, and looked away, ready to listen.
“In three weeks, they’ll have me in the madhouse! I’ll be there if I’m not somewhere worse,” he muttered to himself.
Sonia heard the request and moved hesitantly to the table. She picked up the book anyway.
“You haven’t read it?” she asked, looking up at him across the table.
Her voice grew more tense.
“Long ago... When I was in school. Read!”
“And you haven’t heard it in church?”
“I... haven’t been. Do you go often?”
“N-no,” Sonia whispered.
Raskolnikov smiled.
“I get it... And you won’t go to your father’s funeral tomorrow?”
“Yes, I will. I was at church last week, too... I had a memorial service.”
“For who?”
“For Lizaveta. She was killed with an axe.”
Raskolnikov’s nerves were getting more and more strained. His head started to spin.
“Were you friends with Lizaveta?”
“Yes... She was kind... she used to come... not often... she couldn’t. We used to read together and... talk. She’ll see God.”
The last thing she said sounded strange to him. And now there was something else: these secret meetings with Lizaveta, and both of them—religious fanatics.
“I’m going to become a religious fanatic myself soon! It’s catching!”
“Read!” he demanded, irritated and insistent.
Sonia still hesitated. Her heart was pounding. She almost didn’t dare read to him. He looked at her with something close to anger, thinking she was an “unhappy lunatic.”
“Why? You don’t believe...” she whispered softly, almost breathless.
“Read! I want you to. You used to read to Lizaveta.”
Sonia opened the book and found the place. Her hands shook, her voice failed her. Twice she tried to start and couldn’t even get the first word out.
“Now a certain man was sick named Lazarus of Bethany...” she finally forced herself to say, but her voice broke at the third word, like a snapped string. She gasped for breath.

Raskolnikov partly understood why Sonia couldn’t bring herself to read to him, and the more he saw this, the more roughly he insisted. He knew too well how painful it was for her to expose all that was most private and precious to her. He knew that this was her secret treasure, maybe kept safe since she was a child, while living with a miserable father and a stepmother driven mad by grief, surrounded by starving kids and constant yelling. But he also realized now that, though it hurt her deeply, she still badly wanted to read to him, to let him hear this, right now, no matter what happened.... He saw it in her eyes, in her intense emotion. She forced herself to control her tears and went on reading the eleventh chapter of John. She continued to verse nineteen:
“And many of the Jews came to Martha and Mary to comfort them concerning their brother.
“Then Martha, as soon as she heard that Jesus was coming, went and met Him: but Mary sat still in the house.
“Then said Martha to Jesus, Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
“But I know that even now, whatever you ask of God, God will give you...”
She stopped again, feeling her voice might break.
“Jesus said to her, your brother will rise again.
“Martha said to Him, I know he will rise again at the resurrection, on the last day.
“Jesus said to her, I am the resurrection and the life: whoever believes in Me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.
“And whoever lives and believes in Me shall never die. Do you believe this?
“She said to Him—”
(And, taking a deep, shaky breath, Sonia read clearly and strongly, like she was making a public confession.)
“Yes, Lord: I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God who was to come into the world.”
She stopped and looked up at him quickly, but held herself together and kept reading. Raskolnikov sat motionless, elbows on the table, eyes averted. She read up to verse thirty-two.
“Then when Mary came where Jesus was and saw Him, she fell down at His feet, saying to Him, Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.
“When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews weeping with her, He groaned in the spirit and was troubled,
“And said, Where have you laid him? They said to Him, Lord, come and see.
“Jesus wept.
“Then the Jews said, see how He loved him!
“And some of them said, couldn’t this man who opened the eyes of the blind have kept this man from dying?”

Raskolnikov turned and looked at her, moved. Yes, he’d expected this. She was trembling with a kind of fever. He knew she was reaching the greatest miracle, and she felt a huge sense of triumph. Her voice was loud and clear; excitement and joy gave her strength. The words blurred before her, but she knew them by heart. At the last verse, “couldn’t this man who opened the eyes of the blind...” she lowered her voice, pouring in the doubt and the blame of those who didn’t believe, who in a moment would fall at Jesus’ feet, sobbing and believing. “And he—he too is blind and doesn’t believe, but he’ll hear, he’ll believe too, yes, yes! Right now, right away,” she dreamed, trembling with hope.
“Jesus, again deeply moved, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
“Jesus said, Take away the stone. Martha, the dead man’s sister, said to Him, Lord, by now he smells; he’s been dead four days.”
She emphasized the words four days.
“Jesus said to her, Didn’t I tell you that if you believe, you’ll see the glory of God?
“So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, Father, I thank you that you have heard me.
“I knew that you always hear me, but I said this for the benefit of the people standing here, that they may believe you sent me.
“When he had said this, Jesus called in a loud voice, Lazarus, come out.
“And the dead man came out.”
(She read this loudly, cold and trembling with joy, as if she could see it right in front of her.)
“His hands and feet wrapped with strips of linen, and a cloth around his face. Jesus said to them, Unwrap him and let him go.
“Therefore many of the Jews who came to Mary and saw what Jesus did believed in Him.”
She couldn’t read anymore, closed the book, and quickly stood up from her chair.

“That’s the whole story of the raising of Lazarus,” she said seriously and abruptly, turning away, standing motionless, unable to look at him. She was still trembling. The candle was burning low in the battered holder, barely lighting the poor room with the murderer and the prostitute who had just read the eternal book together. Five minutes or more passed.
“I came to tell you something,” Raskolnikov said aloud, frowning. He got up and went over to Sonia. She looked up at him silently. His face was especially stern, with a kind of wild determination.
“I left my family today,” he said, “my mother and sister. I’m not going to see them again. I’ve completely broken with them.”
“Why?” Sonia asked, shocked. Meeting his family recently had made a big impression on her. She heard his news with almost horror.
“I only have you now,” he added. “Let’s go together... I’ve come to you, we’re both cursed, let’s go down this path together!”
His eyes flashed—“like he was mad,” Sonia thought.
“Go where?” she asked, scared, stepping back without meaning to.
“How should I know? I only know it’s the same path, that’s all I know. The same goal!”
She looked at him, totally confused. She just knew he was terribly, deeply unhappy.
“None of them will understand, if you tell them, but I do. I need you, that’s why I came.”
“I don’t understand,” Sonia whispered.

“You’ll understand later. Haven’t you done the same? You’ve crossed the line too... had the strength to do it. You’ve destroyed a life—your own (it’s the same!). You could have lived with spirit and understanding, but you’ll end up in the Hay Market.... But you can’t take it, and if you stay alone, you’ll go crazy like me. You’re already like someone mad. So we have to go down this path together! Let’s go!”
“Why? What’s all this for?” Sonia asked, agitated by his words.

“Why? Because you can’t keep living like this, that’s why! You need to face things honestly at last, not just cry and say God won’t allow it. What if you really ended up in the hospital tomorrow? She’s crazy and dying, and the children? Do you really think Polenka won’t end up like this? Haven’t you seen kids begging on street corners, sent there by their mothers? I’ve gone and seen where those mothers live, what it’s like. Children can’t stay innocent there! At seven, a child is already stealing. And yet, children are the image of Christ: ‘theirs is the kingdom of Heaven.’ He told us to honor and love them—they’re the future of humanity....”
“What should I do, what should I do?” Sonia cried, sobbing, twisting her hands.

“What should you do? Break what needs to be broken, once and for all, that’s all, and take the suffering on yourself. Don’t you get it? You will, later.... Freedom and power, and above all, power! Over all trembling creatures, over all the ant-hill! That’s the goal, remember that! That’s my goodbye message. Maybe this is the last time I’ll speak to you. If I don’t come tomorrow, you’ll hear about it, and then remember these words. Maybe, years from now, you’ll finally understand what they meant. If I do come tomorrow, I’ll tell you who killed Lizaveta.... Goodbye.”
Sonia flinched in terror.
“Wait—do you know who killed her?” she asked, chilled, looking at him in horror.

“I know, and I’ll tell... you, only you. I picked you. I’m not coming to you for forgiveness, just to tell you. I chose you long ago to hear this, when your father talked about you, even when Lizaveta was alive, I thought about it. Goodbye, don’t shake my hand. Tomorrow!”
He left. Sonia stared after him as if he was insane. But she felt almost the same herself. Her head spun.

“My God, how does he know who killed Lizaveta? What did he mean by that? It’s awful!” But even now, the thought didn’t cross her mind for a second! “Oh, he must be so unhappy!... He left his mother and sister.... Why? What’s happened? And what did he mean? What did he say to her? He kissed her foot and said... yes, he clearly said he couldn’t live without her.... Oh, merciful heavens!”

Sonia spent the whole night feverish and delirious. She kept jumping up, crying and wringing her hands, then falling back into a restless sleep and dreaming of Polenka, Katerina Ivanovna, Lizaveta, reading the Gospel, and him... him with a pale face and burning eyes... kissing her feet, crying.

The next morning, right at eleven o’clock, Raskolnikov arrived at the criminal investigation department and sent word to Porfiry Petrovitch that he was there. He was surprised to be kept waiting for so long—at least ten minutes passed before anyone called for him. He had expected they’d jump on him as soon as he arrived. Instead, he waited in a room where people who clearly had nothing to do with him kept passing by. In the next office, a group of clerks were working, and it was obvious they didn’t know or care who Raskolnikov was. He glanced around nervously, half-expecting to find a guard watching him or someone ready to stop him if he tried to escape, but there was nothing. The clerks were busy with their paperwork, and the others who came and went ignored him. He realized that if that mysterious man from yesterday—the one who’d seemed to appear out of nowhere and saw everything—had actually reported him, they wouldn’t have left him standing around like this. Would they really have waited for him to show up at eleven? Either the man hadn’t said anything, or maybe he didn’t know anything at all (and how could he?), so everything that happened the day before was just a product of Raskolnikov’s anxious, exhausted mind. This idea had been growing stronger since yesterday, even with all his fear. Thinking about it now as he got ready for another confrontation, Raskolnikov noticed he was trembling—and got angry with himself for being so scared to face Porfiry Petrovitch. More than anything, he dreaded seeing Porfiry again; he hated him with a deep, burning hatred and worried that his hatred would give him away. His anger snapped him out of his trembling; he prepared to act cold and arrogant, determined to say as little as possible, to listen and watch, and, just this once, to control his nerves. At that moment, he was called in to see Porfiry Petrovitch.

Raskolnikov found Porfiry Petrovitch alone in his office. The room was neither big nor small, with a large desk in front of a checkered sofa, a bureau, a bookcase in one corner, and a few chairs—all standard government furniture in shiny yellow wood. There was a closed door in the far wall, probably leading to other rooms. As soon as Raskolnikov entered, Porfiry Petrovitch closed the door behind him, leaving them alone. Porfiry greeted him with a friendly, cheerful attitude, but after a few minutes, Raskolnikov noticed hints of awkwardness, as if Porfiry had been caught off guard or interrupted in something secret.

“Ah, my dear fellow! Here you are... in our headquarters,” Porfiry said, holding out both hands. “Come, have a seat, old man... or maybe you don’t like being called ‘my dear fellow’ or ‘old man’—just tell me! Don’t think I’m being too familiar... Here, sit on the sofa.”
Raskolnikov sat down, keeping his eyes fixed on Porfiry. “In our headquarters,” the overly friendly words, and the bit of French, were all typical of him.

“He held out both hands, but didn’t actually shake mine—he pulled them back just in time,” Raskolnikov noticed suspiciously. Both of them were watching each other, but every time their eyes met, they quickly looked away.
“I brought you this paper... about the watch. Here it is. Is it okay, or should I write it again?”

“What? The paper? Yes, yes, don’t worry, it’s fine,” Porfiry said quickly, and after saying that, he took the paper and glanced at it. “Yes, this will do. Nothing else is needed,” he said just as quickly, and set the paper on the table.
A minute later, while talking about something else, he picked up the paper from the table and put it on his bureau.

“I think you said yesterday you wanted to question me... officially... about how I knew the murdered woman?” Raskolnikov started again. “Why did I say ‘I think’?” flashed through his mind. “Why am I so nervous just because I said ‘I think’?” came to him an instant later. Suddenly, he felt his nervousness around Porfiry, with the first words and first looks, had exploded into something huge and dangerous. His nerves were shaking, his emotions rising. “This is bad, really bad! I’m going to say too much again.”

“Yes, yes, yes! There’s no rush, really no rush,” Porfiry muttered, pacing around the table with no clear purpose, sometimes heading toward the window, then the bureau, then the table, avoiding Raskolnikov’s suspicious stares at one moment, then stopping and looking him straight in the eye.
His short, round body looked odd, like a ball rolling from one side of the room to the other and bouncing back.

“We’ve got plenty of time. Do you smoke? Got your own? Here, have a cigarette!” Porfiry said, offering one. “You know, I’m meeting you here, but my own place is just through that door—the official apartment, you know. But I’m staying somewhere else for now, they’re fixing things up here. Almost finished now... Government apartments are a great thing, don’t you think?”
“Yeah, a great thing,” Raskolnikov replied, looking at him almost mockingly.

“A great thing, a great thing,” Porfiry repeated, as if he’d just thought of something completely different. “Yes, a great thing,” he almost shouted at last, suddenly staring hard at Raskolnikov and stopping two steps away.
This ridiculous repetition just didn’t fit with the serious, mysterious look Porfiry gave him.
But this irritated Raskolnikov even more, and he couldn’t help making a sarcastic, slightly reckless challenge.

“Tell me, please,” he said suddenly, looking almost rudely at Porfiry and actually enjoying his own boldness. “Isn’t it a sort of tradition for all investigators to start questioning from a distance, with something irrelevant or trivial, just to get the suspect talking and lower their guard before suddenly hitting them with a big, unexpected question? It’s a sacred tradition, right? I think I’ve read about it in all the investigation manuals.”
“Yes, yes... So, you think that’s why I started talking about government apartments, eh?”

As he said this, Porfiry squinted and winked; a friendly but crafty look crossed his face. The lines in his forehead smoothed, his eyes narrowed, his face grew wider, and suddenly he burst out in a long, nervous laugh, shaking all over and looking Raskolnikov right in the eye. Raskolnikov forced himself to laugh too, but when Porfiry, seeing Raskolnikov was laughing, started laughing even harder—turning almost red—Raskolnikov’s disgust overcame his caution; he stopped laughing, scowled, and stared at Porfiry with hatred, keeping his eyes locked on him while Porfiry’s laughter dragged on. But Porfiry didn’t seem bothered at all by Raskolnikov’s reaction. To Raskolnikov, this was important: Porfiry hadn’t been embarrassed a moment ago, either, but maybe Raskolnikov had fallen into a trap; there must be something going on here that he didn’t understand. Maybe everything was set up and about to come crashing down on him...
He decided to get straight to the point, stood up, and grabbed his cap.

“Porfiry Petrovitch,” he began firmly, though clearly irritated, “yesterday you said you wanted me to come in for some questions” (he emphasized the word “questions”). “I’m here now, so if you have questions, ask them. If not, let me leave. I don’t have time to waste... I have to go to the funeral of that man who was run over, the one you also know about,” he added, getting annoyed at himself for mentioning it, and even angrier about his own irritation. “I’m sick of this, you hear? I’ve been sick of it for a long time. It’s part of what made me ill. In short,” he almost shouted, realizing that talking about his illness made things worse, “in short, question me properly or let me go. And if you’re going to question me, do it by the book! Otherwise, I’m leaving, since there’s nothing keeping us here.”

“Goodness! What are you talking about? What should I ask you?” cackled Porfiry, his tone suddenly changing and his laughter stopping. “Don’t get upset,” he said, fussing around and trying to make Raskolnikov sit. “There’s no rush, really, it’s all nonsense. No, I’m actually glad you’ve come to see me at last... I think of you as just a visitor. And as for my silly laughter, please forgive me, Rodion Romanovitch. Rodion Romanovitch, right? That’s your name? It’s just my nerves, you made me laugh with your clever comment; sometimes I laugh for half an hour straight... I’m worried I’ll have a stroke one day. Please, sit down. If you don’t, I’ll think you’re angry...”
Raskolnikov didn’t say anything; he just listened, still glaring. He sat down, but kept holding his cap.

“I have to tell you something about myself, dear Rodion Romanovitch,” Porfiry went on, walking around the room and avoiding Raskolnikov’s eyes. “You see, I’m a bachelor, nobody special, not used to much company; besides, I don’t have much to look forward to, I’m getting old and... and have you noticed, Rodion Romanovitch, here in Petersburg, if two smart men meet but aren’t close, like us, it takes them half an hour to find something to talk about—they just sit there, feeling awkward. Everyone has their topics, like women or people in high society, they always have something to talk about, it’s required. But regular people like us, thinking people, are always tongue-tied. Why is that? Maybe we’re so honest we don’t want to fake anything, I don’t know. What do you think? And please put down your cap, it looks like you’re about to leave, it makes me uncomfortable... I’m so happy you’re here...”
Raskolnikov put his cap down and kept listening in silence, his face still serious and frowning, to Porfiry’s rambling. “Is he really just trying to distract me with this nonsense?”

“I can’t offer you coffee here; but why not spend five minutes with a friend?” Porfiry went on. “And you know, these official duties... please don’t mind me walking around, forgive me, my friend, but I really need to move. I’m always sitting, so I’m glad to stretch my legs for a bit... I suffer from sitting too much... I always plan to join a gym; they say even the highest-ranking officials go there, skipping and exercising—modern science, right? Yes, yes... But as for my duties, these questions and interviews... you mentioned questions just now... Honestly, these interviews are sometimes more awkward for the interviewer than for the person being questioned... You said so yourself, very cleverly.” (Raskolnikov hadn’t said anything of the sort.) “It gets confusing! A real mess! You just keep repeating yourself, like a drum! They say we’re going to be called something else soon, heh! And about our traditions, as you called it, I agree with you. Every suspect, even a peasant, knows we start with harmless questions before dropping a bombshell, heh, your great comparison! So you really thought I meant something by ‘government apartments’... heh! You’re a sarcastic one. But I won’t go on! Oh, yes, speaking of proper procedures—you mentioned it, about the questions. But what’s the point of being so formal? Sometimes just chatting is more effective. You can always get formal if you need to. And really, what does it matter? An investigator can’t stick to rules at every step. Investigating is an art, you know, heh!”
