Porfiry stopped for a breath. He’d just been babbling, hinting at secrets here and there, then going back to nonsense. He was almost running around the room, his short legs moving faster and faster, looking at the floor with one hand behind his back, while his other hand gestured wildly—totally out of sync with what he was saying. Raskolnikov suddenly noticed that twice as Porfiry moved around, he paused near the door, as if he was listening for something.
“Is he expecting someone?”

“You’re absolutely right about that,” Porfiry said cheerfully, giving Raskolnikov a look of such innocence that it startled him and made him suspicious. “It’s true, it’s ridiculous to follow legal procedures too closely—some of these psychological tricks are just silly and maybe useless if you stick to the rules. Yes... I’m talking about rules again. Well, if I think, or really suspect, that someone is guilty in a case I’m working on... you’re studying law, aren’t you, Rodion Romanovitch?”
“I was...”

“Well, then, consider this a lesson for your future—even though, with all your articles about crime, I shouldn’t be lecturing you! No, I’m just saying, if I thought someone was guilty, why should I rush and arrest him, even if I have some evidence? Sometimes, sure, I have to arrest someone right away, but sometimes it’s different, you know? Why not let him walk around town a bit? Heh! But I see you don’t really get what I mean, so I’ll give you an example. If I arrest him too soon, I might actually give him ‘moral support,’ you know? Are you laughing?”
Raskolnikov wasn’t laughing. He sat there with tight lips, his feverish eyes fixed on Porfiry.

“But it’s true, especially with some people, because everyone’s different. You say ‘evidence’—sure, there might be evidence. But evidence can always be read two ways. I’m an investigator, and I’ll admit I’m not perfect. I’d like to have real, solid proof—like two plus two is four, something you can’t argue with! And if I lock someone up too soon—even if I’m sure he’s guilty—I might actually lose the chance to get more evidence. Why? Because if I put him in a set position, he’ll relax and hide everything again. For example, in Sevastopol after the battle of Alma, people were scared the enemy would attack and win right away. But when they realized the enemy would lay siege instead, they were actually relieved—it would drag out for months. You’re laughing again? You don’t believe me? Well, you’re right, too. These are special cases, I admit. But you should notice this, Rodion Romanovitch: the ‘normal’ case, the one all the textbooks talk about, doesn’t really exist, because every crime turns into a special case. Weird things happen. If I leave a man alone, don’t touch him but let him know—or at least suspect—that I know everything and am watching him, if I keep him nervous and scared, he’ll lose his head. He’ll either come confess or do something that’ll give himself away. It might work with a simple peasant, but with an educated man like us, it’s a sure thing. Because it really matters what kind of education a man has. And then there are nerves—people are all nervous and irritable! And how they all suffer from stress! That’s like a gold mine for us. And I’m not worried about letting him walk around free! He can’t get away. Where could he go? Abroad? A Pole might escape, but not here, especially since I’m watching and have taken precautions. Hide out in the countryside? But the peasants would drive him nuts. An educated man would rather be in jail than live out there. But that’s all just surface stuff. Really, he can’t escape me; it’s like a law of nature. Ever seen a butterfly flying around a candle? That’s how he’ll keep circling around me. Freedom will stop mattering, he’ll start overthinking, tying himself in knots, worrying himself to death! And eventually, he’ll give me that solid proof I’m looking for—if I just give him enough time. He’ll get closer and closer and then—bam! He’ll fall right into my hands, and I’ll catch him, and that’ll be very satisfying, heh! Don’t believe me?”
Raskolnikov didn’t answer; he sat there pale and still, staring intensely at Porfiry.

“It’s a warning,” he thought coldly. “This is more than just the cat-and-mouse game from yesterday. He’s not just showing off. He’s too smart for that... he has another reason. What is it? He’s pretending, trying to scare me! He doesn’t have proof, and that man I saw yesterday doesn’t really exist. He just wants to shake me up, make me lose my cool, and crush me. But he’s wrong, he won’t succeed! But why warn me? Is he hoping my nerves will crack? No, you’re wrong, Porfiry, you won’t break me, even if you have a trap set for me... let’s see what you’ve got.”

He braced himself for a terrible, unknown test. Sometimes he wanted to attack Porfiry and choke him. This rage was what he’d feared from the start. He felt his dry lips frothing, his heart pounding. But he was still determined to stay silent until the right moment. He realized that was the best plan—by saying nothing, he’d irritate his enemy and maybe get Porfiry to reveal something by talking too much. At least, that’s what he hoped.

“No, I see you don’t believe me—you think I’m just joking around with you,” Porfiry said, getting more animated and laughing again as he paced the room. “And you’re probably right: God gave me a body that makes everyone think of a clown; I’m a buffoon! But let me tell you, excuse an old man, Rodion Romanovitch, you’re still young, so you put intelligence above all else, like most young people. You love clever jokes and abstract arguments, just like the old Austrian military planners who, on paper, beat Napoleon and took him prisoner—but then General Mack surrendered with his whole army, heh! I see, I see, Rodion Romanovitch, you’re laughing at a civilian like me, using military history! But I can’t help it, it’s my weakness—I love military history. I should’ve been in the army, really, I should have. Maybe not a Napoleon, but at least a major, heh! Anyway, I’ll tell you the truth about this kind of case: the facts and a man’s personality matter so much, they can throw off even the smartest plans! I—listen to an old man here—I’m being serious, Rodion Romanovitch.” (As he spoke, Porfiry, who was barely thirty-five, seemed to get older; his voice changed, and he seemed to shrink.) “Besides, I’m an honest man... am I not? What do you think? I think I am: I tell you these things for free and don’t expect anything in return, heh! Anyway, wit is a wonderful thing, like an accessory for nature and a comfort in life, but it can play tricks! Sometimes it’s hard for a poor investigator to know what’s going on, especially if he gets caught up in his own imagination, because he’s just a man! But the criminal’s personality trips him up! Young men, caught up in their own cleverness, don’t think of that when they ‘go beyond all limits,’ as you cleverly put it yesterday. He’ll lie—this ‘special case,’ the mysterious one, and he’ll lie really well, you’d think he’d get away with it, but in the most dramatic moment, he faints. Sure, maybe it’s illness or a stuffy room, but still! He gave us a clue! He lied brilliantly, but didn’t count on his own nerves. That’s what betrays him! Or he’ll try to mess with his interrogator, turning pale on purpose, but he’ll do it too naturally, just like the real thing, and again he gives himself away! At every step, he puts himself forward when no one asks, talks all the time when he should be silent, makes all sorts of strange hints, heh! Comes in and asks why he wasn’t arrested long ago! Heh! And this can happen even to the smartest, most educated man. The nerves give everything away! Just look and you’ll see! But why are you so pale, Rodion Romanovitch? Is the room stuffy? Should I open a window?”
“Oh, don’t bother, please,” Raskolnikov cried, suddenly breaking into a laugh. “Please, don’t bother.”
Porfiry stood in front of him, paused for a moment, and then laughed too. Raskolnikov jumped up from the sofa, suddenly stopping his laughter.

“Porfiry Petrovitch,” he said loudly and clearly, though his legs shook and he could barely stand, “I see now that you actually suspect me of killing that old woman and her sister Lizaveta. Let me tell you, I’m sick of this. If you think you have the right to arrest me, then do it. But I won’t let you mock me and torment me...”
His lips shook, his eyes burned with anger, and he couldn’t hold back his voice.
“I won’t allow it!” he yelled, slamming his fist on the table. “Do you hear, Porfiry Petrovitch? I won’t allow it.”
“Good heavens! What’s wrong?” cried Porfiry, sounding truly frightened. “Rodion Romanovitch, my dear fellow, what’s the matter?”
“I won’t allow it,” Raskolnikov shouted again.
“Shhh, my friend! They’ll hear and come in. What would we tell them?” Porfiry whispered in horror, leaning close to Raskolnikov.
“I won’t allow it, I won’t allow it,” Raskolnikov repeated, but now he also whispered.
Porfiry quickly ran to open the window.

“Some fresh air! You need some water, my friend. You’re sick!” He started for the door to call for someone, but then saw a bottle of water in the corner. “Here, drink a little,” he whispered, rushing over with the decanter. “It’ll help.”
Porfiry’s worry and sympathy seemed so real that Raskolnikov was silent and stared at him with wild curiosity. Still, he didn’t take the water.
“Rodion Romanovitch, my friend, you’ll make yourself crazy at this rate! Please, drink some water.”
Porfiry made him take the glass. Raskolnikov lifted it to his lips out of habit, but put it back on the table in disgust.

“You’re having another attack! You’ll bring your illness back again, my friend,” Porfiry said kindly, though he still looked a bit shaken. “You must take better care of yourself! Dmitri Prokofitch was here yesterday—came to see me after you did. I know, I know, I have a nasty, sarcastic temper, but what they made of it!... He came after you’d visited me. We had dinner and he just talked and talked, and I could only throw up my hands! Did he come from you? But please, sit down, please!”
“No, not from me, but I knew he went to you and why,” Raskolnikov answered sharply.
“You knew?”
“I knew. So what?”

“Well, Rodion Romanovitch, I know even more than that; I know everything. I know how you went to look at a flat at night when it was dark, and how you rang the bell and asked about the blood, so the workers and the porter didn’t know what to make of you. Yes, I understand your state of mind then... but you’ll drive yourself crazy like that, honestly! You’ll lose control! You’re full of righteous anger over all the things life and the police have done to you, so you rush into things, trying to force them to just say what they think already, because you’re sick of all this suspicion and nonsense. Isn’t that right? I’ve figured out how you feel, haven’t I? But if you keep doing this, you’ll lose your head and drag Razumihin down with you; he’s too good a guy for that, you know. You’re sick, and he’s a good person, and your illness is rubbing off on him... I’ll talk to you about that when you’re feeling better. But please, sit down, you look terrible, just sit down.”

Raskolnikov sat; he wasn’t shivering anymore—he was hot all over. He listened in amazement, focusing hard on Porfiry, who still seemed concerned and looked after him with friendly care. But he didn’t believe a word, even though part of him wanted to. Porfiry’s surprising mention of the flat had stunned him. “So he knows about the flat,” Raskolnikov thought, “and he tells me himself!”

“Yes, in our legal work, there was a case almost exactly like this, a case of messed-up psychology,” Porfiry went on quickly. “A man confessed to murder and kept it up! It was basically a hallucination; he gave facts, convinced everyone, and why? He was partly, but only partly, the reason a murder happened, and when he realized he’d given the murderers the chance, he got depressed, lost his mind, and started imagining things—he convinced himself he was the killer. But finally the High Court looked into it and the poor guy was found innocent and got medical care. Thank goodness for the High Court! Tut-tut-tut! My friend, you could drive yourself into madness if you keep playing with your nerves, ringing bells at night and asking about blood! I’ve studied all this in my work. Sometimes a person wants to jump out a window or off a tower. Same thing with ringing bells... It’s all illness, Rodion Romanovitch! You’ve started ignoring your sickness. You should see a real doctor—what’s the point of that fat guy? You’re not thinking straight! You were delirious when you did all that!”
For a moment, Raskolnikov felt the world spinning.

“Could it be, could it be,” he thought, “that he’s still lying? He can’t be, he just can’t.” He pushed the idea away, knowing how furious it would make him, and that rage might make him lose his mind.
“I wasn’t delirious. I knew exactly what I was doing,” he shouted, trying desperately to figure out Porfiry’s game. “I was completely in control, do you hear?”

“Yes, I hear, and I get it. You said yesterday you weren’t delirious, you were very clear about it! I understand everything you’re telling me! Listen, Rodion Romanovitch, my friend. If you were actually guilty, or mixed up in this horrible business, would you really insist you weren’t delirious, but totally aware? And so strongly? Would that even make sense? I don’t think so. If you were guilty, you’d probably claim delirium. Isn’t that right?”
There was a sly note in his question. Raskolnikov leaned back on the sofa as Porfiry leaned over him, staring in confusion.
“Another thing about Razumihin—you really should have said he came on his own, and hidden your part in it! But you don’t—you actually stress that you told him to come.”
Raskolnikov hadn’t done that. He felt a chill run down his spine.

“You keep lying,” he said slowly and weakly, twisting his lips into a sick smile. “You’re trying again to show you know all my moves, that you know everything I’ll say before I say it,” he went on, knowing he wasn’t choosing his words carefully. “You want to scare me... or you’re just laughing at me...”
He kept staring as he spoke, his eyes full of deep hatred again.
“You keep lying,” he said. “You know perfectly well that the best thing for the guilty to do is tell as much of the truth as possible... to hide as little as possible. I don’t believe you!”

“What a clever one you are!” Porfiry giggled, “you can’t be caught; you’re obsessed. So you don’t believe me? But you kind of do, at least a little; I’ll make you believe it all soon, because I really do like you and want good things for you.”
Raskolnikov’s lips trembled.

“Yes, I do,” Porfiry went on, patting Raskolnikov’s arm in a friendly way, “you need to take care of your health. Plus, your mother and sister are here now; you need to think of them. You should comfort them, but instead you just scare them...”
“What’s it to you? How do you know? Why do you care? You’re watching me and want me to know it?”

“Good heavens! Why, I got it all from you! You don’t realize it, but when you get worked up you tell me and everyone else everything. I heard a lot from Razumihin yesterday too. No, you interrupted me, but I have to say, for all your cleverness, your suspiciousness keeps you from seeing things clearly. Like the bell-ringing, for example. I, an investigator, gave away an important fact like that, a real clue (because it is one), and you don’t see anything in it! If I had the slightest suspicion about you, would I have done that? No, I would’ve hidden it, distracted you, and then suddenly hit you with it—‘And what were you doing at the murdered woman’s flat at nearly eleven, why did you ring the bell, why did you ask about blood? Why did you ask the porters to come with you to the police?’ That’s what I should have done if I suspected you. I should have taken your statement properly, searched your room, maybe even arrested you... so obviously I don’t suspect you, since I haven’t done any of that! But you can’t see it clearly, you see nothing, I say again.”
Raskolnikov jumped so much that Porfiry couldn’t miss it.
“You’re lying again,” he shouted, “I don’t know why, but you’re lying. You didn’t talk like this a minute ago, and I know I’m right!”

“I’m lying?” Porfiry repeated, pretending to be annoyed, but still smiling as if he didn’t care what Raskolnikov thought. “I’m lying... but how did I treat you just now, as the investigator? I gave you every excuse for your defense: illness, delirium, injury, depression, and the police and all that? Ha! Still, all these psychological excuses aren’t reliable; illness, delirium, ‘I don’t remember’—that’s all fine, but why, my good sir, in your illness and delirium, did you imagine just those things and not others? There could have been other things, right? Heh!”
Raskolnikov stared at him with pride and contempt.
“Enough,” he said loudly and firmly, standing and pushing Porfiry back a little, “I want to know, do you consider me totally cleared of suspicion or not? Tell me, Porfiry Petrovitch, answer me now!”

“What trouble you are!” Porfiry said, his face calm, sly, and friendly. “Why do you want to know? Why so curious, when no one is bothering you? You’re like a kid asking for matches! Why so nervous? Why force yourself on us, eh? Heh!”
“I’m telling you again,” Raskolnikov yelled, “I can’t take this anymore!”
“Take what? The uncertainty?” Porfiry interrupted.
“Don’t mock me! I won’t stand for it, do you hear? I can’t and I won’t!” he shouted, slamming his fist on the table again.
“Quiet! Quiet! They’ll hear! I’m warning you, be careful. I’m not joking,” Porfiry whispered, and this time his face was serious, stern, and for once, without any tricks.
But it lasted only a second. Raskolnikov, confused, almost went wild, but strangely, he obeyed Porfiry’s order to be quiet, even though he was boiling with anger.
“I won’t let you torture me,” he whispered, hating that he couldn’t help obeying and getting even angrier. “Arrest me, search me, but do it properly and don’t play games with me! Don’t you dare!”
“Don’t worry about how it’s done,” Porfiry said, still with his sly smile, enjoying Raskolnikov’s frustration. “I invited you here as a friend.”
“I don’t want your friendship, and I spit on it! Hear me? I’m taking my cap and leaving. What will you do now if you want to arrest me?”
He grabbed his cap and went to the door.
“And won’t you see my little surprise?” Porfiry said with a chuckle, grabbing Raskolnikov’s arm and stopping him at the door.
He seemed to get more playful and cheerful, which only made Raskolnikov angrier.
“What surprise?” Raskolnikov asked, stopping and looking at Porfiry in alarm.
“My little surprise, it’s right behind that door, heh!” (He pointed to the locked door.) “I locked him in so he couldn’t get away.”
“What is it? Where? What?...”
Raskolnikov went to the door and tried to open it, but it was locked.
“It’s locked. Here’s the key!”
And he pulled a key from his pocket.
“You’re lying!” Raskolnikov shouted, losing all control. “You’re lying, you clown!” and he lunged at Porfiry, who backed away toward the other door, not afraid at all.
“I get it! You’re lying and teasing me so I’ll give myself away...”
“You couldn’t give yourself away any more, my dear Rodion Romanovitch. You’re worked up. Don’t shout, or I’ll call the clerks.”

“You’re lying! Go ahead, call them! You knew I was sick and tried to make me lose it so I’d give myself away, that’s your game! Show your evidence! I get it now. You’ve got nothing, just weak suspicions like Zametov’s! You know my character, you wanted to push me into a rage and then trap me with priests and witnesses... Are you waiting for them? Huh? Who are you waiting for? Where are they? Bring them out!”

“Why witnesses, my friend? What ideas people get! And that’s not how it’s done, as you say—you don’t know the business, my good fellow... and you can’t avoid procedures, as you see,” Porfiry muttered, listening at the door where a noise was heard.
“Ah, they’re coming,” Raskolnikov shouted. “You sent for them! You expected them! Fine, bring them all: your witnesses, whoever you want!... I’m ready!”
But just then, something completely unexpected happened—so strange that neither Raskolnikov nor Porfiry Petrovitch could have guessed the interview would end like this.
When Raskolnikov thought back on what happened later, this is how he remembered the scene.
The noise outside the door grew louder, and suddenly the door cracked open a little.
“What’s going on?” Porfiry Petrovitch shouted, sounding annoyed. “I gave instructions...”
No one answered at first, but it was clear that several people were at the door, and it seemed like they were trying to stop someone from coming in.
“What is it?” Porfiry Petrovitch repeated, sounding uneasy.
“The prisoner Nikolay has been brought,” someone finally replied.
“We don’t need him now! Take him out! Make him wait! Why is he here? This is completely out of order!” Porfiry yelled, rushing to the door.
“But he...” the same voice began, but then stopped.
In just a couple of seconds, there was a quick struggle, then someone got shoved hard, and a very pale young man marched into the room.

At first glance, the man looked strange. He stared straight ahead, almost like he couldn’t see anything. There was a determined look in his eyes, but his face was as pale as death, like someone being dragged off to be executed. His lips were white and trembling.

He looked like a worker, about average height, very young and thin, with short-cropped hair and sharp features. The guard he’d pushed back followed him in, grabbing him by the shoulder, but Nikolay pulled free.
Several people tried to look in from the doorway. Some even tried to come inside. All of this happened in just a moment.
“Go away, it’s not time yet! Wait until you’re called!... Why did you bring him now?” Porfiry muttered, really annoyed and thrown off by the interruption.
But suddenly, Nikolay dropped to his knees.
“What’s wrong?” Porfiry asked, surprised.
“I’m guilty! It’s my sin! I am the murderer,” Nikolay said suddenly, a little out of breath but speaking loudly enough for everyone to hear.
For about ten seconds, no one spoke. It was like everyone was frozen. Even the guard stepped back toward the door and just stood there.
“What’s going on?” Porfiry said, snapping out of his shock.
“I... am the murderer,” Nikolay repeated after a short pause.
“What... you... what are you talking about... who did you kill?” Porfiry was clearly confused.
Nikolay was silent again for a moment.
“Alyona Ivanovna and her sister Lizaveta Ivanovna, I... killed them... with an axe. I went dark inside,” he added suddenly, then went quiet again.

He was still on his knees. Porfiry stood there for a few moments, thinking, but then suddenly came to his senses and waved the crowd away from the doorway. They quickly disappeared and shut the door. Porfiry looked at Raskolnikov, who was standing in the corner, staring wide-eyed at Nikolay. Porfiry started toward Raskolnikov, but then stopped, looked from Nikolay to Raskolnikov and back again, and finally rushed at Nikolay, unable to hold himself back.
“You’re too quick to confess,” he yelled at Nikolay, almost angrily. “I didn’t ask you what happened yet... just tell me, did you really kill them?”
“I am the murderer.... I want to give my statement,” Nikolay said.
“Ugh! What did you kill them with?”
“An axe. I had it ready.”
“He’s in a hurry! Did you do it all by yourself?”
Nikolay didn’t seem to understand the question.
“Did you do it alone?”
“Yes, alone. Mitka isn’t guilty and had nothing to do with it.”
“Don’t be so quick to clear Mitka! Ugh! But how did you run down the stairs like that? The porters saw both of you!”
“I did it to throw them off... I ran after Mitka,” Nikolay answered quickly, like he already had the answer ready.
“I knew it!” Porfiry said, annoyed. “He’s not telling his own story,” he muttered, almost to himself, and then his eyes fell on Raskolnikov again.
Porfiry had been so focused on Nikolay that he’d almost forgotten about Raskolnikov. He looked surprised for a second.
“My dear Rodion Romanovitch, I’m sorry!” he hurried over. “You can’t stay, I’m afraid... it’s better if you leave now... you see, what a shock this is!... Goodbye!”
Taking Raskolnikov by the arm, he led him to the door.
“I guess you didn’t see that coming?” Raskolnikov said. Even though he was still processing what had happened, he felt his courage returning.
“You didn’t expect it either, my friend. Look, your hand is shaking! Ha-ha!”
“You’re shaking too, Porfiry Petrovitch!”
“Yes, I am; I didn’t expect this.”
They were already at the door; Porfiry was clearly eager for Raskolnikov to leave.
“And what about your little surprise? Aren’t you going to show me?” Raskolnikov said sarcastically.
“You’re still chattering as you ask! You’re a real joker! All right, see you soon!”
“I guess this is goodbye!”
“That’s up to God,” Porfiry replied with a strange smile.

As Raskolnikov walked through the office, he noticed lots of people staring at him. He even saw the two porters from the house, the ones he’d sent to the police station that night. They were waiting around. But as soon as he started down the stairs, he heard Porfiry Petrovitch calling after him. Turning, he saw Porfiry hurrying to catch up, out of breath.
“One word, Rodion Romanovitch; as for everything else, it’s in God’s hands, but officially I still have a few questions to ask you... so we’ll be seeing each other again, right?”
Porfiry stopped and faced him with a smile.
“Right? We’ll see each other again?”
He looked like he wanted to say more, but couldn’t get the words out.
“You’ll have to forgive me, Porfiry Petrovitch, for what just happened... I lost my temper,” said Raskolnikov, who felt confident enough now to act calm.
“Don’t worry about it, don’t worry,” Porfiry replied, almost cheerfully. “I have a bad temper too, I admit it! But we’ll meet again. If God wants it, maybe we’ll see a lot of each other.”
“And really get to know each other inside and out?” Raskolnikov added.
“Yes, inside and out,” agreed Porfiry, squinting at Raskolnikov as if studying him. “Now, you’re heading to a birthday party?”
“No, a funeral.”
“Oh right, the funeral! Take care of yourself, and get well soon.”
“I’m not sure what to wish for you,” Raskolnikov said, starting down the stairs, but pausing to look back. “I guess I should wish you luck, but your job is so strange.”
“Strange? Why?” Porfiry had started to leave, but perked up at this.

“Well, just think of how you must have messed with poor Nikolay’s mind, pushing him until he confessed! You must have been after him day and night, convincing him he was the killer, and now that he’s confessed, you’ll start picking him apart again. ‘You’re lying,’ you’ll say. ‘You’re not the real killer! This isn’t your own story!’ You have to admit, it’s a strange job!”
“Ha-ha! So you noticed that I just told Nikolay it wasn’t his own story?”
“How could I not notice?”
“Ha! You’re smart. You notice everything! You really have a playful mind! And you always find the funny side... ha-ha! They say that was Gogol’s main trait as a writer.”
“Yes, just like Gogol.”
“Yes, like Gogol... I’ll be looking forward to seeing you again.”
“Me too.”

Raskolnikov went straight home. He was so shaken and confused that when he got there, he sat on the sofa for fifteen minutes, trying to think clearly. He couldn’t even think about Nikolay—he was just stunned. Nikolay’s confession felt impossible, something he couldn’t make sense of. But it was real. He realized right away that it wouldn’t take long for people to see the confession was false, and then they’d be after him again. Until then, at least, he was safe for a little while, and he needed to do something for himself, because the danger was still there.

But how much danger was he really in? The more he thought about what had just happened with Porfiry, the more he shuddered with fear. He didn’t know all of Porfiry’s plans, couldn’t guess at all his ideas. But Porfiry had already shown his hand a bit, and Raskolnikov knew better than anyone how dangerous Porfiry’s “lead” had been. Just a little more, and he might have completely given himself away. Knowing how nervous he was, and how Porfiry could read him so easily, Raskolnikov realized that Porfiry was taking a risk but was likely to win. Raskolnikov had already put himself in a dangerous position, but so far, there were no facts—nothing solid. Still, was he seeing things clearly? Was Porfiry really holding something back? Had he really been expecting something? How would things have ended if Nikolay hadn’t shown up out of nowhere?

Porfiry had shown almost all his cards—he’d taken a risk doing so—and if he’d really had something else, Raskolnikov thought, he probably would have revealed it too. What was that “surprise” he mentioned? Was it just a joke? Or did it mean something more, like real evidence? Was he talking about the man who visited yesterday? Where was he today? If Porfiry had any proof, it had to be about that visitor....
Raskolnikov sat on the sofa with his elbows on his knees, his face in his hands. He was still shivering with nerves. Finally he got up, grabbed his cap, thought for a second, and went to the door.

He had a strong feeling that, at least for today, he was out of danger. He suddenly felt almost happy; he wanted to hurry to Katerina Ivanovna’s. He’d be too late for the funeral, but he’d make it for the dinner afterwards, and he’d see Sonia there.
He stopped for a moment and a sad smile crossed his face.
“Today! Today,” he whispered to himself. “Yes, today! That’s how it has to be....”
But just as he was about to open the door, it started to open by itself. He jumped back. The door swung open slowly, and suddenly a figure appeared—it was yesterday’s visitor from the basement.

The man stood in the doorway, looking at Raskolnikov without saying a word, then took a step into the room. He looked just the same as the day before: same build, same clothes, but his face seemed different—sad and tired. If he’d just put his hand to his cheek and tilted his head, he’d look exactly like a peasant woman.
“What do you want?” Raskolnikov asked, frozen with fear. The man was still silent, but then suddenly bowed down almost to the floor, touching it with his finger.
“What is it?” Raskolnikov shouted.
“I have sinned,” the man said quietly.
“How?”
“With evil thoughts.”
They stared at each other.

“I was angry. When you came, maybe drunk, and told the porters to go to the police and asked about the blood, I got mad that they let you go and just thought you were drunk. I was so upset I couldn’t sleep. Remembering the address, we came by yesterday and asked for you....”
“Who came?” Raskolnikov interrupted, trying to remember.
“I did. I was the one who wronged you.”
“So you’re from that house?”
“I was standing at the gate with the others... don’t you remember? We’ve worked in that building for years, curing and preparing hides, taking work home... but I was really angry....”

Suddenly, Raskolnikov remembered the whole scene from the day before yesterday in the gateway: there had been other people besides the porters, even some women. He remembered that one voice had suggested taking him straight to the police station. He couldn’t remember the speaker’s face, and still didn’t recognize it now, but he remembered turning around and replying....

So that explained yesterday’s scare. The worst part was realizing he had almost ruined himself over something so small. This man couldn’t say anything except that Raskolnikov had asked about the apartment and the blood stains. So Porfiry had nothing but this bit of madness—only psychology, which could be used in different ways, but no real facts. So if nothing else came up (and it mustn’t, it mustn’t!) then... what could they do to him? Even if they arrested him, how could they convict him? And Porfiry had only just learned about the apartment and hadn’t known before.
“Was it you who told Porfiry... that I’d been there?” he suddenly asked.
“Who’s Porfiry?”
“The detective in charge?”
“Yes. The porters didn’t go, but I did.”
“Today?”
“I got there two minutes before you. And I heard everything, how he questioned you.”
“Where? What? When?”
“In the next room. I was sitting there the whole time.”
“What? Then you were the surprise? How did that happen? I can’t believe it!”

“I saw the porters didn’t want to do what I said,” the man began. “‘It’s too late,’ they said, ‘and he might be angry that we didn’t come sooner.’ I was upset and couldn’t sleep, so I started asking around. Yesterday I found out where to go, so I came today. The first time, he wasn’t there. An hour later, he couldn’t see me. I came a third time, and they let me in. I told him everything, just as it happened, and he started jumping around the room and hitting himself on the chest. ‘Why didn’t you come sooner? If I’d known, I would have arrested him!’ Then he ran out, called someone, and talked to him in the corner. Then he turned to me, scolded and questioned me. He scolded me a lot, but I told him everything, even that you didn’t answer me yesterday and didn’t recognize me. Then he started running around again, hitting his chest and getting angry, and when you were announced, he told me to go to the next room. ‘Sit there for a bit,’ he said. ‘Don’t move, no matter what you hear.’ He put a chair there for me and locked me in. ‘Maybe,’ he said, ‘I’ll call you.’ After Nikolay got brought in, he let me out as soon as you left. ‘I’ll call you again and question you,’ he said.”
“And did he question Nikolay while you were there?”
“He got rid of me just like he did with you, before talking to Nikolay.”
The man stood still, then bowed down again, touching the floor with his finger.
“Forgive me for my evil thoughts and for accusing you.”
“May God forgive you,” Raskolnikov replied.
When he said this, the man bowed again—not all the way to the floor—then slowly turned and left the room.
“It can go either way now, it can go either way,” Raskolnikov said to himself, and left, feeling more confident than before.
“Now it’s time to fight,” he said with a bitter smile as he went down the stairs. His anger was aimed at himself; feeling ashamed and disgusted, he remembered his own “cowardice.”

The morning after his disastrous meeting with Dounia and her mother hit Pyotr Petrovitch (Luzhin) hard. As much as he tried to deny it, he had to admit that what seemed impossible yesterday—being dumped—had really happened. He’d spent the night with his pride in knots, feeling angry and hurt. When he got up, Luzhin stared at himself in the mirror, half-worried he’d turned yellow from stress, but he looked fine—his face was still handsome and, if anything, a bit chubbier than before. For a second, he even comforted himself, thinking he could always find another fiancée—maybe an even better one. But the reality sank in, and he spat on the floor, which made his roommate, Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov, smirk sarcastically. Luzhin noticed and mentally added that to a growing list of things he held against Lebeziatnikov. He was even more annoyed that he’d told his roommate about yesterday’s disaster—yet another impulsive mistake. The day kept getting worse: his legal business at the senate ran into trouble, and the landlord of the apartment he’d rented for his wedding refused to cancel the contract, demanding the full penalty, even though the place was now nicely redecorated. The furniture sellers wouldn’t return a single rouble either, even though nothing had been delivered yet.

“Am I supposed to get married just to keep the furniture?” Luzhin muttered, grinding his teeth. Still, some desperate hope flickered in him. “Is it really impossible to fix things? Should I try again?” The thought of Dounia made his heart ache with longing. His pain was so sharp that, if he could have killed Raskolnikov with a wish, he’d have done it instantly.

“It was stupid of me not to give them money,” Luzhin thought grumpily as he walked back to Lebeziatnikov’s room. “Why was I so stingy? I wanted to keep them poor so they’d need me, but look where that got me! If I’d just spent a bit—maybe a thousand or fifteen hundred roubles on gifts and clothes for Dounia, they’d feel guilty breaking things off. They’d find it much harder to return presents and money, and their conscience would bother them. They’d have to wonder, ‘How can we dump a man who’s been so generous?’ Ugh! I really messed up.”
Gritting his teeth again, Luzhin silently called himself an idiot—but only in his head.

He came home feeling twice as angry as before. As he passed by Katerina Ivanovna’s place, he noticed people preparing for a funeral dinner, which made him curious. He’d heard about it yesterday and thought he’d been invited, but he hadn’t paid attention at the time. He asked Madame Lippevechsel, who was setting the table while Katerina Ivanovna was at the cemetery, and learned the dinner would be a big event. All the lodgers were invited, even some who hadn’t known the dead man. Even Lebeziatnikov was invited, despite a recent fight with Katerina Ivanovna. Luzhin himself was not only invited, but apparently everyone was looking forward to him coming, since he was the most important guest. Amalia Ivanovna, the landlady, was invited too; she was dressed up in new black silk and really enjoying herself. All this gave Luzhin an idea, and he went into the room—really Lebeziatnikov’s room—deep in thought. He’d found out that Raskolnikov would also be at the dinner.

Lebeziatnikov had been home all morning. Luzhin’s attitude toward him was complicated, but maybe understandable. He’d always looked down on Lebeziatnikov, even hated him, but was also a little afraid of him. Luzhin hadn’t chosen to stay with him just to save money, though that was a big part of it. He’d heard that Lebeziatnikov, who used to be his ward, was now a leading young progressive, involved in mysterious circles that everyone talked about. This made Luzhin nervous. He’d heard stories about these “progressives” and “nihilists,” and, like many people, blew their reputations way out of proportion. What Luzhin feared most was being exposed or embarrassed by such people, which made him uneasy about moving his business to Petersburg. He remembered two cases from his past where important men had been publicly shamed, one ending in scandal, the other nearly in disaster. That’s why he’d planned to figure things out once he got to Petersburg, maybe even get on the good side of this “younger generation.” He hoped Lebeziatnikov could help with that, and before visiting Raskolnikov, had tried to learn a few trendy phrases. Soon, though, Luzhin realized Lebeziatnikov was basically a naïve fool, but that didn’t calm his nerves. Even if all the progressives were fools, that didn’t mean they couldn’t cause trouble. Luzhin wasn’t interested in their ideas or beliefs—he just wanted to know if he should be worried, and if so, how to protect himself. Could he use them to his advantage somehow? A hundred questions ran through his mind.

Lebeziatnikov was a pale, sickly-looking little man with light blond sideburns he was oddly proud of. He worked as a clerk and always seemed to have some eye problem. He was soft-hearted but overconfident and sometimes full of himself, which looked silly given how small and unimpressive he was. Amalia Ivanovna liked him because he never got drunk and always paid his rent on time. In reality, Lebeziatnikov wasn’t very bright. He clung to “progressive” ideas out of excitement and wanted to be part of the latest trend, but only ended up making those ideas look ridiculous.

Even though Lebeziatnikov was generally good-natured, he was starting to dislike Luzhin, too. It happened without either of them realizing it. Even someone as simple as Lebeziatnikov could tell Luzhin was using him and secretly looking down on him. He’d tried explaining the theories of Fourier and Darwin to Luzhin, but lately Luzhin just listened sarcastically or even rudely. Luzhin had started to suspect that Lebeziatnikov wasn’t just naïve, but maybe a fake, too, with no real connections—just someone who repeated what he’d heard from others, and who probably didn’t really understand what he was talking about. Not much of a threat! Still, Luzhin enjoyed the compliments he got from Lebeziatnikov. He didn’t mind being praised for supporting the “commune,” or for supposedly agreeing not to baptize his future kids, or for being okay if Dounia took a lover a month after marriage. Luzhin liked hearing good things about himself, even if they were ridiculous.

That morning, Luzhin had just cashed in some five-percent bonds and was sitting at the table counting stacks of banknotes. Lebeziatnikov, who almost never had any money himself, walked around the room pretending not to care about the cash on display. Luzhin would never have believed that Lebeziatnikov didn’t envy him, and Lebeziatnikov, on his side, resented the way Luzhin seemed to flaunt his wealth, as if to remind him of their differences.

Lebeziatnikov found Luzhin distracted and cranky, even though he tried to talk about his favorite topic: the idea of starting a new kind of “commune.” Luzhin’s short, sarcastic replies as he counted his money made it clear he wasn’t interested. But Lebeziatnikov thought Luzhin’s bad mood was because of his breakup with Dounia, and was eager to share his own “progressive” thoughts on the subject, hoping it might help his friend “grow.”
“There’s some kind of party being organized at the widow’s place, right?” Luzhin suddenly asked, cutting off Lebeziatnikov in the middle of his speech.
“Don’t you know? I was just telling you last night what I think of those kinds of ceremonies. And she invited you, too! You talked to her yesterday...”

“I can’t believe that foolish woman spent all the money she got from that other fool, Raskolnikov, on this dinner,” Luzhin went on. “I just saw them setting up—wine, food, lots of guests. It’s ridiculous! Wait, you said I was invited? When was that? I don’t remember. But I’m not going. Why should I? I only mentioned the possibility of her getting a pension as a poor widow of a government worker. I guess that’s why she invited me—hoping I’d help. Ha!”
“I’m not going either,” said Lebeziatnikov.
“I’d think not, after you hit her! No wonder you’re hesitating, ha ha!”
“Who hit who?” Lebeziatnikov blurted, flustered and turning red.
“Why, you hit Katerina Ivanovna a month ago. I heard about it yesterday... so much for your convictions and your views on women’s rights, ha!” Luzhin went back to counting his money, clearly amused.

“That’s a lie!” Lebeziatnikov shouted, always nervous when this topic came up. “It wasn’t like that at all! You heard it wrong. It’s a rumor. I was just defending myself—she attacked me first and tried to rip out my sideburns. It’s only fair to defend yourself. I never let anyone use violence against me, it’s the principle. All I did was push her away.”
Luzhin kept laughing in a mean way.

“You keep saying things like that because you’re in a bad mood... But it’s nonsense and has nothing to do with the women’s question! You don’t get it. I used to think that if women are really equal to men, even in strength, then there should be equality in fighting, too. But I later realized that’s silly, since in the future there won’t be fighting at all. Still, there is fighting now... Ugh, you always confuse things! That’s not why I’m not going. I’m not going on principle—I refuse to be part of these old-fashioned memorial dinners. That’s all! Though honestly, I might go just to laugh at it. Too bad there won’t be any priests there—then I’d definitely go.”
“So you’d show up at someone else’s dinner and insult everyone there, huh?”

“Not insult—just protest. For a good cause! It’s everyone’s duty to work toward progress, even if it means being harsh. Maybe I’d plant a new idea, and something good would come from it. How is that insulting? At first, people might be offended, but later, they’d see I did them a favor. You know, Terebyeva (she’s in the commune now) was criticized because when she left her family to live in a free marriage, she wrote a blunt letter to her parents. People said she should’ve been kinder, but I think that’s nonsense. Sometimes you have to protest directly. Take Varents—she left her husband and kids after seven years and wrote him, ‘I can never be happy with you. I only just learned from a great man about a better way of living. I’m leaving to start a new community. Don’t expect me back.’ That’s how such letters should be written!”
“Is this the same Terebyeva you said had a third free marriage?”

“No, only her second! But even if it were the fourth, or the fifteenth, who cares? If I regret anything about my parents dying, it’s that I never got to shock them. I wish they were alive so I could really surprise them with my protest! I’d love to have amazed them. I almost wish I had the chance.”
“To surprise them, huh?” Luzhin cut in. “Anyway, tell me—do you know the dead man’s daughter, the skinny little one? Is what they say about her true?”

“What’s wrong with that? Personally, I think it’s normal for women. Right now, in our society, it’s not really normal, because it’s forced, but in the future it’ll be normal because it’ll be by choice. Even now, she was right to do what she did—her suffering was her only resource, and she had a right to use it. In the future, things will be different, but for now, her actions are a protest against society, and I respect her for it. Honestly, I admire Sonya (Sofya Semyonovna) for what she did.”
“I heard you were the one who got her kicked out of the lodgings.”
Lebeziatnikov got furious.

“That’s another lie!” he yelled. “It’s not true at all. Katerina Ivanovna made that up—she didn’t understand! And I never tried to seduce Sofya Semyonovna. I was just trying to inspire her, to get her to protest! That’s all I wanted. And anyway, she couldn’t have stayed here.”
“Did you ask her to join your commune?”

“You keep laughing, but you’re missing the point. There aren’t ‘roles’ like that in a commune. In a real community, things are totally different. What seems weird here is normal there—it’s all about the environment. I’m still on good terms with Sonya, which proves I never wronged her. I’m trying to get her interested in our community, but in a totally different way. What’s so funny about that? We’re trying to start something new, something bigger than before. We’ve moved beyond the old ideas! And I’m still trying to help Sofya Semyonovna. She’s an amazing person!”
“And you take advantage of her kindness, huh? Ha ha!”
“No, no! It’s the opposite!”
“The opposite? That’s a weird thing to say, haha!”
“I mean it! Why would I lie? Honestly, I’m surprised myself by how shy and proper she is with me, even though she’s so modern!”
“And you’re ‘developing’ her, huh? Trying to convince her that modesty is nonsense?”

“Not at all! That’s not what ‘development’ means. You’re being crude! We want women to be free, and you only think about one thing. Aside from the big questions about modesty, I respect her choices. If she ever told me she wanted me, I’d be happy, because I like her—but as it is, no one has ever treated her with more respect than I have. I’m just waiting and hoping, that’s all.”
“Maybe you should give her a present. I bet that never crossed your mind.”

“You don’t get it! Of course, she’s in a tough spot, but that’s a separate issue. You just look down on her for something that doesn’t deserve contempt. You don’t know her! I’m only sad that she’s stopped reading books lately—I used to lend her some. And even though she’s brave, she still lacks confidence to break free from some old ideas. But she understands some things well—like that it’s insulting for a man to kiss a woman’s hand, because it shows inequality. We debated that, and she listened carefully. She was also interested when I told her about workers’ groups in France. Now I’m explaining to her the question of whether people in the future society can go into anyone’s room.”
“What’s that supposed to mean?”
“We had a debate: should a member of the community be allowed to go into another member’s room at any time—man or woman? We decided yes!”
“Could be awkward if they walked in at the wrong time, huh? Ha!”
Lebeziatnikov was really annoyed now.

“You always think of something unpleasant,” he said, disgusted. “Ugh! I’m annoyed that I even mentioned the privacy question to you. People like you just make fun of it before you understand it, and you’re so proud of that! I’ve always said that beginners shouldn’t discuss this topic until they really believe in the system. And what’s so shameful about cleaning out sewers, anyway? I’d do it myself. It’s not about self-sacrifice—it’s just honest work, and more useful than being an artist or a poet, because it actually helps people.”
“And more honorable, huh? More honorable than anything, ha ha!”

“What do you mean ‘more honorable’? I don’t use words like that. ‘Honorable,’ ‘noble’—those are old-fashioned ideas I reject. If something’s useful to people, it’s honorable. That’s all I care about. Laugh all you want, but it’s true!”

Luzhin laughed hard. He finished counting his money and put most of it away, but left some bills on the table. The “sewer question” had already been an argument between them. It made Lebeziatnikov genuinely angry, but Luzhin found it funny and liked pushing his buttons.

“You’re just grumpy because of what happened yesterday,” Lebeziatnikov blurted out. Even though he liked to talk about “independence,” he still acted a bit deferential toward Luzhin, out of old habit.

“Forget that,” Luzhin said sharply. “Tell me—are you close enough with that young woman to ask her to come in here for a minute? I think everyone’s back from the cemetery now... I heard people coming in. I want to see her—that young woman.”
“Why?” asked Lebeziatnikov, surprised.
“I just do. I’m leaving today or tomorrow and wanted to talk to her about... something. You can stay for the conversation. In fact, it’s better that you do—who knows what people might say otherwise.”
“I won’t get in your way. If you need to say something to her, I’ll go get her right now.”

Five minutes later, Lebeziatnikov came back with Sonya. She looked surprised and incredibly shy, as usual. She had always been timid around new people, even as a kid, and now more than ever. Luzhin greeted her “politely and warmly,” though with a hint of condescending friendliness he thought suited a respectable man dealing with someone as young and interesting as Sonya. He quickly reassured her and invited her to sit at the table. Sonya sat down, glancing at Lebeziatnikov, then at the money on the table, then back at Luzhin—she couldn’t take her eyes off him. Lebeziatnikov started to leave, but Luzhin gestured for Sonya to stay and stopped Lebeziatnikov from going.
“Is Raskolnikov in there? Has he come back?” Luzhin whispered to him.
“Raskolnikov? Yes. Why? He just came in... what’s up?”

“Well, I really want you to stay here with us—don’t leave me alone with this young lady. I only need a few words with her, but who knows what people might say? I don’t want Raskolnikov getting any ideas... You understand?”

“I get it,” Lebeziatnikov said. “Yes, you’re right. Personally, I’m sure you don’t need to worry, but you’re right, just in case. I’ll stand by the window and stay out of the way... I think you’re right.”
Luzhin went back to the sofa, sat facing Sonya, and put on an extra-dignified, almost stern look, as if to say, “Don’t get any ideas, miss.” Sonya felt extremely awkward and embarrassed.

“First of all, Sofya Semyonovna, will you give my apologies to your respected mother... that’s right, isn’t it? Katerina Ivanovna is like your mother?” Luzhin began, trying to sound grand but friendly.
He clearly wanted to come across as helpful.
“Yes, she’s like a mother to me,” Sonya answered quickly and nervously.
“Then please apologize to her for me. Because of circumstances, I won’t be able to attend the dinner, even though your mother kindly invited me.”
“I’ll tell her right away,” Sonya said.
She started to get up from her seat.

“Wait, there’s more,” Luzhin stopped her, smiling at her innocence. “You don’t know me very well, Sofya Semyonovna, if you think I’d call you here just to talk about something that only affects me. I have another reason.”

Sonya sat back down quickly. Her eyes flickered for a second to the colorful money on the table, but she quickly looked away and stared at Luzhin’s gold monocle and the large, flashy ring on his finger. Then she quickly looked away again, not knowing where else to look, and finally just stared at Luzhin’s face. After a pause, Luzhin continued, acting even more important.
“Yesterday, I happened to exchange a few words with Katerina Ivanovna. That was enough for me to understand that she’s in a... well, a very difficult situation.”
“Yes... very difficult...” Sonya agreed quickly.
“Or, to put it simply, she’s sick.”
“Yes, that’s a simpler way to put it. She’s sick.”
“Right. So, out of humanity and compassion, I’d like to help her however I can, since I can see how bad things are. I believe the whole family is depending on you now, right?”
“Can I ask—did you tell her yesterday that she could get a pension? Because she told me you promised to help with that. Is it true?”

“Not at all. That’s just wishful thinking! I only mentioned she might be able to get some temporary help, as the widow of a government worker—if she had the right connections. But your father didn’t serve his full term, and he wasn’t even working lately. So there’s really no hope for a pension. And yet she’s dreaming about it already! She’s really something, isn’t she?”
“Yes, she is. She’s very trusting and kind, and she believes everything people tell her... You have to excuse her,” Sonya said, getting up to leave.
“But you haven’t heard what I want to say yet.”
“No, I haven’t,” Sonya mumbled.
“Then sit down.” Sonya, completely flustered, sat down for the third time.

“Seeing her struggle with her kids, I’d like to help as much as I can—not more than I can, but as much as possible. Maybe we could organize a collection for her, or a lottery, like people do in these cases. That’s what I wanted to discuss with you—it could be done.”
“Yes, yes... God will reward you,” Sonya stammered, staring at Luzhin.

“Maybe, but we’ll talk more about it later. We could start today, lay the groundwork. Come see me at seven o’clock. Mr. Lebeziatnikov will help, I hope. But there’s something I want to warn you about, and that’s why I asked you here. In my opinion, it’s not safe to give Katerina Ivanovna any money directly. Just look at today’s dinner—she spent all her money on the feast, even though she doesn’t have bread for tomorrow, or shoes, or anything. I saw coffee, rum, even Madeira wine. Tomorrow she’ll be broke again, and you’ll be left to pick up the pieces. It’s just not sensible. So, I think the money should be kept secret from her—maybe you could handle it. Do you agree?”

“I don’t know... Today is just a special day. She wanted to honor his memory... She’s usually sensible... But whatever you think is best, we’ll be grateful... God will reward you... and the orphans...” Sonya trailed off.
Sonya burst into tears.

“Alright, just keep that in mind. Now, will you take this small amount from me for your family’s benefit? I’d rather my name not be mentioned. Here... I can’t give more, since I have my own needs...” Luzhin said, handing her a ten-rouble note.

Sonya took it, blushed bright red, jumped up, murmured something, and hurried to leave. Luzhin politely walked her to the door. She finally escaped, flustered and upset, and hurried back to Katerina Ivanovna, overwhelmed.
Meanwhile, Lebeziatnikov had been standing by the window, trying not to interrupt. When Sonya left, he walked over to Luzhin and solemnly reached out his hand.

“I heard and saw everything,” he said, emphasizing the last word. “That was honorable—no, humane! You didn’t want gratitude, I could tell! And while I don’t really believe in private charity, since it doesn’t fix the root problem, I admit I liked what you did—yes, yes, I liked it.”
“That’s all nonsense,” Luzhin muttered, a bit thrown off, and eyed Lebeziatnikov carefully.

“No, it’s not! A man who’s had a bad day like you did yesterday, but still cares about others, deserves respect—even if he’s making a social mistake! I didn’t expect that from you, Pyotr Petrovitch, especially with your ideas... Oh, your ideas really hold you back! You’re so upset about your breakup,” said Lebeziatnikov, who felt suddenly fond of Luzhin again. “And why do you even want marriage, legal marriage, dear Pyotr Petrovitch? Why do you care about legality? Well, you can hit me if you want, but I’m actually glad you didn’t get married, that you’re free, that you’re not lost to humanity. I just had to say it!”
“Because I don’t want to be made a fool of in your ‘free marriage’ and raise another man’s kids—that’s why I want a legal marriage,” Luzhin replied, just to say something.
He seemed distracted by something else.

“Kids? So now you’re talking about kids,” Lebeziatnikov perked up. “That’s a big social issue. Some people refuse to have kids at all because it reminds them of the family system. But that’s a whole other topic. As for ‘honor,’ I admit that’s my weak point. That old-fashioned word is ridiculous—it won’t exist in the future. What does it even mean? It’s nonsense! There’s no cheating in a free marriage—that only happens in legal marriage. In a free marriage, if your wife leaves you for someone else, it just shows she respects you enough to be honest. If I ever got married, I’d be happy if my wife found a new lover. ‘My dear,’ I’d say, ‘I love you, but I want you to respect me, too—see?’ Right?”

Luzhin chuckled as he listened, but not because he thought it was funny—he was barely listening. He seemed distracted and kept rubbing his hands together. Lebeziatnikov noticed this and remembered it later.

It's hard to say exactly why Katerina Ivanovna decided to have that ridiculous dinner after Marmeladov’s funeral. She spent almost half of the twenty roubles that Raskolnikov had given her for the funeral on it. Maybe she felt she had to honor Marmeladov properly, so all the tenants—and especially Amalia Ivanovna, the landlady—would see that her late husband was just as good as any of them, maybe even better, and no one had the right to look down on him. Part of it was probably that strange “poor person’s pride” that makes people spend their last bit of money on things like this, just so they can feel equal to others and not be looked down on. But it was also likely that Katerina Ivanovna, feeling abandoned by everyone, wanted to show the “worthless, stuck-up lodgers” that she actually knew “how to do things right” and that she had grown up in a refined, almost upper-class family—definitely not raised to scrub floors and wash dirty clothes at night. Even the poorest people sometimes have bursts of pride like this, where they just can’t help themselves. And Katerina Ivanovna was not someone whose spirit could be crushed easily, no matter how bad things got for her. In fact, as Sonia had pointed out, Katerina Ivanovna’s mind was a bit unstable—she wasn’t insane, but after a year of constant trouble, it’s no wonder her nerves were worn thin. And people say that the later stages of tuberculosis can affect the mind, too.

There wasn’t much variety in the drinks—no fancy wines like Madeira—but there was wine, vodka, rum, and some cheap Lisbon wine, though none of it was good quality. It was enough, though. Along with the traditional rice and honey, there were three or four dishes, including pancakes, all cooked in Amalia Ivanovna’s kitchen. Two samovars were boiling so there’d be plenty of tea and punch after dinner. Katerina Ivanovna had shopped for all the food herself, helped by one of the lodgers, a sad little Polish man who had somehow ended up living at Madame Lippevechsel’s. He was super eager to help and spent all morning and the day before running errands for her, making sure everyone saw how busy he was. He kept calling her “Pani” (which means “madam” in Polish) every time he rushed up to her, even chasing her down at the market for the smallest things. At first, Katerina Ivanovna said she couldn’t have managed without this “wonderful and generous man,” but by the end she was completely sick of him. That was typical of her—she always described people in the most positive way at first, exaggerating their good points and even making up stories about them, which she believed herself. But just as quickly, she could be disappointed and turn on them, treating them with rude contempt. She was naturally cheerful and wanted everyone to be happy and get along, but after so many disappointments, she now demanded perfect peace, and even the smallest problem would drive her into a frenzy. She’d go from hopeful and excited to furious and cursing her fate in a matter of minutes.

Suddenly Amalia Ivanovna became very important in Katerina Ivanovna’s eyes, probably just because she had thrown herself into helping with the dinner. Amalia had set the table, provided the linens, dishes, and so on, and cooked the food in her own kitchen. Katerina Ivanovna left everything to her and went to the cemetery. Everything was done well—the tablecloth was almost clean, and the dishes, knives, forks, and glasses were all mismatched, borrowed from different lodgers, but at least the table was set right on time. Amalia Ivanovna, proud of her work, dressed up in a black silk dress and a cap with new mourning ribbons, and waited for everyone to return. For some reason, this pride annoyed Katerina Ivanovna: “As if no one but Amalia Ivanovna could set a table!” She also didn’t like the cap with the new ribbons. “Does she think she’s so important just because she’s the landlady and agreed, as a favor, to help her poor tenants? As a favor! Imagine that! My father was a colonel, almost a governor, and sometimes hosted parties for forty people. Back then, someone like Amalia Ivanovna—or Ludwigovna, as she really is—wouldn’t have even been allowed in the kitchen.”

Katerina Ivanovna didn’t say anything about her feelings for now and just treated Amalia Ivanovna coldly, but she made up her mind that she’d have to put the landlady back in her place soon, because who knew what she was thinking of herself. Katerina was also annoyed that almost none of the lodgers she invited had gone to the funeral, except the little Pole who had just made it to the cemetery. But for the dinner, the poorest and most pitiful tenants showed up—some not even fully sober. The older, more respectable ones stayed away, almost like they’d agreed on it. Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin, who was supposed to be the most respectable lodger, didn’t come, even though the night before Katerina had told everyone—Amalia, Polenka, Sonia, and the Pole—that he was the most generous, noble man with lots of money and connections, a friend of her first husband, and a guest in her father’s house, and that he’d promised to help her get a good pension. It should be said that when Katerina bragged about someone’s connections or money, it was just because she liked to, not for any selfish reason—she just enjoyed making them sound important. Maybe, following Luzhin’s example, that “useless guy” Lebeziatnikov didn’t come either. What did he think of himself? He was only invited out of politeness since he shared a room with Luzhin and was his friend, so it would have been awkward not to ask him.

The “genteel lady and her old-maidish daughter” didn’t show up either. They had only been living in the house for two weeks but had already complained a few times about the noise from Katerina Ivanovna’s room, especially when Marmeladov came home drunk. Katerina heard this from Amalia Ivanovna, who once, during an argument, had yelled that Katerina’s family “wasn’t worth the foot” of the respectable lodgers they were disturbing. Katerina decided to invite this lady and her daughter—the same ones who ignored her when they met in the hallway—so they would see she was “nobler in her thoughts” and didn’t hold grudges, and so they’d realize she wasn’t used to living this way. She planned to mention her late father’s important government job during dinner and hint that it was rude of them to ignore her. The fat colonel-major (really just a retired low-ranking officer) was also missing, but it seemed he hadn’t been himself for two days. So, the party was just the Pole, a shabby clerk with a spotted face and greasy coat who never spoke and smelled terrible, and an almost deaf and blind old man who used to work at the post office and had lived off someone’s charity at Amalia Ivanovna’s forever.

A retired commissariat clerk came too. He was drunk, laughed loudly and rudely, and—believe it or not—didn’t even have a waistcoat on! One of the guests sat down at the table without even greeting Katerina Ivanovna. Finally, one man who didn’t even own a suit showed up in his dressing gown, but that was too much, and Amalia Ivanovna and the Pole managed to get him out. The Pole, however, brought along two other Poles who didn’t live at Amalia Ivanovna’s and whom nobody had seen before. All this really got on Katerina Ivanovna’s nerves. “Who did we go to all this trouble for?” To make space for the guests, the children didn’t even get seats at the table; the two youngest sat on a bench in the far corner, eating their dinner off a box, while Polenka, being older, had to take care of them and make sure they ate properly and wiped their noses like proper little kids.

Because of all this, Katerina Ivanovna couldn’t help acting even more proud and formal as she greeted her guests. She looked at some of them with extra seriousness and invited them to sit in the most dignified way. Blaming Amalia Ivanovna for the people who didn’t show up, she treated her with obvious indifference, which Amalia noticed and didn’t like at all. It was clear that this was a bad start. But finally, everyone sat down.

Raskolnikov came in just as they were getting back from the cemetery. Katerina Ivanovna was thrilled to see him—not only because he was the only “educated guest, and everyone knew he’d be a university professor in two years,” but also because he immediately apologized for missing the funeral, in a polite way. She was so happy she practically grabbed him and made him sit on her left (Amalia Ivanovna was on her right). Even though she was constantly worrying that the food was being served properly and that everyone was trying everything, and even though her cough kept getting worse and interrupted her every minute, she couldn’t help whispering all her pent-up feelings to Raskolnikov—her disappointment about how the dinner was turning out—mixed in with sudden bursts of laughter at the expense of the guests and especially her landlady.

“It’s all that cuckoo’s fault! You know who I mean? Her, her!” Katerina Ivanovna nodded towards the landlady. “Look at her, pretending not to notice, but she knows we’re talking about her and doesn’t understand a word. Ha! What’s with that cap? (Cough-cough-cough.) Have you noticed how she acts like she’s doing me a favor by being here, like she’s my patron? I asked her, very sensibly, to invite people—especially those who knew my late husband—and look at the crowd she brought! A bunch of nobodies! Look at that one with the spotty face. And those pathetic Poles—ha-ha-ha! (Cough-cough-cough.) I’ve never even seen them before. Why are they here? Look at them, lined up like that. Hey, pan!” she suddenly shouted to one of the Poles, “tried the pancakes yet? Have some more! Want some beer? Or vodka? Look, he’s jumping up and bowing—he must be starving, poor thing. Never mind, let them eat! At least they’re quiet, though I am worried about the silver spoons… Amalia Ivanovna!” she called out, almost loudly, “if your spoons go missing, it’s not my fault, just so you know! Ha-ha-ha!” She laughed at Raskolnikov, nodding towards the landlady, delighted with her own joke. “She didn’t get it! Look at her, mouth open! An owl, a real owl! An owl in new ribbons, ha-ha-ha!”

Suddenly her laughing turned into an awful fit of coughing that lasted five minutes. Sweat broke out on her forehead and when she wiped her mouth, her handkerchief was stained with blood. She silently showed the blood to Raskolnikov, then, as soon as she could breathe, started whispering to him again, even more animated, her cheeks flushed.

“Do you know, I told her exactly how to invite that lady and her daughter—you know who I mean? It needed so much care, but she managed to mess it up so badly that that stuck-up, ridiculous woman—just because she’s a major’s widow and is trying to get a pension and wears out her skirts going to government offices, and even paints her face at fifty (everyone knows it)—decided not to come and didn’t even reply to the invitation, which any polite person would have done! I don’t get why Pyotr Petrovitch didn’t come. And where’s Sonia? Where have you been, Sonia? It’s weird for you to be late to your own father’s funeral. Rodion Romanovitch, make room for her next to you, that’s her place. Take what you want, Sonia. Try the cold entrée with jelly—it’s the best. Pancakes are coming soon. Did the kids get their food? Polenka, do you have everything? (Cough-cough-cough.) Good. Be good, Lida, and Kolya, stop fidgeting; sit properly. What is it, Sonia?”

Sonia quickly gave Katerina Ivanovna Pyotr Petrovitch’s apologies, speaking loudly enough for everyone to hear and using the most respectful words she could think of, as if quoting Pyotr Petrovitch himself. She added that he had told her to say he would come as soon as possible to talk privately with Katerina Ivanovna about how he could help her and her family.

Sonia knew that this would make Katerina Ivanovna feel better and proud. She sat down next to Raskolnikov and gave him a quick, curious glance but then seemed to avoid looking at or talking to him for the rest of the meal. She seemed distracted, but kept watching Katerina Ivanovna, wanting to please her. Neither Sonia nor Katerina Ivanovna had proper mourning clothes; Sonia wore dark brown, and Katerina Ivanovna wore her only dress, a dark striped cotton one.

Pyotr Petrovitch’s message worked perfectly. Katerina Ivanovna listened to Sonia with dignity and then, just as dignified, asked how Pyotr Petrovitch was doing. Then she leaned over and whispered loudly to Raskolnikov that, honestly, it would have been weird for a man as important as Pyotr Petrovitch to be in such “strange company,” even though he was devoted to her family and had been friends with her father.

“That’s why I’m so grateful to you, Rodion Romanovitch, for not turning down my invitation, even in these conditions,” she added almost out loud. “But I know it was just your special affection for my poor husband that made you keep your promise.”

Then, looking proud again, Katerina Ivanovna looked around at all the guests and suddenly shouted across the table to the deaf old man, asking if he wanted more meat and if he’d had any wine. The old man didn’t answer and couldn’t understand what she wanted for a long time, even though the people next to him kept poking and shaking him. He just sat there staring with his mouth open, which made the others laugh even more.

“What an idiot! Look at him! Why did anyone bring him?” Katerina Ivanovna said, then continued, “But as for Pyotr Petrovitch, I always trusted him. Of course, he’s nothing like—” and here she suddenly turned to Amalia Ivanovna with a sharp, loud voice that startled her, “not like your bunch of ragged nobodies, people my father wouldn’t have hired as cooks, and my husband would only have invited out of charity.”
“He loved to drink, he really did!” shouted the commissariat clerk, gulping down his twelfth glass of vodka.

“My late husband definitely had that weakness, everyone knows it,” Katerina Ivanovna shot back, “but he was a kind and honorable man who loved and respected his family. The problem was he was too trusting and drank with people who weren’t even worth the dirt on his shoes. Would you believe it, Rodion Romanovitch, they found a gingerbread rooster in his pocket; he was completely drunk, but he still remembered the children!”
“A rooster? You said a rooster?” yelled the clerk.
Katerina Ivanovna ignored him, sighing and getting lost in her thoughts.

“You probably think, like everyone else, that I was too harsh with him,” she said to Raskolnikov. “But that’s not true! He respected me, very much! He was a good man. Sometimes I felt so sorry for him, seeing him sitting in the corner, and I wanted to be kind to him. But then I’d think, ‘If I’m kind, he’ll just start drinking again.’ The only way to keep him in line was to be strict.”
“Yeah, he used to get his hair pulled a lot!” the commissariat clerk yelled, downing another glass of vodka.
“Some fools could use a good beating, too—not just hair-pulling. And I’m not talking about my husband!” Katerina Ivanovna snapped at him.

Her face was getting redder and redder, and she was breathing hard. She was about to lose her temper completely. Some of the guests were snickering, clearly enjoying the scene. They started nudging the commissariat clerk and whispering things to him, obviously trying to get him to stir up more trouble.
“Excuse me, but what are you referring to,” said the clerk, “I mean, who… about whom… did you say… But whatever! That’s nonsense! Widow! I forgive you… Forget it!”
And he took another swig of vodka.

Raskolnikov sat there silently, disgusted by everything. He only ate out of politeness, just tasting the food Katerina Ivanovna kept putting on his plate so he wouldn’t hurt her feelings. He watched Sonia closely. But Sonia just looked more and more worried and upset; she could see, just like he could, that the dinner was headed for disaster, and was terrified by Katerina Ivanovna’s growing anger. She knew she herself was the main reason those “respectable” ladies had looked down on Katerina’s invitation. Amalia Ivanovna had even told her that the mother was offended by the invite and had asked, “How could I let my daughter sit beside that kind of girl?” Sonia felt pretty sure Katerina Ivanovna knew this too, and Katerina took insults against Sonia even harder than insults against herself or her own kids. Sonia knew that Katerina wouldn’t be satisfied until she’d put those “snobs” in their place. Then, to make things worse, someone from the other end of the table sent Sonia a plate with two hearts pierced by an arrow, cut out of black bread. Katerina Ivanovna went bright red and shouted across the table that whoever sent it was a “drunken idiot!”

Amalia Ivanovna, sensing trouble and hurt by Katerina’s rudeness, tried to win back the crowd and make herself look good by suddenly telling a story about her friend “Karl from the chemist’s.” She said he was riding in a cab one night when the cabman wanted to kill him, and Karl begged and cried and was so scared he felt his heart was pierced. Even though Katerina Ivanovna smiled, she quickly pointed out that Amalia shouldn’t try to tell stories in Russian, which only made Amalia more upset. Amalia protested that her “father from Berlin was very important and always walked with his hands in his pockets.” Katerina Ivanovna couldn’t help but laugh at this, and Amalia got even more frustrated.

“Did you hear that owl?” Katerina Ivanovna whispered, now in a much better mood. “She meant to say he kept his hands in his pockets, but she said he put his hands in people’s pockets! (Cough-cough.) And have you noticed, Rodion Romanovitch, that all these foreigners in Petersburg, especially Germans, are dumber than we are? Can you imagine one of us telling a story like ‘Karl from the chemist’s’ whose heart was pierced with fear and who, instead of fighting back, just cried and begged? What a fool! She actually thinks it’s a touching story and doesn’t even realize how stupid she sounds. Honestly, that drunk commissariat clerk is smarter—at least he’s just drunk. But these foreigners always try to act so proper and serious. Look at her, glaring! She’s angry—ha-ha! (Cough-cough-cough.)”

Feeling better, Katerina Ivanovna started telling Raskolnikov her plan: when she got her pension, she would open a school for girls from good families in her hometown, T——. This was the first time she’d mentioned it to him, and she launched into all the exciting details. She even pulled out the certificate of honor that Marmeladov had once mentioned to Raskolnikov in the tavern—the one showing that Katerina Ivanovna had danced the shawl dance before the governor and other important people after finishing school. She mainly brought the certificate to prove, especially to those two “stuck-up ladies” if they came, that she came from a noble family—almost upper-class, the daughter of a colonel—and was far above certain people who were now acting so high and mighty. The drunken guests immediately passed the certificate around, and Katerina Ivanovna didn’t even try to get it back, since it actually said her father was a major and had an official title, so she really was nearly the daughter of a colonel.

Getting more and more fired up, Katerina Ivanovna talked about how peaceful and happy their life would be in T——, all about the teachers she would hire for her boarding school, including a very respectable old Frenchman named Mangot, who had taught her as a child and still lived in T——, and who would probably teach in her school for a reasonable price. Then she explained how Sonia would go with her and help her with everything. At that, someone at the far end of the table suddenly burst out laughing.

Even though Katerina Ivanovna pretended she didn’t notice, she immediately raised her voice and started talking very seriously about how Sonia would be perfect for helping, describing her “gentleness, patience, devotion, generosity, and good education.” She patted Sonia’s cheek and kissed her twice. Sonia blushed bright red, and Katerina Ivanovna suddenly began to cry, then said she was “just upset and nervous, that she was being silly, and that the dinner was over and it was time for tea.”

Right then, Amalia Ivanovna, hurt that no one was listening to her, tried one last time to get attention by announcing very seriously that in the future boarding school, they’d have to take special care of the laundry (“die Wäsche”) and make sure the young ladies didn’t read novels at night.

Katerina Ivanovna, who was now exhausted and fed up with the dinner, immediately cut her off, saying, “You don’t know what you’re talking about—it’s the laundry maid’s job to care for the washing, not the headmistress of a good school! And as for reading novels at night, that’s just rude, and please be quiet.” Amalia Ivanovna got angry and insisted that she only “meant well,” and that “it had been a long time since she’d had her rent paid in gold.”

Katerina Ivanovna immediately snapped back, saying it was a lie that Amalia meant well, since just yesterday, while her husband’s body was still in the room, Amalia had bothered her about the rent. Amalia shot back that she had invited “those ladies,” but “those ladies didn’t come because ladies can’t visit someone who isn’t a lady.” Katerina Ivanovna retorted that Amalia was just a nobody and couldn’t tell what made someone a real lady.
