Amalia insisted her “Vater aus Berlin was very, very important, always walked with both hands in his pockets, and always said ‘poof! poof!’” Then she jumped up from the table, stuck her hands in her pockets, puffed out her cheeks, and went “poof! poof!” as the other lodgers laughed, hoping for a fight.

But Katerina Ivanovna had had enough. She loudly declared for everyone to hear that Amalia Ivanovna probably never had a father, was just a drunken Finnish woman from Petersburg, and had probably once been a cook—or maybe something worse. Amalia Ivanovna turned bright red and squealed that maybe Katerina never had a father, but she herself had a Vater aus Berlin who wore a long coat and always said “poof-poof-poof!”

Katerina Ivanovna replied with disdain that everyone knew about her own family, and that her certificate of honor proved her father was a colonel, while Amalia’s father—if he even existed—was probably just a Finnish milkman, or maybe she never had a father at all, seeing as no one even knew if her name was Amalia Ivanovna or Amalia Ludwigovna.

That was the last straw for Amalia Ivanovna, who slammed her fist on the table and screamed that her name was Amalia Ivanovna, not Ludwigovna, and “her father was Johann and a burgomeister, and Katerina Ivanovna’s father was never a burgomeister!” Katerina Ivanovna stood up, pale and breathing hard, and sternly announced that if Amalia dared to compare her father to Katerina’s, she would rip off Amalia’s cap and stomp on it. Amalia ran around the room, yelling that she was the landlady and Katerina should leave her apartment right away, then started grabbing the silver spoons from the table for no clear reason. Chaos broke out—the kids started crying, Sonia tried to hold back Katerina Ivanovna, but when Amalia shouted something about “the yellow ticket,” Katerina shoved Sonia aside and rushed at Amalia, ready to make good on her threat.
Just then, the door opened and Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin appeared in the doorway, looking around at the chaos with sharp, watchful eyes. Katerina Ivanovna rushed over to him.

“Pyotr Petrovitch,” Katerina Ivanovna cried out, “please help me! At least you could stand up for me. Make this foolish woman understand she can’t treat a lady in trouble like this. There are laws! I’ll go to the governor-general himself if I have to. She’ll pay for this. Remember my father’s kindness—help these poor orphans!”

“Excuse me, madam. Please, let me pass,” Pyotr Petrovitch said, waving her off. “As you know, I never even met your father” (someone in the room laughed loudly) “and I don’t intend to get involved in your endless fights with Amalia Ivanovna. I’m here for my own business, and I need to speak to your stepdaughter, Sofya Ivanovna, I think it is? Please let me through.”
Pushing past her, Pyotr Petrovitch crossed the room to where Sonia was standing.

Katerina Ivanovna stood frozen, shocked by Pyotr Petrovitch’s denial about her father’s hospitality. Even though she had made it up, by now she believed it herself. She was also stunned by Pyotr Petrovitch’s cold, businesslike, almost threatening tone. The noisy room fell quiet as he entered. Not only did he seem completely out of place among the other guests, but it was obvious he had come with something important to say. Raskolnikov, standing next to Sonia, moved aside to let him pass. Pyotr Petrovitch didn’t seem to notice him. A moment later, Lebeziatnikov appeared in the doorway, standing still and watching with interest and confusion.

“Sorry to interrupt, but this is very important,” Pyotr Petrovitch announced to everyone. “I’m actually glad there are so many people here. Amalia Ivanovna, as the landlady, please pay close attention to what I’m about to say to Sofya Ivanovna.” He turned to Sonia, who was already anxious. “Right after your visit, I found out a hundred-rouble note was missing from my table, in the room I share with Mr. Lebeziatnikov. If you know anything about where it is, please tell us now, and I promise, in front of everyone, that will be the end of it. If not, I’ll have to take serious action, and you’ll only have yourself to blame.”
The room went completely silent. Even the children stopped crying. Sonia stood there, pale as a ghost, staring at Luzhin. She couldn’t say a word—she seemed too shocked to understand.
“Well, what’s your answer?” Luzhin asked, staring hard at her.
“I... I don’t know. I know nothing about it,” Sonia managed to whisper.

“You know nothing?” Luzhin repeated, pausing again. “Take a moment and think,” he said sternly, as if warning her. “I’ll give you time to consider. Look, I wouldn’t accuse you in front of all these people if I wasn’t completely certain. If it turns out I’m wrong, I’d have to take responsibility for that. This morning, I exchanged some securities for about three thousand roubles. I wrote everything down in my notebook. When I got home, I counted the money—Mr. Lebeziatnikov saw me—and after counting two thousand three hundred roubles, I put the rest in my coat pocket. About five hundred roubles stayed on the table, including three one-hundred rouble notes. Then you came in (I invited you)—and the whole time, you seemed really nervous. You tried to leave three times during our conversation. Mr. Lebeziatnikov saw this, too. Remember, I invited you, through Mr. Lebeziatnikov, only to talk about the difficult situation of your relative, Katerina Ivanovna, since I couldn’t attend the dinner, and to discuss helping her by getting some money together. You thanked me and even cried. I’m telling all this to remind you—and to show I haven’t missed a single detail. Then I took ten roubles from the table and gave them to you as my first donation. Mr. Lebeziatnikov saw that. Then I walked you to the door—you were still very nervous—after that, I talked with Mr. Lebeziatnikov for about ten minutes. Then he left, and I went back to the table to count the money. That’s when I noticed a hundred-rouble note was gone. Think carefully. I can’t suspect Mr. Lebeziatnikov. I couldn’t have miscounted, because I’d just finished counting before you came in. Given your nervousness, the way you kept your hands on the table, and considering your social situation and what comes with it, I was—unfortunately—forced to suspect you. It’s a horrible thing for me to think, but I had no choice! Still, I know I risk something by accusing you, but I couldn’t ignore it. And do you know why I went through all this? Because of your incredible ingratitude! I invite you to help your relative, I give you ten roubles, and you pay me back by stealing. It’s too much! You need to learn a lesson. Please—think! I’m your friend right now, and you won’t find a better one. If you don’t confess, I won’t back down. Now, what do you say?”
“I didn’t take anything,” Sonia whispered, terrified. “You gave me ten roubles—here, take it back.”
Sonia pulled a handkerchief from her pocket, untied a corner, took out the ten-rouble note, and handed it to Luzhin.
“And you’re not going to admit to taking the hundred roubles?” he pressed, looking disappointed and accusing.

Sonia looked around. Everyone in the room was staring at her with harsh, judgmental, even mocking eyes. She looked over at Raskolnikov—he was standing against the wall, arms crossed, his eyes burning.
“Oh God!” Sonia cried.
“Amalia Ivanovna, we’ll need to call the police, so please send for the house porter,” Luzhin said softly, almost kindly.
“God have mercy! I knew she was the thief!” Amalia Ivanovna shouted, throwing her hands in the air.
“You knew?” Luzhin snapped. “Then you must have had some reason to think so before. Please, Amalia Ivanovna, remember that you said this in front of everyone.”
The room erupted with loud conversation. Everybody started moving around.
“What!” Katerina Ivanovna suddenly realized what Luzhin was saying and rushed at him. “What! You’re accusing her of stealing? Sonia? Oh, you monsters!”
She ran to Sonia and wrapped her thin arms around her, holding her tight as if to protect her.
“Sonia! How could you take ten roubles from him? Silly girl! Give it to me, give me the ten roubles, right now—here!”

Snatching the note from Sonia, Katerina Ivanovna crumpled it up and threw it right in Luzhin’s face. It hit him in the eye and fell to the floor. Amalia Ivanovna hurried to pick it up. Pyotr Petrovitch lost his temper.
“Somebody restrain this crazy woman!” he shouted.
Just then, a few more people, including the two ladies, appeared in the doorway along with Lebeziatnikov.

“What! You say I’m crazy? Me? You idiot!” Katerina Ivanovna shrieked. “You’re the idiot, you sneaky lawyer, you rotten man! Sonia, take his money? Sonia, a thief? She’d give away her last coin!” Katerina Ivanovna started to laugh hysterically. “Have you ever seen such a fool?” she shouted, spinning around. “And you?” She spotted the landlady. “You too, sausage-eater, you say she’s a thief, you silly Prussian chicken leg in a dress! She hasn’t left this room—she came straight here from you and sat by me, everyone saw it. She sat by Rodion Romanovitch. Search her! If she hasn’t left, then the money must be on her! Go ahead, search her! But if you don’t find it, you’ll answer for this! I’ll go to the Tsar himself if I have to! I’m alone in the world, but they’ll let me in! You think they won’t? You’re wrong! You thought you could count on her being quiet—but I’m not! You’ve gone too far. Search her, search her!”
In a frenzy, Katerina Ivanovna shook Luzhin and dragged him over toward Sonia.

“Fine, I’ll take responsibility... but please calm down, madam, calm down. I see that you’re not quiet at all!... Well, well, but as for that...” Luzhin mumbled, “that should be done by the police... though there are enough witnesses here.... I’m ready... but it’s awkward for a man... because she’s a woman.... Maybe Amalia Ivanovna could help... but this isn’t really the right way.... How should we do this?”

“However you want! Anyone can search her!” Katerina Ivanovna yelled. “Sonia, empty your pockets! Look, monster, her pocket is empty—her handkerchief was here! Here’s the other pocket—look! Do you see?”

Katerina Ivanovna turned Sonia’s pockets inside out—really, she nearly tore them open. Suddenly, a piece of paper flew out of the right pocket, floated through the air, and landed at Luzhin’s feet. Everyone saw it; some people cried out. Pyotr Petrovitch bent down, picked up the paper with two fingers, held it up for everyone to see, and opened it. It was a hundred-rouble note, folded up small. He showed it to the whole room.
“Thief! Out of my house! Police, police!” Amalia Ivanovna yelled. “They should be sent to Siberia! Out!”

Everyone started shouting. Raskolnikov stayed silent, his eyes fixed on Sonia, only glancing quickly at Luzhin now and then. Sonia stood still, almost in a daze, barely able to react. Suddenly, her face flushed; she screamed and covered her face with her hands.
“No, it wasn’t me! I didn’t take it! I know nothing about it!” she sobbed, her voice breaking. She ran to Katerina Ivanovna, who hugged her tightly, as if to shield her from the world.

“Sonia! Sonia! I don’t believe it! Do you hear me? I don’t believe it!” Katerina Ivanovna cried, rocking Sonia like a child, kissing her face and hands, “You took it! How stupid these people are! Oh, you’re all fools,” she yelled at everyone, “you don’t know what a heart she has, what kind of girl she is! She take it? She’d sell her last piece of clothing, go barefoot, just to help someone! She ended up with that yellow passport because my children were starving—she did it for us! Oh, husband, do you see? What a funeral dinner for you! Oh, God! Please, help her—why are you all just standing there? Rodion Romanovitch, why don’t you defend her? Do you believe it too? None of you are worth her little finger! Oh God, please, help her now!”

The desperate cries of the sick, helpless woman touched everyone in the room. Her thin, pale face, cracked lips, hoarse voice, and childlike tears and pleading were so sad that even Pyotr Petrovitch was moved.

“Madam, madam, this doesn’t reflect on you,” he said loudly. “No one would dare say you had anything to do with this, especially since you proved her guilt by turning out her pockets yourself. I’m willing to show mercy if poverty drove Sofya Semyonovna to this, but why didn’t you confess?” he said to Sonia. “Were you afraid of the shame? Maybe you panicked? I can understand that. But how could you do such a thing? Everyone,” he addressed the whole room, “I’m willing, out of pity, to forgive this, despite how I was insulted! May this disgrace be a lesson to you,” he said to Sonia, “and I won’t take it any further. That’s enough!”

Pyotr Petrovitch glanced at Raskolnikov. Their eyes met, and Raskolnikov’s look was so fierce it could burn him up. Meanwhile, Katerina Ivanovna seemed not to hear anything—she was hugging and kissing Sonia like she was losing her mind. The children clung to Sonia, and Polenka, though she didn’t understand what was happening, was sobbing on Sonia’s shoulder.
“How disgusting!” a loud voice shouted from the doorway.
Pyotr Petrovitch turned quickly.
“What filth!” Lebeziatnikov repeated, staring him straight in the face.
Pyotr Petrovitch jumped—everyone noticed, and they remembered it later. Lebeziatnikov marched into the room.
“And you dared to call me as a witness?” he said, coming up to Pyotr Petrovitch.
“What do you mean? What are you talking about?” Luzhin muttered.
“I mean you’re a liar, that’s what I mean!” Lebeziatnikov shot back, glaring at him with his nearsighted eyes.
He was furious. Raskolnikov watched him closely, paying attention to every word. Again, the room fell silent. For the first time, Pyotr Petrovitch seemed stunned.
“If that’s meant for me...” he started, stammering. “What’s wrong with you? Are you out of your mind?”

“I’m perfectly sane, but you’re the scoundrel! How disgusting! I heard everything. I waited on purpose to figure it out, and I still don’t really get your logic... Why you did all this, I can’t understand.”
“What have I done then? Stop talking in your crazy riddles! Or maybe you’re drunk!”

“Maybe you’re a drunk, but I’m not! I never touch vodka—it’s against my beliefs. Listen—he, he himself, with his own hands, gave Sofya Semyonovna that hundred-rouble note—I saw it, I witnessed it, I’ll swear to it! He did it!” Lebeziatnikov told everyone.
“Are you out of your mind, you little fool?” Luzhin shouted. “She just said herself, in front of everyone, that I only gave her ten roubles. How could I have given her a hundred?”

“I saw it, I saw it,” Lebeziatnikov repeated. “And even though it goes against my principles, I’ll swear in court if you want, because I saw you slip it into her pocket. I thought you were just being generous! When you were saying goodbye at the door, while you held her hand, you used your other hand—your left hand—and slipped the note into her pocket. I saw it, I saw it!”
Luzhin turned pale.
“What lies!” he shouted, “how could you, standing by the window, see the note? You just imagined it with your bad eyesight. You’re crazy!”

“No, I didn’t imagine it. I was standing a little far, but I saw everything. And yes, it would be hard to tell a hundred-rouble note from a distance, but I knew it was a hundred because when you were going to give Sofya Semyonovna ten roubles, you actually picked up a hundred-rouble note from the table (I saw because I was close then, and it stuck in my mind). You folded it and kept it in your hand. I didn’t think about it again until you were getting up—you switched it from your right to your left hand and nearly dropped it! I noticed because it reminded me again, and I thought you were giving her a secret gift. So I watched, and I saw you slip it into her pocket. I saw it, I saw it, I’ll swear it.”
Lebeziatnikov was almost out of breath. People shouted from all sides, some surprised, some angry. Everyone crowded around Pyotr Petrovitch. Katerina Ivanovna rushed to Lebeziatnikov.
“I was wrong about you! Help her! You’re the only one standing up for her. She’s an orphan—God sent you!”
Katerina Ivanovna, not knowing what she was doing, dropped to her knees in front of him.

“Nonsense!” Luzhin yelled, his anger boiling over. “All this about ‘you thought’ and ‘you noticed’—what does it even mean? So I gave her money on purpose, in secret? Why? What for? What do I care about this?”

“Why? That’s what I can’t figure out, but what I’m telling you is the truth, that’s for sure! Right after I thanked you and shook your hand, I was wondering—why did you secretly put it in her pocket? Was it just so I wouldn’t see, since you know I don’t believe in private charity? Maybe you were embarrassed to give so much in front of me. Or maybe you wanted to surprise her when she found it in her pocket. Some people love doing good deeds in secret. Or maybe you wanted to test her, to see if she’d come thank you. Or maybe you didn’t want thanks at all. I thought of all these possibilities. I even thought she might lose the money before noticing it, so I decided to come here and tell her you’d put a hundred roubles in her pocket. But on the way I stopped by Madame Kobilatnikov’s to bring a book, and then I came here—and look what I found! Would I have all these thoughts if I hadn’t seen you put the note in her pocket?”

When Lebeziatnikov finally finished his long speech, he was sweating and exhausted. He wasn’t even able to speak properly, but his words made a big impact. He spoke so passionately and convincingly that everyone believed him. Pyotr Petrovitch could tell the situation was turning against him.

“What do I care if you had silly ideas?” he shouted. “That’s not proof! You probably dreamed it! And I say you’re lying—lying and slandering me because you’re mad I don’t agree with your godless, radical ideas!”
But this comeback didn’t help Pyotr Petrovitch. Everyone around him started murmuring in disapproval.

“Ah, so that’s your excuse now!” Lebeziatnikov shouted. “That’s nonsense! Call the police, I’ll swear to what I saw! The only thing I don’t get is why he risked doing something so disgusting. What a pitiful, shameful man!”
“I can explain why he did it, and if needed, I’ll swear to it too,” Raskolnikov finally said in a steady voice, stepping forward.
He looked calm and determined. Everyone could see just by looking at him that he truly knew what was going on, and that the mystery would soon be solved.

“Now everything makes sense to me,” Raskolnikov said to Lebeziatnikov. “From the start, I suspected there was something sneaky going on—based on some things only I knew, which I’ll now explain to everyone. Your testimony makes it all clear. Please, everyone, listen: This man (he pointed at Luzhin) was recently engaged to my sister, Avdotya Romanovna Raskolnikov. But when he got to Petersburg, he argued with me the day before yesterday at our first meeting, and I kicked him out of my room—there are two witnesses. He’s very spiteful. That same day, I didn’t even know he was staying here, and that means he saw me give money to Katerina Ivanovna for the funeral, as a friend of Mr. Marmeladov. He immediately wrote to my mother and told her I’d given all my money not to Katerina Ivanovna, but to Sofya Semyonovna, and hinted at terrible things about my relationship with her. He did this to turn my mother and sister against me, to make them think I was wasting the money they sent me on unworthy people. Yesterday, in front of my mother, my sister, and him, I said I gave the money to Katerina Ivanovna for the funeral and didn’t even know Sofya Semyonovna. I also said that, for all his so-called virtues, Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin wasn’t worth Sofya Semyonovna’s little finger. When he asked if I’d let Sofya Semyonovna sit next to my sister, I said I already had. When my mother and sister didn’t take his side, he started getting really rude, and finally he was thrown out of the house. That was yesterday evening. Now, pay attention: if he had managed to prove that Sofya Semyonovna was a thief, he would have shown my mother and sister he was right, that he had a reason to be mad at me for treating my sister and Sofya Semyonovna as equals, and that he was protecting my sister’s honor. Maybe he even thought this would win him back their trust, and he could get revenge on me—since he knows how much Sofya Semyonovna’s happiness means to me. That’s what he was up to! That’s the whole reason for this!”

That’s about how Raskolnikov finished his speech, which everyone listened to carefully, even though people interrupted with shouts and exclamations. Still, he spoke clearly, calmly, and firmly, and his confidence and seriousness made a big impression.

“Yes, yes, that’s it!” Lebeziatnikov said excitedly. “That must be it! He asked me, as soon as Sofya Semyonovna came into our room, if you were here, if I’d seen you at Katerina Ivanovna’s dinner. He pulled me aside and asked in private. He needed you here! That’s it, that’s it!”

Luzhin gave a contemptuous smile and stayed silent, but he was very pale. He seemed to be looking for a way out. He probably wished he could just leave, but that would make him look guilty. Besides, the crowd—many of whom were drunk—was too fired up to let him slip away. The commissariat clerk, though he didn’t really understand everything, was yelling louder than anyone and making rude suggestions about Luzhin. But not everyone was drunk; lodgers from other rooms had come in, and the three Polish men were shouting at Luzhin, calling him a “lajdak” and muttering threats in Polish. Sonia listened closely, even though she seemed overwhelmed; she kept her eyes on Raskolnikov, as if her whole safety depended on him. Katerina Ivanovna was breathing heavily and looked exhausted. Amalia Ivanovna stood staring with her mouth open, completely confused, only noticing that Pyotr Petrovitch was in trouble.

Raskolnikov tried to speak again, but people wouldn’t let him. Everyone crowded around Luzhin, shouting threats and insults. But Pyotr Petrovitch didn’t back down. Seeing his plan against Sonia had failed, he tried to act tough:

“Let me through, gentlemen! Don’t block my way!” he said, pushing through the crowd. “No threats, please! I promise you, it’s pointless—you’ll only get in trouble for stopping justice. The thief has been completely exposed, and I’ll press charges. Our judges aren’t blind or drunk, and they won’t believe the word of two notorious atheists who are only accusing me out of revenge, which they’ve admitted.... Now let me through!”
“I don’t want to see you in my room again!” Lebeziatnikov snapped. “Get out right now, and we’re done! After all I’ve put up with, all I’ve explained to you these past two weeks!”
“I told you earlier today I was leaving, when you tried to make me stay; now I’ll just add that you’re an idiot. You should see a doctor for your brain—and your eyesight. Let me through, everyone!”

He forced his way out. But the commissariat clerk wasn’t going to let him off easily—he grabbed a glass from the table, swung it in the air, and threw it at Pyotr Petrovitch; but it hit Amalia Ivanovna instead. She screamed, and the clerk fell heavily under the table. Pyotr Petrovitch went to his room and, half an hour later, left the house. Sonia, always timid, had already felt that she was easy to mistreat, but until today she’d hoped that by being gentle and polite, she could avoid trouble. Now she realized how wrong she was. She could put up with almost anything without complaint, but this was too much. Even though she’d been proven innocent, the pain of being so helpless and wronged made her burst into tears. Finally, unable to take any more, she rushed out and ran home, just after Luzhin left. When the glass hit Amalia Ivanovna and people laughed, it was more than the landlady could handle. She screamed and, furious, attacked Katerina Ivanovna, blaming her for everything.
“Get out of my house! Right now! Move it!”

With that, she started grabbing anything that belonged to Katerina Ivanovna and throwing it on the floor. Katerina Ivanovna, pale, almost passing out, gasping for breath, jumped up from the bed where she’d collapsed and rushed at Amalia Ivanovna. But she was too weak: the landlady pushed her away easily.

“What! As if that horrible accusation wasn’t enough—now this awful woman attacks me! What! On the day of my husband’s funeral, I’m thrown out of my home! After eating my bread and salt, she throws me and my orphans into the street! Where am I supposed to go?” the poor woman sobbed. “Oh God!” she cried, her eyes blazing. “Is there no justice in this world? Who else should be protected if not us orphans? We’ll see! There is law and justice—I’ll find it! Wait, you heartless woman! Polenka, stay with the children—I’ll be back. Wait for me, even if you have to wait in the street. We’ll see if there’s justice in this world!”

Throwing the green shawl (the one Marmeladov had mentioned to Raskolnikov) over her head, Katerina Ivanovna pushed her way through the noisy, drunken crowd, wailing and crying as she ran into the street—determined to find justice. Polenka, with the little ones in her arms, crouched in a corner, terrified, waiting for her mother to come back. Amalia Ivanovna stormed around the room, screaming and throwing things. The lodgers chattered, argued, and even broke into song, each reacting in their own way to what had just happened.
“Now it’s time for me to go,” thought Raskolnikov. “Well, Sofya Semyonovna, let’s see what you’ll say now!”
And he set off toward Sonia’s place.

Even though Raskolnikov was carrying so much guilt and horror inside, he had defended Sonia fiercely against Luzhin. After everything that had happened that morning, it was almost a relief to focus on something else, even if deep down he still cared a lot about Sonia. He was nervous too, especially when he remembered he needed to talk to Sonia soon and tell her who had killed Lizaveta. He knew it would be a terrible moment, and kept trying not to think about it. So when he left Katerina Ivanovna’s and said, “Well, Sofya Semyonovna, we’ll see what you say now!” he was still pumped up and defiant from beating Luzhin. But, strangely, by the time he reached Sonia’s place, he suddenly felt weak and scared. He hesitated at her door, asking himself, “Do I really have to tell her I killed Lizaveta?” The question felt weird, because he knew he couldn’t stop himself from telling her, and he couldn’t delay it either. He didn’t even understand why—he just knew he had to, and the helplessness of it almost crushed him. To end his own torment, he quickly opened the door and looked at Sonia. She was sitting at the table, her face in her hands, but as soon as she saw him, she stood up and came toward him, like she’d been waiting for him.
“What would I have done without you?” she said quickly, meeting him in the middle of the room.
It was obvious she’d been dying to say this to him. She’d been waiting for it.
Raskolnikov walked to the table and sat in the chair she’d just left. She stood facing him, just a couple steps away, just like the day before.
“Well, Sonia?” he said, his voice shaking. “It was all because of ‘your social status and the things that come with it.’ Did you get that just now?”
Her face showed how upset she was.
“Just please don’t talk to me like you did yesterday,” she cut in. “Don’t start that again. There’s already enough misery.”
She tried to smile, worried he might be hurt by her complaining.
“I shouldn’t have left there. What’s happening now? I wanted to go back right away, but I kept thinking... you would come.”
He told her that Amalia Ivanovna was kicking them out of their apartment and that Katerina Ivanovna had run off somewhere “to find justice.”
“Oh my God!” Sonia cried. “Let’s go right now...”
She grabbed her cape.
“It’s always the same with you!” Raskolnikov said irritably. “You only think about them! Stay with me for a bit.”
“But... Katerina Ivanovna?”
“You won’t lose Katerina Ivanovna, trust me. She’ll come to you since she ran off,” he added grumpily. “If you’re not here when she comes back, you’ll get blamed for it...”
Sonia sat down, anxious and tense. Raskolnikov stayed silent, staring at the floor and thinking.

“Luzhin didn’t want to press charges against you this time,” he started, not looking at Sonia, “but if he had wanted to, if it fit his plans, he would have sent you to jail if it weren’t for Lebeziatnikov and me. Right?”
“Yes,” she agreed in a weak voice. “Yes,” she repeated, lost in thought and looking worried.
“But I might not have been there at all. And Lebeziatnikov only showed up by accident.”
Sonia didn’t say anything.
“And if you had gone to jail, then what? Remember what I said yesterday?”
She still didn’t answer. He waited.

“I thought you’d shout at me again, ‘don’t talk about it, stop.’” Raskolnikov gave a little laugh, but it sounded forced. “What, still nothing?” he asked a minute later. “We have to talk about something, you know. I’d really like to know how you’d solve a certain ‘problem,’ as Lebeziatnikov would say.” (He was starting to lose track of what he was saying.) “No, really, I mean it. Imagine, Sonia, that you knew all along what Luzhin planned. Knew for sure that his actions would ruin Katerina Ivanovna, her kids, and you too—since you don’t think you matter—Polenka as well, because she’d end up the same. Now, if it was all up to you, if you had to choose who would live—Luzhin or them—like, Luzhin keeps on doing bad things or Katerina Ivanovna dies? Who would you pick to die? I’m asking you.”
Sonia looked at him nervously. The weird way he was asking made it feel like he was circling something important.
“I had a feeling you’d ask something like that,” she said, eyeing him curiously.
“I bet you did. But how would you answer it?”
“Why do you ask about something that could never happen?” Sonia said, not wanting to answer.
“So you think it’s better for Luzhin to keep living and doing bad things? You can’t even choose that!”
“But I don’t know God’s plan... And why do you ask such impossible questions? What’s the point of them? How could it ever depend on me—who made me the judge of who gets to live or die?”
“Oh, if you bring God’s plan into it, then you can’t do anything,” Raskolnikov grumbled.
“Just say what you mean!” Sonia cried, distressed. “You’re leading up to something again... Did you come here just to torture me?”
She couldn’t help herself and started crying hard. He looked at her, miserable. Five minutes passed.

“You’re right, Sonia,” he said softly at last. Suddenly, he was different. The false confidence and defiance were gone. Even his voice was weak. “I told you yesterday I wasn’t coming to ask forgiveness, and almost the first thing I do is ask for forgiveness... I brought up Luzhin and God’s plan for myself. I was asking for forgiveness, Sonia...”
He tried to smile, but it was pale and broken. He bowed his head and hid his face in his hands.

Suddenly, he felt a strange, sharp feeling—almost like bitterness toward Sonia. Surprised and scared by this, he looked up at her. But he saw only her anxious, loving eyes fixed on him; and with that, his bitterness vanished like smoke. It wasn’t real hatred; he’d just mixed up one feeling for another. It just meant the moment had come.
He hid his face in his hands again and lowered his head. Then suddenly he went pale, stood up from his chair, looked at Sonia, and without a word sat down on her bed.
The feeling was terribly similar to how he’d felt standing over the old woman with the axe in his hand, thinking, “I can’t waste another minute.”
“What’s wrong?” Sonia asked, terrified.

He couldn’t say a word. This wasn’t at all the way he’d planned to confess, and he didn’t understand what was happening to him now. She quietly came over, sat on the bed beside him, and waited, never taking her eyes off him. Her heart was pounding and sinking. She couldn’t take it; he turned his deathly pale face to her. His lips trembled, struggling to say something. A jolt of fear ran through Sonia.
“What’s wrong?” she repeated, scooting a little away from him.

“Nothing, Sonia, don’t be scared... It’s nothing, if you think about it,” he muttered, like someone sick with fever. “Why did I come here to torture you?” he suddenly asked, looking at her. “Why, really? I keep asking myself, Sonia...”
Maybe he’d asked himself that question fifteen minutes before, but now he spoke helplessly, barely aware of what he was saying, shaking all over.
“Oh, you’re in so much pain!” she whispered, watching him closely.
“It’s all nonsense... Listen, Sonia.” He suddenly managed a pale, helpless smile for a moment. “Remember what I was going to tell you yesterday?”
Sonia watched him nervously.
“I said when I left yesterday that maybe I was saying goodbye forever, but that if I came today, I’d tell you who... who killed Lizaveta.”
She started shaking all over.
“Well, I’m here to tell you.”
“So you really meant it yesterday?” she whispered, barely able to speak. “How do you know?” she asked quickly, as if suddenly snapping out of it.
Sonia’s face got even paler, and her breathing was ragged.
“I know.”
She paused for a minute.
“Did they find him?” she asked quietly.
“No.”
“Then how do you know?” she asked again, barely making a sound, after another minute.
He turned and looked at her very seriously.
“Guess,” he said, with that same sad, awkward smile.
She shivered.
“But you... why are you scaring me like this?” she said, forcing a childlike smile.

“I must be a close friend of his... since I know,” Raskolnikov went on, still staring at her as if he couldn’t look away. “He... didn’t mean to kill Lizaveta... he... killed her by accident... He meant to kill the old woman when she was alone, and he went there... and then Lizaveta came in... so he killed her too.”
Another horrible moment passed. They just stared at each other.
“So you can’t guess?” he asked suddenly, feeling like he was jumping off a cliff.
“N-no...” Sonia whispered.
“Look carefully.”

As soon as he said that again, he felt that same old chill in his heart. He looked at Sonia and suddenly thought he saw Lizaveta’s face in hers. He remembered perfectly the look on Lizaveta’s face when he came at her with the axe—how she backed up to the wall, holding out her hand, her face full of childlike terror, like a kid about to cry, staring at what scared her. Sonia was looking at him almost the same way now, helpless and terrified. She pressed her left hand softly to his chest and slowly got up from the bed, moving further away, her eyes glued to him even more. Her fear was contagious. The same fear showed on his face. He stared at her, almost with the same childlike, helpless smile.
“Do you know now?” he whispered.
“Oh God!” Sonia wailed.

She fell onto the bed, hiding her face in the pillows, but a moment later jumped up, hurried to him, grabbed both his hands, and stared into his face, gripping his hands tightly with her thin fingers. In this desperate look, she was searching for some last bit of hope. But there was none; it was all true. Later, looking back, she wondered why she hadn’t doubted him for even a second. She couldn’t have said she’d expected it, and yet, after he told her, it was like she’d always known.
“Stop, Sonia, enough! Don’t torture me,” he begged.
This wasn’t at all the way he thought it would go, but this was how it happened.

She sprang up, not even knowing what she was doing, wringing her hands, pacing the middle of the room; then she rushed back and sat down next to him, almost touching his shoulder. Suddenly, she cried out and collapsed on her knees in front of him, not even knowing why.
“What have you done—what have you done to yourself?” she cried in despair. She jumped up and threw herself around his neck, hugging him tightly.
Raskolnikov pulled back and looked at her with a sad smile.
“You’re a strange girl, Sonia—you hug and kiss me even though I’ve just told you all this... You don’t even realize what you’re doing.”
“There’s no one—no one in the whole world as unhappy as you!” she cried, almost wild, not even hearing his words, and burst into uncontrollable sobs.
A feeling he hadn’t had in a long time rushed into his heart, softening it at once. He didn’t try to fight it. Two tears filled his eyes and clung to his lashes.
“So you won’t leave me, Sonia?” he asked, looking at her hopefully.
“No, no, never, nowhere!” Sonia cried. “I’ll follow you, I’ll follow you anywhere. Oh, God! Oh, I’m so miserable! Why, why didn’t I meet you sooner? Why didn’t you come before? Oh, dear!”
“Well, I’m here now.”
“Yes, now! What do we do now?... Together, together!” she repeated, almost without realizing it, hugging him again. “I’ll follow you to Siberia!”
He pulled away at that, and a strange, proud, almost harsh smile appeared on his lips.
“Maybe I don’t want to go to Siberia yet, Sonia,” he said.
Sonia looked at him quickly.

After her first wave of wild sympathy for him, the terrible thought of the murder hit her again. His new tone sounded like a murderer’s. She stared at him in confusion. She didn’t know anything yet about why or how it happened. All these questions hit her at once. She still couldn’t believe it: “He, he’s a murderer? Could it really be?”
“What does it mean? Where am I?” she said, totally lost, as if she still couldn’t believe it. “How could you, you, a man like you... How could you do it?... What does it mean?”
“Oh, just for the money. Stop, Sonia,” he answered tiredly, almost annoyed.
Sonia was stunned into silence, but suddenly she cried:
“You were starving! It was... to help your mother? Wasn’t it?”
“No, Sonia, no,” he said, turning away and hanging his head. “I wasn’t starving... I did want to help my mother, but... that’s not the real reason either... Don’t torture me, Sonia.”
Sonia clasped her hands together.

“Could it—could it all be true? Oh God, what a truth! Who could believe it? And how could you give away your last bit of money and then rob and murder! Wait,” she cried suddenly, “the money you gave Katerina Ivanovna... that money... Was it...?”

“No, Sonia,” he cut in quickly, “that money wasn’t it. Don’t worry! That money was from my mother, it came when I was sick, the day I gave it to you... Razumihin saw it... he got it for me... That money was mine—my own.”
Sonia listened, confused, trying her best to understand.

“And the other money... I don’t even know if there was any real money,” he added softly, as if thinking aloud. “I took a purse from her neck, made of chamois leather... it was stuffed with something... but I didn’t look in it; I guess I didn’t have time... And the stuff—chains and trinkets—I buried under a stone with the purse the next morning in a yard off V—— Prospect. They’re still there now...”
Sonia strained to catch every word.
“Then why...? You said you did it to rob, but you took nothing?” she asked quickly, desperate for some hope.
“I don’t know... I still haven’t decided whether to take that money or not,” he said, lost in thought; then, snapping out of it, he gave a quick, bitter smile. “Ugh, what nonsense I’m talking, huh?”
Sonia wondered for a second if he was insane. But she dismissed it immediately. “No, it’s something else.” She just couldn’t figure it out.

“You know, Sonia,” he said suddenly, sounding sure, “I’ll tell you this: if I’d killed just because I was starving,” he emphasized every word and looked at her with a strange, honest expression, “I’d be happy now. You have to believe that! Why does it matter to you,” he cried in despair a moment later, “why does it matter to you if I admit I did wrong? What do you get from seeing me suffer like this? Oh, Sonia, did I come to you today just for that?”
Sonia tried to say something, but couldn’t speak.
“I asked you to come with me yesterday because you’re all I have left.”
“Go where?” Sonia asked shyly.

“Not to steal or kill, don’t worry,” he said with a bitter smile. “We’re so different... And you know, Sonia, it’s only now, at this moment, that I understand what I asked you yesterday! Yesterday, I didn’t know why. I came for one thing—not to be alone. You won’t leave me, Sonia?”
She squeezed his hand.

“And why, why did I tell you? Why did I let you know?” he cried a minute later, looking at her with endless pain. “You want an explanation from me, Sonia; you’re just sitting there waiting for one, I can see it. But what can I tell you? You wouldn’t understand and it would just make you miserable... because of me! And now you’re crying and hugging me again. Why do you do that? Because I couldn’t handle my burden and I came to dump it on you: now you suffer too, and maybe I’ll feel better! And how could you love someone as rotten as me?”
“But aren’t you suffering, too?” Sonia cried.
Again, that same feeling washed over him, and for a moment, softened his heart.

“Sonia, I have a bad heart, remember that. Maybe that explains a lot. I came to you because I’m bad. Some people wouldn’t have come at all. But I’m a coward and... a pathetic loser. But... never mind, that’s not the point. I have to talk now, but I don’t know where to start.”
He paused, lost in thought.
“Ugh, we’re so different,” he cried again, “we’re nothing alike. And why did I come? I’ll never forgive myself for that.”
“No, no, it was good you came,” Sonia said. “It’s better I know, much better!”
He looked at her with pain.
“But what if that’s really it?” he said, as if realizing something. “Yes, that’s it! I wanted to be a Napoleon, that’s why I killed her... Do you get it now?”
“N-no,” Sonia whispered, innocent and scared. “Just say it, say it, I’ll understand, I’ll understand, I promise!” she begged.
“You’ll understand? Okay, we’ll see!” He paused and was quiet for a while, deep in thought.

“Here’s how it was: One day I asked myself—what if Napoleon, for example, was in my place, and if he hadn’t had battles or big adventures to start his career, but just some ridiculous old woman, a pawnbroker, he needed to kill for money (for his career, you know). Would he have done it if there was no other way? Would he have felt bad because it wasn’t heroic and... and was sinful? Well, I tormented myself with that question for so long, and then suddenly I realized—he wouldn’t have cared at all, it wouldn’t even have crossed his mind that it wasn’t heroic... he would have strangled her in a second without thinking! So I... stopped worrying about it... and killed her, following his example. That’s exactly what happened! Do you think it’s funny? Yeah, Sonia, the weirdest thing is, maybe that’s really how it was.”
Sonia didn’t think it was funny at all.
“Just tell me straight... without all these examples,” she begged, even more softly.
He looked at her sadly and took her hands.

“You’re right again, Sonia. Of course it’s nonsense, it’s almost all talk! You see, you know my mother has almost nothing, my sister got a good education but ended up as a governess. All their hopes were on me. I was a student, but I couldn’t support myself at university and had to drop out for a while. Even if I’d stayed, maybe in ten or twelve years, if I was lucky, I could hope to be some kind of teacher or clerk with a thousand roubles salary” (he repeated it like a lesson) “and by then my mother would be worn out from worry and I wouldn’t be able to help her, and my sister... well, she might have ended up even worse! And it’s so hard to spend your whole life just passing by everything, turning your back, forgetting your mother and politely accepting the insults your sister faces. Why should I? Even if I got married, had kids, I’d just leave them poor too. So I decided to take the old woman’s money, use it for my first years, stay in university, and after that, build a new life of my own... That’s all... Of course, killing the old woman was wrong... That’s enough.”
He forced himself to finish, exhausted, and let his head drop.
“No, that’s not it, that’s not it,” Sonia cried in distress. “How could someone... no, that’s not right, not right.”
“You see, even you know it’s not right. But I told the truth.”
“Like that could be the truth! Oh God!”
“I only killed a louse, Sonia, a useless, disgusting, harmful thing.”
“A human—a louse!”

“I know she wasn’t just a louse,” he said, looking at her strangely. “But I’m talking nonsense, Sonia,” he added. “I’ve been talking nonsense for a long time... That’s not it, you’re right. There were other reasons! I haven’t talked to anyone for so long, Sonia... My head hurts so much now.”

His eyes shone with fever. He was almost delirious; a weird, uneasy smile wandered across his lips. His exhaustion showed through his excitement. Sonia saw how much he was suffering. She was getting dizzy too. And the way he talked was so strange; it sort of made sense, but still... “But how, how! Oh God!” She wrung her hands in despair.

“No, Sonia, that’s not it,” he started again suddenly, lifting his head, as if a new thought had just hit him—“that’s not it! Better... imagine—yes, it’s better—imagine that I’m vain, jealous, mean, cruel, bitter, and... maybe kind of crazy. (Let’s admit it all! They’ve called me crazy already, I noticed.) I told you before I couldn’t keep going at university. But you know, maybe I could have. My mom would’ve sent me enough for fees, and I could’ve earned money for clothes, shoes, and food. Jobs were out there at half a rouble. Razumihin works! But I got sulky and refused. (Yeah, sulky, that’s the word!) I sat in my room like a spider. You saw my place... And you know, Sonia, low ceilings and tiny rooms just crush a person? Oh, how I hated that attic! And yet I wouldn’t leave it! I stayed inside for days, wouldn’t work, wouldn’t eat, just lay there. If Nastasya brought food, I ate it; if not, I went without, on purpose! At night, no light, I lay in the dark and wouldn’t earn money for candles. I should’ve studied, but I pawned my books; now dust is an inch thick on my notebooks. I just lay there, thinking... and I kept thinking... And I had all kinds of weird dreams, no need to describe them! Only then I started to believe that... No, that’s not it! Again I’m saying it wrong! You see, I kept asking myself: why am I so dumb that even though others are dumb—and I know they are—I won’t be smarter? Then I realized, Sonia, if you wait for everyone to get smarter, it’ll take forever... Later, I saw that’ll never happen, people won’t change, and no one can change it, so it’s not worth the effort. Yes, that’s how people are, Sonia... that’s just it! And now I know, Sonia, that anyone strong in mind and spirit can rule others. The bravest ones are always seen as right. The ones who care least about rules become leaders, and the boldest are always right! That’s how it’s always been and always will be. You’d have to be blind not to see it!”

Even though Raskolnikov looked at Sonia as he said this, he hardly cared if she understood. The fever had taken over; he was in a kind of dark excitement (he definitely hadn’t talked to anyone for too long). Sonia could see that this gloomy idea had become his whole way of thinking.

“I realized then, Sonia,” he went on eagerly, “that power only goes to the person who dares to take it. There’s only one thing you need: you just have to dare! That was the first time in my life that I had an idea I thought no one had ever had before me, no one! I saw so clearly how strange it is that no one in this crazy world has ever dared to just go for it all and wreck the whole thing! I... I wanted to be brave... and I killed her. I just wanted to be brave, Sonia! That’s the real reason!”
“Oh stop, stop,” cried Sonia, wringing her hands. “You turned away from God and He’s punished you, given you over to the devil!”
“So, Sonia, when I used to lie there in the dark and all this came to me, was it the devil tempting me, huh?”
“Stop, don’t joke, blasphemer! You don’t get it, you just don’t get it! Oh God! He’ll never understand!”

“Quiet, Sonia! I’m not joking. I know it was the devil leading me. Quiet, Sonia, quiet!” he repeated, dark and insistent. “I know all of it, I’ve thought it over and over, whispered it to myself in the dark... I’ve argued with myself about every detail, and I know it all, every bit! And how sick I got of thinking it all through! I’ve wanted to forget it all, start over, stop thinking. And you mustn’t think I just ran into this like a fool. I went into it like a smart man, and that was my downfall. And don’t think I didn’t know, for example, that if I started asking myself whether I had the right to grab power—I definitely didn’t—or that if I wondered if a human being is just a louse, it proved I didn’t see them as one, even if someone else could. If I struggled for days wondering if Napoleon would have done it, it was obvious I wasn’t Napoleon. I had to put up with all that mental pain, Sonia, and I wished I could just be rid of it. I wanted to murder without all this debating, just for myself! I didn’t even want to lie to myself. It wasn’t to help my mother that I did it—that’s crap—I didn’t do it to get rich or powerful and help humanity. Nonsense! I just did it; I killed for myself, only for me, and whether I helped people or trapped them like a spider, I didn’t care at that moment... And it wasn’t the money I wanted, Sonia, when I did it. It wasn’t really about the money, but something else... I get it now... Understand me! Maybe I’d never have murdered again. I wanted to find out something else; something else drove me. I wanted to know, right then, if I was a louse like everyone else or a man. If I could step over boundaries or not, if I dared to take what I wanted, if I was a trembling thing or if I had the right...”
“To kill? To have the right to kill?” Sonia cried, wringing her hands.

“Ugh, Sonia!” he said, irritated, about to say something but then falling silent. “Don’t interrupt, Sonia. I just want to prove one thing: that the devil led me, and he’s shown me now that I had no right to take that path, because I’m just as much a louse as everyone else. He was mocking me, and now I’ve come to you! Welcome your guest! If I weren’t a louse, would I have come to you? Listen: when I went to the old woman’s, I just went to try... You can be sure of that!”
“But you killed her!”

“But how did I kill her? Is that how people commit murder? Do people go to kill like I did? I’ll tell you someday how it happened! Did I kill the old woman? I really killed myself, not her! I destroyed myself forever... But it was the devil who killed the old woman, not me. Enough, Sonia, enough! Leave me alone!” he cried suddenly, in agony. “Leave me alone!”
He put his elbows on his knees and pressed his head in his hands like a vice.
“What suffering!” Sonia wailed.
“So what do I do now?” he asked, suddenly looking up at her with a face twisted by despair.

“What should you do?” she cried, jumping up, and her tear-filled eyes suddenly started shining. “Stand up!” (She grabbed his shoulder; he stood, almost in a daze.) “Go right now, this minute, stand at the crossroads, bow down, first kiss the earth you’ve stained, then bow to everyone and say out loud, ‘I’m a murderer!’ Then God will give you new life. Will you do it, will you?” she asked, trembling, grabbing both his hands and staring at him with burning eyes.
He was shocked by her sudden passion.
“You mean Siberia, Sonia? I should turn myself in?” he asked darkly.
“Suffer and make up for your sin by doing that, that’s what you have to do.”
“No! I’m not going to the police, Sonia!”

“But how will you live? What will you live for?” Sonia cried. “How is that possible now? How can you talk to your mother? (Oh, what will become of them?) But what am I saying? You already abandoned your mother and sister. He’s abandoned them! Oh, God!” she cried, “he knows it himself. How, how can he live alone! What’s going to happen to you now?”

“Don’t be a child, Sonia,” he said softly. “What have I done to them? Why should I go to them? What would I say? That’s just a ghost... They destroy millions and call it good. They’re all thieves and liars, Sonia! I’m not going to them. And what would I say—that I murdered her, but didn’t even take the money and hid it under a stone?” he added with a bitter smile. “They’d laugh at me, call me stupid for not taking it. A coward and a fool! They wouldn’t understand and don’t deserve to. Why go to them? I won’t. Don’t be a child, Sonia...”
“It’ll be too much for you, too much!” she repeated, reaching out desperately.
“Maybe I’ve been too hard on myself,” he said darkly, thinking. “Maybe I am a man, not a louse, and I judged myself too quickly. I’ll try to fight it out.”
A proud smile crossed his lips.
“What a burden! And your whole life, your whole life!”

“I’ll get used to it,” he said grimly, thinking. “Listen,” he said a minute later, “stop crying, it’s time to talk about real things: I came to tell you the police are after me, they’re on my trail...”
“Oh!” Sonia gasped in fear.

“Why are you so shocked? You want me to go to Siberia, but now you’re scared? But listen: I’m not turning myself in. I’ll fight, and they won’t get me. They don’t have real evidence. Yesterday I was in real danger and thought I was done for, but today things look better. All the facts they know could be explained away—I can use their accusations to defend myself, you understand? And I will, I’ve learned my lesson. But they’ll definitely arrest me. If something hadn’t happened, they would have today for sure; maybe they still will, even now... But that’s not important, Sonia; they’ll let me go again... because they don’t have real proof, and they won’t get it, I promise. They can’t convict me with what they have. That’s it... I just wanted you to know... I’ll try to explain things to my mother and sister so they don’t get scared... My sister’s future is safe now, I think... and my mother’s should be too... Well, that’s all. Be careful, though. Will you come visit me in prison if I’m there?”
“Oh, I will, I will.”

They sat side by side, both sad and depressed, like they’d been washed up alone on a deserted shore after a storm. Raskolnikov looked at Sonia and realized how much she truly loved him—and strangely, he felt that being so loved hurt and weighed him down. Yes, it was a strange and terrible feeling! On his way to Sonia, he’d thought all his hope was in her; he expected to get rid of at least some of his pain, and now, when she gave him all her love, he suddenly felt even more miserable than before.
“Sonia,” he said, “maybe you shouldn’t visit me in prison.”
Sonia didn’t answer; she was crying. Several minutes passed.
“Do you have a cross?” she asked, like she’d just remembered.
He didn’t get the question at first.

“No, of course not. Here, take this one—it’s made of cypress wood. I have another, a copper one that belonged to Lizaveta. I swapped with Lizaveta: she gave me her cross and I gave her my little icon. I’ll wear Lizaveta’s now and give you this one. Take it... it’s mine! It’s mine, you know,” she begged him. “We’ll go through this together, and together we’ll carry our cross!”
“Give it to me,” said Raskolnikov.
He didn’t want to hurt her feelings. But right away, he pulled back the hand he’d held out for the cross.
“Not now, Sonia. Better later,” he added gently.
“Yes, yes, better,” she agreed, “when you go to face your suffering, then put it on. You’ll come to me, I’ll put it on you, we’ll pray and go together.”
Just then, someone knocked three times at the door.
“Sofya Semyonovna, may I come in?” they heard a very familiar, polite voice say.
Sonia rushed to the door in a panic. Mr. Lebeziatnikov’s blond head poked in the doorway.
Lebeziatnikov looked upset and worried.

“I came to see you, Sofya Semyonovna,” he began. “Sorry... I figured you’d be here,” he added, suddenly glancing at Raskolnikov. “Not for any... weird reason... I just thought...” Then he blurted out, turning back to Sonia, “Katerina Ivanovna has lost her mind.”
Sonia let out a scream.

“At least, it looks that way. But... we don’t know what to do! She came back—seems like she was thrown out somewhere, maybe even beaten. She tried to find your dad’s old boss, but he wasn’t home—he was having dinner at another general’s place. Can you believe it? She chased after him there, and somehow managed to get him pulled out of dinner. You can imagine what happened next. She was thrown out, of course, but she says she yelled at him and threw something at him. That sounds about right... I don’t know how she didn’t get arrested! Now she’s telling everyone—including Amalia Ivanovna—but it’s hard to understand her; she’s screaming and flailing around. Oh, and she keeps shouting that since everyone’s abandoned her, she’ll take the kids and go out in the street with a barrel organ. The kids will sing and dance for money, and she will too, right under the general’s window, so everyone can see ‘well-bred children whose father was an official, begging in the street.’ She keeps beating the children, and they’re all crying. She’s teaching Lida to sing ‘My Village,’ and the boy to dance, and Polenka too. She’s tearing up their clothes to make costumes, like little actors, and wants to bang a tin basin for music. She won’t listen to anything. Just imagine! It’s completely out of control!”

Lebeziatnikov would have kept going, but Sonia, who had listened almost without breathing, grabbed her cloak and hat, and rushed out, trying to put them on as she ran. Raskolnikov followed her, and Lebeziatnikov hurried after them.

“She’s definitely lost her mind!” he told Raskolnikov as they walked out. “I didn’t want to scare Sofya Semyonovna, so I said it just ‘seemed like it,’ but there’s no doubt. I’ve heard that with tuberculosis, sometimes it gets into the brain. Too bad I know nothing about medicine. I tried to talk to her, but she wouldn’t listen.”
“Did you actually mention the tuberculosis to her?”

“Not exactly the tuberculosis. Besides, she wouldn’t have understood! But I think, if you can logically explain to someone that there’s nothing to cry about, they’ll stop crying. That’s just obvious, right? Don’t you think so?”
“If only it were that simple,” Raskolnikov replied.

“Excuse me, excuse me; of course, it’d be hard for Katerina Ivanovna to get it, but did you know that in Paris they’ve actually tried to cure insane people just by reasoning with them? A famous professor—he died recently—believed insanity was just a logical mistake, like seeing the world wrong. He would talk to the patient and show them their errors, and they say he actually got results! Though he also used cold showers, so maybe that helped too... At least, that’s what it seems.”
Raskolnikov had stopped listening a while ago. When they reached his building, he nodded to Lebeziatnikov and went inside. Lebeziatnikov snapped out of his thoughts, looked around, and hurried off.

Raskolnikov entered his small room and stood in the middle, uncertain why he’d come back. He glanced at the yellowed, torn wallpaper, the dust, his old sofa. From the yard, he heard loud, steady hammering—someone was banging on something. He went to the window, stood on tiptoes, and stared down into the yard, fully focused, but the yard was empty and he couldn’t see who was making the noise. In the house next door, windows were open, sick-looking geraniums sat on the sills, and laundry hung out. He knew it all by heart. He turned away and sat on the sofa.
He had never, ever felt so terribly alone.
Again, he felt that maybe he’d end up hating Sonia, now that he had made her even more miserable.
“Why did I go to her, begging for her tears? Why did I have to make her life worse? How low can I get?”
“I’ll stay alone,” he said firmly. “She shouldn’t come to visit me in prison.”
Five minutes later, he lifted his head with a strange little smile. That was such a strange idea.
“Maybe Siberia really would be better,” he thought all of a sudden.

He couldn’t have said how long he sat there, lost in confused thoughts, when suddenly the door opened and Dounia came in. She paused in the doorway, watching him, just as he had watched Sonia before. Then she came in and sat in the same chair as yesterday, right in front of him. He stared at her in silence, almost as if he wasn’t really seeing her.
“Don’t be mad, brother; I’ve only come for a minute,” said Dounia.
Her face looked serious, but not harsh. Her eyes were bright and gentle. He realized she had come out of love for him.

“Brother, now I know everything. Dmitri Prokofitch (Razumihin) explained it all to me. They’re bothering and accusing you because of some stupid suspicion. Dmitri Prokofitch said there’s no real danger, and that you’re wrong to be so afraid. I’m not so sure, and I can see why you’re so upset—and I worry that this anger might stay with you forever. That’s what scares me. About you cutting yourself off from us—I don’t blame you, and I’m sorry I ever did. If I had such a big problem, I’d probably hide from everyone too. I won’t tell Mother about this, but I’ll talk about you all the time and tell her you’ll come soon. Don’t worry about her; I’ll calm her down. But please don’t make her wait too long—come at least once. Remember, she’s your mother. And I came now just to say—” (Dounia started to stand up) “that if you ever need me, or need... anything, even my whole life... just call me, and I’ll come. Goodbye!”
She turned quickly and went to the door.
“Dounia!” Raskolnikov called after her and walked toward her. “That Razumihin—Dmitri Prokofitch—is really a good guy.”
Dounia blushed a little.
“Well?” she asked, pausing.
“He’s smart, hardworking, honest, and truly capable of loving someone... Goodbye, Dounia.”
Dounia blushed bright red, then suddenly looked worried.
“What’s that supposed to mean, brother? Are we really saying goodbye forever, that you... tell me something like that?”
“Don’t worry about it... Goodbye.”
He turned away and walked to the window. She stood there for a second, looked at him anxiously, and left, troubled.
No, he hadn’t been cold to her. For a brief second—the last one—he’d wanted to hug her and say goodbye, maybe even tell her everything, but he hadn’t dared to even touch her hand.
“Later, she’d probably shudder remembering I hugged her, and feel like I stole a kiss.”
“Would she really be able to handle the truth?” he thought a few minutes later. “No, she wouldn’t; girls like her can’t handle things like this. They never do.”
Then he thought of Sonia.
A breath of fresh air drifted in from the window. It was getting dark. He grabbed his cap and went out.

Of course, he couldn’t and wouldn’t admit how sick he really was. But all the constant stress and worry were taking a toll. If he wasn’t flat in bed with a fever, it was probably only because this constant tension kept him moving and thinking straight. But he couldn’t keep this up much longer.

He wandered the streets without any purpose. The sun was setting. Lately, a special kind of misery had started weighing him down. It wasn’t sharp or sudden, but it felt endless, like it would last forever—a taste of hopeless years ahead, stuck in a tiny space. Toward evening, this feeling always got worse.
“With this stupid, purely physical weakness—maybe it’s the sunset or something—you can’t help but do something dumb! You’ll end up going to see Dounia, and Sonia too,” he muttered bitterly.
He heard someone call his name. He turned. Lebeziatnikov rushed up.

“You won’t believe it—I went to your room looking for you. She’s actually done it—she took the kids! Sofya Semyonovna and I had a hard time tracking them down. She’s banging on a frying pan and making the kids dance. The kids are crying. They keep stopping at intersections and in front of shops, and a crowd of idiots is following them. Come on!”
“And Sonia?” Raskolnikov asked anxiously, hurrying after Lebeziatnikov.

“She’s frantic. Well, not as frantic as Katerina Ivanovna—she’s totally lost it. I’m telling you, she’s mad. They’re going to get taken to the police. Just think what that’ll do... They’re on the canal bank near the bridge now, not far from Sofya Semyonovna’s place, really close.”

On the canal bank near the bridge, just a couple of houses from Sonia’s building, a crowd had gathered—mostly street kids. From the bridge, you could hear Katerina Ivanovna’s hoarse, broken voice. It was a crazy scene, the kind that draws a crowd. Katerina Ivanovna, in her old dress and green shawl, a torn straw hat smashed crooked on her head, was truly frantic. She was exhausted and out of breath. Her thin, sickly face looked even worse in the daylight. But she never stopped, and kept getting more worked up. She rushed at the kids, yelled at them, begged them, explained in front of everyone how to dance and what to sing, and when they didn’t get it, she hit them. Then she’d rush at the crowd, and if she saw anyone well-dressed, she’d beg them to see what “good, well-bred children” had been reduced to. If anyone laughed, she’d yell at them too. Some people laughed, others shook their heads, but everyone was curious about the crazy woman and the scared kids. The frying pan Lebeziatnikov had mentioned wasn’t there—at least, Raskolnikov didn’t see it. Instead, Katerina Ivanovna clapped her thin hands to make Lida and Kolya dance and Polenka sing. She tried singing too, but broke off coughing so badly that she cursed and even cried. What made her angriest was Kolya and Lida crying in terror. The kids had been dressed up like street performers. The boy wore a homemade red-and-white turban to look like a Turk. Lida just had a red knitted cap—really an old nightcap of Marmeladov’s—decorated with a broken piece of white ostrich feather from Katerina Ivanovna’s grandmother. Polenka wore her everyday dress, looking at her mother with scared confusion, staying close and hiding her tears. She sort of understood her mother wasn’t right and kept looking around nervously. She was terrified of the street and the crowd. Sonia followed Katerina Ivanovna, crying and begging her to go home, but Katerina Ivanovna wouldn’t listen.

“Stop it, Sonia, stop!” she shouted, talking fast, panting and coughing. “You don’t get it; you’re like a little kid! I told you before, I’m not going back to that drunken German woman. Let everyone, all Petersburg, see these children begging—even though their father was an honest man who served all his life and died in service.” (Katerina Ivanovna had made this story up and believed it now.) “Let that awful general see! And you’re silly, Sonia—what are we supposed to eat? We’ve already been a burden to you, and I won’t let it go on! Oh, Rodion Romanovitch, is that you?” she called, seeing Raskolnikov and running up to him. “Tell this silly girl that what I’m doing is the only thing left! Even organ-grinders earn money, and people will see right away that we’re different—a good family brought down to this. That general will lose his job, you’ll see! We’ll perform under his window every day, and if the Tsar goes by, I’ll get down on my knees, show him the kids, and say, ‘Help us, Father.’ He’s the father of orphans; he’s merciful—he’ll protect us, you’ll see. And that general... Lida, stand up straight! Kolya, you’re going to dance again. Why are you crying? Crying again! What are you scared of, you silly thing? Good grief, what am I supposed to do with them, Rodion Romanovitch? If you only knew how hopeless they are! What’s anyone supposed to do with such kids?”

She pointed at the crying children, almost crying herself, but she couldn’t stop talking. Raskolnikov tried to persuade her to go home, even saying that it wasn’t right for someone hoping to run a boarding school to act like a street performer.

“A boarding school, ha-ha-ha!” laughed Katerina Ivanovna, ending in a cough. “No, Rodion Romanovitch, that dream’s over! Everyone’s abandoned us!... And that general—you know, I threw an inkpot at him! It was just sitting there in the waiting room by the sign-in paper. I wrote my name, tossed it at him, and ran. Oh, those scoundrels! But never mind about them—I’ll take care of the kids myself! No more begging! She’s already done enough for us!” She pointed at Sonia. “Polenka, how much did you get? Show me! What, only two farthings? Oh, these people are so cheap! They just follow us, sticking out their tongues. Why is that fool laughing?” (She pointed at someone in the crowd.) “It’s all Kolya’s fault—he’s impossible. What do you want, Polenka? Tell me in French, parlez-moi français! I’ve taught you, you know some phrases. That’s how people will see you’re well-brought-up kids, not just street performers. We’re not putting on a puppet show, but singing something classy. Ah, yes—what should we sing? You’re confusing me! We’re standing here trying to figure out what to sing to get money, something Kolya can dance to. Obviously, this is all improvised... We need to talk it out and practice, then we’ll go to Nevsky Prospect, where there are more fancy people and they’ll notice us. Lida only knows ‘My Village’—everyone sings that! We need something more refined. Well, have you thought of anything, Polenka? If only you’d help your mother! My memory’s useless now, or I’d have thought of something. We can’t sing ‘An Hussar.’ Oh, let’s sing in French: ‘Cinq sous,’ I taught you that! People will know you’re from a good family, and it’ll be even sadder. Or ‘Marlborough s’en va-t-en guerre’—that’s a child’s song, a lullaby in rich houses.”

“Marlborough s’en va-t-en guerre Ne sait quand reviendra...” she started to sing. “No, better do ‘Cinq sous.’ Now, Kolya, hands on your hips—hurry up! Lida, turn the other way. Polenka and I will sing and clap!”
“Cinq sous, cinq sous Pour monter notre menage.”

(Cough-cough-cough!) “Polenka, fix your dress—it’s slipping off your shoulders,” she said, panting from the coughing. “Now more than ever you have to act proper so people see you’re well-bred. I said the dress should have been longer, made with two pieces. It’s your fault, Sonia, you said to make it shorter, and now look, the child looks all weird... Why are you all crying again? What’s wrong with you? Come on, Kolya, start! Hurry up! Oh, what a hard child to deal with!”
“Cinq sous, cinq sous.
“Oh no, a policeman! What do you want?”

A policeman really was pushing through the crowd. But just then, a well-dressed man in uniform with a medal around his neck—obviously an important official—stepped up and silently handed her a green three-rouble note. He looked genuinely sympathetic. Katerina Ivanovna took the money, giving him a polite, almost formal bow.

“Thank you, honored sir,” she began grandly. “The reasons that have brought us here—(Take the money, Polenka! See, there are decent people who help a poor gentlewoman in trouble.) These orphans are from a good family—aristocratic, even—and that awful general sat eating fancy food and got angry at me for bothering him. ‘Your excellency,’ I said, ‘protect these orphans; you knew my late husband, Semyon Zaharovitch, and on the day of his death the worst people slandered his only daughter...’ Oh, that policeman again! Help me, sir!” she cried to the official. “Why is the policeman coming near me? We just got away from one. What do you want, idiot?”
“You’re not allowed to make a scene in the street.”
“You’re the one making a scene. It’s just like playing an organ in the street. Why is it your business?”
“You need a license to play an organ, and you don’t have one. You’re drawing a crowd. Where do you live?”
“A license?” wailed Katerina Ivanovna. “I buried my husband today. Why would I need a license?”
“Calm down, madam, please,” said the official gently. “Come on, I’ll help you. This isn’t the place for you and the children. You’re sick.”

“Honored sir, you don’t understand!” screamed Katerina Ivanovna. “We’re going to Nevsky Prospect... Sonia! Where is she? She’s crying too! What’s wrong with all of you? Kolya, Lida, where are you going?” she suddenly cried, alarmed. “Oh, silly kids! Kolya, Lida, where are they running off to?...”

Kolya and Lida, terrified by the crowd and their mother’s crazy behavior, grabbed each other’s hands and ran as soon as they saw the policeman coming for them. Crying, poor Katerina Ivanovna chased after them, sobbing and gasping for breath. Sonia and Polenka ran after her.
“Bring them back, Sonia! Oh, stupid, ungrateful children!... Polenka! Catch them! I’m doing this for you...”
As she ran, she tripped and fell down.
“She’s hurt! She’s bleeding! Oh no!” cried Sonia, leaning over her.

Everyone crowded around. Raskolnikov and Lebeziatnikov were the first to reach her, and the official hurried over too, followed by the policeman, who grumbled, “Great,” realizing this was going to be a mess.
“Move along! Move along!” he told the crowd pressing in.
“She’s dying!” someone shouted.
“She’s lost her mind,” said another.
“God have mercy,” said a woman, crossing herself. “Did they catch the kids? The older one got them... Ah, those naughty children!”
When they checked Katerina Ivanovna, they saw she hadn’t cut herself on a stone like Sonia thought. The blood staining the pavement was coming from her chest.

“I’ve seen that before,” the official muttered to Raskolnikov and Lebeziatnikov. “That’s tuberculosis—the patient coughs blood and can’t breathe. Happened to someone in my family recently... nearly a pint of blood in a minute. What can you do? She’s dying.”
“This way, to my room!” Sonia begged. “I live just there—see, the second house from here. Come with me, hurry!” She turned from person to person. “Send for a doctor! Oh, please!”

Thanks to the official’s help, they agreed to Sonia’s plan. The policeman even helped carry Katerina Ivanovna. She was nearly unconscious and they laid her on Sonia’s bed. The blood was still coming, but she seemed a bit more awake. Raskolnikov, Lebeziatnikov, and the official came in behind Sonia, with the policeman, who first pushed back the crowd outside. Polenka came in holding Kolya and Lida, who were shaking and crying. Several people from the Kapernaumovs’ room came in too: the landlord, a strange-looking, lame, one-eyed man with wild hair and whiskers; his wife, who always looked scared; and a bunch of wide-eyed kids. Suddenly, Svidrigaïlov showed up. Raskolnikov stared at him in surprise, not understanding how he’d gotten there or how he hadn’t noticed him before. Someone mentioned a doctor and a priest. The official whispered to Raskolnikov that it was probably too late for a doctor, but he ordered someone to get one anyway. Kapernaumov ran off to fetch help himself.

Meanwhile, Katerina Ivanovna managed to catch her breath. The bleeding stopped for now. She looked with sick, sharp eyes at Sonia, who stood pale and shaking, wiping sweat from her face with a handkerchief. Finally, Katerina Ivanovna asked to be sat up. They propped her up on the bed, holding her upright.
“Where are the kids?” she asked weakly. “Did you bring them, Polenka? Oh, you silly things! Why did you run away... Oh!”
Again, blood covered her dry lips. She moved her eyes around, searching.
“So this is where you live, Sonia! I’ve never been in your room before.”
She looked at Sonia with a suffering face.
“We ruined your life, Sonia. Polenka, Lida, Kolya, come here! Well, here they are, Sonia, take them all! I can’t do it anymore. The party’s over.” (She coughed.) “Lay me down—let me die in peace.”
They laid her back on the pillow.
“What, the priest? I don’t want a priest. You don’t have a ruble to spare. I have no sins. God has to forgive me for free. He knows how much I’ve suffered. And if He won’t forgive me, I don’t care!”

She slipped deeper and deeper into confused, feverish talk. Sometimes she shivered, looked around, recognized people for a moment, then drifted back into delirium. Her breathing was harsh and rough, almost rattling.

“I said to him, your excellency,” she gasped out, pausing for breath after every word. “That Amalia Ludwigovna, ah! Lida, Kolya, hands on your hips, quick! Glissez, glissez! pas de basque! Tap your heels, be graceful!
“Du hast Diamanten und Perlen
“What next? That’s what we should sing.
“Du hast die schönsten Augen Mädchen, was willst du mehr?”
“What an idea! Was willst du mehr? What a silly song! Ah, yes!
“In the heat of midday in the vale of Dagestan.

“Oh, I loved that! I loved that song so much, Polenka! Your father used to sing it when we were engaged... Oh, those days! That’s the song for us! How does it go? I’ve forgotten. Remind me! How does it go?”
She got extremely worked up and tried to sit up. Finally, in a broken, hoarse voice, she started shrieking the words, gasping for air and looking more and more terrified.
“In the heat of midday... in the vale!... of Dagestan!... With lead in my breast!...”

“Your excellency!” she wailed suddenly, her voice breaking and tears streaming down her face, “protect the orphans! You were their father’s guest... almost like family...” She stopped, suddenly aware of where she was, and stared at everyone in terror, but then she saw Sonia and recognized her.
“Sonia, Sonia!” she said softly and lovingly, like she was surprised Sonia was there. “Sonia darling, are you here, too?”
They lifted her up again.
“Enough! It’s over! Goodbye, poor thing! I’m done—I’m broken!” she cried with desperate anger, her head falling heavily back onto the pillow.
She went unconscious again, but this time it didn’t last long. Her pale, yellow face sagged, her mouth fell open, her leg jerked, she gave a deep, deep sigh—and died.

Sonia threw herself on Katerina Ivanovna, wrapped her arms around her, and stayed there with her head pressed against the dead woman’s thin chest. Polenka fell at her mother’s feet, kissing them and sobbing. Kolya and Lida, though too young to understand, sensed something terrible had happened; they put their arms around each other’s shoulders, stared at each other, and both started screaming at the top of their lungs. They were both still in their dress-up costumes: one in a turban, the other in the cap with an ostrich feather.
And how did “the certificate of merit” end up on the bed next to Katerina Ivanovna? It was lying by the pillow—Raskolnikov saw it.
He walked to the window. Lebeziatnikov hurried over to him.
“She’s dead,” he said.
“Rodion Romanovitch, I need a word with you,” said Svidrigaïlov, coming up.
Lebeziatnikov quickly stepped aside, giving them space. Svidrigaïlov drew Raskolnikov further away.

“I’ll handle everything—the funeral and so on. It’s a money issue, and like I told you, I’ve got plenty. I’ll put those two little ones and Polenka in a good orphanage, and I’ll set aside fifteen hundred roubles for each when they grow up, so Sofya Semyonovna won’t have to worry about them. And I’ll help her too, because she’s a good girl, right? Tell Avdotya Romanovna (Dounia) that’s what I’m doing with her ten thousand.”
“Why are you being so generous?” Raskolnikov asked.

“Ah, you don’t trust me!” Svidrigaïlov laughed. “I told you I don’t need the money. Can’t you accept it’s just out of kindness? She wasn’t a ‘louse’”—he nodded at the corner where Katerina Ivanovna’s body lay—“not like some old pawnbroker woman, right? Come on, tell me: should Luzhin keep living and doing bad things, or should she die? If I didn’t help them, Polenka would end up the same way.”
He said this with a sly, almost cheerful look, staring at Raskolnikov

A strange time began for Raskolnikov. It was like he was trapped in a fog, cut off from everyone, with no way out. When he thought back on this period much later, he realized his mind hadn’t always been clear—sometimes he was almost confused or lost, and this lasted on and off until everything finally fell apart.
