He knew he’d gotten lots of things mixed up, like when certain things happened. When he tried to remember it all later, he had to rely on what other people told him to fill in the blanks. He’d confused events and blamed things on circumstances that only existed in his own head. Sometimes he was tortured by nervous panic, but he also remembered long stretches when he felt totally numb, almost like someone close to dying. In those moments, he just wanted to hide from the truth about what was happening to him. There were some important problems that needed attention, but he found them especially annoying to think about. He wished he could just forget about those worries, even though ignoring them could ruin him completely.

One thing that really bothered him was Svidrigaïlov—he thought about him constantly. Ever since Svidrigaïlov had spoken those threatening, unmistakable words in Sonia’s room when Katerina Ivanovna died, Raskolnikov’s mind seemed to stop working right. But even though this new threat made him extremely anxious, he didn’t rush to deal with it. Sometimes, sitting alone in some shabby café in a far-off part of the city, he’d suddenly think of Svidrigaïlov and realize, with fear, that he really needed to talk to the man and figure things out. Once, walking outside the city gates, he actually thought he was supposed to meet Svidrigaïlov there and was waiting for him. Another time, he woke up before dawn, lying on the ground under some bushes, and couldn’t even remember how he’d gotten there.

In the two or three days after Katerina Ivanovna’s death, Raskolnikov ran into Svidrigaïlov a few times at Sonia’s place, where Raskolnikov had gone without any real reason. They spoke a little, but didn’t mention the important topic between them. It was almost as if they silently agreed not to talk about it—at least for now.

Katerina Ivanovna’s body was still in her coffin, and Svidrigaïlov was busy arranging the funeral. Sonia was busy, too. During their last meeting, Svidrigaïlov told Raskolnikov he had worked out something really good for Katerina Ivanovna’s kids—he’d used his connections to get the three orphans into good institutions, and the money he’d given them helped a lot, since it’s easier to place kids who have some money. He also mentioned Sonia and promised he’d visit Raskolnikov himself in a day or two, saying, “There are things we need to discuss... I’d like to consult with you.”

This conversation happened in the hallway on the stairs. Svidrigaïlov looked closely at Raskolnikov and, after a short pause and lowering his voice, asked, “But what’s wrong, Rodion Romanovitch? You don’t seem like yourself. You look and listen, but it’s like nothing’s getting through. Cheer up! We’ll talk things over. I’m just sorry I’m so busy with my own business and with helping others. Ah, Rodion Romanovitch,” he suddenly added, “what everyone really needs is fresh air, fresh air… more than anything!”

He stepped aside to let the priest and his helper pass—they were coming up for the requiem service. Svidrigaïlov had ordered that the service be held twice a day, right on time. Svidrigaïlov went his way. Raskolnikov stood still for a moment, thinking, then followed the priest into Sonia’s room. He stood at the door while the priests began their quiet, slow, and sad prayers. Since he was a child, the thought and presence of death had always felt heavy and mysterious to him, and it had been a long time since he’d heard the requiem. But there was something else here—something even more frightening. He looked at the children: they were all kneeling by the coffin, Polenka was crying, and behind them Sonia prayed softly, almost as if she was afraid, tears running down her face.

“She hasn’t said a word to me in these last two days, hasn’t even looked at me,” Raskolnikov thought suddenly. Sunlight filled the room, incense floated in the air, and the priest read, “Give rest, oh Lord....” Raskolnikov stayed through the whole service. As the priest finished, blessed them, and left, he gave Raskolnikov a strange look. Afterward, Raskolnikov went up to Sonia. She took both his hands and rested her head on his shoulder. This small, kind gesture surprised Raskolnikov. He was struck by how she showed no disgust, no fear, not even a shiver. To him, it felt like the ultimate self-sacrifice.

Sonia didn’t say a word. Raskolnikov squeezed her hand and left. He felt miserable. If he could have escaped to some deserted place forever, he would have gladly done it. But even though he was almost always alone lately, he never really felt alone. Sometimes he’d walk out of town to the highway, and once he even reached a small forest, but the more deserted the place, the more he felt some uneasy presence nearby. It didn’t scare him, but it annoyed him so much that he hurried back to the city, wanting to lose himself in crowds, restaurants, or busy streets. There, he actually felt a bit better—and even lonelier. One evening, he sat in a tavern for an hour, listening to people sing, and remembered actually enjoying it. But suddenly, the same anxiety crept back, like his conscience was nagging him. “Here I am, listening to singing—is this really what I should be doing?” he thought. But he knew that wasn’t the only thing bothering him. There was something else, something urgent, but he couldn’t figure out what exactly. It was a mess in his mind. “No, better to face it again! Better to deal with Porfiry… or Svidrigaïlov. Better to have some kind of confrontation, some challenge. Yes, yes!” he thought. He rushed out of the tavern, almost running. Thinking of Dounia and his mother made him nearly panic. That night, he woke up before dawn among bushes on Krestovsky Island, shaking with fever. He walked home and arrived early in the morning. After a few hours of sleep, the fever was gone, but he woke up late—at two in the afternoon.

He remembered that today was Katerina Ivanovna’s funeral and was actually glad he wasn’t there. Nastasya brought him food; he ate and drank hungrily. His head felt clearer and he was calmer than he’d been for days. He even wondered for a moment why he’d been so panicked before.
The door opened and Razumihin walked in.
“Ah, so you’re eating—not sick, then,” said Razumihin. He pulled up a chair and sat across from Raskolnikov at the table.
Razumihin seemed worried and didn’t try to hide it. He sounded annoyed, but he wasn’t rushing or raising his voice. He looked like he’d made up his mind about something.

“Listen,” he said firmly. “As far as I’m concerned, you can all go to hell, but from what I see, I just can’t figure you out. Don’t think I came here to ask questions—I don’t even want to know! If you tried to tell me your secrets, I’d probably walk out. I’m only here to find out, once and for all, if you’re actually crazy. Everyone seems convinced you’ve lost your mind, or are close to it. Honestly, I kind of thought so too, judging by your weird, awful, and totally confusing behavior lately—especially how you’ve treated your mother and sister. Only a monster or a madman could act like that, so you must be crazy.”
“When did you last see them?”

“Just now. Haven’t you seen them since? What have you been doing? Tell me, please. I’ve already come to see you three times. Your mother’s been really sick since yesterday. She wanted to come to you; Avdotya Romanovna tried to stop her, but she wouldn’t listen. ‘If he’s sick, if he’s losing his mind, who can take care of him like his mother?’ she said. We all came here together, because we couldn’t let her come alone. We kept begging her to stay calm. We came in, but you weren’t here. She sat down, waited ten minutes while we stood there in silence. Then she got up and said, ‘If he’s out, that means he’s fine, but if he’s forgotten his mother, it’s humiliating for me to stand at his door asking for kindness.’ She went home and went straight to bed—now she has a fever. ‘I see,’ she said, ‘that he has time for his girl.’ She means Sofya Semyonovna, your fiancée or your mistress—I don’t know. I went to see Sofya Semyonovna right away to see what was going on. I saw the coffin, the kids crying, Sofya Semyonovna putting them in mourning clothes. No sign of you. I apologized and left, then told Avdotya Romanovna all about it. So, that’s all nonsense, you don’t have a girl—you’re probably just crazy. But here you are, eating boiled beef like you haven’t eaten in three days. Madmen eat too, I guess, but even though you still haven’t said a word to me, you’re not crazy! I’d swear it. So, you can all go to hell—there’s some mystery, some secret, and I’m not going to break my head trying to figure it out. I just came to yell at you,” he finished, getting up, “to get it off my chest. And now I know what I need to do.”
“What are you going to do now?”
“Why do you care what I’m going to do?”
“You’re planning to go get drunk.”
“How… how did you know?”
“It’s pretty obvious.”
Razumihin paused for a moment.
“You’ve always been a level-headed person—never crazy, not once,” he said suddenly, sounding more passionate. “You’re right: I’m going to drink. Goodbye!”
And he started toward the door.
“I was talking with my sister—the day before yesterday, I think—about you, Razumihin.”
“About me? But… how could you have seen her the day before yesterday?” Razumihin stopped and even turned a little pale.
You could see his heart was pounding, slow and strong.
“She came here by herself, sat there, and talked with me.”
“She did?”
“Yes.”
“What did you say to her… I mean, about me?”
“I told her you’re a good, honest, hardworking guy. I didn’t say you’re in love with her, because she already knows that.”
“She knows that?”

“It’s obvious. No matter where I go or what happens to me, you’ll stay and take care of them. I’m basically leaving them in your hands, Razumihin. I’m saying this because I know you love her and your heart is pure. I think she might love you, or maybe she already does. Now you decide for yourself if you still need to go drink or not.”

“Rodya! You see… well… Ah, never mind! But where are you planning to go? If it’s a secret, fine… But I’ll figure out your secret, I’m sure it’s all some silly nonsense you’ve made up. Anyway, you’re a great guy—a really great guy!”

“That’s exactly what I was going to say, except you interrupted me. It’s good you decided not to try to find out these secrets. Let time take care of it; don’t worry. You’ll know everything when you need to. Yesterday, someone told me what people really need is fresh air, fresh air, fresh air. I’m going to see that person now and find out what he meant.”
Razumihin stood there, lost in thought and excitement, coming to his own silent conclusion.
“He’s a political conspirator! That must be it. He’s about to do something desperate, I’m sure of it. That’s the only explanation! And… and Dounia knows,” he suddenly thought.

“So Avdotya Romanovna comes to see you,” he said, carefully choosing his words, “and you’re going to see a man who says we need more air, and so that letter… that must be part of it, too,” he finished, thinking to himself.
“What letter?”

“She got a letter today. It really upset her—a lot. Too much. I tried to talk about you, but she begged me to stop. Then… she said maybe we’d have to part soon… then thanked me for something, then locked herself in her room.”
“She got a letter?” Raskolnikov asked, thinking hard.
“Yeah, and you didn’t know? Hmm…”
They both sat in silence.
“Goodbye, Rodion. There was a time, brother, when I… Never mind, goodbye. See, there was a time… Well, goodbye! I have to go, too. I’m not going to drink. There’s no reason now… That’s all nonsense!”
He hurried out, but just as he was nearly out the door, he opened it again and, looking away, said:

“Oh, by the way, do you remember that murder—Porfiry’s case, the old woman? They’ve got the killer—he confessed and gave proof. He’s one of those workmen, the painter, can you believe it? Remember how I defended them here? Turns out, all that fighting and joking with his friends on the stairs while the porter and the witnesses were going up—he did it on purpose to avoid suspicion. The nerve, the quick thinking of that guy! Hard to believe, but that’s what he says—he confessed everything. And I was such a fool about it! He’s just a genius at fooling the lawyers—so I guess it makes sense! Of course, there are people like that. And the fact that he couldn’t keep up the act and confessed makes his story easier to believe. But what an idiot I was! I was so sure he was innocent!”
“Tell me, please, who told you that, and why does it interest you so much?” Raskolnikov asked, clearly anxious.
“Why does it interest me?… Well, I heard it from Porfiry, among others… He told me most of it.”
“From Porfiry?”
“From Porfiry.”
“What… what did he say?” Raskolnikov asked, looking worried.
“He explained it all really well. Psychologically, you know, in his usual way.”
“He explained it? Explained it himself?”

“Yes, yes; goodbye. I’ll tell you all about it later, but I’m busy now. There was a time I thought… But never mind, another time! Why do I need to drink now? You’ve made me drunk without any alcohol. I’m drunk, Rodya! Goodbye, I’m leaving. I’ll come back soon.”
He left.

“He’s definitely a political conspirator, no doubt about it,” Razumihin decided as he slowly walked down the stairs. “And he’s gotten his sister involved; that really fits Avdotya Romanovna’s personality. There have been secret meetings between them! She hinted at it, too… So many of her words and hints point that way! How else can all this mess be explained? Hm! And to think what I almost believed… Good grief, what was I thinking! I really lost my mind and treated him unfairly! It was that scene under the lamp in the hallway that did it. Ugh! What a stupid, nasty idea I had! Nikolay is a good guy, for confessing… And now it’s all clear! Raskolnikov’s illness, all his weird behavior… even before, in the university, how moody he was, how gloomy… But what about that letter? There’s something in that, too, maybe. Who was it from? I need to find out!”
He thought about Dounia, realizing everything he’d heard, and his heart started pounding—then he suddenly broke into a run.

As soon as Razumihin left, Raskolnikov got up, went to the window, paced from one corner of the tiny room to another, then sat down again on the sofa. He felt almost renewed; the struggle was back, and now, suddenly, there was a way out.

“Yes, there was a way out! Everything had been so suffocating, so tight, the pressure almost unbearable. Sometimes he’d just felt numb. Ever since what happened with Nikolay at Porfiry’s, he’d felt trapped, with no hope. And after Nikolay confessed, on that same day, there was the scene with Sonia; his actions and words had been nothing like he’d planned—they were weak, and deep down, he agreed with Sonia: he couldn’t go on living alone with this on his conscience!

“And Svidrigaïlov was still a mystery… He worried Raskolnikov, but not in the same way. There might be another showdown with Svidrigaïlov. Maybe Svidrigaïlov could even be a way out. But Porfiry was a whole different problem.

“So Porfiry had explained everything to Razumihin, explained it using his psychological tricks. Porfiry again! But to think Porfiry could really believe Nikolay was guilty, after everything that happened between the two of them before Nikolay showed up, after that private interview that could only mean one thing? (During those days, Raskolnikov often thought back to his encounter with Porfiry; he hated to dwell on it.) The words, the gestures, the looks they’d exchanged—Nikolay, whom Porfiry saw through from the first moment, couldn’t have changed Porfiry’s mind.

“And even Razumihin had started to suspect! That scene under the lamp in the corridor really had an effect. He ran straight to Porfiry… But why did Porfiry treat him that way? What was his goal in distracting Razumihin with Nikolay? He must have some plan—some scheme—but what is it? It’s true, it’s been a while since that morning—too long—and Porfiry hasn’t shown up. That’s not a good sign…”

Raskolnikov grabbed his cap and left his room, still deep in thought. It was the first time in a long while he felt his mind was clear, at least. “I need to settle things with Svidrigaïlov,” he thought, “and soon; he seems to be waiting for me, too.” At that moment, he was so full of hate for both Porfiry and Svidrigaïlov that he felt like he could kill either of them—if not now, then maybe soon.
“We’ll see, we’ll see,” he repeated to himself.

But as soon as he opened the door, he ran straight into Porfiry himself in the hallway. Porfiry was coming to see him. Raskolnikov was shocked for a moment, but only for a moment. Strangely, he didn’t feel that surprised or even afraid to see Porfiry. He was just startled, but quickly put himself on guard. “Maybe this is the end? But how did Porfiry sneak up so quietly, like a cat, so I didn’t even hear him? Was he listening at the door?”

“You weren’t expecting a visitor, Rodion Romanovitch,” Porfiry said, laughing. “I’ve been meaning to drop by for a while; since I was passing, I thought I’d stop in for five minutes. Are you going out? I won’t keep you long. Just let me have a cigarette.”
“Sit down, Porfiry Petrovitch, sit down.” Raskolnikov offered him a seat with such a friendly, welcoming look that he would have been amazed at himself if he could’ve seen his own face.

The final moment had come—he had to face the last drop of trouble! It’s like a man who has spent half an hour terrified that a robber will kill him, but once the knife is at his throat, he feels no fear.
Raskolnikov sat right across from Porfiry and stared him down. Porfiry squinted and began to light a cigarette.
“Say something

"Ugh, these cigarettes!" Porfiry Petrovitch finally said, lighting one up. "They're terrible for me—just awful—but I can't quit! They make me cough, my throat gets scratchy, and it's getting hard to breathe. You know I'm a bit of a coward. I went to see Dr. B——n recently—he spends at least half an hour with every patient. He actually laughed when he checked me over. He listened to my chest and said, 'Tobacco's bad for you; your lungs aren't in good shape.' But how am I supposed to give it up? What can replace it? I don't even drink—that's the problem, ha ha! Everything in life is relative, Rodion Romanovitch, everything!"
"He's playing his detective games again," Raskolnikov thought, feeling annoyed. The memory of their last meeting hit him all at once, bringing back the same rush of emotions.

"I came to see you the night before last, in the evening. You didn't know?" Porfiry continued, looking around the room. "I came right into this very place. I was walking by, just like today, and thought I'd return your visit. Your door was wide open, so I walked in, looked around, waited, and left without telling your servant. Don't you ever lock your door?"
Raskolnikov's face grew darker and more tense. Porfiry seemed to notice how he was feeling.
"I've come to clear things up with you, Rodion Romanovitch, my friend! I owe you an explanation and I'm going to give it," he said, giving Raskolnikov's knee a gentle pat and a quick smile.
But right away, Porfiry's face changed—he suddenly looked serious and tired. Raskolnikov was surprised to see a hint of sadness there. He had never seen Porfiry look like that before.

"Last time we met, things got pretty weird between us, Rodion Romanovitch. Our first meeting was strange too, but then... well, things just kept piling up! Here's the thing: I may have been unfair to you, and I feel bad about it. Do you remember how we parted? Both our nerves were shot—your knees were shaking, and so were mine. Honestly, our behavior was pretty embarrassing, not very gentlemanly at all. But we are gentlemen, after all, and that matters. Remember what happened? It was really out of line."
"What's he trying to do? What does he think of me?" Raskolnikov wondered, confused, lifting his head to look Porfiry in the eye.

"I've decided it's better for us to be honest with each other," Porfiry went on, turning his head away and lowering his eyes, like he didn't want to make Raskolnikov uncomfortable, and as if he was done with his mind games. "Suspicions and scenes like that can't go on forever. If Nikolay hadn't shown up, who knows where things would have gone? That workman was sitting in the next room at the time—can you imagine? Of course you know all this; I know he came to see you later. But what you thought wasn't true: I hadn't sent for anyone or set anything up. Why not? I don't know—I was caught off guard. I had just called for the porters (you probably saw them as you left). Suddenly, I got an idea. At the time, I was really sure about you, Rodion Romanovitch. I thought—even if I missed something, I'd catch you another way—I wouldn't lose what I was after. You're naturally jumpy and sensitive, Rodion Romanovitch—it's kind of extreme, compared to the rest of your character, which I think I've figured out a bit. Of course, I knew even then that it's rare for someone to just stand up and spill everything. Sometimes it happens, if you push hard enough, but not often. I knew that. If only I had a single fact, even a tiny one, something solid—not just psychology. If someone's guilty, there has to be something real you can get from them—sometimes, you get surprising results. I was counting on your temperament, Rodion Romanovitch, more than anything! I had high hopes for you then."
"But what are you getting at now?" Raskolnikov finally muttered, not even thinking about his words.
"What is he talking about?" he wondered, almost dizzy with confusion. "Does he seriously think I'm innocent?"

"What am I getting at? I'm here to explain myself—I feel I owe you that. I want you to understand how this whole mess and misunderstanding started. I've made you suffer a lot, Rodion Romanovitch. I’m not some kind of monster. I know what it's like for someone proud, strong-willed, and impatient to go through what you did. I think you have a noble character, and you're not without kindness, even if I don't agree with all your ideas. I wanted to tell you that honestly, because I really don't want to trick you. When I first met you, I actually liked you. Maybe you'll laugh at that—you have every right. I know you never liked me, and I get why. Think what you want, but I want to erase that bad impression and show you that I’m a decent person with feelings and a conscience. I'm being straight with you."
Porfiry paused, looking serious. Raskolnikov suddenly felt a wave of fear. The idea that Porfiry actually believed he was innocent started to make him nervous.

"There's no need to go over every little detail," Porfiry continued. "I couldn't even if I tried. It started with rumors. Who spread them, how, or when—I don't need to explain. My suspicions started from a total accident; it might not have even happened. What was it? Hm, I don't think that's important either. Those rumors and that accident gave me an idea. I admit it—I was the first to suspect you. The old woman's notes about the pawned stuff and everything—they didn’t prove anything. Yours was just one pledge among many. I also heard about what happened at the office, from a guy who described it really well, almost like he was reliving it. One thing after another, Rodion Romanovitch! How could I not start connecting the dots? But a hundred suspicions don't make proof, like the English say. Still, lawyers are human; it's hard not to get caught up in ideas. I also thought about that article you wrote for the journal—remember, we talked about it the first time you visited? I made fun of you then, but only to get you talking. I saw you were bold, stubborn, and had felt a lot. I’ve felt the same way, so your article struck a chord with me. I could tell it was written during sleepless nights, with a pounding heart, and hidden excitement. That kind of quiet passion in young people can be risky! I teased you, but honestly, I love reading those intense first essays—you can feel the youthful pride and desperation. Your article is gloomy and kind of wild, but that's what makes it interesting. After reading it, I thought, ‘this guy won't follow the usual path.’ So, after all that, how could I not notice what happened next? But I'm not accusing you now—I'm just telling you what I thought back then. And really, there was nothing solid to go on. A prosecutor shouldn't let himself get carried away by ideas. Meanwhile, here was Nikolay, with actual evidence against him—believe what you want, but it's evidence. He brought his own psychology into it, too, and I had to consider him—it's life or death. Why am I telling you all this? Because I want you to understand, and not think I was being cruel. I wasn't, really! Do you think I didn't search your room back then? I did, I did! I was here when you were sick in bed, not officially, but I was here. We searched your room from top to bottom right away, but found nothing! I thought, he'll come on his own—if he's guilty, he’ll come. Another guy wouldn’t, but you would. Remember how Razumihin started talking about the case with you? We planned that to make you react—we spread rumors on purpose so Razumihin would bring it up, and he's not one to hide his feelings. Zametov was stunned by your anger and your boldness. Imagine blurting out in a restaurant, 'I killed her.' That was so reckless! Even I thought, if he's guilty, he's a real challenge. I was waiting for you. But you totally shocked Zametov and—well, here's the thing: this kind of psychology can be seen both ways! So I kept waiting, and you did come! My heart was beating so fast. Oh!"

"Why did you even come? And your laugh when you walked in—do you remember? I saw it all so clearly, but if I hadn’t been expecting you, I might not have noticed anything strange. That’s how much your mood can affect things! Then there’s Razumihin—and that stone, the one where you hid the stuff! I keep picturing it in a backyard garden. Wasn’t it in a garden? You told Zametov, and then you repeated it to me? And when we started picking apart your article, your explanations could be taken two different ways, like you were hiding another meaning."

"So that’s how, Rodion Romanovitch, I went as far as possible, then stopped myself and wondered what I was even doing. After all, you could explain everything in another way, and honestly, that seemed more likely. I had to admit it. So I thought, 'No, I need a real fact.' Then, when I heard about you ringing the bell, I got all excited. 'Here’s my fact,' I thought, and I didn’t even think it through. I would have paid a thousand roubles to see you walking with that workman after he called you a murderer, and you didn’t even ask him a question the whole way. And then there’s your shaking, and the bell-ringing when you were sick and half out of your mind."

"So, Rodion Romanovitch, can you blame me for playing tricks on you? And what made you show up at just that moment? It was like someone sent you, honestly! If Nikolay hadn't interrupted us... do you remember Nikolay then? That was a shock—a real shock! How could I believe it? Even after you left and he started giving really believable answers about some things, even then I didn't trust his story! See how stubborn I am? No, I thought, tomorrow morning. What does Nikolay have to do with it?"
"Razumihin just told me you think Nikolay is guilty, and that you told him so yourself..."

His voice trailed off, and he stopped. He had been listening, completely wound up, as this man who seemed to see right through him kept changing his story. He was afraid to believe Porfiry, but kept searching his words for something more definite.

"Mr. Razumihin!" Porfiry exclaimed, sounding glad that Raskolnikov finally said something. "Heh! But I had to keep Razumihin out of this—two people is company, three is a crowd. Besides, Razumihin is an outsider. He came running to me, looking terrified... But forget about him. Back to Nikolay—do you want to know what kind of person he is, as I see him? First, he’s still a kid—not exactly a coward, but kind of an artist. Seriously, don’t laugh! He’s innocent and easily influenced. He has a good heart and is a dreamer. He sings, dances, and tells stories—people come from other villages just to listen. He goes to school, and if you wag a finger at him, he’ll laugh until he cries. He can drink himself silly—not all the time, but when people treat him, like a child. And he stole things without even realizing it—‘how can it be stealing if you just pick something up?’ You know, he’s an Old Believer, or really more like a religious dissenter. Some of his family were Wanderers[*], and he spent two years in his village under the guidance of a religious elder. I learned all this from Nikolay and people from his village. What’s more, he even wanted to run off into the wilderness! He prayed at night, read old religious books—the ‘true’ ones—until he nearly drove himself crazy."
[*] A religious group that split off from the main Russian Orthodox Church.—TRANSLATOR'S NOTE.

"St. Petersburg really changed him, especially the women and the drinking. He reacts to everything, and he forgot all about the elder and that stuff. I found out that an artist here took a liking to him, used to visit him, and then this whole mess happened."

"Well, he got scared—he tried to hang himself! He ran away! People are terrified of Russian law; even the word 'trial' scares them. Is that their fault? We’ll see what the new juries do. I hope they help! Anyway, in jail, it seems he remembered the old elder, and the Bible came back into his life, too. Do you know how powerful the word 'suffering' is for some of these people? They don’t suffer for someone else—they just believe ‘one must suffer.’ If the authorities make them suffer, that’s even better. I knew a very quiet prisoner once who spent a whole year in jail, reading his Bible every night on the stove, until he lost his mind. One day, for no reason, he picked up a brick and threw it at the warden—not to hurt him, though; he aimed a yard off on purpose. We all know what happens to someone who attacks an officer. So he ‘took his suffering.’"

"So now, I think Nikolay wants to suffer, or something like that. I know it for sure, from the facts. He doesn’t know I know, of course. What, you don’t believe there are such dreamers among the peasants? There are plenty! The elder has started influencing him again, especially after Nikolay tried to hang himself. But he’ll come and tell me everything himself. You think he’ll stick to his story? Wait, he’ll take it all back. I’m waiting for him to change his mind any hour now. I’ve gotten to like Nikolay and I’m studying him closely. And you know what? He gave me some very convincing answers about a few things—he obviously prepared and collected evidence. But about other things, he’s totally clueless and doesn’t even know it!"

"No, Rodion Romanovitch, Nikolay isn’t the one! This is a weird, dark story—a modern problem, one that shows how troubled people are now, with all these ideas about blood 'renewing' things and comfort being the point of life. Here, we have crazy book ideas, someone’s mind messed up by theories. There’s determination, but a special kind: he decided to do it like jumping off a cliff, and his legs were shaking the whole time. He forgot to shut the door, killed two people because of an idea, but couldn’t even take the money, and what little he did grab, he hid under a rock. It wasn’t enough to suffer behind the door while people banged and rang the bell—no, he had to go back to the empty apartment, half out of his mind, to relive the bell ringing. Sure, that was because he was sick, but look: he’s a murderer who still thinks of himself as an honest man, looks down on others, and acts like he’s the real victim. No, that’s not Nikolay’s work, my dear Rodion Romanovitch!"
Everything Porfiry had said before sounded almost like he was taking it all back, so these last words hit Raskolnikov like a slap. He shuddered as if he'd been stabbed.
"Then... who... who is the murderer?" he asked, out of breath, unable to stop himself.
Porfiry Petrovitch leaned back in his chair, as if he was shocked by the question.
"Who is the murderer?" he repeated, sounding like he couldn't believe what he'd heard. "Why, you, Rodion Romanovitch! You are the murderer," he almost whispered, but with real certainty in his voice.
Raskolnikov jumped up from the sofa, stood for a few seconds, and sat down again without saying a word. His face twitched uncontrollably.

"Your lip is twitching, just like before," Porfiry said, almost sympathetically. "I think you've misunderstood me, Rodion Romanovitch," he added after a pause. "That's why you're so surprised. I came here to tell you everything and be open with you."
"It wasn't me—I didn't kill her," Raskolnikov whispered, like a frightened kid caught doing something wrong.
"No, it was you, Rodion Romanovitch, and nobody else," Porfiry whispered back, stern and sure.

They both fell silent, and the quiet lasted strangely long, almost ten minutes. Raskolnikov leaned his elbow on the table and ran his fingers through his hair. Porfiry just sat there, waiting patiently. Suddenly, Raskolnikov looked at him scornfully.
"You're using your old tricks again, Porfiry Petrovitch! The same old methods. Aren't you tired of them yet?"

"Oh, come on, what does that matter now? It would be different if there were witnesses here, but we're just whispering alone. You can see that I haven't come to hunt you down like some animal. Whether you confess or not doesn't matter to me now; for myself, I'm already convinced."
"If that's true, then why are you here?" Raskolnikov snapped. "Let me ask again: if you think I'm guilty, why don't you arrest me?"
"Ah, that's your question! I'll answer you, step by step. First, arresting you right away isn't in my best interest."
"Why not? If you're so sure, you should..."

"Well, what if I am sure? That's just what I think for now. Why should I put you somewhere safe? That's what it would be, since you ask. If I brought in that workman and you said, 'Were you drunk or not? Who saw me with you? I thought you were drunk, and you really were.' What could I say to that, especially since your story sounds more believable than his? All we have is psychology to back him up—and that's not much, considering how he looks. You, on the other hand, fit the story perfectly, and he's a known drunk. I've already admitted that psychology can be taken two ways, and the second one makes more sense. Besides that, I have nothing solid against you. And even though I could put you in jail—and I've come here, against the rules, to tell you first—honestly, that wouldn't help me. Now, secondly, I came because..."
"Yes, yes, secondly?" Raskolnikov listened, barely breathing.

"Because, like I said, I feel I owe you an explanation. I don't want you to think I'm some kind of monster—I actually like you, believe it or not. And third, I've come with a direct and honest offer: you should turn yourself in and confess. It will be much better for you, and for me too—my job will be done. So, isn't that honest of me?"
Raskolnikov thought for a moment.
"Listen, Porfiry Petrovitch. You just said all you have is psychology, but now you're acting like you have proof. What if you're wrong?"
"No, Rodion Romanovitch, I'm not wrong. I actually have a little fact, a clue that came to me—maybe even from fate."
"What clue?"

"I'm not going to tell you, Rodion Romanovitch. And anyway, I shouldn't wait any longer—I have to arrest you soon. So think about it; it doesn't matter to me anymore, and I'm only saying this for your own good. Believe me, it's better this way."
Raskolnikov gave a bitter, mean little smile.
"That's not just silly, it's actually shameless. Even if I was guilty—which I don't admit—why would I confess, if you just said I'd be safer in prison?"

"Oh, Rodion Romanovitch, don't trust words too much—maybe prison won't be that comfortable. That's just theory, my theory, and who am I to you? Maybe I’m still hiding something from you! I can't reveal everything, ha! And why do you ask about the benefit? Don't you know it would reduce your sentence? You'd be confessing at a time when someone else has already confessed and messed up the whole case. Think about that! I swear to God I'll make sure your confession is a complete shock to everyone. We'll clear away all the psychological stuff and suspicions, so your crime looks like a moment of madness—because honestly, that's what it was. I'm an honest man, Rodion Romanovitch, and I'll keep my promise."
Raskolnikov sat in gloomy silence, his head drooping. He thought for a long time and finally smiled again, but this time it was a sad, gentle smile.
"No," he said, apparently giving up on pretending with Porfiry, "it's not worth it. I don't care about a lighter sentence."
"That's exactly what I was afraid of!" Porfiry burst out, like he couldn't help himself. "That's what I feared—that you wouldn't care about making your punishment less."
Raskolnikov looked at him sadly, his eyes saying everything.
"Oh, don't give up on life!" Porfiry said. "You've got so much still ahead of you. How can you say you don't want a lighter sentence? You're so impatient!"
"A lot of what lies ahead?"
"Life, of course! Are you a fortune teller? Do you really know what your future will be? 'Seek and you shall find.' Maybe this is how God reaches you. Besides, it's not forever, being locked up..."
"My time will get cut short," Raskolnikov laughed.
"Is it that you're scared of public shame? Maybe you're afraid of it without even knowing, because you're still young. But anyway, you shouldn't be afraid of giving yourself up and confessing."
"Ugh, forget it," Raskolnikov muttered in disgust, as if he didn't even want to speak.
He stood up like he was going to leave, but then sat down again, looking hopeless.

"Say what you want! You've lost faith, and you think I'm just flattering you. But how much of life have you lived? How much do you really understand? You dreamed up a theory, and then you were ashamed when it failed and turned out to be nothing special. Sure, it ended up being something ugly, but you're not hopelessly lost. Not at all! At least you didn't fool yourself for long—you went straight to the worst part in one jump. How do I see you? I think you’re the kind of person who would smile at his torturer, as long as he believed in something or someone. If you find faith, you'll live. You really need a change of air. Suffering is good sometimes—suffer! Maybe Nikolay is right to want to suffer. I know you don't believe in that, but don't be too clever—just throw yourself into life, don't overthink it; don't be afraid—life will carry you to safety somehow. Where? Who knows? I just believe you have a long life ahead. You probably think I'm just making a big speech, but maybe you'll remember these words someday. Maybe they'll help. That's why I say them. It's lucky you only killed the old woman. If you’d had a different theory, maybe you'd have done something even worse. Maybe you should thank God. How do you know? Maybe God's got some plan for you. But try to stay positive, and don't be afraid! Are you scared of facing justice? No, that would be shameful. Now that you’ve gone this far, you have to be strong. It's only fair. You have to face justice. I know you don't believe it, but life will fix things over time. You’ll get through it. What you need now is fresh air—fresh air, fresh air!"
Raskolnikov actually jumped in surprise.
"But who are you? What kind of prophet do you think you are? What gives you the right to say all this?"

"Who am I? I'm just a man with nothing left to hope for, that's all. Maybe I have some feelings and a bit of knowledge, but my time is up. You're different—life is waiting for you. Still, who knows, maybe your life will amount to nothing. So what if you end up in a different class of people? It's not comfort you miss, with your heart! So what if no one sees you for a long time? It's not time, it's you that decides. Be the sun and everyone will notice. The sun has to be the sun, first and foremost. Why are you smiling again? Because I sound like a poet? You probably think I'm trying to flatter you. Maybe I am, ha ha ha! Maybe you shouldn't believe a word I say—I'm just made that way. But you can judge for yourself whether I'm a bad man or an honest one."
"So when are you planning to arrest me?"
"Well, I can let you walk around for another day or two. Think it over, my friend, and pray to God. It's really in your best interest, believe me."
"And what if I run away?" Raskolnikov asked, with a strange smile.

"No, you won't run away. A peasant would, or someone following another person's ideas would, ready to believe anything you tell them. But you've already stopped believing in your own theory—what would you run away with? And what would you do in hiding? You’d hate it, and what you need most is a clear place in the world, an atmosphere that fits you. What kind of atmosphere would you have on the run? If you did run, you’d end up coming back. You can’t live without us. And if I put you in jail—even if it’s a month, two, or three—mark my words, you’ll eventually confess, maybe even surprising yourself. You won’t even see it coming. I’m sure you’ll decide ‘to take your suffering.’ You don’t believe me now, but you’ll get there. Suffering, Rodion Romanovitch, is a big deal. Never mind that I’ve gotten fat, I still know what I’m talking about. Don’t laugh—there’s something to suffering; Nikolay is right. No, you won’t run away, Rodion Romanovitch."
Raskolnikov stood up and grabbed his cap. Porfiry Petrovitch stood up, too.
"Going for a walk? The evening should be nice, unless we get a storm. It’d be good to clear the air."
He picked up his own cap.

"Porfiry Petrovitch, don't go thinking I confessed to you today," Raskolnikov said stubbornly. "You're a strange man, and I listened to you just out of curiosity. But I haven't admitted anything—remember that!"

"Oh, I know, I'll remember. Look at you, you're shaking! Don't worry, my friend—do what you want. Go for a walk, but you won’t get too far. If anything happens, I have one request," he added, dropping his voice. "It's awkward, but important. If, by any chance (though I really doubt it), you suddenly decide to end things in some crazy way—hurt yourself or something—please leave a short, clear note, just two lines, and mention the stone. It would be the decent thing to do. Well, until we meet again! Good thoughts and wise choices to you!"

Porfiry left, stooping and not looking at Raskolnikov. Raskolnikov went to the window and waited impatiently, counting the time until he guessed Porfiry was outside and had gone. Then he hurried out, too.

He rushed to Svidrigaïlov’s place. Raskolnikov wasn’t sure what to expect from him, but Svidrigaïlov had some mysterious power over him. Now that Raskolnikov recognized this, he couldn’t relax, and something told him the moment to face it had finally come.
As he walked, one question kept bothering him: had Svidrigaïlov already visited Porfiry?

As far as he could tell, he was almost certain Svidrigaïlov hadn’t gone yet. He kept remembering Porfiry’s visit and going over the details in his mind—no, it wasn’t possible, Svidrigaïlov hadn’t been there.

But if Svidrigaïlov hadn’t gone yet, would he go soon? For now, Raskolnikov felt he wouldn’t, though he couldn’t explain why. Still, he couldn’t stop worrying about it, even if he didn’t have the energy to focus on it. Oddly enough, even though his future was uncertain, he only felt a faint, distant anxiety about it. Something else, more urgent, was eating at him from inside. He was also completely worn out, even though his mind was clearer that morning than it had been recently.

Was it even worth it, after everything that had happened, to deal with these new little problems? Should he bother trying to keep Svidrigaïlov from seeing Porfiry? Was there any point in investigating, getting more information, or wasting time on someone like Svidrigaïlov?
He was so tired of all of it!

Yet here he was, hurrying to Svidrigaïlov anyway. Was he hoping for some new information or a way out? People will grab onto anything when they’re desperate. Was it fate, or just instinct, that brought them together? Maybe it was just exhaustion and hopelessness. Maybe Svidrigaïlov just happened to cross his path, and it could have been someone else. Sonia? But what could he possibly want from Sonia now? To beg her for tears again? He was afraid of Sonia, too. She was like a final judgment hanging over him. He had to choose his own path or go along with hers, and right now, he couldn’t face her at all. So wouldn’t it be better to see Svidrigaïlov? Deep down, he had always known he needed to meet with him for some reason.

But what could they possibly have in common? Even the wrong things they’d done were different. Svidrigaïlov was an unpleasant man—clearly corrupt, definitely clever and tricky, maybe even evil. People told all sorts of stories about him. Sure, he was helping Katerina Ivanovna’s kids, but who knew why or what he really wanted? Svidrigaïlov always seemed to have some plan.

Another thought had been bugging Raskolnikov lately, making him anxious. It was so upsetting that he had to work hard to push it away. Sometimes he wondered if Svidrigaïlov was following him. He knew Svidrigaïlov had figured out his secret and had targeted Dounia. What if Svidrigaïlov still wanted something from her? Wasn’t that almost certain? And what if, now that he knew Raskolnikov’s secret, he used it as blackmail against Dounia?

This idea had even haunted his dreams, but it had never felt as real as it did now, on the way to Svidrigaïlov. The thought filled him with dark anger. If that happened, it would change everything—even his own situation. He might have to confess everything to Dounia right away. Would he have to turn himself in just to stop her from doing something reckless? The letter? Dounia had gotten a letter that morning. Who could it be from in Petersburg? Maybe Luzhin? Sure, Razumihin was there to protect her, but Razumihin didn’t know the whole story. Maybe Raskolnikov should tell him? The idea made him cringe.

Either way, he decided, he needed to see Svidrigaïlov as soon as possible. Thankfully, the details of the meeting didn’t matter as much as getting to the heart of the issue. But if Svidrigaïlov was scheming against Dounia—then...
Raskolnikov was so worn out from everything he’d been through that he could only come to one conclusion: “Then I’ll kill him,” he thought, feeling cold and hopeless.

Suddenly, a wave of panic hit him. He stopped in the middle of the street and looked around to see where he was. He was on X. Prospect, just thirty or forty steps from the Hay Market, which he had just passed through. The whole second floor of the house on the left was a tavern. All the windows were wide open, and from the people moving around inside, it looked packed. He could hear singing, a clarinet, a violin, and the deep thump of a Turkish drum. Women were shouting. He was about to turn around, wondering why he’d even come here, when he suddenly spotted Svidrigaïlov at one of the end windows, sitting at a tea table with a pipe in his mouth. Raskolnikov was shocked and almost scared. Svidrigaïlov was silently watching him, and it looked like he was thinking about getting up and slipping away unnoticed. Raskolnikov quickly pretended not to see him, acting distracted and looking away, but still watching from the corner of his eye. His heart was pounding. One thing was clear: Svidrigaïlov didn’t want to be seen. He took the pipe from his mouth and started to hide, but as he moved his chair, he seemed to realize Raskolnikov had seen him. Just like their first meeting in Raskolnikov’s room, they both knew they were watching each other. A sneaky smile spread across Svidrigaïlov’s face, getting wider and wider, until he finally burst out laughing.
“Well, well, come in if you want me; I’m here!” he shouted from the window.

Raskolnikov went inside the tavern. He found Svidrigaïlov in a tiny back room next to the main hall, where merchants, clerks, and all sorts of people were drinking tea at twenty little tables, while a loud chorus of singers performed. He could hear billiard balls clacking in the distance. On the table in front of Svidrigaïlov was an open bottle and a glass half full of champagne. There was also a boy with a small hand organ, and a healthy-looking, red-cheeked girl of about eighteen wearing a striped skirt and a Tyrolean hat with ribbons. Even with all the noise from the other room, she was singing a servant’s song with a husky contralto voice, accompanied by the organ.

“That’s enough, stop now,” Svidrigaïlov said, cutting her off as Raskolnikov entered. The girl immediately stopped and stood there, waiting politely. She had been singing her rough song with a serious, respectful look on her face.
“Hey, Philip, a glass!” Svidrigaïlov called.
“I’m not drinking anything,” Raskolnikov said.
“As you wish, it’s not for you. Drink, Katia! I don’t want anything else today, you can go.” He poured her a full glass and put a yellow banknote on the table.

Katia drank her wine all in one go, not setting the glass down, took the note, and kissed Svidrigaïlov’s hand, which he let her do seriously. She left, and the boy followed her out with his organ. Both of them had just been brought in from the street. Svidrigaïlov hadn’t even been in Petersburg for a week, but everything around him already seemed like it belonged to him; the waiter, Philip, was already acting like an old friend and was extremely eager to please.
The door to the main hall had a lock on it. Svidrigaïlov seemed completely at home in this room and might even spend whole days there. The tavern itself was dirty and miserable, not even second-rate.

“I was going to look for you,” Raskolnikov began, “but I don’t know why I turned from the Hay Market into X. Prospect just now. I never come this way. I always turn right from the Hay Market, and this isn’t the way to your place. I just turned and there you were. It’s strange!”
“Why not just say it’s a miracle?”
“Because it could just be a coincidence.”

“That’s how everyone is around here,” Svidrigaïlov laughed. “Even if you secretly think it’s a miracle, you won’t admit it! You say it could just be chance. Everyone’s scared to have their own opinion here, you wouldn’t believe it, Rodion Romanovitch. I’m not talking about you—you do have your own opinions and aren’t afraid to show it. That’s what made me interested in you.”
“Nothing else?”
“Well, that’s enough, isn’t it?” Svidrigaïlov was clearly in a good mood, though he’d only had half a glass of wine.
“I think you came to see me before you even knew I had what you call my own opinion,” Raskolnikov said.

“Well, that was a different reason. Everyone has their own plans. And about the miracle—I actually think you’ve been half-asleep these past two or three days. I told you about this tavern myself; it’s no miracle you came straight here. I explained the way, told you where to find me, and when. Remember?”
“I don’t remember,” Raskolnikov said, surprised.

“I believe you. I told you twice. The address stuck in your mind without you realizing. You came here on autopilot, even if you’re not aware of it. When I told you, I barely thought you understood me. You’re too easy to read, Rodion Romanovitch. And another thing, I’m sure there are lots of people in Petersburg who talk to themselves as they walk. This is a city full of strange people. If only we had more scientists, doctors, or lawyers—Petersburg would give them so much to study. There aren’t many places with so many gloomy, strong, and weird influences on the soul. Even the climate affects people. And since it’s the capital of all Russia, it shapes the whole country. But anyway, that doesn’t matter now. The point is, I’ve watched you several times. You leave your house with your head up, but after twenty steps you drop your head, fold your hands behind your back, and stare into space. You don’t see anything around you. Then you start moving your lips, talking to yourself, sometimes waving your hand and speaking out loud, and finally stopping right in the middle of the street. That’s not good. Someone else might be watching you too, and it won’t help you. Not that it’s my business or that I can help you, but you get what I mean.”
“Do you know I’m being followed?” Raskolnikov asked, looking at him curiously.
“No, I don’t know anything about that,” Svidrigaïlov said, sounding surprised.
“Well then, let’s not talk about me,” Raskolnikov muttered, frowning.
“Fine, let’s drop it.”
“But tell me this: if you come here to drink, and you told me twice to come here, why did you hide and try to sneak away when I saw you at the window? I noticed it.”
“Ha! And why did you lie on your sofa pretending to be asleep when I showed up at your door, even though you were totally awake? I saw that too.”
“I might have had... reasons. You know that.”
“And maybe I had my own reasons, even if you don’t know them.”

Raskolnikov leaned his right elbow on the table, resting his chin on his fingers, and stared intently at Svidrigaïlov. He studied his face for a full minute. It was strange, almost like a mask—pale and red, with bright red lips, a pale blond beard, and still thick blond hair. His eyes were too blue and had a heavy, fixed look. There was something disturbing about his handsome face, which looked oddly young for his age. Svidrigaïlov was dressed sharply in light summer clothes, with clean linen and a huge ring with a gemstone.

“Do I need to start worrying about you now, too?” Raskolnikov suddenly blurted out, impatient and nervous. “Even if you are the most dangerous person for me, I’m done caring. I’ll show you right now that I don’t value my own life as much as you might think. If you keep going after my sister, and if you plan to use what you know against me, I’ll kill you before you can get me arrested. You can count on that—I keep my word. And second, if you have anything to tell me—I keep thinking you have something to say—then hurry up and say it, because time is running out.”
“Why are you in such a rush?” Svidrigaïlov asked, watching him closely.
“Everyone has their own plans,” Raskolnikov answered darkly and impatiently.

“You just told me to be honest, but now you refuse to answer my questions,” Svidrigaïlov said with a smile. “You keep thinking I have some secret agenda, so you watch me with suspicion. That’s normal, given your situation. I’d rather be friends with you, but I won’t go out of my way to prove anything. It’s not worth the effort, and I didn’t plan to talk about anything important with you anyway.”
“Then why did you want to see me? You’re the one who’s been hanging around me.”

“Just because you’re interesting to watch. I liked the strange situation you’re in—that’s all! Besides, you’re the brother of someone I care about, and she’s told me a lot about you. I learned you have a lot of influence over her; isn’t that enough? Ha-ha-ha! Still, your question is kind of complicated and hard to answer. For example, you came to me not just for a specific reason, but also to hear something new. Right? Isn’t that right?” Svidrigaïlov pressed, grinning slyly. “Well, can’t you imagine I was hoping for something new from you too, maybe some benefit for myself? See how rich we both are!”
“What kind of benefit could you get?”

“How should I know? Look at this place—I spend all my time here, and it’s not exactly fun, but you have to sit somewhere. That poor Katia you saw... If I were a gourmet, I’d at least enjoy the food, but look at what I eat.”
He pointed at a small table in the corner, where the remains of a terrible-looking steak and potatoes were on a tin plate.

“Have you eaten, by the way? I’ve had something and don’t want more. I don’t really drink at all. Except for champagne—I never touch anything else, and only one glass a night, which is enough to give me a headache. I ordered it now just to pep myself up, since I’m just about to go out and you caught me in a weird mood. That’s why I tried to hide like a schoolboy; I was afraid you’d slow me down. But I think,” he checked his watch, “I can spend an hour with you. It’s half-past four now. If only I were something—a landowner, a father, a cavalry officer, a photographer, a journalist... But I’m nothing, I have no specialty, and sometimes I’m just bored. I really thought you’d have something new to say.”
“So what are you, and why are you here?”
“What am I? You know, just a gentleman. I served two years in the cavalry, then wandered around Petersburg, then married Marfa Petrovna and lived in the country. That’s my whole life story!”
“You’re a gambler, right?”
“No, a lousy gambler. More like a card-cheater than a real gambler.”
“So you’ve been a card-cheater?”
“Yes, I’ve been a card-cheater too.”
“Didn’t you ever get beaten up?”
“It happened sometimes. Why?”
“Well, you could have challenged them... It must have been exciting at least.”
“I won’t argue with you. Besides, I’m not much of a philosopher. Honestly, I rushed here because of the women.”
“Right after you buried Marfa Petrovna?”
“Exactly,” Svidrigaïlov smiled openly. “So what? Are you bothered by how I talk about women?”
“You’re asking if I think there’s something wrong with being a creep?”

“A creep! So that’s where you’re going with this. But I’ll answer you, first about women in general; you know I like to talk. Tell me, why should I hold back? Why should I give up women if that’s what I like? It’s something to do, anyway.”
“So you’re just here for vice and nothing else?”

“Alright, call it vice if you want. I appreciate a direct question. At least vice is permanent, built into human nature, not just some fantasy. It’s like a spark in your blood, always burning and hard to put out, even as you get older. You have to admit, it’s something to do.”
“That’s nothing to be proud of. It’s a sickness—a dangerous one.”

“So that’s what you think! I agree, it’s a sickness if you go too far. Of course, you have to go too far in this. But honestly, everyone goes too far in something. And yeah, you should be careful and moderate, even if it’s boring. But what can I do? If I didn’t have this, maybe I’d have to shoot myself. I know decent people should put up with being bored, but still...”
“Could you really shoot yourself?”

“Come on,” Svidrigaïlov said, sounding disgusted. “Don’t talk about that,” he added quickly, suddenly losing his previous bragging attitude. He looked different now. “I know it’s a terrible weakness, but I can’t help it. I’m scared of death and hate talking about it. Did you know I’m a little bit superstitious?”
“Ah, Marfa Petrovna’s ghost? Do you still see her?”

“Don’t bring that up; I haven’t seen her in Petersburg, thank goodness!” he snapped, sounding irritated. “Let’s talk about something else... though... Hm! I don’t have much time and can’t stay long. That’s a shame, I have plenty I could tell you.”
“Are you meeting a woman?”
“Yes, a woman, just a random thing... But that’s not what I wanted to talk about.”
“And all this filth and ugliness around you—doesn’t it get to you? Can’t you stop yourself?”

“And you think you’re strong? Ha-ha-ha! You surprised me, Rodion Romanovitch, even though I knew you’d say that. You’re lecturing me about vice and morals! You—a Schiller, an idealist! Of course, that’s how it should be, and I’d be shocked if it wasn’t, but it’s still funny in real life... What a pity I don’t have time, you’re such an interesting type! By the way, do you like Schiller? I’m a big fan.”
“What a bragger you are,” Raskolnikov said, a little disgusted.

“Honestly, I’m not,” Svidrigaïlov laughed. “But fine, let’s say I am. Why not brag if it doesn’t hurt anyone? I spent seven years in the country with Marfa Petrovna, so when I meet someone smart and interesting like you, I’m just happy to talk! And besides, that half glass of champagne has gone to my head a little. Also, there’s something that has me all worked up right now, but I’ll keep that to myself. Where are you going?” he asked, sounding alarmed.
Raskolnikov had started to get up. He felt trapped, suffocated, and uncomfortable for coming here. He was sure Svidrigaïlov was the worst scoundrel in the world.
“Ah! Sit down, stay a bit!” Svidrigaïlov begged. “Let them bring you some tea, at least. Stay—I won’t keep talking about myself. I’ll tell you a story. If you want, I’ll

“Maybe you already know—I think I told you myself,” Svidrigaïlov began, “that I once landed in debtors’ prison here, owing a huge amount of money with no hope of paying it back. No need to explain how Marfa Petrovna got me out; do you know how crazy in love a woman can get? She was honest and smart in her own way, though totally uneducated. Would you believe it, this honest and jealous woman, after all kinds of drama and arguments, agreed to a sort of contract with me that we kept all through our marriage? She was much older than I was—and she always had a clove or something in her mouth, by the way. I was honest enough, or maybe just awful enough, to admit to her that I couldn’t promise to be completely faithful. That made her furious, but in a strange way, she liked my bluntness. She thought it meant I wasn’t trying to trick her, since I warned her up front—and for a jealous woman, that matters most. So after many tears, we made this unwritten agreement: first, I’d never leave Marfa Petrovna and would always be her husband; second, I’d never go away without her permission; third, I wouldn’t have a permanent mistress; fourth, in return for all that, Marfa Petrovna let me do as I wanted with the maidservants—as long as she secretly knew about it; fifth, I was never to fall in love with someone from our own class; and sixth, if I ever did fall really in love—God forbid—I had to tell Marfa Petrovna. But she wasn’t worried about that last one. She was smart enough to believe I was a hopeless scoundrel, not capable of real love. Still, being sensible and being jealous are two totally different things—so we had our problems. But to judge people fairly, you have to put aside your usual ideas and see them as they really are. I’d rather trust your judgment than anyone else’s. Maybe you’ve heard a lot of ridiculous things about Marfa Petrovna. She did have some silly habits, but honestly, I feel bad for all the trouble I caused her. Well, that’s enough for a decent little funeral speech for the most loving wife of the most loving husband. When we fought, I usually kept quiet and avoided making her angrier. That almost always worked—she liked it, in fact. Sometimes she was even proud of me. But your sister—she just couldn’t deal with her. I still can’t figure out why she risked hiring someone as beautiful as your sister to be a governess. My guess is Marfa Petrovna was such a passionate and emotional person that she just fell in love—with your sister, I mean. Really, can you blame her? Just look at Avdotya Romanovna! I saw trouble coming right away, so I decided not to even look at her. But believe it or not, Avdotya Romanovna made the first move. And would you believe Marfa Petrovna actually got mad at me at first because I didn’t say anything about your sister or react at all to her endless praise of Avdotya Romanovna? I have no idea what she wanted! Of course, Marfa Petrovna told Avdotya Romanovna everything about me. She had this bad habit of sharing all our family secrets with everyone and constantly complaining about me. How could she not open up to such a wonderful new friend? I bet they talked about nothing but me, and Avdotya Romanovna heard all the dark rumors people whispered about me... I’m sure you’ve heard some of that, too, haven’t you?”
“I have. Luzhin accused you of causing a child’s death. Is that true?”
“Please don’t bring up those gross rumors,” said Svidrigaïlov, looking both annoyed and disgusted. “If you really want to hear all that nonsense, I’ll tell you one day, but not now…”
“I also heard about a footman you had in the country and how badly you treated him.”
“Let’s drop the subject,” Svidrigaïlov cut in again, clearly impatient.
“Was that the footman who came to you after he died, to fill your pipe?... You told me about it yourself.” Raskolnikov was getting more and more irritated.
Svidrigaïlov looked at him closely, and Raskolnikov thought he saw a flash of mean amusement in his eyes. But Svidrigaïlov held back and answered politely:

“Yes, it was. I see you’re really interested, so I’ll have to satisfy your curiosity one day. Honestly! With some people I could seem like a real romantic. Imagine how grateful I must be to Marfa Petrovna for telling Avdotya Romanovna such mysterious and juicy gossip about me. I can’t guess what Avdotya Romanovna thought of it, but in the end, it actually helped me. Even though Avdotya Romanovna naturally disliked me—and I always looked gloomy and unpleasant—she at least felt sorry for me, for a lost soul. And when a girl starts to feel sorry for a man, that’s the most dangerous thing. She’ll want to ‘save him,’ change him, give him a better life, and make him useful—well, we all know how far those kinds of dreams can go. I saw right away she was trapping herself. And I started preparing, too. Are you frowning, Rodion Romanovitch? There’s no need. You know it all came to nothing in the end. (Wow, I’m really drinking a lot!) You know, I’ve always regretted that your sister wasn’t born in the second or third century, as a prince’s daughter or a governor’s daughter in Asia Minor. She would have been one of those people who go through suffering and even smile when tortured. She would have walked into the desert in the fourth or fifth century and lived there for thirty years, surviving on roots and visions. She’s just desperate to suffer for someone, and if she can’t, she’d probably throw herself out a window. I’ve heard of a Mr. Razumihin—he sounds like a smart guy; even his name suggests it. Maybe he studies theology. He’d better take care of your sister! I think I understand her, and I’m proud of that. But at the beginning, people can be careless and stupid. You don’t see things clearly. Why is she so beautiful? It’s not my fault. Honestly, at first, what drew me to her was just irresistible physical attraction. Avdotya Romanovna is extremely pure, almost unbelievably so. Remember that—I’m telling you a fact. She’s almost obsessed with being pure, even though she’s smart, and that will actually be a problem for her. Back then, there was a girl in the house named Parasha, dark-eyed and pretty, but so dumb—she’d just moved from another village. She cried and screamed so much, everyone heard her, and it caused a scandal. One day after lunch, Avdotya Romanovna followed me into the garden and, eyes blazing, demanded I leave Parasha alone. That was almost the first time we talked alone. Naturally, I was happy to do what she wanted, and I acted all awkward and embarrassed—I played my role pretty well. After that, there were meetings, serious talks, arguments, begging, even tears—would you believe it, actual tears? That’s what some girls will do for a cause! I, of course, blamed it all on fate, pretended I was searching for meaning, and finally pulled out my best weapon for winning a woman’s heart—flattery. Telling the truth is hard, but flattery is easy. Even if the truth is a tiny bit off, it can cause problems. But if flattery is all lies, it still sounds good and people like it—maybe in a shallow way, but still. Even the most obvious flattery feels half true to most people. That’s true at every level of society. Even a girl who’s sworn to be pure could be won over by flattery. I still laugh remembering how I once seduced a woman who was devoted to her husband, her kids, and her morals. It was fun and barely any work! And she really did have her own morals. My whole plan was to act totally defeated and humble in front of her innocence. I flattered her like crazy, and as soon as I got even a handshake or a glance, I’d act guilty, saying I’d forced it, and only got it because I was so shameless. I’d say she was so innocent she didn’t even realize what I was doing, and so on. I won, while she kept believing she was innocent, pure, and loyal, and that anything that happened was just an accident. And she got so mad when I finally told her I thought she wanted it as much as I did. Poor Marfa Petrovna was a sucker for flattery, too. If I’d wanted, I could’ve gotten her to give me all her money while she was alive. (I’m drinking too much now and talking even more.) I hope you won’t be mad if I say I was starting to have the same effect on Avdotya Romanovna. But I was stupid and impatient and messed it all up. Avdotya Romanovna had already gotten upset with the way I looked at her—would you believe it? Sometimes my eyes scared her, and it got worse until she hated it. No need to explain, but that’s when we split up. Again, I was an idiot. I started making fun of all her attempts to change me; Parasha got involved again, and not just her—there was a whole mess. Oh, Rodion Romanovitch, if you could see how your sister’s eyes can flash! Never mind that I’m tipsy and have had a whole glass of wine—I’m telling the truth. That look haunted my dreams; even the sound of her dress drove me crazy. I really thought I might have a seizure. I never thought I could get so worked up. I needed to make up with her, but by then it was too late. And guess what I did next! See how stupid a man can get when he’s obsessed? Never do anything when you’re like that, Rodion Romanovitch. I remembered that Avdotya Romanovna was basically poor (ugh, sorry, not the best word... but you get what I mean), and that she supported her mother and you (ugh, you’re frowning again), so I decided to offer her all my money—thirty thousand roubles I could have gotten at the time—if she’d run away with me to Petersburg. Of course, I would have promised her eternal love and happiness and all that. I was so crazy about her then, if she’d told me to poison Marfa Petrovna or cut her throat and marry her, I’d have done it right away! But it ended in the disaster you already know about. Imagine how desperate I was when I heard that Marfa Petrovna had found that sleazy lawyer Luzhin and almost set up a marriage between them—which would really have been the same thing I was proposing. Wouldn’t it? Wouldn’t it? I see you’re finally paying close attention... you interesting young man…”

Svidrigaïlov slammed his fist on the table, impatient. His face was red. Raskolnikov could tell that even just a glass or two of champagne was affecting him—and decided to use the chance to get more out of him. He was feeling very suspicious of Svidrigaïlov.
“After everything you’ve said, I’m sure you came to Petersburg because you have plans for my sister,” Raskolnikov said straight out, trying to irritate Svidrigaïlov even more.
“Oh, come on,” Svidrigaïlov said, snapping out of his daze. “I told you already… Plus, your sister can’t stand me.”
“Yes, I’m sure she can’t, but that’s not the point.”

“Are you so sure?” Svidrigaïlov squinted and smiled in a mocking way. “You’re right, she doesn’t love me. But you can never really know what goes on between a husband and wife, or lovers. There’s always a secret corner only they know about. Are you really sure Avdotya Romanovna hated me?”
“From what you’ve said, it sounds like you still have plans—bad ones—about Dounia, and you’re going to act on them soon.”
“What, did I say something like that?” Svidrigaïlov asked, pretending to be surprised, and not reacting at all to how Raskolnikov described his plans.
“You’re saying it right now. Why are you so scared? What are you afraid of?”

“Me—afraid? Afraid of you? You should be more afraid of me, my friend. But that’s silly… I’ve just had a bit too much to drink, that’s all. I was about to say too much again. Curse this wine! Hey, water!”
He grabbed the champagne bottle and casually tossed it out the window. Philip brought some water.
“It’s all nonsense!” Svidrigaïlov said, wetting a towel and putting it on his head. “But I can prove you’re wrong about me with one sentence. Do you know I’m getting married?”
“You told me that before.”

“Did I? I forgot. But I couldn’t have really told you, because I hadn’t even met my fiancée yet; I just meant to. But now I really do have a fiancée, and it’s official. If I didn’t have urgent business, I’d take you to meet them right now, because I’d actually like your advice. Ah, hang on, only ten minutes left! Look, see the time? But I have to tell you anyway, it’s kind of an interesting story, this marriage of mine. Where are you going? Leaving again?”
“No, I’m not leaving now.”

“Really? We’ll see. I’ll take you to meet my fiancée, just not right now. Because soon you’ll have to go one way and I’ll go the other. You know Madame Resslich, the woman I’m renting a room from? I know what you’re thinking—she’s the one whose girl supposedly drowned herself last winter. Listen, are you paying attention? She set it all up for me. She said, ‘You’re bored, you need something to keep you busy.’ I am a gloomy, depressed person, you know. Do you think I’m cheerful? No, I’m gloomy. I don’t hurt anyone, but I can sit silently in a corner for three days straight. And Resslich is a sly one, let me tell you. I know what she’s hoping—she thinks I’ll get tired of marriage, leave my wife, and then she can get her hands on the girl and make a profit—someone of our class, or higher. She told me the father is a retired official, paralyzed for three years, just sits in a chair. The mother is smart. There’s a son in the provinces who doesn’t help; a daughter who’s married but never visits. They already have enough kids, but they’re even taking care of two little nephews. They pulled their youngest daughter out of school—she’ll be sixteen soon—so she can get married. She was meant for me. We went to meet them. It was so funny! I showed up—a landowner, a widower, with a famous name, connections, and money. Who cares if I’m fifty and she’s not even sixteen? Who notices that? But it’s fascinating, right? It sure is! You should’ve seen how I talked to the parents. It was worth paying just for that. Then she comes in, does a little curtsy—imagine, still in a short dress, just a kid! Blushing bright red—she’d been told, obviously. I don’t know how you feel about girls’ faces, but I think sixteen-year-old shyness and tears are even better than beauty; and she’s adorable. Blonde curls, rosy lips, tiny feet, just a little charmer!... So, we got along. I told them I was in a hurry because of family reasons, and the very next day—just two days ago—we got engaged. Now, when I visit, she sits on my knee, and I keep her there... She blushes bright red and I kiss her all the time. Her mom keeps telling her, ‘This is your husband, this is how it should be.’ It’s just wonderful! Being engaged is maybe even better than being married. This is what they call la nature et la vérité, ha-ha! I’ve talked to her twice, she’s not dumb at all. Sometimes she looks at me in a way that burns right through me. Her face is like Raphael’s Madonna—you know, that painting, the Sistine Madonna, with that mystical, sad look? She looks like that. The day after we got engaged, I bought her gifts worth 1,500 roubles—a set of diamonds, pearls, a huge silver case full of things—her Madonna face even lit up at that! Yesterday, I put her on my knee, maybe a bit too boldly—she blushed bright red and tears came to her eyes, but she tried to hide it. When we were alone, she suddenly threw her arms around my neck (for the first time on her own), hugged me, kissed me, and promised to be a good, loyal wife, to make me happy, to devote her whole life to me, to give up everything, and all she wants in return is my respect, ‘nothing else, no gifts.’ Admit it, hearing that from a sixteen-year-old girl in a muslin dress, with curls and blushing cheeks and shining eyes, is pretty irresistible! Isn’t it? It’s worth paying for, right? Well… anyway, we’ll go see my fiancée, but not just now!”
“This huge gap in age and maturity, that’s what excites you! Are you really going to go through with this marriage?”

“Why not? Everyone looks out for themselves, and the happiest people are the ones who fool themselves best. Ha-ha! But why are you so obsessed with virtue? Have some mercy, my friend. I’m a sinner. Ha-ha-ha!”
“But you did help Katerina Ivanovna’s kids. Though… you had your reasons. I get it now.”

“I always like children, really like them,” Svidrigaïlov laughed. “Let me tell you something interesting. The first day I got here, I visited a bunch of places—I just rushed to them after being away seven years. You’ve probably noticed I’m not eager to see old friends. I’ll avoid them as long as I can. You know, when I was in the country with Marfa Petrovna, I kept thinking about these places where anyone who knows the city can find all sorts of things. Yes, honestly! The peasants have vodka, young educated people waste away with impossible dreams, Jews have popped up and are getting rich, and everyone else just gives in to vice. From the first hour, the city smelled just like I remembered. I ended up in a horrible dive—I like them dirty—a dance place, and they were doing a cancan like I’ve never seen. That’s progress for you. Suddenly I saw a thirteen-year-old girl, dressed nicely, dancing with some ‘specialist’—another one was her partner. Her mother was sitting by the wall. You can’t imagine what that cancan was like! The girl was embarrassed, blushed, finally felt humiliated, and started crying. Her partner grabbed her and started spinning her around, showing off in front of her; everyone laughed, and—even in that crowd—they all shouted, ‘Serves her right! Don’t bring kids!’ I don’t know if that makes sense, but whatever. I quickly came up with a plan, sat by the mother, and told her I was a stranger too, that people here were rude, couldn’t tell decent folks and treat them right, hinted that I had plenty of money, offered them a ride home. I took them home and got to know them. They were in a miserable little room, just arrived from the country. The mother said meeting me was an honor. I found out they had nothing and had come to town about some legal business. I offered to help and give money. I found out they’d gone to the dance place by mistake, thinking it was a real dance class. I offered to pay for the girl’s lessons in French and dance. They accepted, thrilled, and now we’re friends… If you want, we can go visit them, but not right now.”
“Stop! I’ve had enough of your disgusting, filthy stories, you depraved, nasty man!”
“Schiller! You’re a true Schiller! O la vertu va-t-elle se nicher? But you know, I tell you these stories just to get a rise out of you!”
“I believe it. I must look pretty ridiculous myself,” Raskolnikov muttered angrily.
Svidrigaïlov laughed loudly; then he called for Philip, paid his bill, and started getting up.
“I must be drunk. That’s enough talking,” he said. “It’s been a pleasure.”

“I bet it is a pleasure!” Raskolnikov snapped, standing up too. “Of course it’s fun for a worn-out creep to brag about these adventures, especially when he’s planning something just as bad—and talking about it to someone like me… It’s thrilling!”

“Well, if you say so,” Svidrigaïlov replied, studying Raskolnikov in surprise, “if you say so, you’re just as much a cynic as I am. You have plenty of reason to be, too.
