You understand a lot… and you can do a lot, too. But that’s enough. I honestly wish we could talk more, but I won’t lose track of you… Just wait.”

Svidrigaïlov left the restaurant. Raskolnikov followed him. Svidrigaïlov wasn’t actually very drunk anymore—the wine had only affected him for a moment, and he was quickly sobering up. He seemed distracted and tense, like he was waiting for something big. He was clearly excited and uneasy. He’d become ruder and more sarcastic with Raskolnikov in the last few minutes. Raskolnikov noticed this and felt uneasy, too. He became even more suspicious of Svidrigaïlov and decided to keep following him.
They stepped out onto the sidewalk.
“You go right, and I’ll go left—or the other way, if you want. Anyway, goodbye, my pleasure, maybe we’ll meet again.”
And Svidrigaïlov walked off to the right toward the Hay Market.
Raskolnikov followed Svidrigaïlov down the street.
“What’s this?” Svidrigaïlov shouted, spinning around. “Didn’t I tell you—?”
“It means I’m not letting you out of my sight now,” Raskolnikov said.
“What?”
They both stopped and stared each other down, measuring each other’s resolve.

“From all your half-drunk stories,” Raskolnikov snapped, “I’m sure you haven’t given up on my sister. In fact, you’re working even harder to go after her. I know she got a letter from you this morning. You haven’t been able to sit still all day... Maybe you found yourself a wife, but that doesn’t mean anything. I want to see for myself what’s really going on.”
Truthfully, Raskolnikov wasn’t even sure himself what exactly he wanted or what he needed to find out.
“I swear, I’ll call the police!” Svidrigaïlov threatened.
“Go ahead, call them!” Raskolnikov shot back.
They faced off in silence for another minute. Then Svidrigaïlov’s expression changed. He realized Raskolnikov wasn’t scared by his bluff. Svidrigaïlov switched to a friendly, joking manner.

“What a guy you are! I was actually trying not to bring up your situation, even though I’m dying to know what happened. It’s such a wild story. I was saving it for another time, but you’re impossible. Anyway, let’s go. I’m warning you, though—I’m just going home for a minute to grab some money, then I’m locking up, getting a cab, and heading out to the Islands for the evening. Are you really going to come after me everywhere?”
“I’m coming to your place, but I’m not here to see you. I want to see Sofya Semyonovna (Sonya), to say sorry for missing the funeral.”

“Suit yourself, but Sofya Semyonovna isn’t home. She took the three kids to see an old lady—she’s some kind of big deal, runs orphanages, used to know me years ago. I impressed her by giving her money to help Katerina Ivanovna’s children and by signing up to donate to her charity. I also told her Sonya’s whole story, every detail. She was completely blown away. That’s why Sonya was invited to meet her today at the X. Hotel where the lady is staying.”
“Doesn’t matter. I’ll come anyway.”

“Whatever, it’s all the same to me. But I’m not coming with you. Here we are at my place, by the way. You know, I bet you only suspect me because I’ve been so polite and haven’t bothered you with questions... right? You thought it was odd. I’d wager that’s the reason. Just goes to show, being polite isn’t always smart!”
“And eavesdropping at doors is polite, too?”

“Ah, so that’s what you’re mad about!” Svidrigaïlov laughed. “I figured you’d bring that up after everything that’s happened. Ha! I did pick up parts of your ‘adventures’—the ones you were telling Sonya about. What was that all about? Maybe I’m just out of touch. Come on, explain it to me. Teach me the latest theories!”
“You didn’t hear anything. You’re making it up!”

“I’m not talking about that—though I did hear a bit. I mean how you’re always sighing and groaning now. Your inner poet keeps rebelling, and now you’re telling me not to eavesdrop. If you feel that strongly, maybe you should turn yourself in to the police and say you made a little mistake with your theory. But if you think eavesdropping is wrong but murder is fine, then you better get out of here fast—go to America! Run, young man! There’s still time. Don’t have the money? I’ll buy you the ticket.”
“That’s not what I’m thinking at all,” Raskolnikov interrupted, disgusted.

“I get it—don’t stress about it if you don’t want to talk. I know what’s bothering you—moral questions, right? Your duties as a citizen and a man? Forget about all that. None of it matters now, ha! You’ll say you’re still a man and a citizen? Then you shouldn’t have gotten yourself tangled up in this mess. No point taking on a job you’re not made for. Maybe you should just shoot yourself—unless you don’t want to?”
“Are you trying to make me angry so I’ll leave you alone?”

“What a strange guy! But here we are. Welcome to the stairs. That’s the way to Sofya Semyonovna’s room. See, nobody’s home. Don’t believe me? Ask Kapernaumov. Sonya leaves the key with him. Here’s Madame de Kapernaumov herself. She’s deaf—can you hear me, ma’am? Has Sonya gone out? Where? Did you hear? See? She’s not in and won’t be until late. Well, come to my room if you want. Madame Resslich isn’t home—she’s always busy, but she’s a great woman, could’ve helped you if you’d been smarter. Now look, I’m taking this five-percent bond out of the bureau—see, I still have a lot of them—this one I’ll cash today. I can’t waste more time. The bureau is locked, the flat is locked, and here we are back on the stairs. Should we take a cab? I’m off to the Islands. Want a ride? No? Tired of this? Come, let’s take a drive, it might rain soon. No worries, we’ll put the top up...”

Svidrigaïlov had already gotten into the carriage. Raskolnikov decided his suspicions were probably unfair for now. Without saying anything, he turned and walked back toward the Hay Market. If he’d glanced back, he would have seen Svidrigaïlov get out of the carriage less than a hundred steps away, send the cab away, and walk off down the street. But Raskolnikov turned the corner and couldn’t see. His disgust for Svidrigaïlov pulled him away.
“How could I even think about asking for help from that disgusting brute, that pervert, that criminal?” Raskolnikov muttered to himself.

But Raskolnikov was judging Svidrigaïlov too quickly. There was something strange, even mysterious, about him. As for his sister, Raskolnikov was sure Svidrigaïlov wouldn’t leave her alone. But thinking about all this was just too much—he couldn’t stand it.

Alone again, Raskolnikov hadn’t gone twenty steps before he slipped back into deep thought. When he got to the bridge, he leaned against the railing and stared at the water. His sister was standing nearby.

He had passed her at the entrance to the bridge without noticing her. Dounia had never run into him on the street like this before and was shocked. She stood frozen, unsure whether to call out to him. Suddenly, she saw Svidrigaïlov hurrying up from the Hay Market.

He was moving carefully, not stepping onto the bridge, but standing off to the side, making sure Raskolnikov didn’t see him. He had been watching Dounia for a while and was signaling her. She thought he was begging her not to talk to her brother, but to come to him instead.
That’s exactly what Dounia did. She slipped past her brother and went up to Svidrigaïlov.

“Let’s hurry away,” Svidrigaïlov whispered. “I don’t want Rodion Romanovitch (Raskolnikov) to know we’re meeting. I have to tell you, I’ve been sitting with him in a restaurant nearby where he tracked me down—it was hard to get rid of him. Somehow he found out about my letter to you and suspects something. You didn’t tell him, did you? Then who did?”
“Well, we’ve turned the corner now,” Dounia interrupted, “he won’t see us. But I’m not going any further with you. Say whatever you want right here, in the street.”

“First, I can’t say it in the street. Second, you need to hear it with Sofya Semyonovna. Third, I have some documents to show you. If you won’t come, I won’t explain anything and I’ll just leave. But remember, I have a very important secret about your beloved brother.”
Dounia stopped, hesitating, and looked closely at Svidrigaïlov.
“What are you afraid of?” he said quietly. “This is the city, not the countryside. Besides, in the country you did me more harm than I did to you.”
“Have you told Sofya Semyonovna?” Dounia asked.

“No, I haven’t said a word to her, and I’m not even sure if she’s home. But she probably is. She buried her stepmother today—it’s not likely she’d go out visiting. Right now, I don’t want to talk to anyone else about this and I almost regret talking to you. Even the smallest mistake is as bad as betrayal in a situation like this. I live right there in that building. We’re almost there. That’s the porter—he knows me, see, he’s bowing. He sees I’m with a lady and probably recognizes you, which you’ll be glad for if you’re nervous about me. Sorry if I sound blunt. I don’t have an apartment to myself; Sonya’s room is next to mine, she rents the next flat. The whole floor is rented out. Why are you so scared? Am I really that terrifying?”

Svidrigaïlov gave a condescending smile, but he was far from calm. His heart was pounding and he could barely breathe. He spoke loudly to cover up his nerves, but Dounia didn’t notice—she was just annoyed that he called her childish and was scared of him.
“Even though I know you’re not an honorable man, I’m not afraid of you,” she said, pretending to be calm, but her face was very pale.
Svidrigaïlov stopped at Sonya’s door.

“Let me check if she’s in... No, she isn’t. Too bad! But I know she’ll be back soon—if she’s out, it’s only to visit a lady about the orphan kids. Their mother just died. I’ve been trying to help them. If Sonya doesn’t come back in ten minutes, I’ll send her to you today if you want. This is my place—two rooms. Madame Resslich, my landlady, has the other room. Now, look here. I’ll show you the main evidence: this door from my bedroom leads to two empty rooms that are for rent. Here they are... Take a good look.”

Svidrigaïlov rented two pretty big furnished rooms. Dounia looked around, suspicious, but the rooms looked normal—nothing odd about the furniture or layout. Still, there was something to notice: Svidrigaïlov’s place was in between two nearly empty apartments. You couldn’t get to his rooms straight from the hallway, only by passing through the landlady’s almost empty rooms. Unlocking a door from his bedroom, Svidrigaïlov showed Dounia the two vacant rooms. She stopped in the doorway, confused about what she was supposed to see, but Svidrigaïlov explained quickly.

“Look at this second big room. See that door? It’s locked. Right by the door there’s a chair—that’s the only chair in these two rooms. I brought it here from my rooms so I could listen more easily. On the other side of that door is Sonya’s table; she sat there talking to Rodion Romanovitch. I sat here, listening, two nights in a row, for two hours each time. So, I learned a thing or two—what do you think?”
“You listened in?”
“Yes, I did. Now let’s go back to my room; we can’t stay here.”

He led Avdotya Romanovna (Dounia) back to his sitting room and offered her a chair. He sat on the other side of the table, at least seven feet away, but probably had the same intense look in his eyes that used to scare Dounia. She shivered and glanced around the room nervously. It was an automatic reaction; she clearly didn’t want to show her fear. But now she noticed how isolated Svidrigaïlov’s apartment was. Part of her wanted to ask if his landlady was at least home, but her pride held her back. Besides, she had something much bigger and scarier on her mind.

“Here’s your letter,” she said, putting it on the table. “Is what you wrote true? You hint that my brother committed a crime—too clearly to deny now. I’d heard this stupid rumor before you wrote, and I don’t believe a word of it. It’s disgusting and ridiculous. I know where the story came from and why. You can’t have any proof. You promised you’d prove it. Speak! But I’m warning you—I don’t believe you! I don’t!”
Dounia said all this quickly, and her face turned red for a moment.
“If you didn’t believe it, why would you risk coming here alone? Why are you here? Just curious?”
“Don’t torture me—just talk! Tell me!”

“You really are brave, you know. I figured you’d ask Mr. Razumihin to come with you. But he wasn’t with you, or even nearby—I was watching. It’s bold of you, which shows you want to protect Rodion Romanovitch. Everything about you is amazing.... As for your brother, what can I say? You just saw him yourself—what did you make of him?”
“That can’t be all you’re basing this on, right?”

“No, not just that—also on what he said himself. He came here two evenings in a row to see Sonya. I showed you where they sat. He confessed everything to her. He’s a murderer. He killed an old pawnbroker woman—someone he used to pawn things with. He also killed her sister, Lizaveta, who walked in while he was murdering the old woman. He killed them both with an axe he brought. He did it to rob them, and he stole money and other things. He told Sonya every detail—word for word. She’s the only person who knows. But she had nothing to do with it and was as horrified as you are now. Don’t worry—she won’t betray him.”
“No way,” Dounia muttered, lips white. She could barely breathe. “No way. There wasn’t any reason, no cause at all... It’s a lie, a lie!”

“Robbery was the reason. He took money and things. He admits he never used the money or sold the things—he hid them under a stone, and they’re still there. But that’s because he was too scared to use them.”
“But how could he steal? How could he even think of it?” Dounia cried, jumping up. “You know him—you’ve seen him—could he be a thief?”
She was practically begging Svidrigaïlov now, forgetting to be afraid.

“There are thousands—millions—of reasons and possibilities, Avdotya Romanovna. A thief steals and knows he’s a scoundrel, but I once heard of a gentleman who robbed the mail. Maybe he thought he was being honorable! I wouldn’t have believed it myself if someone just told me, but I believe my own ears. He explained everything to Sonya, and at first she couldn’t believe it, either, but eventually she had to believe her own eyes.”
“What... were his reasons?”

“It’s a long story, Dounia. How do I explain it... It’s a kind of theory—just like I believe that a single crime is okay if the main goal is good, one bad deed for a hundred good ones! Imagine how hard it is for a smart, proud young man to know that if he just had, say, three thousand rubles, his whole life could be different—but he doesn’t have it. Add to that the misery of being hungry, living in a dump, wearing rags, and watching his mother and sister suffer too. And, most of all, pride and vanity—though he does have good qualities, too. I’m not judging him—don’t think that; it’s not my business. He also had a special little theory—a theory that people are divided into ordinary folks and great ones, and that the great ones can break the law because it doesn’t apply to them—they make the laws for others. It’s just a theory, like any other. Napoleon was his hero, or at least he liked the idea that lots of geniuses broke the law and didn’t care. He thought he was a genius, at least for a while. Now he’s suffering because he found out he couldn’t really cross the line, so he’s not a genius after all. That’s tough on a proud young man—especially nowadays....”
“But what about guilt? You don’t think he has any conscience? Is he really like that?”

“Ah, Dounia, everything’s a mess now—not that it was ever that organized. Russians in general are broad-minded, like our country, and love wild, chaotic ideas. But it’s a problem to be broad without being a genius. Remember how we talked about this so much, sitting on the terrace after supper? You used to tease me for being ‘broad.’ Maybe we were talking about it at the very time he was lying here, making his plan. We don’t really have sacred traditions—not among educated people, anyway. At best, people make up their own from books or old stories. But even that’s for the old and the learned, so it’s almost unfashionable these days. You know my views—I never judge anyone. I don’t do anything; I just keep going. But we’ve talked about this a lot before. I was lucky you were interested in my ideas.... You’re very pale, Dounia.”
“I know his theory. I read that article he wrote about ‘men to whom everything is allowed.’ Razumihin brought it to me.”
“Mr. Razumihin? Your brother’s article? In a magazine? Really? I didn’t know. Must be interesting. But where are you going, Dounia?”
“I want to see Sonya,” Dounia said weakly. “How can I get to her? Maybe she’s come back. I need to see her right away. Maybe she can...”
Dounia couldn’t finish. She almost couldn’t breathe.
“Sonya won’t be back until tonight, at least I think so. She planned to return earlier, but if not, it’ll be late.”
“You’re lying! I see it now... you’ve been lying... lying this whole time. I don’t believe you! I don’t!” Dounia cried, completely losing control.
Barely conscious, she collapsed into a chair Svidrigaïlov rushed to offer her.
“Dounia, what is it? Get a hold of yourself! Here, drink some water...”
He sprinkled water on her. Dounia shivered and snapped back to herself.

“That had a strong effect,” Svidrigaïlov muttered, frowning. “Calm down, Dounia! Trust me, he has friends. We can save him. Want me to help him escape abroad? I have money—I can get him a ticket in three days. And as for the murder, he’ll do all kinds of good things to make up for it. Calm down. He could still become great. So, how are you feeling?”
“You’re cruel! How can you joke about this? Let me go...”
“Where are you going?”
“To him. Where is he? Do you know? Why is this door locked? We came in that way and now it’s locked—when did you lock it?”

“We couldn’t shout about this all over the building. I’m not making fun; I’m just tired of these talks. But how can you go out like this? Do you want to betray him? You’ll only make him panic and give himself up. I’m telling you, he’s already being watched—they’re on his trail. You’d just be handing him over. Wait a minute: I just saw him and talked to him. He can still be saved. Wait, sit down; let’s think this through. I asked you here so we could talk it out in private. Please, sit!”
“How can you save him? Can he really be saved?”
Dounia sat down. Svidrigaïlov sat beside her.
“It all depends on you—just you, and nobody else,” he began, eyes shining with excitement, barely able to get the words out.
Dounia shrank away from him in fear. He was shaking all over, too.

“You... one word from you, and he’s safe. I... I’ll save him. I have money and friends. I’ll get him out of here right away. I’ll get a passport—two passports, one for him and one for me. I have friends—good people. If you want, I’ll get a passport for you, for your mother... Why do you need Razumihin? I love you, too. I love you more than anything... Let me kiss the hem of your dress, let me, please... Just hearing it rustle is almost too much for me. Tell me to do something, anything, and I’ll do it. I swear! I’ll do the impossible. Whatever you believe, I’ll believe. Anything! Don’t look at me like that. Do you know you’re killing me?”
He was almost raving now, totally losing control. Dounia jumped up and ran to the door.
“Open it! Open it!” she yelled, shaking the door. “Open up! Is anyone there?”
Svidrigaïlov snapped out of it, his lips twisting into a cold, mocking smile.
“There’s no one home,” he said, quietly but firmly. “The landlady’s out. Shouting is pointless. You’re just wearing yourself out.”
“Where’s the key? Open the door right now, you scoundrel!”
“I’ve lost the key and can’t find it.”
“This is outrageous!” Dounia cried, turning as pale as death. She ran to the far corner and quickly pulled a little table in front of her as a barrier.
She didn’t scream, but she kept her eyes locked on Svidrigaïlov, watching his every move.
Svidrigaïlov stood on the other side of the room, facing her. He looked calm, at least on the outside, but his face was still pale, and he never lost his mocking smile.

“You just called this ‘outrage,’ Dounia. If that’s the case, you should know I’ve taken precautions. Sonya isn’t home. The Kapernaumovs are far away—there are five locked rooms between us. I’m at least twice as strong as you and have nothing to fear. You wouldn’t actually accuse me after this—you wouldn’t want to betray your brother, would you? Besides, nobody would believe you. How could a girl end up alone in a man’s apartment? Even if you did report me, you wouldn’t be able to prove anything. It’s very hard to prove an assault, Dounia.”
“Monster!” Dounia whispered, furious.

“As you like. I was just speaking generally. I actually agree with you—violence is awful. I only said all this to show you that you wouldn’t have to feel guilty, even if you decided to save your brother the way I suggested. You’d just be giving in to circumstances—giving in to force, if you want to put it that way. Think about it. Your brother’s and your mother’s fate are in your hands. I’d be your slave for life... I’ll wait here.”

Svidrigaïlov sat down on the sofa, about eight steps from Dounia. She had no doubt now that he was completely serious. She also knew what he was capable of. Suddenly, she pulled a revolver out of her pocket, cocked it, and set it on the table in her hand. Svidrigaïlov jumped.

“Ah! So that’s how it is?” he shouted, surprised but grinning wickedly. “Well, that changes everything, Dounia. You’ve just made things a lot simpler for me. Where’d you get the gun? Was it Razumihin? Wait, that’s my revolver! I’ve been looking for it everywhere! All those shooting lessons I gave you in the country weren’t wasted after all.”

“It’s not yours—it belonged to Marfa Petrovna, the woman you killed, you fiend! There was nothing of yours in her house. I took it when I started to suspect what you might do. If you come one step closer, I swear I’ll shoot you.” She was frantic.
“But what about your brother? Just curious,” Svidrigaïlov said, still standing back.
“Tell whoever you want! Don’t move! Don’t come any closer! I’ll shoot! You poisoned your wife, I know it—you’re a murderer!” She kept the revolver ready.
“Are you so sure I poisoned Marfa Petrovna?”
“You did! You basically admitted it; you talked to me about poison... I know you went to get it... you had it ready... It had to be you... Monster!”
“Even if that’s true, I did it for you—you would have been the reason.”
“You’re lying! I always hated you, always!”
“Oh, Dounia! Have you forgotten how you warmed up to me back then? I saw it in your eyes. Remember that moonlit night, with the nightingale singing?”
“That’s a lie!” Dounia’s eyes flashed with rage. “That’s a lie and slander!”
“A lie? Fine, if you say so, it’s a lie. I made it up. I shouldn’t remind women of things like that,” he smiled. “I know you’ll shoot, you wild thing. Go ahead, shoot!”

Dounia raised the revolver, deadly pale, staring at him, judging the distance and waiting for him to move. Her lower lip was white and trembling, her large dark eyes burning with fire. He had never seen her look so beautiful. The fire in her eyes seemed to set something off in him—he felt a sharp pain in his heart. He took a step forward, and a gunshot rang out. The bullet just grazed his hair and hit the wall. He stood still and laughed quietly.
“The wasp stung me. She aimed right at my head. What’s this—blood?” He pulled out his handkerchief to wipe away a thin trickle of blood down his right temple. The bullet had barely scratched him.
Dounia lowered the gun and stared at Svidrigaïlov—not in fear, but almost in wild shock. She seemed lost, not really understanding what she’d just done or what was happening.
“You missed! Shoot again, I’ll wait,” Svidrigaïlov said softly, still smiling, though his smile was darker now. “But if you take too long, I’ll be able to grab you before you cock the gun again.”
Dounia jerked, quickly cocked the revolver, and raised it again.
“Stay away!” she cried desperately. “I’ll really shoot this time. I’ll kill you!”
“Well, at this distance you probably won’t miss. But if you don’t shoot... then—” His eyes flashed, and he took two steps forward. Dounia fired again: the gun misfired.
“You didn’t load it right. Doesn’t matter, you have another shot. Get it ready, I’ll wait.”

He stood in front of her, just two steps away, staring intensely, eyes burning with stubborn passion. Dounia realized he’d rather die than let her go. “At this distance, she’d definitely kill him now!” she thought. Suddenly, she threw the revolver aside.

“She dropped it!” Svidrigaïlov said in surprise, taking a deep breath. A huge weight seemed to lift from his heart—maybe not only the fear of death, but something darker and more painful that he couldn’t name.

He walked over to Dounia and gently put his arm around her waist. She didn’t resist, but trembled like a leaf, looking up at him with pleading eyes. He tried to speak, but his lips just moved without any words coming out.
“Let me go,” Dounia begged. Svidrigaïlov shuddered. Her voice was completely different now.
“So you don’t love me?” he whispered. Dounia shook her head.
“And... and you never could? Not ever?” he asked, hopeless.
“Never!”

There was a long, silent struggle in Svidrigaïlov’s heart. He stared at her with a look she couldn’t describe. Suddenly, he let go, turned quickly to the window, and stood facing it. Another moment passed.
“Here’s the key.”
He pulled it out of his left coat pocket and set it on the table behind him, still not looking at Dounia.
“Take it! Hurry up!”
He kept staring out the window. Dounia walked to the table and grabbed the key.
“Hurry! Hurry!” Svidrigaïlov repeated, still not turning around or moving. But there was something frightening in the way he said “hurry.”
Dounia understood, snatched up the key, ran to the door, unlocked it fast, and rushed out. A minute later
Svidrigaïlov spent that evening wandering from one cheap bar to another until ten o’clock. Katia showed up again and sang another street song about how
“a villain and a tyrant,”
“started kissing Katia.”

Svidrigaïlov bought drinks for Katia, the organ-grinder, some singers, the waiters, and two young office clerks. He felt oddly connected to the clerks because both of them had crooked noses—one bent to the left, the other to the right. They ended up taking him to an outdoor amusement park, where he paid for their tickets. The park had just one tall, skinny pine tree and three scraggly bushes, plus a “Vauxhall” that was really just a bar serving tea and alcohol, with some green tables and chairs outside. A group of awful singers and a gloomy, drunk German clown with a big red nose tried to entertain the crowd. The clerks got into an argument with some other clerks, and a fight almost broke out. Svidrigaïlov was asked to settle the quarrel. He listened for fifteen minutes, but everyone yelled so loudly he couldn’t understand a thing. The only clear detail was that one clerk had stolen something and sold it right there to a Jewish man, but refused to split the money. It turned out the stolen item was a teaspoon from the Vauxhall. When the staff noticed it was missing, things got complicated. Svidrigaïlov paid for the lost spoon, stood up, and left the park. By then it was about six o’clock. He hadn’t touched any alcohol, just ordered tea to blend in.

The evening was dark, muggy, and suffocating. By ten o’clock, heavy storm clouds covered the sky. There was a loud clap of thunder, and then the rain poured down in sheets. It didn’t just drip—it flooded the streets. Lightning flashed every minute, each bolt lasting as long as you could count to five.

Soaked all over, Svidrigaïlov went home, locked himself in, opened his desk, took out all his money, and tore up a few papers. He put the money in his pocket and was about to change into dry clothes. But when he looked out at the storm and listened to the thunder and rain, he decided not to bother. He grabbed his hat and left, not even locking the door behind him. He went straight to visit Sonia, who was at home.

She wasn’t alone—the four Kapernaumov children were with her, and she was giving them tea. When Svidrigaïlov walked in, Sonia greeted him quietly, looking at his dripping clothes in surprise. The children immediately ran away, terrified.
Svidrigaïlov sat at the table and asked Sonia to sit next to him. She sat down, nervous and ready to listen.

“I might be going to America soon, Sofya Semyonovna,” Svidrigaïlov said, “and since this could be the last time I see you, I wanted to settle a few things. Did you see the lady today? I know what she told you, you don’t have to say it.” (Sonia shifted in her seat and blushed.) “People like that do things their own way. As for your sisters and brother, they’re taken care of. The money set aside for them is safely stored, and I’ve got signed receipts. You should keep the receipts, just in case. Here, take them. That’s done. Now, here are three bonds, each worth a thousand roubles at five percent interest. These are for you—just for you—and please, don’t tell anyone about it, no matter what you hear. You’ll need the money, because living the way you have been isn’t necessary anymore, Sofya Semyonovna.”
“I’m so grateful to you, and so are the children and my stepmother,” Sonia said quickly, “and if I haven’t said much... please don’t think...”
“That’s enough! That’s enough!”

“But about the money, Arkady Ivanovitch, I really appreciate it, but I don’t need it now. I can earn my own living. Please don’t think I’m ungrateful. If you want to help someone, maybe give the money...”

“It’s for you, Sofya Semyonovna, just for you, and please, don’t argue. I don’t have time for it. You’ll need it. Rodion Romanovitch (Raskolnikov) only has two options: shoot himself or go to Siberia.” (Sonia stared at him, shocked.) “Don’t worry, I know everything from him, and I’m not a gossip. I won’t tell anyone. You gave him good advice when you told him to confess—it really would be better for him. If he goes to Siberia, you’ll go after him, right? You’ll need money then. You’ll need it for him, understand? Giving it to you is like giving it to him. Also, you promised Amalia Ivanovna you’d pay what’s owed. I heard you. Why do you take on such debts so carelessly, Sofya Semyonovna? It was Katerina Ivanovna’s debt, not yours, so you shouldn’t have listened to that German woman. You can’t go through life like that. If anyone asks about me—maybe tomorrow or the next day—don’t mention that I visited and don’t show the money to anyone or even talk about it. All right, goodbye.” (He stood up.) “Say hello to Rodion Romanovitch for me. By the way, you should give the money to Mr. Razumihin for safekeeping for now. You know Razumihin, right? Of course you do. He’s a good guy. Take it to him tomorrow or... when you need to. Until then, hide it well.”
Sonia stood up too, staring at Svidrigaïlov in alarm. She wanted to say something, to ask a question, but for a moment, she was too scared and didn’t know where to start.
“How can you... how can you go out now, in such heavy rain?”

“What, should I let some rain stop me from going to America? Ha, ha! Goodbye, Sofya Semyonovna, my dear! Live a long life—you’ll help others. Oh, and... tell Mr. Razumihin I say hello. Tell him Arkady Ivanovitch Svidrigaïlov sends his greetings. Don’t forget.”
He left, and Sonia was left standing there, filled with confusion and a sense of dread.

Later, it turned out that at twenty past eleven that same night, Svidrigaïlov made another strange and unexpected visit. The rain was still coming down. Soaking wet, he went to the tiny apartment where his fiancée’s parents lived, on Third Street in Vassilyevsky Island. He knocked for a long time before they let him in, and his visit at first caused a lot of worry. But Svidrigaïlov could turn on the charm when he wanted, so the parents quickly dropped their first guess—that he was just drunk and didn’t know what he was doing. The frail father was wheeled in by the gentle and practical mother, who, as usual, started talking with random small talk. She never asked anything directly, but would start by smiling and rubbing her hands, then slowly get around to her real question—for example, when Svidrigaïlov wanted to set the wedding date, she’d begin by asking about Paris and life at court, and only eventually mention Third Street. Usually, this way of talking was impressive, but tonight Arkady Ivanovitch seemed especially impatient and insisted on seeing his fiancée right away, even though they told him she was already in bed. Of course, she came out.

Svidrigaïlov told her immediately that he had urgent business that forced him to leave Petersburg for a while, and that he’d brought her fifteen thousand roubles as a gift, something he’d always planned to give her before their wedding. It didn’t really make sense why he needed to give her the money just because he was leaving, especially in the middle of the night during a rainstorm, but no one questioned it. They all accepted it happily; even the usual exclamations of surprise and regret were kept to a minimum. The mother, especially, was glowing with gratitude and even shed tears. Svidrigaïlov got up, laughed, kissed his fiancée, patted her on the cheek, and promised to be back soon. When he saw in her eyes a mix of childlike curiosity and a deeper, silent question, he thought for a moment and kissed her again, although he felt secretly annoyed knowing her mother would immediately lock the money away. He left them all buzzing with excitement, but the mother, in a quiet whisper, calmed everyone, saying Svidrigaïlov was a very important, wealthy man—no one could guess what he was up to. He could just decide to travel and give away money whenever he wanted, so it wasn’t that strange. Sure, it was odd that he was soaking wet, but Englishmen were even weirder, and rich people didn’t care what others thought or follow the usual rules. Maybe he even came in the rain on purpose to show he wasn’t afraid of anything. Above all, no one should talk about it, since who knew what could happen, and the money needed to be locked up right away. They were glad the cook, Fedosya, hadn’t left the kitchen, and absolutely nothing should be said to that nosy Madame Resslich. They whispered about it until two in the morning, but the girl went to bed early, amazed and a little sad.

Meanwhile, Svidrigaïlov crossed the bridge back to the mainland exactly at midnight. The rain had stopped, but a strong wind was blowing. He started shivering and, for a moment, stared at the dark waters of the Little Neva, oddly interested. But he soon felt too cold standing by the water, so he turned and walked toward Y. Prospect. He walked for almost half an hour, stumbling a couple times on the wooden sidewalk, but always looking for something on the right side of the street. He remembered seeing a wooden hotel near the end called something like Adrianople. He found it easily—the place stood out, even in the dark, as a big, blackened wooden building with lights in the windows, showing people were still awake. He went inside and asked a shabby man in the hallway for a room. The man, sizing up Svidrigaïlov, led him straight to a tiny, stuffy room at the end of the corridor under the stairs, saying it was the only one available. The ragged man looked at him, waiting for instructions.
“Can I have some tea?” Svidrigaïlov asked.
“Yes, sir.”
“What else do you have?”
“Veal, vodka, snacks.”
“Bring me tea and veal.”
“Don’t you want anything else?” the man asked, surprised.
“No, nothing else.”
The ragged man left, a little disappointed.
“This place is interesting,” Svidrigaïlov thought. “How did I not know about it? I probably look like I just came from some nightclub and got into trouble. I wonder who else stays here?”

He lit the candle and checked out the room. The ceiling was so low he could barely stand up. There was one small window. The dirty bed, plus a plain chair and table, filled almost the whole space. The walls were made of rough boards, covered with torn, faded yellow wallpaper. One wall sloped because of the stairs overhead, so the room wasn’t an attic, just wedged under the stairs.

Svidrigaïlov set the candle down, sat on the bed, and started thinking. But a weird, continuous noise from the next room kept grabbing his attention. It got louder at times, almost like shouting, and hadn’t stopped since he got there. He listened carefully: someone was angrily complaining, almost crying, but only one voice.

Svidrigaïlov got up, shielded the candle with his hand, and noticed a crack of light in the wall. He peeked through. The next room was a little bigger and had two people in it. One was a man with curly hair and a red, puffy face, standing like he was giving a speech, without his coat, legs spread to keep his balance, pounding his chest. He yelled at the other guy for being a beggar with no status, claiming he’d rescued him from the streets and could kick him out whenever he wanted, and only “the finger of Providence” was watching. The man being yelled at sat in a chair, looking like he was about to sneeze but couldn’t. Sometimes he looked up with confused, sheepish eyes, but clearly had no idea what the other was ranting about. A candle burned on the table, surrounded by wine glasses, a nearly empty vodka bottle, bread, cucumber, and dirty tea glasses. After watching for a bit, Svidrigaïlov lost interest and sat back down on his own bed.

The ragged attendant came back with the tea and asked again if Svidrigaïlov wanted anything else. Getting another “no,” he finally left. Svidrigaïlov drank a cup of tea to warm up but couldn’t eat. He started to feel feverish. Taking off his coat, he wrapped himself in the blanket and lay on the bed, annoyed. “It would’ve been better to feel good for this,” he thought with a smile. The room was stuffy, the candle barely flickered, the wind howled outside, a mouse scratched in the corner, and the place smelled like mice and old leather. His mind wandered: one thought after another, trying to focus. “There must be a garden outside the window,” he thought. “I can hear trees. I hate the sound of trees on a stormy night—it gives me the creeps.” He remembered how much he disliked it when he walked past Petrovsky Park earlier. That reminded him of standing by the Little Neva bridge and feeling cold. “I’ve never liked water,” he thought, “not even in paintings.” Suddenly he laughed at himself. “Shouldn’t all these comforts not matter now? But I’m getting picky, like an animal looking for the perfect spot... for something important. I should have gone to Petrovsky Park! Guess it was too dark and cold—ha! As if I’m looking for comfort... Oh, why haven’t I put out the candle?” He blew it out. “Looks like the people next door went to bed.” He couldn’t see any light through the crack. “Well, Marfa Petrovna, now’s the time for you to appear—it’s dark, perfect for a ghost. But you won’t come now!”

He suddenly remembered how, just an hour before trying to force himself on Dounia, he had told Raskolnikov to trust her with Razumihin. “I bet I really did say that, just as Raskolnikov guessed, to tease myself. But what a sly guy that Raskolnikov is! He’s been through a lot. He might even turn into a successful schemer when he gets over his wild ideas. But right now he’s too hungry for life. Young men are the worst that way. Oh well, let him do what he wants, it’s none of my business.”

He couldn’t fall asleep. Dounia’s face kept appearing in his mind, giving him chills. “No, I have to let all that go now,” he told himself, trying to focus on something else. “It’s strange. I never truly hated anyone, never even wanted revenge much, and that’s a bad sign. I never liked fighting, never lost my temper—that’s a bad sign too. And the promises I just made her—damn it! But who knows—maybe she could have changed me somehow....”

He clenched his teeth and went silent again. Dounia’s image came back: how she’d looked after firing the revolver at him and then lowering it in shock, staring at him blankly—how he could have grabbed her again and she wouldn’t have stopped him if he hadn’t reminded her. He remembered feeling almost sorry for her then, feeling a sharp pain in his heart...
“Ugh! Enough of these thoughts! I need to stop thinking about this!”

He started drifting off to sleep; the fever chills had stopped, when suddenly something ran over his arm and leg under the blanket. He jumped. “Ugh! Must be a mouse,” he thought, “drawn by the veal I left on the table.” He didn’t want to pull off the blanket, get up, and get cold, but then something crawled over his leg again. He threw off the blanket and lit the candle. Shivering, he checked the bed: nothing. He shook out the blanket, and suddenly a mouse darted onto the sheet. He tried to catch it, but it zigzagged around, slipped through his fingers, ran over his hand, and suddenly shot under his pillow. He threw the pillow aside, but instantly felt something scurry across his chest, down his body, and under his shirt. He panicked—and woke up.
The room was dark. He was in bed, wrapped in the blanket like before. The wind howled outside the window. “Gross,” he thought, annoyed.

He sat up and perched on the edge of the bed, back to the window. “I’d better not sleep at all,” he decided. There was a cold, damp breeze from the window, so he pulled the blanket tighter around him. He didn’t want to think about anything, but random images and broken thoughts drifted through his mind as he grew drowsy. Maybe it was the cold, the damp, or the wind outside, but he started daydreaming. He pictured a beautiful flower garden, a sunny, almost hot day, like a holiday. There was a fancy country house, English-style, covered in flowers, with flower beds all around. The porch was surrounded by climbing plants and roses. Inside, the stairs had thick rugs and rare plants in pots. He especially noticed vases of white, fragrant narcissus flowers in the windows. He didn’t want to leave them, but he climbed the stairs into a big, bright living room—again, with flowers everywhere: in the windows, on the doors to the balcony, and even on the balcony itself. The floors were scattered with fresh hay, the windows were open, cool air came in, and birds chirped outside. In the middle of the room, on a table covered in white satin, was a coffin. It was decorated with white silk and surrounded by flowers. Inside was a girl in a white dress, arms folded on her chest, as still as a statue. Her loose, fair hair was wet, and she wore a wreath of roses. Her face, pale and serious, looked like marble, and her sad smile showed deep, grown-up suffering. Svidrigaïlov recognized the girl; there were no icons, candles, or prayers—she had drowned herself. She was only fourteen, but her heart had been broken by an insult so shocking and unfair that she couldn’t bear it, and in her despair, she ended her life on a cold, rainy night, while the wind howled....

Svidrigaïlov snapped out of it, got up from the bed, and went to the window. He opened it, and the wind whipped into the room, stinging his face and chest through his shirt as if it were freezing. Below the window there seemed to be a garden, maybe even an amusement garden where people had tea and music during the day. Now, rain blew in from the trees and bushes; it was so dark he could barely see shapes outside. Leaning on the windowsill, he stared into the darkness for five minutes. Suddenly, the sound of a cannon echoed through the night, then a second shot. “Ah, that’s the signal! The river is flooding,” he thought. “By morning, water will be rushing down the street, flooding basements. Rats will swim out, people will curse as they move their stuff upstairs. What time is it?” Just then, he heard a clock nearby strike three.
“Aha! It’ll be light in an hour. Why wait? I’ll go out now, right to the park. I’ll pick a big bush soaked with rain, so when I touch it, tons of drops fall on my head.”

He left the window, closed it, lit the candle, put on his vest, coat, and hat, and went into the hallway to find the ragged attendant—who was probably sleeping somewhere among candle stubs and junk—to pay for the room before leaving. “This is the right moment; I couldn’t pick a better time.”

He walked for a while down a long, narrow hallway, not seeing anyone. He was about to call out when, in a dark corner between an old cupboard and the door, he spotted something strange—something alive. He bent down with the candle and saw a little girl, not older than five, shivering and crying, her clothes soaked. She didn’t seem scared of Svidrigaïlov, just stared at him with wide, amazed black eyes. She sobbed now and then like kids do when they’re almost done crying but not quite comforted. Her face was pale and tired, and she was numb with cold. “How did she end up here? Must have hidden here, not sleeping all night.” He started asking her questions. Suddenly she became lively and babbled in her childish way about “mammy” and how “mammy would beat her,” and something about breaking a cup. From what he could gather, she was a neglected child whose mother—probably a drunk cook who worked at the hotel—beat and scared her. The girl had broken her mom’s cup, got terrified, ran away, hid outside in the rain, then finally sneaked in here, hid behind the cupboard, and spent the whole night there, crying and shaking from the cold, dark, and fear. He picked her up, carried her to his room, sat her on the bed, and began taking off her wet clothes. Her shoes, with no socks, were as soaked as if she’d stood in a puddle all night. Once she was undressed, he put her on the bed, wrapped her in the blanket from head to toe, and she fell asleep immediately. He went back to his gloomy thoughts.

“Why am I bothering with this?” he suddenly thought, annoyed. “What nonsense!” He grabbed the candle, planning to go find the ragged attendant and leave quickly. “Forget the child!” he muttered as he opened the door, but turned back to check if the girl was asleep. He lifted the blanket carefully. She was sleeping soundly, warmed up now, and her cheeks were flushed. But strangely, the flush looked harsher than a normal child’s rosy cheeks. “It’s a fever,” thought Svidrigaïlov. It looked almost like she’d been drinking alcohol—her lips were hot and bright red. But then, he thought he saw her eyelashes twitch, like she was peeking with a sly, adult look, pretending to sleep. Yes, her lips curled in a smile, the corners of her mouth trembling as she tried to hide it. Suddenly, it turned into a full grin—there was something shameless, even wicked, in her face. It was like the face of a prostitute, a French harlot, but on a child. Now both her eyes opened wide, looking at him with a bold, mocking stare, laughing, inviting him.... There was something horribly wrong and disgusting in that look, in those eyes, in such nastiness on a child’s face. “What, at five years old?” Svidrigaïlov whispered, horrified. “What’s happening?” She turned toward him, her face glowing, holding out her arms.... “Cursed child!” Svidrigaïlov shouted, raising his hand to hit her—but woke up at that moment.
He was in the same bed, still wrapped in the blanket. The candle hadn’t been lit, and daylight was streaming in through the window.

“I’ve had nightmares all night!” he said angrily, feeling completely exhausted; his bones ached. It was thick with fog outside, so he couldn’t see a thing. It was almost five o’clock. He had overslept! He got up, put on his still-damp jacket and overcoat. Feeling the revolver in his pocket, he took it out, then sat down, took out a notebook, and wrote a few big lines on the front page. After reading them over, he propped his elbows on the table and thought. The revolver and notebook lay beside him. Some flies, now awake, landed on the untouched veal on the table. He stared at them, and then, almost without thinking, started trying to catch one with his hand. He kept at it until he was tired, then realized what he was doing, jolted, got up, and walked out of the room. A minute later, he was outside.

A thick, milky fog covered the city. Svidrigaïlov walked down the slippery, dirty wooden sidewalk toward the Little Neva. He pictured the river, swollen from the storm, Petrovsky Island, the wet paths, the soaked grass, trees, and bushes, and finally the bush he had picked.... He stared grumpily at the houses, trying to distract himself. There wasn’t a single cab or person on the street. The small yellow wooden houses looked dirty and sad with their shutters closed. The cold and damp seeped into his bones, making him shiver. Sometimes he stopped to read shop signs carefully. Finally, he reached the end of the wooden sidewalk and came to a big stone building. A dirty, shivering dog slunk past him, tail between its legs. A man in a big coat lay facedown on the sidewalk, dead drunk. Svidrigaïlov glanced at him and kept walking. A tall tower rose on the left. “Aha!” he said, “here’s a spot. Why does it have to be Petrovsky? There will be an official witness here, anyway....”

He almost smiled at this new idea and turned down the street with the big house and tower. At the closed gates, a short man leaned against them, wearing a gray soldier’s coat and a shiny bronze helmet. He looked at Svidrigaïlov sleepily, with the sour, tired look seen on many Jewish faces. The two of them stared at each other in silence for a few minutes. At last, the man realized it was odd for someone not drunk to just stand there staring at him.
“What do you want here?” he asked, not even moving.
“Nothing, brother. Good morning,” Svidrigaïlov replied.
“This isn’t the place.”
“I’m going abroad, brother.”
“Abroad?”
“To America.”
“America.”
Svidrigaïlov took out his revolver and cocked it. The man’s eyebrows shot up.
“Hey, this isn’t the place for jokes like that!”
“Why not?”
“Because it just isn’t.”
“Well, brother, that doesn’t matter to me. It’s a good spot. When they ask you, just say he said he was going to America.”
Svidrigaïlov put the revolver to his right temple.
“You can’t do that here, it’s not the place!” the man yelled, wide awake now, his eyes huge.
Svidrigaïlov pulled the trigger.

That same day, around seven in the evening, Raskolnikov was heading to his mother’s and sister’s apartment—the one Razumihin had found for them in Bakaleyev’s building. The stairs led up straight from the street. Raskolnikov walked slowly, almost as if he was still debating with himself about whether to go. But nothing could make him turn back now: he had made up his mind.
“Anyway, it doesn’t matter. They don’t know anything yet,” he thought. “And they’re used to me acting strange by now.”

He looked terrible: his clothes were ripped and dirty, soaked from the rain the night before. His face was twisted from exhaustion, being out in the weather, and from the constant struggle inside him for the past twenty-four hours. No one knew where he’d spent the night. But at least, now, he had decided what to do.

He knocked at the door, and his mother opened it. Dounia wasn’t home. Even the servant was out. At first, Pulcheria Alexandrovna was too happy and surprised to speak; then she grabbed his hand and pulled him into the room.

“You’re here!” she said, her voice trembling with happiness. “Don’t be mad at me, Rodya, for welcoming you like this, crying. I’m not really crying—I’m laughing! Did you think I was upset? No, I’m just so happy, but I’ve gotten into the habit of crying over everything ever since your father died. I cry at anything these days. Sit down, my dear, you must be tired. Oh, look at you—how muddy you are.”
“I got caught in the rain yesterday, Mother…” Raskolnikov started to explain.

“No, no,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna interrupted quickly, “you think I’m going to start questioning you like I used to, but don’t worry, I get it now. I’ve learned how things work here, and I see for myself it’s better not to poke at you. I’ve decided I can’t really understand your plans or expect you to explain everything—who knows what thoughts you have, or what you’re working on! So I shouldn’t keep bothering you about it. But, oh my goodness! I’m running around like a crazy person… I’ve been reading your article in that magazine, Rodya—Dmitri Prokofitch (Razumihin) brought it to me. As soon as I saw it, I thought, ‘There, you silly woman, that’s what he’s been up to—that’s the secret!’ Smart people are always like this. Maybe you’ve got new ideas you’re thinking about, and I just get in your way. I read it, my dear, and of course I didn’t understand most of it—but that’s normal, isn’t it?”
“Can I see it, Mother?”

Raskolnikov took the magazine and glanced at his article. Even though it didn’t fit his mood or situation at all, he still felt that weird, bittersweet feeling every author gets the first time they see their own words in print—and he was only twenty-three. The feeling only lasted a moment. After reading a few lines, he frowned, and his heart started pounding with pain. He remembered all the inner struggles of the past months. Suddenly, he threw the article down on the table in anger and disgust.

“But even if I don’t understand everything, Rodya, I can see with my own eyes that you’ll soon be one of the top thinkers in Russia—maybe even the best! And to think, people actually thought you were insane! You don’t know, but they really did. How could they understand someone as smart as you? And Dounia, she almost believed them—can you believe it? Your father once sent poems and even a whole novel to magazines (I still have the manuscript and can show you), and we prayed they would accept it—but they never did. Just a week ago I was heartbroken about your food, your clothes, and the way you’re living. But now I see how silly that was, because you can achieve anything you want with your mind and talent. I know you don’t care about that right now, and you’re busy with more important things…”
“Is Dounia not home, Mother?”

“No, Rodya. I hardly ever see her—she’s always out. Dmitri Prokofitch visits me, though, which is so kind of him, and he always talks about you. He really likes and respects you, my dear. I’m not saying Dounia doesn’t care—she just has her own way. She seems to have some secrets lately, but I never keep secrets from either of you. I’m sure she loves you and me… but who knows where all this is leading. You’ve made me so happy by coming now, Rodya, but she missed you by going out; when she gets home I’ll tell her: ‘Your brother came while you were out! Where have you been all this time?’ But don’t spoil me, Rodya, come when you can, and if you can’t, it’s okay—I’ll know you love me and that’s enough. I’ll read your writing, hear about you from others, and sometimes you’ll visit. What more could I want? You came today just to make your mother happy, I know you did.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna started to cry again.

“There I go again! Don’t pay attention to me. Oh goodness, why am I just sitting here?” she said, suddenly standing up. “There’s coffee and I haven’t even offered you any. That’s just me being selfish and old. I’ll get it right now!”
“Mother, don’t worry about that, I’m leaving soon. I didn’t come for coffee. Please, listen to me.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna came over to him, a little nervous.

“Mother, no matter what happens, no matter what you might hear about me, or what anyone tells you, will you always love me like you do now?” he suddenly asked, his heart full, not really thinking about the words as he said them.
“Rodya, Rodya, what’s wrong? Why would you ask me something like that? Who would ever say anything against you? Besides, I wouldn’t believe them—I wouldn’t even listen.”

“I just wanted you to know that I’ve always loved you, and I’m glad we’re alone right now—even glad Dounia isn’t here,” he continued, still speaking from the heart. “I want you to know that even though you might be unhappy, you have to believe your son loves you more than himself, and all those things you thought about me—that I was cruel and didn’t care—were all wrong. I’ll never stop loving you… That’s all. I needed to say this, to start with this…”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna hugged him tightly and silently, holding him close and crying softly.

“I don’t know what’s wrong with you, Rodya,” she finally said. “I kept thinking we were just bothering you, but now I see something terrible must be coming, and that’s why you’re so unhappy. I’ve felt it for a long time, Rodya. I’m sorry to say it, but I worry about it all the time, even when I’m lying in bed at night. Your sister was talking in her sleep last night—all about you. I couldn’t understand everything, but I caught a few things. All morning I felt like something awful was about to happen, and now here it is! Rodya, are you leaving? Are you going somewhere?”
“Yes.”

“I thought so! I’ll come with you, if you want. And Dounia, too—she loves you so much. Even Sofya Semyonovna (Sonya) can come if you want. I’d be happy to treat her like a daughter. Dmitri Prokofitch will help us all go together. But… where are you going?”
“Goodbye, Mother.”
“What, today?” she cried, as if she’d lost him forever.
“I can’t stay. I have to go now…”
“And I can’t come with you?”
“No, but kneel down and pray for me. Maybe your prayer will reach God.”
“Let me bless you and make the sign of the cross. Yes, that’s right… Oh God, what are we doing?”

He was glad—really glad—that no one else was there and he was alone with his mother. For the first time in months, his heart softened. He dropped to his knees in front of her, kissed her feet, and they both hugged each other, crying. She wasn’t surprised or questioning this time. For days, she’d known something terrible was happening to her son, and now the awful moment had finally come.

“Rodya, my dear boy, my firstborn,” she sobbed, “this is just like when you were little. You’d run to me like this, hug me, and kiss me. When your father was alive and we were poor, you made us happy just by being there. And when I buried your father, how many times did we cry together at his grave, hugging like this? If I’ve been crying lately, it’s because a mother just knows when something bad is coming. The first evening I saw you after we arrived here, I could tell just from your eyes—my heart sank. And today, when I opened the door and saw you, I thought the terrible moment had come. Rodya, you’re not leaving today, are you?”
“No!”
“You’ll come again?”
“Yes… I’ll come.”
“Rodya, don’t be mad, I won’t ask you questions—I know I shouldn’t. Just tell me one thing: is it far, where you’re going?”
“Very far.”
“What’s waiting for you there? Is it a job, a new life?”
“Whatever God sends… just pray for me.” Raskolnikov headed for the door, but his mother grabbed onto him, staring into his eyes with fear. Her face was full of terror.
“Enough, Mother,” Raskolnikov said, deeply wishing he hadn’t come.
“It’s not forever—not yet forever, is it? You’ll come, you’ll come tomorrow?”
“I will, I will—goodbye.” He finally pulled himself away.

It was a warm, clear, bright evening. The weather had improved since morning. Raskolnikov hurried back to his apartment; he wanted to finish everything before sunset. He didn’t want to run into anyone on the way. As he went up the stairs, he noticed Nastasya watching him closely from the samovar. “Has someone come to see me?” he wondered. He had a nasty image of Porfiry in his mind. But when he opened his door, he saw Dounia. She was sitting there alone, deep in thought, and it looked like she’d been waiting a long time. He stopped in the doorway. She stood up from the sofa, shocked, and faced him. Her eyes were full of horror and sadness. Just from her eyes, he knew she understood everything.
“Should I come in, or should I leave?” he asked uncertainly.
“I was with Sofya Semyonovna (Sonya) all day. We were both waiting for you. We thought you’d definitely come there.”
Raskolnikov walked into the room and collapsed into a chair, exhausted.
“I feel weak, Dounia. I’m really tired, and I wish I was able to control myself right now.”
He looked at her with suspicion.
“Where were you all night?”

“I don’t remember clearly. You see, sister, I wanted to make a final decision, and I walked along the Neva several times. I remember I was thinking about ending it all there, but… I couldn’t do it,” he whispered, looking at her suspiciously again.
“Thank God! That’s what Sonya and I were so afraid of. So you still want to live? Thank God, thank God!”
Raskolnikov gave a bitter smile.
“I don’t really believe in anything, but I just cried in Mother’s arms; I don’t have faith, but I asked her to pray for me. I don’t know what’s going on, Dounia, I just don’t get it.”
“You went to see Mother? Did you tell her?” Dounia cried, horrified. “Please tell me you didn’t!”

“No, I didn’t tell her… not directly; but she figured out a lot. She heard you talking in your sleep. I’m sure she understands at least half of it already. Maybe it was a mistake to visit her. I don’t even know why I went. I’m a pathetic person, Dounia.”
“Maybe, but you’re brave enough to face what’s coming! You are, aren’t you?”

“Yes, I’m going. Right now. I even thought about drowning myself to escape the shame, Dounia, but as I stood by the water, I realized that if I thought I was strong before, I shouldn’t be afraid of disgrace,” he said quickly. “It’s just pride, Dounia.”
“Pride, Rodya.”
There was a spark in his tired eyes; he seemed almost happy to think he still had his pride.
“You don’t think I was just scared of the water, do you?” he asked, looking at her with a dark, twisted smile.

“Oh, Rodya, stop!” Dounia cried, nearly in tears. They were silent for two minutes. He stared at the floor; Dounia stood at the other end of the table, watching him with pain in her eyes. Suddenly he stood up.
“It’s late. It’s time to go. I’m going right now to confess. But I don’t even know why I’m doing it.”
Big tears rolled down Dounia’s cheeks.
“You’re crying, sister, but can you shake my hand?”
“You really doubted it?”
She hugged him tightly.
“Aren’t you already half making up for your crime by facing what’s coming?” she cried, holding him close and kissing him.

“Crime? What crime?” he shouted, suddenly furious. “That I killed a horrible, useless insect—an old pawnbroker woman, who was no good to anyone! Killing her made up for forty other sins. She was draining the life from poor people. Was that really a crime? I’m not thinking about it, and I’m not thinking about making up for it. Why does everyone keep bringing it up—‘crime, crime!’? Only now I see how stupid my cowardice was, now that I’ve decided to face this pointless disgrace. It’s just because I’m pathetic and I have nothing inside me that I’m doing this—maybe even for my own benefit, like Porfiry suggested!”
“Brother, what are you saying? You killed someone—you spilled blood!” Dounia cried in despair.

“Everyone spills blood,” he said almost wildly, “it’s been happening forever, it flows like champagne, and people get medals for it and are called heroes. Think about it! I wanted to help people and would have done hundreds, thousands of good deeds to make up for that one mistake—not even a mistake, just clumsiness, because the idea itself wasn’t as stupid as it seems now that it failed. (Everything seems stupid when it fails.) I only wanted to put myself in a position where I wouldn’t be poor, to take the first step, to get the money, and then I could’ve done so much good. But I… I couldn’t even do that first step, because I’m pathetic, that’s the truth! But I won’t see it the way you do. If I had succeeded, I’d be celebrated, but now I’m trapped.”
“But that’s not true, not true! Brother, what are you saying?”

“Oh, it’s not pretty, not poetic enough! I don’t get why killing people by bombing them in wars is considered more honorable. Worrying about appearances is the first sign of weakness. I’ve never seen that more clearly than now, and I’m further than ever from believing what I did was a crime. I’ve never felt stronger or more sure than I do right now.”

His pale, exhausted face flushed with color, but as he said those last words, he happened to meet Dounia’s eyes and saw such deep pain there that it stopped him. He felt, at least, that he had made these two women miserable, that he was the cause of their suffering…

“Dounia, if I’m guilty, forgive me (even though I know I can’t be forgiven if I am). Goodbye! Let’s not argue anymore. It’s time—past time—to go. Don’t follow me, please, I have somewhere else to go… But you, go right now and stay with Mother. Please, I’m begging you, it’s my last request. Don’t leave her, not even for a moment; I left her anxious, and she can’t handle it; she’ll die or lose her mind. Be with her! Razumihin will stay with you. I’ve talked to him. Don’t cry for me: I’ll try to be honest and brave all my life, even if I’m a murderer. Maybe someday I’ll make a name for myself. I won’t shame you, you’ll see; I’ll prove it… Now goodbye for now,” he finished quickly, noticing once more the strange look in Dounia’s eyes at his last words and promises. “Why are you crying? Don’t cry, don’t cry—we’re not saying goodbye forever! Oh, wait, I almost forgot!”

He went to the table, picked up a thick, dusty book, opened it, and took out a little watercolor portrait painted on ivory. It was a picture of his landlady’s daughter, the strange girl who had wanted to be a nun, who died of fever. For a moment, he stared at her delicate, expressive face, kissed the portrait, and handed it to Dounia.

“I used to talk a lot to her, only to her,” he said quietly. “I told her so much that’s now turned out so horribly. Don’t worry,” he said to Dounia, “she was against it all, just like you, and I’m glad she’s gone now. The main thing is, everything is going to change now—it’s all going to be split in two,” he said, suddenly sounding hopeless again. “Everything, everything, and am I ready for it? Do I even want it? They say I have to suffer! What’s the point of all this pointless suffering? Will I understand any better after twenty years of hard labor, when I’m weak as an old man? What will I have to live for then? Why am I agreeing to that life now? Oh, I knew I was pathetic this morning when I stood by the Neva at dawn!”

At last, they both left. It was hard for Dounia, but she loved him. She walked away, but after fifty steps she turned to look at him again. He was still visible. At the corner, he turned too, and for the last time their eyes met; but when he saw her looking, he waved her off impatiently, even a little angrily, and quickly turned the corner.

“I’m awful, I see that,” he thought, feeling ashamed a moment later for snapping at Dounia. “But why do they love me so much if I don’t deserve it? If only I was alone and nobody cared about me, and I never cared for anyone

When Raskolnikov walked into Sonia’s room, the sun was already setting and it was getting dark. Sonia had been waiting anxiously for him all day, and Dounia (his sister) had been with her. Dounia had come to see Sonia that morning, remembering what Svidrigaïlov had said—that Sonia knew the truth. We won’t go into all the details of their conversation or how they cried together and grew close, but Dounia did find some comfort: at least her brother wouldn’t have to go through his troubles alone. He had confessed to Sonia first, turned to her when he needed someone, and Dounia could tell that Sonia would stay with him, wherever fate took them. Dounia didn’t need to ask; she just knew. She looked at Sonia with so much respect that, at first, it almost embarrassed Sonia. Sonia felt like she wasn’t even worthy to look at Dounia. The way Dounia had treated her with respect and kindness the first time they met in Raskolnikov’s room had left a lasting impression on Sonia.

Eventually, Dounia got impatient and left Sonia’s place to wait for her brother in his own room. She kept thinking he’d go there first. As soon as Dounia left, Sonia grew terrified Raskolnikov would kill himself, and Dounia was afraid of that too. Still, they’d spent most of the day trying to convince each other that he wouldn’t do that, and when they were together, their fear seemed smaller. But once alone, neither could think of anything else. Sonia remembered how Svidrigaïlov had told her the day before that Raskolnikov really only had two options—Siberia or... something worse. She also knew how proud and stubborn he could be, and how he didn’t really believe in anything.
“Is it really possible that it’s only fear and cowardice that makes him stay alive?” Sonia thought desperately.

The sun was almost gone. Sonia stood sadly at the window, staring out, but all she could see was the dirty, blank wall of the building next door. Just when she started to feel sure that Raskolnikov must be dead, he walked in.
Sonia cried out with joy, but when she looked closely at his face, she turned pale.
“Yes,” Raskolnikov said with a strange smile. “I’ve come for your cross, Sonia. You told me to go to the crossroads—so why are you scared now that the time has come?”
Sonia stared at him in shock. His voice sounded odd to her; a chill ran through her, but she realized quickly that he was putting on an act. He wouldn’t look her in the eyes.

“Listen, Sonia, I’ve decided it’s better this way. There’s a reason... but it’s a long story and there’s no point going into it now. You know what really annoys me? It’s that all those stupid, nosy people are going to be staring at me, asking dumb questions that I’ll have to answer—they’ll point and gossip... Ugh! I’m not going to Porfiry, I’m sick of him. I’d rather go to my friend, the Explosive Lieutenant; imagine the surprise! What a scene I’ll make! But I need to calm down, I’m getting too edgy. I nearly shook my fist at my own sister just now, just because she looked back at me. That’s horrible! What’s happening to me? Anyway, where are the crosses?”
He barely seemed to know what he was doing. He couldn’t stay still or focus; his thoughts raced around wildly, his words came out jumbled, and his hands shook a little.

Without speaking, Sonia took two crosses out of a drawer—one made of wood and one of copper. She made the sign of the cross over herself and over Raskolnikov, then put the wooden cross around his neck.

“So this is me ‘taking up the cross,’” he laughed. “Like I haven’t already suffered enough! The wooden one is the peasant’s cross; the copper one was Lizaveta’s—you’ll wear that one, right? Show me. So she had it on... when it happened? I remember she had something like that and a little icon. I threw them back on the old woman’s neck. Those would fit now, really, those are what I should be wearing... But now I’m just rambling and forgetting what matters; my mind’s all over the place. Anyway, I came to warn you, Sonia, just so you’d know... that’s it—that’s why I came. I thought I had more to say, but I don’t. You wanted me to go, remember? Well, now I’m going to the police, and you’ll get your wish. Why are you crying? You too? Stop it! Oh, I hate this!”

But seeing her cry made something hurt inside him. “Why is she so upset?” he thought. “What am I to her, really? Why does she care? Why does she look after me, like my mother or Dounia? It’s like she’s my nurse.”
“Cross yourself, say at least one prayer,” Sonia whispered, her voice shaking.
“Oh sure, as many as you want! And honestly, Sonia, really...”
But what he really wanted to say was something totally different.

He made the sign of the cross several times. Sonia picked up her green drap de dames shawl—the one Marmeladov used to call “the family shawl”—and put it over her head. Raskolnikov noticed the shawl and thought about it, but didn’t say anything. He could feel himself getting more forgetful and nervous, and it scared him. Suddenly, it hit him that Sonia was planning to go with him.
“What are you doing? Where are you going? Stay here, stay! I’ll go alone,” he snapped, almost angry and embarrassed, moving to the door. “Why should we go in a parade?” he muttered as he left.
Sonia stood frozen in the middle of the room. He hadn’t even said goodbye—he’d just forgotten about her. Raskolnikov’s heart filled with a sharp, rebellious doubt.
“Was this really right, all of this?” he wondered as he went down the stairs. “Couldn’t I just stop and take it all back... and not go?”

But still, he kept walking. He suddenly felt that he couldn’t let himself ask questions anymore. As he turned onto the street, he remembered he hadn’t said goodbye to Sonia, leaving her standing there in her green shawl, too scared to move after he yelled. He stopped for a second. Then, another thought hit him, as if it had been waiting for this moment.

“Wait—why did I even go to her just now? I said I had business with her; what business? I had no real reason! Was it to tell her I was going? But why did she need to know? Do I love her? No, no, I just pushed her away like she was nothing. Did I want her crosses? Ugh, how far I’ve fallen! No, I wanted to see her cry, to see her scared, to watch her heart break! I just needed something to hold onto, something to slow me down, any friendly face! And I actually thought I was something special, dreamed about what I’d do! I’m just a miserable, pathetic loser!”
He walked along the canal, not much farther to go. But when he reached the bridge, he stopped and, instead of going straight, turned off toward the Hay Market.

He looked around, staring at everything, but couldn’t really focus; everything seemed to slip by. “In a week or a month, I’ll be driven over this bridge in a prison cart. How will I look at the canal then? I want to remember this!” he thought. “Look at that sign! How will I read those letters then? It says ‘Campany’—I should try to remember that ‘a’ and look for it again in a month. How will I feel then? What will I be thinking? How silly all my worries seem now! I guess it’ll all be interesting... in a way... (Ha-ha-ha! What am I even thinking?) I’m acting like a little kid, putting on a show for myself; why am I embarrassed? Ugh, people keep bumping into me! That fat guy—he must be German—he doesn’t know who he pushed. There’s a poor woman with a baby begging. It’s funny that she probably thinks I’m happier than she is. Maybe I’ll give her something, just because it’s so weird. Oh, here’s a five-kopeck piece in my pocket—where did that come from? Here, take it, lady.”
“God bless you,” the beggar woman said in a watery, sing-song voice.

He went into the Hay Market. It was awful to be in a crowd, but he kept walking where the most people were. He would have done anything to be alone, but he knew that if he was, he wouldn’t last a second. In the crowd, a drunk man was trying to dance and kept falling, and people gathered around him. Raskolnikov pushed through, stared at the drunk for a few minutes, then gave a weird, short laugh. A moment later, he’d forgotten all about the drunk, even though he still stared in that direction. He wandered off, not really knowing where he was going, but when he reached the middle of the square, a powerful feeling took over his whole body and mind.

Suddenly, he remembered Sonia’s words: “Go to the crossroads, bow to the people, kiss the earth, because you’ve sinned against it too, and say out loud to everyone, ‘I am a murderer.’” The memory made him shiver. All the misery and stress of these last hours had been so heavy that he almost grabbed onto this new, strong feeling like it was something pure. It hit him all at once, like a spark that set his whole soul on fire. His heart softened, tears filled his eyes, and he dropped to the ground right there.
He knelt down in the middle of the square, bowed to the ground, and kissed the dirty earth with a strange joy and relief. Then he stood up and bowed down again.
“He’s drunk,” a young guy nearby said.
People burst out laughing.
“He’s going to Jerusalem, brothers, saying goodbye to his family and Russia. He’s bowing to everyone and kissing St. Petersburg and its pavement,” a slightly drunk worker joked.
“He’s pretty young, too!” said another person.
“And a gentleman,” someone else added more seriously.
“These days, who even knows who’s a gentleman and who’s not?”

These comments stopped Raskolnikov, and the words “I am a murderer,” which he might have been about to say, died on his lips. He just took it quietly, didn’t look back, and headed for the street that led to the police station. On the way, he saw something that didn’t even surprise him—he’d half expected it. When he bowed down in the Hay Market the second time, he noticed Sonia, about fifty steps away, hiding behind a wooden stall. She had followed him! In that instant, Raskolnikov knew for sure that Sonia would never leave him, that she’d follow him anywhere, no matter where his fate took him. The thought hurt him... but now he was almost at the final destination.

He walked into the police yard, trying to look determined. He had to climb up to the third floor. “It’ll take me a while to get up there,” he thought. He felt like the moment of truth was still far away, as if he had more time to think things over.

Again, the same old trash, the same broken eggshells on the spiral staircase, the same open doors, the same kitchens with their awful smells. Raskolnikov hadn’t been there since that day. His legs felt numb and weak, but they kept moving. He stopped to catch his breath and steady himself, wanting to walk in like a man. “But why? What’s the point?” he wondered. “If I have to go through with this, why not make it as bad as possible?” For a second, he pictured the Explosive Lieutenant, Ilya Petrovitch. Was he really about to go to him? Couldn’t he see someone else, like Nikodim Fomitch? Maybe he could just go straight to Nikodim Fomitch’s place and confess privately... No, no! To the Explosive Lieutenant! If he had to do it, better to get it over with fast.

Feeling cold and barely aware of himself, he opened the office door. There weren’t many people inside—just a house porter and a peasant. The doorkeeper didn’t even bother to look up. Raskolnikov went to the next room. “Maybe I don’t have to say anything,” crossed his mind. Some clerk, not in uniform, was sitting down to write at a desk. Another clerk sat in a corner. Zametov wasn’t there, nor, of course, Nikodim Fomitch.
“No one in?” Raskolnikov asked the guy at the desk.
“Who are you looking for?”
“A-ah! ‘Not a sound was heard, not a sight was seen, but I smell a Russian...’ How does that go in the fairy tale? I forget! ‘At your service!’” a familiar voice suddenly called out.
Raskolnikov flinched. The Explosive Lieutenant, Ilya Petrovitch, was standing there. He’d just come in from the other room. “It’s fate,” thought Raskolnikov. “Why is he here?”

“You’ve come to see us? What’s up?” Ilya Petrovitch said loudly. He was clearly in a great mood, maybe a bit tipsy. “If it’s official business, you’re a little early. It’s just luck that I’m here... but I’ll help you if I can. I have to admit, I... well, what is it? Excuse me...”
