“Raskolnikov.”
“Of course, Raskolnikov. You didn’t think I’d forgotten, did you? I’m not like that... Rodion Ro—Ro—Rodionovitch, right?”
“Rodion Romanovitch.”

“Yes, yes, Rodion Romanovitch! That’s it. I’ve asked about you a lot, you know. I really felt bad about how I acted that day... Later I was told you’re a writer... and a smart guy too... just starting out. Every educated man is a little strange at first! My wife loves literature, she’s obsessed! Literature and art! If a man’s a gentleman, the rest can be learned—talent, brains, genius. And a hat—who cares about a hat? I can buy a hat anytime, but what’s under the hat can’t be bought! I even thought about coming to apologize, but I thought you might... But never mind that. Is there something you want? I heard your family arrived?”
“Yes, my mother and sister.”

“I had the honor of meeting your sister—she’s very smart and charming! I’m sorry I got so worked up with you before. It happens! And about me thinking your fainting was suspicious—that’s been cleared up! Old-fashioned thinking, that’s all. I get why you were upset. Maybe you’re moving because your family’s here?”
“No, I just stopped by... I wanted to ask... I thought I’d find Zametov here.”

“Oh, right! You’re friends, I heard. Well, no, Zametov’s not here. He hasn’t been since yesterday—left in a rage, fighting with everyone. He’s just a silly kid, all talk. He says he wants to take some exam, but it’s just talk. Not like you or your friend Razumihin. You’re serious, and you don’t let failure stop you. You—life’s temptations mean nothing to you—you’re a monk, a scholar! A book, a pen behind your ear, some research—that’s your world! I’m the same way, you know... Ever read Livingstone’s Travels?”
“No.”
“Oh, I have. There are so many Nihilists these days, you know, but that’s no surprise. What times these are! But you’re not a Nihilist, are you? Tell me honestly!”

“Really, you can speak to me as if you’re talking to yourself! My job is one thing, but... you think I’m going to say friendship is another? No, you’re wrong! It’s not about friendship, it’s about being a man and a citizen, caring about people and God. I might be an official, but I’m also a person like everyone else... You were asking about Zametov. He’ll make a scene at some shady place over a glass of champagne—that’s all he’s good for! But me, I’m full of passion and noble feelings, plus I have rank and a job! I’m married, I have kids, and I do my duty. But who is he? I ask you, as an educated man... And don’t get me started on these young girls with short haircuts, studying to be doctors—midwives, I call them.”

Raskolnikov raised his eyebrows, confused. Most of Ilya Petrovitch’s words, especially since he’d been drinking, just sounded like nonsense. Still, he understood some of it and looked at him, not sure where this was going.

“I mean those girls with the cropped hair,” Ilya Petrovitch went on. “I call them midwives. I think it’s a good name, ha-ha! They go to college, study anatomy. If I get sick, am I supposed to call a young lady to treat me? What do you think? Ha-ha!” He laughed at his own joke. “People are too obsessed with education, but once you’ve got it, that’s enough. Why use it to insult decent people, like that jerk Zametov? Why did he insult me? And look at all these suicides—so common now, you can’t imagine! People spend their last penny and kill themselves—kids, old folks, everyone. This morning we heard about a gentleman who had just arrived in town. Nil Pavlitch, what was the name of the man who shot himself?”
“Svidrigaïlov,” someone mumbled from the other room.
Raskolnikov jumped.
“Svidrigaïlov! Svidrigaïlov shot himself!” he exclaimed.
“What, you know Svidrigaïlov?”
“Yes... I knew him... He hadn’t been here long.”

“That’s right. He lost his wife, lived recklessly, then just killed himself out of nowhere... and in such a horrible way. He left a note saying he was sane and no one was to blame for his death. They say he had money. How did you know him?”
“I... met him... my sister was a governess for his family.”
“Wow! Then you probably know something about him. Did you have any idea?”
“I saw him yesterday... he... was drinking; I didn’t know anything.”
Raskolnikov felt like something heavy had landed on him, making it hard to breathe.
“You’ve gone pale again. The air in here is terrible...”
“Yes, I should go,” Raskolnikov muttered. “Sorry to bother you...”
“Not at all, come by anytime. I’m glad to see you, really.”
Ilya Petrovitch offered his hand.
“I just wanted... I came to see Zametov.”
“I get it, I get it. Still, it’s good to see you.”
“I... am glad too... goodbye,” Raskolnikov said with a weak smile.

He left, dizzy and barely aware of what he was doing. He went down the stairs, steadying himself with his hand on the wall. He thought he saw a porter brush past him on the stairs, heard a dog barking downstairs, and a woman shouting and throwing something at it. He walked out into the yard. Not far from the door stood Sonia, pale and terrified. She stared at him with wild eyes. He stopped in front of her, and saw agony and despair on her face. She clasped her hands. His mouth twisted into a strange, awkward smile. He stood there a moment, grinned, and went back inside to the police office.
Ilya Petrovitch was sitting and shuffling through some papers. The same peasant who’d passed Raskolnikov on the stairs was standing in front of him.
“Hey! Back again? Did you forget something? What’s wrong?”
With white lips and wide eyes, Raskolnikov slowly moved closer. He walked right up to the desk, leaned on it, tried to speak, but only managed some confused sounds.
“You look sick, take a seat! Here, sit down! Get some water!”
Raskolnikov dropped into a chair, but kept staring at Ilya Petrovitch, who looked pretty surprised and uncomfortable. They stared at each other for a minute. Someone brought water.
“It was me...” Raskolnikov began.
“Drink some water.”
Raskolnikov waved the water away, and in a shaky but clear voice, said:

Siberia. On the banks of a wide, lonely river stands a town, one of Russia’s main centers. In that town is a fortress, and inside the fortress, there’s a prison. That’s where Rodion Raskolnikov, a second-class convict, has been locked up for the last nine months. It’s been almost a year and a half since he committed his crime.

Raskolnikov’s trial wasn’t very difficult. He stuck firmly and clearly to his confession. He didn’t get confused, lie, or try to make himself look better. He told everything about the murders in detail—even the secret of the pledge (a piece of wood with a strip of metal) found in the old woman’s hand. He explained how he took her keys, what they looked like, described the chest and what he found inside. He explained how Lizaveta was killed, exactly what Koch and the student said when they knocked, and how he ran downstairs and heard Nikolay and Dmitri shouting. He described hiding in the empty apartment and then going home. He even showed where, under a stone in a yard off Voznesensky Prospect, he had hidden the purse and the trinkets. Everything made sense. The lawyers and judges were especially surprised that he’d hidden the purse and jewelry under a stone and never used them, and that he didn’t even remember what the stolen things were or how many there were. He’d never opened the purse and didn’t know how much money was inside—which seemed unbelievable. When they opened it, there were three hundred and seventeen roubles and sixty copecks. Some of the money was ruined from being under the stone for so long. For a while, everyone wondered why he would lie about this when he’d told the truth about everything else. Finally, some lawyers, who understood psychology, admitted it was possible he really hadn’t looked inside the purse. They decided the murders must have happened because of temporary insanity, a kind of madness with no real purpose or plan to get money. This fit with the current theories of mental illness in criminal cases. Also, many witnesses, including Dr. Zossimov, his old classmates, his landlady, and her servant, proved that Raskolnikov had been very depressed and sick. All this showed that Raskolnikov was not a typical murderer or robber—something else was going on.

Much to the frustration of people who believed this theory, Raskolnikov barely tried to defend himself. When asked what made him kill and rob the old woman, he answered straight out that his reasons were his miserable situation, his poverty, and his wish to get three thousand roubles to help him start his life. He said his weak and cowardly nature, made worse by struggle and failure, had led him to murder. When asked why he confessed, he said it was because he truly felt sorry for what he’d done. He answered everything plainly, almost harshly.

In the end, his sentence was lighter than anyone expected—maybe because he didn’t try to excuse himself and almost seemed to make his guilt sound even worse. The court considered all the strange details of the case. It was clear that Raskolnikov had been poor and not in his right mind at the time. The fact that he never used what he stole was seen as proof of his guilt and his mental state. Lizaveta’s murder, which happened almost by accident, only made this clearer: he killed two people but forgot the door was open! Also, his confession came at the exact moment when the case was hopelessly confused by false evidence from Nikolay, and when no one suspected the real killer—just like Porfiry Petrovitch had promised. This helped him a lot. Other good things came out too. Razumihin managed to find proof that Raskolnikov, while at university, had helped a sick classmate and spent all his own money to support him for six months. When that student died, Raskolnikov found his old father a hospital and paid for his funeral. Raskolnikov’s landlady also testified that, when they lived at Five Corners, Raskolnikov once saved two little kids from a burning building and got burned himself. Many people confirmed this story. All these facts made people feel more sympathy for him.
So, in the end, because of these special circumstances, Raskolnikov was sentenced to eight years of penal servitude in the second class—not as harsh a sentence as many had expected.

At the very start of the trial, Raskolnikov’s mother became ill. Dounia and Razumihin managed to get her out of St. Petersburg during the trial. Razumihin picked a town on the railway not far away, so he could still keep up with the trial and see Avdotya Romanovna (Dounia) as much as possible. Pulcheria Alexandrovna’s illness was strange and nervous, and partly affected her mind.

When Dounia came back from her last visit to her brother, she found her mother already sick, with a fever and delirium. That evening, she and Razumihin agreed on what to tell her mother about Raskolnikov. They made up a whole story about him having to go far away on business, which would bring him money and make him respected.

But they noticed that Pulcheria Alexandrovna never asked about Raskolnikov—not then, and not later. Instead, she had her own explanation for her son’s sudden disappearance. She told them, crying, that he had come to say goodbye, hinting that she alone knew important secrets, and that Rodya had powerful enemies, so he needed to hide. As for his future, she was sure he’d become famous once certain bad influences were gone. She told Razumihin her son would be a great leader one day, and his article and writing talent proved it. She was always reading this article, even reading it aloud, almost taking it to bed with her. She hardly ever asked where Rodya was, even though everyone else avoided the subject, which should have made her suspicious.

Eventually, Dounia and Razumihin started getting worried about Pulcheria Alexandrovna’s odd silence about certain things. She didn’t complain about not getting letters from Rodya, even though before, she lived for his letters. This made Dounia uneasy; she began to think her mother suspected something terrible had happened to Rodya and was afraid to ask, fearing the truth would be even worse. No matter what, Dounia could see her mother wasn’t entirely in her right mind.

A couple of times, Pulcheria Alexandrovna steered the conversation in a way that made it impossible to answer without mentioning where Rodya was. When she got suspicious or vague answers, she became gloomy and silent, sometimes for days or weeks. Dounia realized it was hard to fool her mother and decided it was better to just avoid certain topics. But it became more obvious that her mother feared something awful had happened. Dounia remembered her brother telling her that their mother had overheard her talking in her sleep after her meeting with Svidrigailov and before his confession—had she figured something out from that? Sometimes Pulcheria Alexandrovna would go days, even weeks, silent and crying, then suddenly become excited and talk endlessly about her son and her hopes for his future. Her thoughts were sometimes very strange, but they humored her and pretended to agree (maybe she knew they were pretending), and she kept talking anyway.

Five months after Raskolnikov confessed, he was sentenced. Razumihin and Sonia visited him in prison as often as possible. At last, the time came for them to say goodbye. Dounia promised her brother that they wouldn’t be separated forever, and Razumihin did the same. In his passionate way, Razumihin decided he would work hard for the next three or four years, save up money, and then move to Siberia—a place full of natural resources and in need of people to help build a new life. They would all live together in the same town as Rodya and start over. Everyone cried when they parted.

Raskolnikov had been lost in thought for days before this. He asked a lot about his mother and worried constantly about her, so much that it scared Dounia. When he heard about her illness, he became even more depressed. With Sonia, he was especially distant. Thanks to the money Svidrigailov had left her, Sonia was already prepared to follow the group of convicts to Siberia. Raskolnikov and Sonia didn’t talk about it, but both knew she would go. When saying goodbye, he smiled in a strange way at his sister and Razumihin’s hopeful talk about their future together when he got out. He predicted that their mother’s illness would soon end in death. Then Sonia and he left for Siberia.

Two months later, Dounia married Razumihin. It was a small, sad wedding, but Porfiry Petrovitch and Zossimov attended. During this time, Razumihin was completely determined. Dounia trusted that he would make his plans work—and she couldn’t help believing in him. He showed real strength of character. He even started going to university lectures again to get his degree. They were always making plans for the future; both expected to move to Siberia within five years. Until then, they relied on Sonia.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna was happy to give her blessing to Dounia’s marriage to Razumihin, but after the wedding, she became even more sad and anxious. To cheer her up, Razumihin told her about how Raskolnikov had helped the poor student and his old father, and how, a year ago, he’d been burned rescuing two children from a fire. These stories excited Pulcheria Alexandrovna’s imagination—she talked about them all the time, even to strangers on the street, though Dounia always went with her. In buses, in stores, anywhere she could find a listener, she would start talking about her son, his article, how he’d helped the student, the fire, and so on! Dounia didn’t know how to stop her. Besides the danger of her mother getting too worked up, there was the risk that someone might recognize Raskolnikov’s name and mention the trial. Pulcheria Alexandrovna found out where the mother of the two rescued children lived and insisted on visiting her.

Eventually, her restlessness got worse. She would sometimes start crying for no reason and was often sick and feverish. One morning, she announced that, by her calculations, Rodya should be home soon—she remembered him saying when he left that they should expect him back in nine months. She began getting her room ready for him, cleaning the furniture, putting up new curtains, and so on. Dounia was worried but didn’t say anything, and helped her. After a tiring day spent in dreams and tears, Pulcheria Alexandrovna got sick during the night and by morning was feverish and delirious. She had brain fever and died within two weeks. In her delirium, she said things that showed she knew much more about her son’s fate than anyone thought.

For a long time, Raskolnikov didn’t know his mother had died, even though he and his family had been writing letters since he got to Siberia. Sonia wrote to the Razumihins every month and always got a reply. At first, they thought Sonia’s letters were dry and didn’t say much, but later they realized her letters were actually perfect, because they gave a clear picture of what was happening to Raskolnikov. Sonia’s letters gave all the basic facts—exact details about his life in prison, his health, what he said during their visits, what he asked her to bring, and so on. She wrote about everything with great detail, painting a clear picture of their unlucky brother’s life, because she stuck to the facts and nothing else.

Still, Dounia and Razumihin didn’t find much comfort in these letters, especially at first. Sonia wrote that Raskolnikov was always gloomy and didn’t talk much, that he barely seemed interested in news from home, that sometimes he asked about his mother, and that, when Sonia finally told him the truth about her death—after realizing he’d guessed it—he didn’t seem very upset, at least on the outside. She told them that, although he seemed to shut himself off from everyone, he accepted his new life simply. He understood his situation, didn’t expect things to get better soon, and had no false hopes, which was unusual for someone in his position. Sonia wrote that his health was okay, he did his work without trying to avoid it or do extra, and he didn’t care much about food. Except on Sundays and holidays, the food was so bad he finally agreed to take some money from Sonia to buy his own tea every day. He asked her not to worry about anything else, saying all this attention just annoyed him. Sonia also wrote that he slept in the same room as the other prisoners, though she’d never seen their barracks, but guessed they were crowded and unhealthy. He slept on a wooden plank with just a rug under him and didn’t want any better. He lived so simply and roughly, not because he was trying to, but just because he didn’t care.

Sonia wrote that, at first, Raskolnikov wasn’t interested in her visits and was almost annoyed she came, acting cold and rude. But eventually, her visits became a habit, almost something he needed, and he was upset when she was sick for a few days and couldn’t come. She used to see him on holidays at the prison gates or in the guard-room, where he was brought out for a few minutes. On working days, she’d watch him at work, whether in the prison workshops, the brick kilns, or the sheds on the banks of the Irtish River.

About herself, Sonia wrote that she’d made some friends in the town, did sewing work, and since there was barely a dressmaker in the area, she was needed in many houses. But she never mentioned that the authorities were interested in Raskolnikov because of her, or that his work was made easier because of her.

Finally, the letters started mentioning that Raskolnikov kept away from everyone. Dounia had already noticed signs of worry and tension in earlier letters. The other prisoners didn’t like him, he wouldn’t talk for days, and he was getting paler. In the last letter, Sonia said he was seriously ill and in the prison hospital.

He was sick for a long time. But it wasn’t the prison hardships, hard labor, bad food, shaved head, or patched clothes that crushed him. He didn’t care about those things—even welcomed the hard work because it let him sleep for a few quiet hours. He’d gone hungry as a student before, so the terrible soup didn’t bother him. His clothes were warm enough for prison life. He didn’t even notice the shackles. Was he ashamed of his shaved head and prison coat? Who would he be ashamed in front of? Sonia? Sonia was afraid of him, so he wouldn’t be ashamed around her. And yet he was embarrassed, even in front of Sonia, and treated her coldly because of it. But it wasn’t the prison uniform or chains that hurt him; it was his wounded pride. He was sick because his pride was crushed. He would have been happier if he could just blame himself—then he could have handled the shame and humiliation. But he judged himself harshly and couldn’t find any terrible crime in his past except for one stupid mistake that anyone could make. He was ashamed only because he, Raskolnikov, had failed so badly, as if fate had ruined him, and now he had to accept the “idiocy” of his sentence if he wanted any peace.

Now, all he could see ahead was a vague, pointless anxiety in the present, and a future full of endless sacrifice leading to nothing. What comfort was it that in eight years he’d only be thirty-two and could start over? What did he have to live for? What was there to hope for? Why bother? He’d been ready to give up his life a thousand times before for an idea, a hope, or even a dream. Just existing was never enough for him; he always wanted more. Maybe it was because he wanted so much out of life that he thought he was allowed to do more than other people.

If only fate had given him real repentance—the kind that tears at your heart and keeps you awake at night, the kind of guilt that makes people want to hang themselves or drown! He would have welcomed it. Tears and suffering would at least have felt like being alive. But he didn’t feel sorry for his crime.

At least he might have found some comfort in being angry at his own stupidity, like he’d been when he first got caught. But now, in prison, when he thought over everything that happened, he didn’t even see his actions as so ridiculous or stupid as they had seemed during those awful days.

“How is my theory any dumber,” he asked himself, “than all the others that have been argued about since the beginning of time? If you look at it with an open mind, without everyday prejudices, my idea doesn’t seem so strange. Oh, doubters and cheap philosophers, why do you stop halfway?”

“Why does what I did seem so terrible to them?” he wondered. “Is it just because it was a crime? What does ‘crime’ even mean? My conscience is clear. Sure, I broke the law and spilled blood. Fine, punish me for breaking the law and leave it at that. If that’s the rule, then even the people who changed history and grabbed power should have been punished at the start. But they succeeded, so they were right—and I failed, so I had no right to do what I did.”
That was the only way he saw himself as a criminal—because he failed and admitted it.

He also tortured himself wondering why he hadn’t killed himself. Why did he stand by the river and then decide to confess instead? Was the urge to live really that strong? Hadn’t Svidrigailov killed himself, even though he was afraid of death?

He asked himself this question in misery, not understanding that, even when he stood by the river, he might have sensed deep down that his beliefs were false. He didn’t get that this feeling could be the start of a huge change inside him, a new way of seeing life, a coming back to life.

He preferred to blame it on his natural instincts, which he was too weak to fight. He looked at the other prisoners and was amazed by how much they loved life. It seemed like they valued life even more in prison than when they were free. Some of them, like the tramps, had suffered more than he could imagine. Did they really care that much about a bit of sunshine, the wild woods, or a hidden spring in the forest that they’d dreamed about for years? He saw even more examples that he couldn’t explain.

In prison, of course, there was a lot he didn’t see—and didn’t want to see. He kept his head down. It was disgusting and unbearable to look at it all. But eventually, things started to surprise him, and he began to notice things he’d never thought about before. What shocked him most was the huge, impossible gap between himself and everyone else. The other prisoners seemed like a different species, and they looked at him with suspicion and hostility. He knew why he was an outsider, but hadn’t realized until then how deep and strong those reasons were. There were some Polish political prisoners who looked down on everyone else as ignorant, but Raskolnikov couldn’t look at them that way—he saw that many of the “ignorant” men were actually wiser than the Poles. There were some Russians who were just as stuck-up—a former officer and two seminary students. Raskolnikov saw their mistakes too. He was disliked and avoided by everyone; eventually, they even started to hate him—and he didn’t know why. Even men who had done worse things made fun of his crime.
“You’re a gentleman,” they told him. “You shouldn’t go chopping people up with an axe; that’s not something a gentleman does.”

During the second week of Lent, it was his group’s turn to take communion. He went to church and prayed with the others. One day, a fight broke out—he wasn’t even sure how it started. Suddenly, everyone was angry at him.
“You’re an infidel! You don’t believe in God,” they shouted. “You should be killed.”

He had never talked to them about God or his beliefs, but they wanted to hurt him for being an “infidel.” He stayed silent. One prisoner rushed at him, furious. Raskolnikov just waited calmly, not flinching. The guard managed to get between them before there was real violence.

There was another thing he couldn’t explain: why did all the prisoners like Sonia so much? She didn’t try to win them over and barely saw them—sometimes she only came by for a minute to see Raskolnikov at work. Still, everyone knew about her, knew she had come to Siberia just for him, knew where and how she lived. She never gave them money or did anything special for them. Only once, at Christmas, did she send everyone pies and rolls. Little by little, though, she became closer to them. She would write and mail letters for them to their families. Whenever relatives of the prisoners visited, they left gifts and money with Sonia for the men. Their wives and girlfriends visited Sonia, too. Whenever she came to see Raskolnikov at work or passed a group of prisoners, they all took off their hats to her. “Little mother Sofya Semyonovna, you’re our dear, good mother,” even the roughest criminals said to the fragile, small Sonia. She would smile and nod, and everyone was happy when she smiled. They even admired the way she walked; they admired her for being so small, and didn’t know what they admired most. They even came to her for help when they were sick.

He was in the hospital from the middle of Lent through Easter. When he started feeling better, he remembered the dreams he’d had while he was sick and delirious. He dreamed that the whole world was being destroyed by a strange new plague that had spread from Asia to Europe. Almost everyone was doomed, except for a few chosen people. New kinds of germs attacked people’s bodies, but these germs had their own minds and wills. Anyone infected went mad and violent right away. But even as people went crazy, they were sure they were smarter and more right than ever before. No one could agree on what was right or wrong, or who to blame or forgive. People killed each other out of pure anger. Armies gathered to fight each other, but even as they marched, soldiers would turn on each other, stabbing and biting and fighting for no reason. The alarm bells rang all day in the cities; people rushed together, but no one knew why or who called them. Ordinary jobs were abandoned because everyone had their own new ideas and couldn’t agree. Even the land was left uncared for. People tried to stick together, made promises, but immediately broke them and did something else. They blamed and fought and killed each other. There were fires and famine. Everything and everyone was destroyed. The plague kept spreading. Only a handful of people could survive—pure, chosen ones, meant to start a new life and world, but nobody had seen or heard these new people.

Raskolnikov was bothered that this crazy dream wouldn’t leave his mind, and the feeling from his fever stayed with him for a long time. The second week after Easter arrived. The spring days were warm and bright; the hospital windows below the guard’s walkway were open. Sonia had only been able to visit him twice while he was sick; each time she needed special permission, which was hard to get. But she often came to stand in the hospital yard, especially in the evenings, sometimes just to look up at the windows of his ward.

One evening, when he was almost well, Raskolnikov woke up and went to the window. He saw Sonia far away at the hospital gate, waiting for someone. Something stabbed at his heart. He shivered and turned away from the window. The next day Sonia didn’t come, nor the day after; he realized he was waiting for her and felt uneasy. Finally, he was released from the hospital. When he got back to prison, he heard from the other convicts that Sofya Semyonovna was sick at home and couldn’t go out.

He was very worried and sent to ask about her. Soon he learned her illness wasn’t serious. When Sonia heard he was worried, she sent him a quick note, telling him she was much better, just had a slight cold, and would come see him at work soon. His heart pounded as he read it.

Once again, it was a warm, bright day. Early in the morning, at six o’clock, he went to work by the river, where they crushed alabaster and baked it in a kiln in a shed. Only three convicts were sent. One went with a guard to the fortress to get a tool; another began preparing wood for the kiln. Raskolnikov sat on a pile of logs by the shed, staring at the wide, empty river. From the high bank, he could see a huge landscape and hear faint singing from the other side. In the sunny steppe, he could just make out the nomads’ tents—black dots in the distance. Out there was freedom; people lived their lives differently, as if time had stood still. Raskolnikov gazed, lost in daydreams, thinking of nothing in particular, but feeling restless inside. Suddenly, Sonia appeared beside him—she had come quietly and sat down next to him. It was still early and chilly. She wore her old cloak and green scarf; her face was still thin and pale from being sick, but she smiled at him. She held out her hand shyly—she was always nervous about offering her hand, almost afraid he’d push it away. In the past, he’d always taken it reluctantly, sometimes barely speaking to her, sometimes making her leave in tears. But this time, their hands stayed together. He glanced at her quickly, then looked down, silent. They were alone; the guard had turned away.

He didn’t know how it happened, but suddenly something seemed to grab him and throw him at her feet. He cried and hugged her knees. For a moment, she was terrified and turned pale. She jumped up, shaking. But instantly, she understood, and a look of pure happiness filled her eyes. She knew, without a doubt, that he loved her more than anything, and that the moment had finally come.

They wanted to speak, but couldn’t—tears filled their eyes. They were both thin and pale, but their sick faces shone with hope for a new future, for a fresh start and a new life. Their love had brought them back to life; each heart now held endless life for the other.

They decided to wait and be patient. They still had seven years to go, and who knew what suffering—or what happiness—was ahead? But Raskolnikov knew he had been reborn, and he felt it in every part of himself, while Sonia lived only for him.

That evening, when the barracks were locked, Raskolnikov lay on his plank bed and thought about Sonia. He even thought that the other convicts, who used to dislike him, looked at him differently that day. He’d even talked to them, and they’d answered him kindly. He remembered this and thought it must be a sign—wasn’t everything going to change now?

He thought of Sonia. He remembered how much he’d hurt her and made her suffer. He remembered her pale, thin face. But those memories didn’t bother him much now; he knew how much love he would give her to make up for everything. And what did all the pain of the past matter now? Even his crime, his sentence, and his time in prison seemed like something outside himself, something that didn’t really matter anymore. But he couldn’t think about anything for long that night—he was just feeling, not analyzing. Life itself had replaced all his old theories, and something new was beginning to take shape inside him.

Under his pillow was the New Testament. He picked it up automatically. It belonged to Sonia; it was the one she’d used to read him the story of Lazarus. At first, he’d been afraid she would try to talk to him about religion or bother him with books, but to his surprise, she had never brought it up and hadn’t even offered him the book. He’d asked her for it himself before he got sick, and she brought it without a word. Until now, he hadn’t opened it.
He didn’t open it now, either, but one thought passed through his mind: “Could her beliefs become mine, too? At least her hopes and dreams...”

Sonia, too, had been deeply shaken that day, and at night she got sick again. But she was so happy—so unexpectedly happy—that it almost scared her. Seven years—only seven years! At the start of their happiness, it even felt like those seven years would go by as quickly as seven days. Raskolnikov didn’t realize that a new life wouldn’t come easily; he’d have to struggle and suffer to earn it.

But this is just the beginning of a new story—the story of a man slowly being renewed, changing from one world to another, starting a new and unknown life. That could be the start of a whole new tale, but for now, this story is over.
